events.title: CoreWeave shares tumble as bond yields near 15% on concern about AI borrowing binge
events.summary: Elon Musk responded, "yikes" to the moves, pointed out on X by Chamath Palihapitiya late Tuesday. CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. Oracle shares also dropped. CoreWeave's stock and bonds were both hit on Wednesday as investor fear grew that some technology companies are borrowing too heavily for the artificial intelligence build-out. CEO Mike Intrator dismissed the market moves in a memo obtained by CNBC. "When you are building a new type of technology company there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally," he wrote. "We are confident in our backlog which more than supports all of our debt obligations." While investors were once excited about getting in on the AI action, investor sentiment has started to shift, said Luis Alvarado, co-head of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo Investment Institute. Now, investors are demanding more risk compensation, he said. "The era of easy money, which we experienced in the first nine months of the year, is starting to disappear and dissipate," Alvarado noted. "Now the extra dollar or the marginal dollar is going to be more looked at with a microscope into the concessions that the issuer is giving you back." Tech investor Chamath Palihapitiya , founder and CEO of investment firm Social Capital and CEO of AI company 8090, called out CoreWeave's soaring yields on X late Tuesday. That prompted Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to respond, "yikes." Palihapitiya shared a chart of the 2032 bond, noting that the yield "touched 15%" and then "closed at a new high" on Tuesday. He also included part of his deep dive into whether the AI build-out is creating a private credit bubble, in which he noted "how little extra lenders appear to charge for AI risk." CoreWeave's balance sheet is "relatively bad" compared to its neocloud peers, said Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets. That's because CoreWeave has done more borrowing and is currently building more data centers, he explained. "The yields have blown out because there's just more and more concern — that I don't share — about the wherewithal of these guys [being] able to over time pay back their interest expense," Meeks said. "It's definitely not a deteriorating situation," he added. "Maybe it's not improving, and I didn't really expect it to improve until these data centers get up and running." He expects the company to report flat margins from June to September and guide for margins to have a pretty significant improvement between September and December. CoreWeave's next quarterly results are expected in November. CoreWeave's overall credit rating is a B+ at S&P Credit Ratings, which is junk bond territory. With rates in general having risen lately, it's natural that highly-leveraged companies, such as CoreWeave, are affected, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. CoreWeave "has capital expenditure levels that are almost hyperscaler-like, but it doesn't have the hyperscaler balance sheet," Nolan said. CoreWeave isn't the only tech company seeing fallout from concerns over AI debt loads. For instance, shares of Oracle closed down nearly 9% on Wednesday. Yields on its bonds were also higher, with the yield to maturity on its 6.25% bond due in Nov. 2032 sitting at 7.24%. The overall tech sector brought down the stock market on Wednesday with the Nasdaq Composite closing down 1.9%. The debt concern seems to be hitting the shakier stocks outside of the "Magnificent Seven" the hardest. Another neocloud stock, Nebius , dropped 10%. Dell cratered by roughly 11%. Companies are in a race to build AI infrastructure and have turned to the credit market to finance their projects, leading to surging supply of new bonds. For instance, hyperscalers Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms and Oracle together have issued more than $228 billion in bonds, as of Oct. 14, according to LSEG. That is more than double the amount seen in all of 2025. All but Oracle have investment-grade ratings at S&P Credit Ratings. Overall, hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion this year, according to JPMorgan . By 2027, it is expected to exceed $1 trillion annually, the bank said. — CNBC's Seema Mody contributed reporting.

After sales tanked following the cancellation of tax credits last year, they’ve been growing for the last three consecutive quarters, according to a new report from Cox Automotive . EV’s captured 6.1% of the U.S. market, their best showing since the third quarter of 2025. The data shows that the EV market is “finding its footing again,” Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said in an analysis that accompanied the new report. EV prices have become more competitive, and high gas prices have sparked renewed consumer interest, she added. Toyota, Rivian, and Subaru led the pack. Sales of the Toyota bZ and Lexus RZ about doubled following a refresh that hit dealerships late last year. The updated models adopted Tesla-style charging ports and received larger batteries, more powerful motors, and faster charging times. Meanwhile, Tesla’s sales dropped by 20% year-over-year. Tesla still retains the first-mover advantage, though, selling over half of all EVs during the third quarter. The recovery in the U.S. mimics what occurred in Germany after the government stopped incentives for EV purchases in November 2023, a year earlier than expected. The following month, sales fell by more than half. But after hitting that low, the market steadily recovered. events.title: Ukraine says a sudden Starlink speed limit disrupted its most important drone missions
events.summary: Ukraine is heavily reliant on Starlink for military operations. Inna Varenytsia/REUTERS Ukrainian officials said on Wednesday that Kyiv's access to Starlink has been disrupted. Slower-than-normal speeds have affected military operations, the officials said. Ukraine is heavily reliant on Starlink, specifically for communications and drone missions. Ukraine's access to Starlink internet service was suddenly disrupted for unknown reasons, interfering with military operations, sources in the country's defense ministry and a top presidential advisor said Wednesday morning. Serhii Beskrestnov, a top advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said in a social media post that Elon Musk's SpaceX had implemented speed limits for Starlink terminals overnight. Beskrestnov said the restriction throttles the operation of  Starshield , the company's dedicated satellite network for military services, at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or roughly 161 kilometers per hour. Sources in Ukraine's defense ministry confirmed the disruption and told Business Insider that SpaceX had restricted the Starshield operations without warning the military. They said some units have experienced a loss of connection when drones reach speeds as low as 45 mph. The sources said that the disruption has complicated military operations , particularly drone missions. This includes mid-range strikes, front-line logistics, and air defense intercepts, some of Ukraine's most important drone missions. Because Starlink does not work inside Russia, the disruption is limited to drone operations within Ukrainian territory and Russian-occupied territory. Later in the day on Wednesday, the Ukrainian defense ministry reported that SpaceX continues to enforce a speed limit of 161 km/h, though restrictions were significantly tighter earlier in the day. Communication quality has since improved at speeds up to 160 km/h. Ukraine has said it is in contact with the US, SpaceX, and NATO partners and is working to install backup communication channels. Starlink antennas are a common sight in Ukraine. Yan Dobronosov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Amid questions about the Starlink service disruptions, Musk responded to former Ukrainian defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov's concerns and gratitude for partial restoration on social media, saying that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he said. "Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX," Musk said. "Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company." Critical in combat As the technology has in military and industrial sectors worldwide, SpaceX's Starlink has become critically important to Ukraine's military. Kyiv has adopted it as a battlefield communications tool and also uses it in drone warfare. Drones equipped with Starlink dishes, which can be controlled remotely by pilots hundreds of miles away and adapted to new targets mid-mission, have become one of the country's most potent weapons in the battle against Russian forces. Ukraine's dependence on Starlink has made it reliant on Musk and SpaceX, however. As Business Insider recently reported , Starlink has provided Musk a vital source of influence and soft power that stretches the globe. In 2023, the world's richest man said he refused a request from Ukraine's military to activate Starlink to assist a Ukrainian assault on Crimea, and Reuters reported last year that SpaceX jeopardized a 2022 Ukrainian counteroffensive by cutting Starlink access to front-line troops. Recently, Musk has proven to be more supportive. In February, SpaceX clamped down on Russian forces' use of Starlink terminals in Ukraine after Ukraine's then-defense minister made a personal appeal to the billionaire CEO, a move that allowed Ukrainian forces to wage a successful counteroffensive. 'It is clear this action is not coincidental' On Saturday, Musk reignited past criticisms of Zelenskyy with a post on X that the Ukrainian president had "gone too far" with his strikes on Russian refineries. The Starlink disruption comes after a series of Russian ballistic missile attacks against Kyiv on Monday and Tuesday nights. Ukrainian officials said that in both cases, international partners did not provide an advance warning about their launch, breaking from standard practice. Elon Musk receives the National Medal of Science from President Donald Trump. Win McNamee/Getty Images Asked by reporters before the attack on Tuesday if the US would cut intelligence with Ukraine over its strikes on Russian energy sites , President Donald Trump said that Washington continued to share it. Zelenskyy's advisor suggested that the Starlink disruption could be linked to tensions between the US and Ukraine. "It is clear that this action is not coincidental and is related to the current political situation," Beskrestnov said on Telegram, according to a translation of his statement. The cause, however, remains unclear. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Dell stock plunges 11%, leading data center sell-off on concerns about 'enterprise AI timing'
events.summary: Barclays downgraded Dell, HPE, and NetApp on concerns that enterprise AI adoption is lagging. Dell tumbled 11%, leading the drop on Wall Street. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time," the Barclays analysts wrote. Dell shares plummeted 11% on Wednesday and dragged down other data center equipment names on mounting concerns that enterprise spending on artificial intelligence won't justify the AI buildout. Hewlett-Packard Enterprise , Oracle and Super Micro all joined in the downward slide. In a report to clients on Wednesday, analysts at Barclays downgraded its rating on Dell, HPE and NetApp , "after a significant run and on enterprise AI timing." Makers of data center servers and other backend equipment have been favored on Wall Street this year on optimism that they'll be selling huge volumes of gear tied to demand for AI chips and systems for years into the future. Dell has been one of the top performers on the market, up more than 300% this year, while HPE has jumped about 160% and NetApp has doubled. However, sentiment toward the AI infrastructure space has shifted of late due in part to concerning revenue figures out of OpenAI and more broadly out of fear that rising interest rates will create a challenging environment as so much of the buildout is reliant on debt. Oracle, a heavy borrower, dropped 9% on Wednesday and is now down 33% for the year while neocloud CoreWeave plunged 15%, wiping out its gains for 2026. The Barclays analysts said they haven't seen a "meaningful AI inflection" when it comes to enterprise spending for Dell, HPE and NetApp, lowering the rating on each to the equivalent of a hold from buy. They instead attribute increased revenue to the global memory shortage and noted that infrastructure companies have passed the higher price of memory along to customers. "There is growing sentiment about enterprise AI adoption creating a hardware refresh," the Barclays analysts wrote, adding that businesses are typically allocating just 5% of their IT budgets to AI. "We believe the strong enterprise revenues are more of a function of memory costs than a move to enterprise AI at this time." The Barclays analysts also found that only about a quarter of total enterprise AI spend is going towards hardware. They said normalizing and eventually declining memory prices could weigh on infrastructure-related revenue. Memory is a notoriously cyclical business, and stocks were hit this week after China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, reported progress over the weekend on a new chip structure. Micron is down 11% for the week, while South Korea's SK Hynix has tumbled 13% in U.S. trading and Western Digital has dropped more than 8%. events.title: Bank of America hired 1,000 contractors to patch software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos
events.summary: Bank of America added 1,000 third-party consultants to support 3,000 internal staff in patching proprietary and vendor software flaws exposed by Anthropic's Mythos. Software patching, combined with anti-money laundering compliance, added hundreds of millions in third-quarter costs, which CEO Brian Moynihan expects will decline over time. While defensive patching creates short-term expenses, BofA’s 130 internal AI projects are projected to drive $700 million in savings next year. Bank of America has hired an army of external contractors to help it patch software vulnerabilities exposed by advanced artificial intelligence models including Anthropic's Mythos , the bank's CEO, Brian Moynihan , told CNBC on Wednesday. In an interview after the bank's third-quarter earnings release , Moynihan said that earlier this year the company rushed to bolster a wide spectrum of its internal and vendor code using thousands of employees and outside personnel. "That risk is real risk, and that's why when the frontier-type models came out. … A lot of us sat down and said, 'How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?" Moynihan told CNBC's Leslie Picker . "We put on 1,000 contractors to help us do the patching work in the second quarter, and those people remain here today, helping us, on top of the 3,000 people we have in that area," he said. The bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" on the software remediation and regulatory issues related to anti-money laundering compliance in the third quarter, Moynihan told analysts earlier Wednesday. The comments are some of the first by a major U.S. corporation to specify the manpower and dollars spent to protect software systems from Mythos, which was released to a small group of banks, technology firms and government agencies in April. They also highlight the dual-edged nature of AI: While it can help companies save money by boosting productivity, the ability of models like Mythos to uncover and exploit decades-old software flaws has also forced firms into a costly defensive scramble. "We've got to stay ahead of them, and we've got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services," Moynihan said. Still, Moynihan — speaking as his company's shares slumped as much as 8% Wednesday — sought to reassure investors that the spending increase was temporary. "Once you patch, you don't have to patch as much. … The pipeline moves through," Moynihan said, adding that the bank expects remediation costs to decline over time. In other places, AI is helping to reduce expenses. Bank of America has about 130 internal AI projects, and savings from those efforts are expected to rise from $300 million this year to $700 million in 2027, Moynihan told analysts. Bank of America's head count fell by about 3,400 employees in the past year as the firm cut roughly 5% of managers, he said. It's unclear how much of that workforce reduction is attributable to AI.

events.title: 10-year Treasury yield dips as traders look ahead to Thursday economic reports
events.summary: The 10-year Treasury note yield fell on Wednesday after jumping earlier in the day as traders awaited more inflation data due out Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note — the benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — slid more than 2 basis points to 5.19%. Earlier in the day, yields had climbed in reaction to a stronger-than-expected September consumer price index report. The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury yield — which tends to react most to geopolitical events — was down more than 4 basis points at 5.517%. The 2-year Treasury yield — which closely tracks the Fed's interest rate decisions — gained more than 1 basis point to 4.808% after earlier hitting its highest level since Sept. 29. One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely. The midday reversal came as equities sold off, with the S&P 500 dropping more than 1%, leading some investors to rotate back into the relative safety of the bond market. On Thursday, investors will get the September reading for the producer price index, September retail sales data and weekly initial jobless claims figures. For PPI, economists polled by Dow Jones are expecting a 0.6% rise on the month and a 5.5% gain on the year. The data will follow Wednesday's September consumer price index report, which rose 3.7% year over year , higher than the Dow Jones consensus estimate of 3.6%. Core inflation, excluding food and energy prices, came in at 2.6% on an annualized basis, versus the 2.5% consensus estimate. The latest inflation reading comes just two weeks before the Fed's next interest rate decision. With inflation remaining sticky, the central bank may need to raise rates higher and keep them there for longer in 2027, said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The bond bulls have turned around and are running the other way as 10-year yields have shot higher after today's shocking inflation report," he said. "Inflation is alive and the only way the Warsh Fed knows how to kill it is with another dose of higher rates." Odds for an October 28 quarter-point hike in the fed funds rate — currently 3.75% to 4.00% — increased to roughly 35% from just 22.1% a day ago, according to futures trading measured by CME's FedWatch tool . There is now more than a 90% likelihood of at least one more rate hike before the year is out, and included in that is a 40% chance that rates are higher by a half-percentage point — double the odds seen just one day ago. — With additional reporting by CNBC's John Melloy.

Defense tech startup Anduril will give employees a chance to sell stock through a tender offer that would value the company at roughly $90 billion, CNBC has confirmed. Bloomberg was the first to report the news, citing sources familiar with the matter. Anduril confirmed the report to CNBC. Employees participating in the offering can sell shares at $94.80 apiece. The offer, which opened on Oct. 13 and closes Nov. 9, is capped at $1.3 billion, according to the report. Bloomberg reported that employees from 16 countries are eligible to participate. Anduril has been a major winner of the growing U.S. defense tech boom and President Donald Trump 's plans to reindustrialize the U.S. military. In May, the company closed a $5 billion funding round that doubled its valuation to $61 billion. Co-founder and Oculus headset creator Palmer Luckey is among a growing group of defense tech leaders taking on advisory roles in Washington as they compete for key Department of Defense contracts. This month, the company inked a U.S. Navy shipyard contract worth up to $2.9 billion, shortly after Luckey was named a co-director of Project Meridian, which aims to develop and scale military capabilities. SpaceX rocket maker CEO Elon Musk also joined the initiative. Founded in 2017, Anduril has gained prominence for its drones, augmented reality headsets and AI software it's developing for the U.S. government and allied governments. Last month, the company made headlines after Iran said it had captured one of its underwater vehicles. events.title: TimeTeller puts our internal clocks at the center of personalized medicine
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. At-home health testing has been mired in overblown claims and outright fraud. But German startup TimeTeller , which has developed a saliva test kit to help anyone understand their circadian rhythm, is led by CEO Angela Relógio, who is the polar opposite of Theranos’ disgraced founder Elizabeth Holmes. Relógio is a physicist-engineer and molecular biologist who spent years researching oncology, circadian biology, and systems medicine in Germany before leaving academia to build TimeTeller. She is careful about what the test can and can’t do today. It would be easy to oversell: Relógio’s last name means “clock” in her native Portuguese, and TimeTeller has the potential to reduce side effects from cancer treatment and improve outcomes by timing treatment to each patient’s internal clock. That’s also why she’s careful to warn that TimeTeller itself operates on two timelines. The long-term goal is to determine when cancer treatments will be better tolerated and most effective, and doing so much more granularly than just telling whether someone is a morning person or a night owl. But its direct-to-consumer kit won’t help patients figure that out on their own. “That is something that we need to calculate for every single medicine; we do that in the context of clinical studies,” Relógio cautioned. According to Relógio, TimeTeller started accepting direct orders because of demand from longevity clinics, which focus on healthy aging and understand that individual data on a person’s circadian rhythm can be used to offer personalized advice on sleep, nutrition, light exposure, and physical activity. TimeTeller could also apply to metabolic diseases (such as diabetes) and neurodegenerative diseases (such as Alzheimer’s), performance, and women’s health, but cancer is its core mission. It was while studying cancer that Relógio made the discovery that led her to leave academia. She noticed that many cancer patients stopped or started their treatment because of side effects. “As a scientist, that was just impossible to watch, particularly when I was convinced that part of the problem might not only be what treatment we give, but when we give it,” Relógio said. This led her to develop the circadian rhythm test at the core of TimeTeller — which she knew had to become a company. “I personally funded our first patent because I strongly believed that this discovery should not remain in scientific publications,” she said. The he startup spun out of Berlin’s Charité university hospital but has since moved to Medical School Hamburg, which provided access to patients and funding. It also offered a fallback: backup employment for TimeTeller’s team of 10 if the company couldn’t pay them. That’s a safety net TimeTeller may not need. Having enlisted biochemist and market access specialist Benjamin Dose as a cofounder, the startup secured a partnership with Techniker Krankenkasse, one of Germany’s largest health insurance providers. The partnership started out as a reimbursement deal in which the insurer pays back the cost of the test for a subset of cancer patients, and both sides are now ready to expand it to more of the insurer’s 12 million members, Relógio said. Despite her caveats about the direct-to-consumer test, TimeTeller has become a solution that cancer patients can actually access. Ahead of her appearance at TechCrunch Disrupt, where Relógio appeared on stage today in San Francisco as part of our storied Startup Battlefield competition, she made clear that the company has broader ambitions: a future in which asking “when” is central to precision medicine, because “almost every process in our body is timed.” You aren’t too late to join the action at Disrupt . events.title: White House played central role in antitrust probe of TV networks
events.summary: The Scoop The White House played a central role in the Justice Department’s antitrust investigation into major TV networks’ temporary suspension of pooled coverage of the president, three people familiar with the matter told Semafor. While the probe is progressing, some inside the DOJ are concerned about its legal merits. Two former DOJ officials said that the networks suspending their pool participation after three news outlets got barred from the White House are likely protected by the First Amendment — one cited a 1982 Supreme Court ruling that afforded those constitutional protections to group boycotts for political purposes. Two of the people familiar with the matter suggested that the idea of an antitrust inquiry was first discussed inside the White House, which ultimately pushed for it from the DOJ. A third described the White House-DOJ interplay as a “distinction [without] a difference,” given how closely the two are intertwined under President Donald Trump’s administration. A DOJ official disputed that the White House first raised the idea of a probe, saying that “seasoned attorneys within the Justice Department, including the antitrust division, first discussed this.” The official added that any requests for information from networks which may have been sent were written “because there is sound legal footing to investigate.” In addition to the longstanding Trump-era blur between the DOJ and White House, the department’s antitrust division has close ties to presidential priorities. Sara Matar, formerly the division’s chief of staff, joined the White House counsel’s office in August as an associate. Notably, Laura Loomer — a staunch MAGA ally whose outside influence has occasionally resulted in changes within the White House — tweeted last month wondering why the DOJ hadn’t “filed an antitrust lawsuit” against outlets that “colluded to refuse to cover” Trump. Loomer attacked Woodward in her post; the following week, she traveled with Trump to Alabama, though it’s unclear whether she raised the issue with the president personally during that trip. The White House referred Semafor to the DOJ in response to a request for comment. Know More The Trump administration has long argued that the Justice Department is not wholly separate from the White House, counter to the norms that took root after the Nixon era. At Semafor’s World Economy Summit in April, Attorney General Todd Blanche indicated that it is Trump’s “right” to suggest targets for investigation — a stance he has echoed repeatedly since settling into his role at the top of the department. “Certainly if the leader of the Free World learns about something or hears about something or wants us to focus on something, a certain area, that is, of course, what every Department of Justice has done,” Blanche told Semafor at the time. “This idea that President Trump has some sort of outsized control because of things that he says, that that’s absolutely his right and his duty to do that,” Blanche added. Notable Legal experts view the antitrust probe as a potential rationale for the DOJ to secure internal records from TV networks, Axios reported .

The move by US Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) comes amid major US-Venezuela energy pacts and other talks with the Latin American country’s government. list 1 of 3 Venezuelans rally for opposition leader’s return and presidential elections list 2 of 3 Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro and his wife charged over torture allegations list 3 of 3 US charges Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro over torture allegations The delisting notice was posted on the federal agency’s website on Wednesday, officially removing Jorge Rodriguez’s name from OFAC’s Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) blacklist. He served as vice president under Venezuela’s late President Hugo Chavez, among other posts. Jorge and Delcy Rodriguez had been sanctioned under US President Donald Trump’s first administration due to their ministerial roles under Maduro, who now faces several federal charges, including a sweeping superseding indictment adding torture to his other alleged crimes. In 2018, the State Department said that Jorge Rodriguez was given prominent government positions by Maduro “to help him maintain power and solidify his authoritarian rule”. A source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that the decision to lift sanctions on Jorge Rodriguez is part of Washington’s wider diplomatic recognition of the interim Venezuelan government, and Trump’s three-phase plan for Venezuela’s stabilisation and political transition. During a press briefing at the US State Department on Friday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the next round of negotiations on Venezuela’s future was scheduled to begin on Wednesday. He also urged all Venezuelan opposition factions to join US-backed political talks with the interim president. Earlier this year, the US Treasury dropped sanctions against Delcy Rodriguez and later lifted the restrictions on Venezuela’s central bank and its state-owned national airline, signalling Washington’s pivot from economic warfare to backroom bargaining . She has largely complied with Trump’s demands for Caracas to open up its energy industry to American companies. As interim president, Delcy Rodriguez has promised to hold elections – including in her recent remarks at the United Nations General Assembly – but no firm date has been set. Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado has demanded they take place by July. Jorge Rodriguez has shepherded several major reforms through the ruling party-controlled legislature since his sister took power, including a law that facilitated the entry of more foreign oil companies, a similar law for the mining sector and an effort to allow private investment for the country’s battered power grid. Since Maduro’s ouster, Caracas and Washington have cut a deal giving the US access to 17 Venezuelan oil fields, while international energy firms have separately committed to expanding projects in the Latin American country. In August, Trump announced a plan to secure direct US access to a large share of Venezuela’s vast oil to refill the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.

Ambrosia Energy has begun work on a massive, 10 gigawatt-hour battery factory near Austin, Texas, co-founder and CEO Ben Longmier announced onstage Tuesday at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco. “That allows us to build about a 300 megawatt power plant per year out at our field sites,” he said. The factory will occupy 150,000 square feet, and Longmier said that Ambrosia plans to reach full production in two to three years. The startup emerged from stealth in June to build power plants for data centers at a cost of $100 per megawatt hour. Longmier and his co-founder, Sara Spangelo, had settled on solar plus batteries as the cheapest option that’s the fastest to deploy. Solar panels power the load during the day and charge the batteries, which discharge at night and on cloudy days to keep the data center operating round the clock. Longmier and Spangelo previously founded the satellite constellation startup Swarm, which they sold to SpaceX. Ambrosia is also beginning work on its first commercial power plant in West Texas later this year, Longmier said. The facility will pair 300 megawatts of solar panels with 660 megawatt-hours of batteries to deliver 30 megawatts of continuous power, with a goal of 99.3% uptime. Even with “overbuilding” solar and batteries to deliver continuous uptime, Longmier said the company can be profitable at $100 per megawatt-hour, making it competitive with natural gas turbines that many hyperscalers are planning to use to power their data centers. events.title: This is the $24 gizmo the FBI says was used to bug OpenAI's offices
events.summary: OpenAI's offices in San Francisco. Authorities say an OpenAI employee installed a recording device in an executive office. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images The device the FBI says an employee used to bug OpenAI's office isn't exactly state-of-the-art. You can buy the model for $24 on Amazon or even less from its Chinese manufacturer. ChatGPT can help hone its surreptitious recording ability. Gone are the days of Watergate, when Richard Nixon's "plumbers" used government-provided, state-of-the-art recording devices tucked into Chapstick containers to bug the Democratic National Committee. Now, anyone with some pocket change and an Amazon account can get their hands on a far more advanced recording device. One such gizmo, a postage-stamp-sized microcontroller that authorities say a now-former employee used to bug an executive conference room at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters, sells for $24 on Amazon . It has rave reviews. If you buy directly from the China-based manufacturer, it's even cheaper, selling for about $14, not including sales tax and shipping fees. And these days, you don't even need a background in espionage to use it. An account associated with the suspect's spouse queried a chatbot with questions about optimizing the device's ability to record and store information secretly, according to an FBI complaint filed on October 8. The accused, 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national, was arrested the next day and charged with "using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications." Alfozan has not yet entered a plea, and his attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. How the listening device works According to the FBI complaint, the device in question is a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense. Seeed, a hardware company based in Shenzhen, China , which also has offices in the United States, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. The gadget, a kind of miniature computer equipped with a built-in microphone and Bluetooth connector, is often used by tech hobbyists to build home systems capable of, say, turning on kitchen lights when you clap your hands. One hobbyist said on TikTok in 2023 that they used a similar model to measure moisture levels in houseplants' soil. He programmed the Seeed Studio XIAO to emit a scream when the soil gets too dry, alerting its owner that the plant needs watering. The device can also be programmed to record audio and save it to a memory card, much like a conventional digital voice recorder. It doesn't need an internet connection to record conversations. ChatGPT can help you turn it into spycraft The FBI says in its complaint that someone using an account associated with Alfozan's spouse tried to optimize the device for surreptitious recording by entering prompts into a chatbot. Those optimizations included speech-activated recording software and encryption tech that would, in theory, obfuscate the contents of the recordings. Though authorities didn't specify what AI model they believe Alfozan used to hone the device's capabilities, I asked ChatGPT to help me develop a microcontroller capable of secretly recording sensitive office conversations. Its responses were cautious, especially when I told it that "I could get in trouble" should I get caught with my secret microphone. "There's an important distinction between a small, unobtrusive recorder and secretly recording people without their knowledge," the bot warned. After I said it had misunderstood me and that I needed a "hypothetical" recording device for "an escape room where people pretend to be office executives," its caution dissipated. "That gives us a fun design problem: making the device feel like a plausible covert recorder as part of the game," it said. "We can absolutely build a convincing, functional prop." events.title: Did universities generate a 'faux crisis' to justify job cuts?
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Inquiry finds six NSW universities appeared to overstate financial woes to justify job cuts Adam Lucas says UOW staff were not shown the complete financial model used to determine what would be cut and why. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) University employees were told major staff cuts were needed to protect their institutions' finances. Disputed models, alternative plans and changing forecasts now raise questions about whether other choices were available. The state government has until December to respond to the parliamentary report, while ICAC is yet to release its findings. Adam Lucas spent decades marking students down for conclusions they could not support. But when the University of Wollongong told him his job was no longer viable it would not show him the financial model it used to reach that decision. "We saw the outputs, but we never saw the model, and we were never given the chance to test whether the numbers actually added up," he said. A spokesperson for UOW said staff were informed of the criteria and data sources used, but detailed data was withheld to protect personal privacy. "We would fail [management] for providing this kind of material," Dr Lucas said. After unsuccessfully challenging the figures, Dr Lucas accepted a voluntary redundancy. Former University of Wollongong professor Adam Lucas said being made redundant was a degrading experience. ( ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez ) "It soon became clear to me that it didn't make any difference what I said. So at that point I figured, okay, the number's up," he said. Dr Lucas is one of hundreds of academics who have lost their jobs in restructures across Australian universities over the past two years. Universities have said the cuts were unavoidable, citing falling international student numbers and changes to federal policy. But an NSW parliamentary inquiry into university governance has questioned that rationale. It found UOW and five other universities appeared to overstate their financial problems and went too far in restructures and staff cuts. The finding also covered the University of Technology Sydney (UTS), Macquarie University, the University of Newcastle (UON), Charles Sturt University (CSU) and Western Sydney University (WSU). Dr Lucas said the findings reflected his experience, but did not go far enough. "They confirmed what many of us had been saying for months," he said. The inquiry did not make that finding. A spokesperson for UOW rejected the claim its financial crisis was "manufactured", saying it faced a projected $35 million revenue shortfall in 2024 because of falling international enrolments and rising costs. It also denied the framework produced predetermined outcomes, saying only four of the 25 disciplines initially assessed as unviable were ultimately discontinued following consultation. The university said the changes delivered $22 million in recurrent savings. The inquiry accepted universities were operating in a difficult environment, but questioned the accuracy of the financial information used to justify restructures. It found the way some universities calculated their finances painted a worse picture than their official audited accounts. The committee found some forecasts used to justify cuts were later significantly revised. In at least one case the university's own modelling showed job cuts were not the only option. At Macquarie University, internal modelling obtained by the National Tertiary Education Union included a "no workplace change" scenario that the union said could have achieved the university's $55 million savings target. Management instead selected the full-redundancy scenario, accompanied by the words: "Why not go all the way?" Macquarie said the no-cuts scenario was hypothetical and did not represent a formal plan or decision. The NSW parliamentary inquiry was critical of the role of consultants found to have benefited from the crisis at universities. ( Four Corners: Nick Wiggins ) Inquiry chair and Labor MLC Sarah Kaine has described some of the financial cases as "faux crisis narratives". Speaking on a recent Australia Institute webinar she said university councils had displayed a "lack of genuine inquisitiveness" and sometimes failed to adequately challenge the information presented by senior management. Dr Kaine was also critical of the role played by consultants, describing them as "at best complicit in the crisis" and "at worst architects of it", while benefiting financially from reform programs. NTEU NSW secretary Vince Caughley said the findings vindicated union members who had challenged the cuts and pushed for the inquiry.

events.title: AI tools are aiding would-be spies
events.summary: AI tools are now exacerbating a largely hidden problem that frontier AI companies have been contending with for years: the risk that employees will exploit their access to spy on their employers. Why it matters: The same AI tools that companies are racing to release can also help people plan crimes and develop the technology to carry them out, creating another security headache for the companies building them. Driving the news: Federal prosecutors charged Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national who has been an OpenAI engineer since July 2025, with allegedly attempting to intercept private conversations at OpenAI. Around Sept. 30, the company found a "surreptitious audio recording device" that was plugged into a USB port in the back of a television in an executive conference room. OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its own AI models to help "understand the device and where it had come from." Zoom in: Investigators allege Alfozan used AI tools to research company meeting rooms and develop recording equipment, according to an FBI affidavit . Alfozan used a "productivity agent" to ask basic information about OpenAI's offices, the documents say. Those queries included: "What meeting was this presented at and when was it record?," "List meeting rooms in (company) that are 6+", and "can you list today's meeting in this room." Investigators also said that an AI chatbot account tied to his spouse asked the model to build a "continuous audio recorder" and to add "browser access an controls," as well as encrypt the memory card where the recordings were saved. The complaint didn't say whether any sensitive conversations were successfully recorded. The big picture: This is just the latest case where AI tools have helped people carry out alleged crimes. Prosecutors say they discovered a Nebraska man's use of ChatGPT before a bank robbery, including asking the model for assistance with stripping and repairing a handgun. He was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison in August. Last year, authorities said a man used ChatGPT to help plot the explosion of a Tesla Cybertruck outside of the Trump International Hotel in Las Vegas. Flashback: Alfozan's case has caught viral attention across news sites and social media, but it isn't the first time a tech employee has been arrested for allegedly stealing AI trade secrets. In 2024, the Justice Department indicted ex-Google software engineer Linwei Ding for stealing AI technology secrets and sharing them with two Chinese companies. Earlier this year, a federal jury found Ding guilty on several counts of economic espionage and theft of trade secrets. Threat level: Now, AI tools are adding a new dimension to corporate espionage, potentially making it easier for less-sophisticated actors to build spying devices while giving investigators new ways to retrace their steps. The bottom line: AI models are creating security headaches for companies not only when they break out of containment , but also when people use them to plan and carry out crimes — including espionage against their own internal workings.

events.title: 5 reasons Netflix is struggling as it cuts about 1,000 staffers
events.summary: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos is looking to kickstart growth at the streaming giant. Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images; Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images Netflix shares have struggled amid slower engagement growth and intensifying competition. The paid streaming leader laid off about 1,000 on Wednesday, its biggest round of cuts in years. Here are reasons Wall Street is uneasy about Netflix's outlook. Netflix is in a slump — and it's not just because you can't find a hot new show to watch. The streaming titan's shares are down 42% in the last 12 months and have been nearly cut in half from their all-time high last summer. Netflix had its biggest round of layoffs in four years on Wednesday, cutting about 1,000 employees, roughly 6% of the company. So, what's going wrong? Netflix's viewership growth has slowed as free competitors like YouTube gain momentum, and initiatives like games and podcasts have yet to become breakout hits. Add in the company's surprise bid for Warner Bros., which it later abandoned, and some investors are feeling on edge. Co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said in a memo that entertaining the world "requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources" but added that the company is still on track to reach its financial goals this year. Many of Netflix's struggles aren't unique to the "Stranger Things" maker, which disrupted Hollywood by pioneering paid TV streaming and has a major influence over culture. "Even the top streaming companies are not immune to stagnation and financial difficulties," said Ross Benes, a media analyst at EMARKETER, Business Insider's sister company. Other entertainment giants like Disney and NBCUniversal have turned to layoffs recently. Here are five of the biggest challenges facing Netflix right now. 1. Engagement growth is slowing Although Netflix is still growing revenue at a healthy pace while generating billions in profits, Wall Street is concerned about its viewership trends. Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos told Bloomberg at an event last month that "we're not growing as fast as I want us to, and we're working on making that move faster." Netflix grew global viewing hours by 2% year over year to 97 billion in the first half of 2026. The streaming giant also announced last quarter that it would share its engagement report only once a year, down from twice a year. When announcing the move, Netflix told investors that "engagement is not just the quantity of view hours, but also refers to the quality and variety of our offering." Investors are worried that slowing engagement growth could hurt Netflix's ability to retain customers and persuade them to pay more, though the streamer has an industry-low cancellation rate. Engagement is also "the golden compass for advertisers" since higher usage helps them reach broader audiences, said Brandon Katz, an analyst at Greenlight Analytics. If Netflix keeps growing viewership, it could charge advertisers higher rates. The lack of a new breakout hit is also troubling for Netflix analysts. "Stranger Things," the platform's biggest show ever, ended last year, and the streamer needs to find new franchises and buzzy hits that can replace it. "Entertainment is an inherently subjective and streaky industry," Katz said. 2. Competition is heating up from free streamers and social media While Netflix is still leading its paid peers in viewership and profits, free streaming services like YouTube, Tubi, and The Roku Channel are gaining popularity , especially among younger audiences. YouTube's viewership share on US TVs was 14.2% in July — nearly double Netflix's 7.8% share, according to Nielsen. Roku's free streamer and Tubi are also formidable competitors with shares of 2.9% and 2%, respectively. These no-cost services have grown as paid streamers like Netflix have raised their prices . Netflix is considering starting a free offering in some markets, co-CEO Greg Peters has said. Then there's the popularity of social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram, which are hoovering up viewership hours. Netflix is looking to counter social-media foes by investing in video podcasts and creators to increase engagement and connect with younger viewers without breaking the bank. "With pressure mounting, Netflix will look to turn the tide by getting a boost from low-cost content," Benes said. 3. The Wall Street narrative soured after Netflix's failed bid for Warner Bros. Netflix spooked some shareholders by making an $82.7 billion bid for the Warner Bros. studio and streaming assets. Paramount Skydance eventually bought the whole company. Although adding HBO Max and the Warner Bros. studio could have given Netflix a boost, investors worried that its leaders had run out of ideas for growth since Netflix hasn't historically turned to major dealmaking. Besides that narrative, shareholders were concerned about Netflix taking on a massive debt load and going through a complex integration process, Katz said. Even though Netflix pocketed a $2.8 billion breakup fee when the deal fell apart, the stock never fully recovered. 4. Games and podcasts haven't become runaway hits Netflix has made major pushes into games and podcasts, though neither has been a game changer so far. The streamer shut down a pair of game studios this summer and laid off some staffers in October 2024 as well. Netflix hasn't shared many details about how its games or podcasts are performing. The company said in its July shareholder letter that it had successfully launched games like "FIFA World Cup: Launch Edition" and "Unhinged," and that the kids app Netflix Playground tripled its daily user count, but it didn't specify how much time those games generated. Neither games nor podcasts were on last quarter's engagement report. If either were a substantial hit, company leadership would likely want to share specific metrics of their success to investors eager to see new growth areas. Games are "not a bad idea" but likely are "not going to get any subs," said Alan Wolk, a media analyst at research firm TVREV. He added that it "remains to be seen if people will start watching podcasts on Netflix," saying the streamer should adjust its mobile app interface to improve the experience. Still, podcasts are a cheap way to expand into verticals like news and are also "laundry folding programming" that can form habits, Katz said. 5. events.title: Container ship sinks in Strait of Hormuz as Iran steps up attacks
events.summary: The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries have been reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore. More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. A container ship sank in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday as Iran escalated its attacks on commercial vessels. The GFS Pride, registered in Singapore, sank after it was struck by an unidentified projectile and caught fire. The ship's 21 crew members were safely evacuated and no injuries were reported, according to the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore . "Such attacks are unprovoked, unjustifiable and a breach of international law," the Singapore maritime authority said in a statement Wednesday. Containers were floating in the water after the vessel sank, Pakistani maritime authorities warned in a navigational alert . It is the third commercial ship sunk during the Iran war, according to the International Maritime Organization , a United Nations' agency. A second Singapore-registered container ship, the GFS Giselle, sustained damage to its hull after it was hit by an unidentified projectile on Wednesday. The ship has arrived at safe anchorage and none of its crew were hurt, the Singapore maritime authority said. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed early Wednesday that a container ship exploded and sank after hitting a naval mine, according to the state news agency Tasnim . But there is no independent evidence to confirm that a mine is what caused the Pride to sink, according to the maritime security firm Marisks. Iran's claims are "consistent with an ongoing psychological operations campaign aimed at generating fear, increasing uncertainty and discouraging commercial shipping" in Hormuz, Marisks said in a security alert. Iran has escalated its strikes on commercial ships transiting Hormuz in recent weeks, as it tries to choke off a rebound in crude oil exports through the strait. More than 20 vessels, mostly oil tankers, have come under attack this month in Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman, according to incident reports from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre. The attacks this month have left two sailors missing and more than a dozen injured, according to the IMO. Crude oil exports through Hormuz hit prewar levels in September as the U.S. military guided tankers through the strait, but shipments have since pulled back as attacks have increased. Oil prices closed slightly higher Wednesday. Exports through Hormuz averaged 8.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in the week ended Oct. 12, nearly 40% below normal levels before the Iran war, according to data from Kpler . Shipments from the Middle East, including pipelines to the Gulf of Oman and Red Sea, stood at 14 million bpd, or nearly 20% below prewar levels, the data showed. Daily crude flows are very volatile, with only 3 million barrels of crude transiting Hormuz on Monday while 6 million barrels passed through the strait on Friday, according to Kpler.

events.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang responds to Pope Leo’s AI safety criticism— ‘We all care about the same thing’
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang responded to criticism by Pope Leo XIV regarding AI safety and regulation, saying that the questions raised by the pontiff were necessary and important, while stressing Nvidia’s efforts to make AI a safe and positive technology for society. “He’s asking all the right questions and he’s thinking about all the right issues,” Huang told Fortune in an interview Wednesday, when asked about the pope’s remarks. “I’m looking forward to seeing them.” Pope Leo made the earlier comments in a press conference in late September. He told reporters concerns that AI could destroy the world are not “fake news” and should be taken seriously, in an apparent rebuke of President Donald Trump, who had told the UN General Assembly the previous week that he believed fears about AI’s dangers were a “hoax.” The pope also directly criticized Huang, saying he was skeptical of Nvidia’s announcement about AI guardrails because Huang has argued there should be no limits and no government regulation. Huang told CBS News earlier this month that he agreed with Trump that AI safety concerns were overblown. Nvidia has also launched a software platform that is aimed at stopping AI agents from breaching containment. Huang told Fortune he was unsure what the pope meant, but defended Nvidia’s record. “I’m not exactly sure what was intended, but the facts are that few are doing as much in advancing AI safety in a way that helps the entire industry as we are,” he said. He pointed to Nvidia’s open-source safety technology, its work on a framework for improving the quality of companies, and its efforts on audit, governance and standards-setting. “We are doing as much as we can, and the things that we’re doing are going to dramatically help,” he said. Huang argued the tools would have helped in incidents that have already occurred. “We can always talk about hypothetical incidents that have not happened, but as an engineer, we should develop the technology and methodologies and practices to deal with the incidents that have happened,” he said. He also said he had common ground with some of the pope concerns. “We all care about the same thing, which is an optimistic future where this technology has great positive impact in society while doing it with great responsibility, safety, and accountability,” Huang said. The pope, who has warned of the dangers of A I throughout his 16-month papacy, urged the world “to promote dialogue, study, investigation” on the technology. events.title: From Substack to YouTube, here are the social platforms cracking down on AI slop
events.summary: Companies running social platforms are updating their guidelines on AI-generated content, especially for monetized accounts. Milan Surkala/Getty Images Social platforms are updating their guidelines on AI-generated content. AI has been a point of tension across the creator community for years. Here's how social platforms are handling AI-generated content and monetization. As tech companies race to weave AI into every inch of their products, they're discovering there's a fine line between embracing new technology and flooding users with low-quality, machine-generated content. The shifting guidelines reflect a broader tension across the creator economy. Not long ago, social platforms competed aggressively for influencers with creator funds, exclusive programs, and monetization tools. Many of those same companies are now investing billions in AI products and infrastructure, leaving some creators worried they're becoming less central to the platforms they helped grow. Here's how major social platforms that rely on creators, including YouTube and Substack, are dealing with the proliferation of AI content. YouTube Illustration by Avishek Das/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images YouTube is sharpening its stance on AI-generated content. In an update from the company's trust and safety team, on July 20, YouTube said it wants to reward creators who use AI to enhance original storytelling, as opposed to those who mass-produce generic content or AI personas designed to game the platform. A YouTube spokesperson told Business Insider that the policy isn't new but an important clarification of YouTube's long-standing "inauthentic content" policy, intended to reduce ambiguity for content creators who have been demonetized for repetitive, low-effort, or emotionally manipulative videos. In October, YouTube Music also rolled out labels to identify music generated primarily by AI or music in which generative AI played a significant role. Listeners can tap a label on the player screen to learn how the technology contributed to a track, including its composition or vocals. Music partners can choose to disclose whether their content uses generative AI entirely or partly, but YouTube can supplement those disclosures with its own signals. Standard pitch correction, such as Auto-Tune, doesn’t count as generative AI under YouTube's policies. YouTube has spent years pitching itself to advertisers as the future of television , and a surge of AI-generated spam threatens to undermine that message. In January, the platform removed more than a dozen popular channels that had amassed millions of views by pumping out AI-generated videos featuring characters like cats and Jesus. Video editing platform Kapwing published a report estimating that 21% of YouTube's feed was AI-generated videos. TikTok Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images TikTok isn't shying away from generative AI. The company and its owner, ByteDance, offer an array of AI tools for content creators on its marquee app and video editor CapCut. Creators who post on its e-commerce platform, TikTok Shop, have been ramping up the use of AI to sell products this year. Much of the company's tech is built around ByteDance's AI video model, Seedance 2.0. Still, TikTok is taking a variety of steps to keep generative AI under control across its ecosystem. The company requires creators to label AI-generated content and appends an invisible watermark to the metadata of some videos to indicate they are artificially generated. In November, the company introduced the ability for users to toggle the amount of AI content  that appears in their feeds. In July, the company said it's beginning to test "improved detection systems to target accounts dedicated to posting AI-generated spam that crowds out original creators." Substack Bloomberg/Getty Images The newsletter platform announced on July 21 that it would help readers identify AI-generated content . Substack will now let readers scan content to estimate how much AI may have been used in its writing. Substack is partnering with Pangram, an AI detector tool, to power its AI identification tools. Creators on Substack can also add a disclosure to their content explaining how they made it, such as noting that they used Claude for copyediting, or if they don't use AI at all. However, users can fairly easily disable this tool for their Substack content by turning off AI analysis in their publication settings. Creators can opt out of Pangram's automated scanning, meaning readers will no longer see an AI-use estimate on those posts. Pinterest Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Pinterest is no stranger to AI slop. In 2025, the platform began adding AI labels to content. Pinterest lets creators label content as AI-modified or -generated, and has its own detection systems to flag content that may have been AI-generated. Pinterest also added a tool that lets users limit the amount of AI-generated content appearing in their feeds. In June, Pinterest's CEO Bill Ready told Business Insider's editor in chief, Jamie Heller, at Cannes Lions that while there are "so many great uses of AI," there is also a "bit of a counter movement to that with consumers." "We provide users with controls to decide whether they want to see more or less GenAI content in their feed," a Pinterest spokesperson told Business Insider. "Additionally, our Community Guidelines apply to GenAI content, and our recommendation system prioritizes high-quality content, regardless of if it's human-created or GenAI." Meta Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto via Getty Images Meta wants users to create and engage with content made with its own AI tools, so, for the most part, it has let content like the famed Shrimp Jesus run free. However, the company has been labeling content as AI-generated since 2024. Across Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, Meta adds an "AI info" label to content it detects as AI-generated. It doesn't automatically do the same for content that was modified with AI, though. Meta "may require" its AI labels on content with "photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio that was digitally created, modified or altered, including with AI," per the company's help page explaining its AI policies. People can also voluntarily add the label to their content. In June, Meta started putting its "AI info" label on advertisements that use AI, whether they're created by Meta's own tools or third-party editing services. LinkedIn Illustration by Avishek Das/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images If your LinkedIn posts sound a little too polished, readers may be taking notice. AI detector Pangram estimates that 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts and 30% of short-form posts from April through June were AI-generated, which is the highest share among platforms it analyzed, including X, Reddit, Substack, and Medium. events.title: Bangladesh arrests two for luring locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine
events.summary: Twenty Bangladeshi victims have been killed after being used by Russia as ‘bait’ to locate enemy positions, police say. Police in Bangladesh have arrested two people they say are linked to a trafficking network that deceptively recruited locals to fight for Russia in Ukraine. The suspects, identified as Mizanur Rahman and Abu Taher, trafficked at least 30 people to Russia with false promises of high-paying jobs, Mohammad Asaduzzaman, commander of the elite police force Special Response Battalion, said on Wednesday. Once abroad, the victims’ passports and phones were taken, and they were handed over to the Russian military, he said. list 1 of 3 Trump’s diesel deal opens a new rift with Europe over Ukraine list 2 of 3 Trump says Putin and Zelenskyy both want to end Russia’s war on Ukraine list 3 of 3 Russia arrests Japanese reporter for alleged espionage Seventeen of the trafficking victims, who arrived in Russia in early May, were killed on the first day of deployment after being given minimal training, Asaduzzaman said. A total of 20 Bangladeshis have been confirmed dead. “Bangladeshis were used as bait to locate enemy positions,” he said. “Russian forces determined their next course of action after the Bangladeshis fell victim to drone attacks.” In addition to the 20 Bangladeshis killed, two more are being treated in a Moscow hospital while six others are still on the battlefield, police cited a survivor who was injured and managed to return home as saying. The victims were from poor backgrounds and had paid around $8,000 for the fake jobs that brought them to Russia, Bangladeshi media reported. Both Russia and Ukraine have recruited thousands of foreign nationals into their armies since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago. An estimated 28,000 foreigners from 136 countries are said to be fighting in the Russian army, and officials believe Moscow deployed some 14,000 North Korean troops to battle Ukraine’s 2024 incursion into the Kursk region. Meanwhile, Ukraine says 16,000 foreign nationals from more than 70 countries – including nearly 40 percent from Latin America – are currently serving in its army. Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly last month , Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia deceptively recruits people from 47 countries for an “absolutely brutal” campaign and urged countries not to let Moscow “drag” them into the war. Amnesty International has also accused Russia of using “deceptive, coercive and exploitative practices” to recruit foreigners to fight on the Ukrainian front. Russia has previously dismissed accusations of coercing foreigners into joining its army. Amnesty says it cannot conduct inquiries about foreigners in Ukraine’s army as it has no access to prisoners of war held in Russia, which designates the rights group as a “foreign agent”.

events.title: OpenAI says it found a 'hidden' recording device planted in its office
events.summary: OpenAI said it found a recording device "hidden" in one of its offices and reported the matter to the FBI. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI said the device was "concealed in toilet paper" and planted in one of its offices. The company said it then used its own models to determine who planted the device. The Department of Justice said an employee was arrested on October 9. OpenAI said it found a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in one of its offices and used its own AI to identify who planted the device. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," OpenAI wrote in an X post on Tuesday. "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work." A statement from the Justice Department said that the employee in question is allegedly 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national. Alfozan was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan made his first appearance in federal court on Tuesday, the statement said. A complaint filed in the Northern District of California said that an employee found a USB device surreptitiously placed on the back of a television located in an " executive conference room ." The device was concealed in toilet paper, the complaint said. Photos attached to the court documents and DOJ statement showed the device positioned behind what appears to be a television. The complaint said the device consists of a "thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage." An FBI affidavit filed in the Northern District of California included photos of what prosecutors said was a recording device surreptitiously hidden in an executive conference room. Department of Justice The complaint further said that CCTV footage showed Alfozan near the conference room on multiple dates prior to the device's discovery. "According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the DOJ said. An FBI affidavit included an image of what prosecutors said is Abdulrahman Alfozan looking behind a television located in the conference room where the recording device was planted. Department of Justice Prosecutors allege that Alfozan used a productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses and meeting rooms, and used a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse to submit prompts related to building and hiding an audio recording device. Some of the queries to the productivity agent included a list of "today's meetings in this room" and "what meeting was this presented at and when was it recorded," the complaint said. A screenshot of the criminal complaint shows a list of queries federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan made to a "productivity agent." Department of Justice A LinkedIn account with the same name as the defendant in the complaint showed that Alfozan was an engineering lead at OpenAI and is a partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm that invests in early-stage tech startups across the Middle East and North Africa. A contact associated with the LinkedIn account and a spokesperson for Raed did not immediately return a request for comment. In a statement, William Pernik, Aflozan's attorney, said the government's allegations "appear wholly out of character" for his client and clarified Alfozan's charges. "He is charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent," Pernik wrote. "There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us. Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws." OpenAI said that it found no evidence that the employee improperly accessed or manipulated model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was fired, OpenAI said in the social media post. OpenAI told Business Insider that its models were used to help with the technical investigation of the incident, including analyzing forensic images of the device's storage. It also said it has evidence that the employee intended to plant more recording devices throughout OpenAI's offices. OpenAI said in the X post that the case was an example of how AI can help address " sophisticated security threats ." The announcement comes on the heels of a cluster of firings at OpenAI unrelated to the recording device. In the prior case, the company let go of three safety and alignment employees who it alleged had "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." The workers, Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni, and Tomek Korbak, published a letter disputing some of the claims circulating about their conduct. They wrote that they were concerned about the lack of clarity around their firings, as well as the way they might chill transparency at the company. OpenAI stood by the dismissals. The company published an internal note that said, "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." events.title: Trump to appeal order blocking White House from banning MS NOW, CNN and Politico
events.summary: The Department of Justice said it is appealing a federal judge's order indefinitely blocking the White House from enforcing its ban on MS NOW, CNN and Politico. Judge Timothy Kelly, whom President Donald Trump nominated, ruled that the three targeted outlets can keep their access to the White House complex. The Department of Justice said Wednesday it is appealing a federal judge's decision to extend his order blocking the White House from enforcing its ban on MS NOW, CNN and Politico. The notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit came less than a day after U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the three outlets targeted by President Donald Trump can keep their access to the White House complex. That ruling, a preliminary injunction, replaces Kelly's temporary restraining order against the ban that Trump first announced on Sept. 18. It is not a final ruling in the ongoing lawsuit that the three news outlets filed against Trump, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, U.S. Secret Service Director Sean Curran and White House communications director Steven Cheung. Kelly, in an opinion filed Tuesday night, said the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on their claims that Trump and his co-defendants violated their First Amendment rights through unlawful retaliation and viewpoint discrimination. "It is likely that Plaintiffs were selected by President Trump for revocation of their access to the White House press area because he believes their coverage of him and his administration is generally inaccurate and biased," wrote Kelly, whom Trump nominated in 2017 for his current seat. "In other words, it was 'an effort to suppress the speaker's activity due to disagreement with the speaker's view' ... rather than to vindicate any other purportedly 'compelling governmental interest,' ... including maintaining professional standards for journalists or protecting national security," he wrote. "Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination," the judge wrote. This is breaking news. Please refresh for updates.

events.title: ‘The way work gets done is changing across every industry’: Kroger cites AI efficiency push as it cuts 3,000 corporate jobs
events.summary: Kroger wants to make grocery shopping cheaper, and part of its plan is a smaller corporate workforce.  The supermarket giant plans to eliminate about 3,000 corporate roles over the next three years as it expands its use of AI and overhauls operations. CEO Greg Foran says the restructuring will help fund lower prices and investment in frontline workers as Kroger competes with discount giants Walmart and Aldi. But shoppers may see only modest savings unless the company targets that investment toward the products where price matters most, retail analyst Neil Saunders told Fortune . “Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” Foran wrote in a memo to employees Monday, according to Business Insider , which reported the planned cuts . “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology.” The cuts amount to roughly 37% of Kroger’s approximately 8,200 corporate employees, according to Business Insider . However, they’re a small share of its total workforce of 409,000, which supports more than 2,700 stores under banners including Ralphs, King Soopers, and Fred Meyer. Will shoppers notice the savings? Trimming corporate overhead can help fund lower prices, but only up to a point, Neil Saunders, who has tracked Kroger’s turnaround under Foran, told Fortune . “If spread across various products this kind of investment would take only cents off the price of an average basket,” he said. The effect could be bigger if Kroger continues to concentrate the savings on the products and categories where value matters most to shoppers—which Saunders expects it to do. These job cuts are also only a piece of a wider push to run more efficiently, which he said makes them important in the bigger picture. Where those savings land matters because Kroger is fighting Walmart and Aldi for shoppers’ grocery budgets. Foran, who became CEO in February, previously led Walmart’s U.S. business from 2014 to 2019. After the abrupt resignation of Kroger’s previous CEO, he now faces a crucial task: giving shoppers a reason to choose Kroger instead. Walmart is also using technology to streamline store operations. As Fortune previously reported , its digital shelf labels let employees update prices without replacing paper tags by hand. Beyond the AI headline Kroger outlined its AI strategy in September , describing tools that forecast demand, personalize savings, and help customers plan meals and build shopping carts around their budgets and dietary needs. But Foran’s memo speaks broadly about technology and doesn’t specify how many roles AI will replace. This puts its technology push on two tracks, helping store workers do their jobs while at the same time reshaping how its corporate operation works. The company also said it’s developing AI agents to help frontline teams prioritize daily tasks and notifications, while making AI training and tools available to more than 400,000 employees. This puts its technology push on two tracks: helping store workers do their jobs while reshaping its corporate operation. Saunders cautioned against treating the reductions as purely a consequence of automation. “There is a degree to which Kroger’s corporate structure was bloated and inefficient, so some of these cuts would have happened regardless of any technological innovation,” he said. To Saunders, meaningful AI gains should allow Kroger to move faster with fewer people and make better decisions about sourcing, forecasting, and its supply chain. “It will take some time before we see whether these things materialize,” Saunders said. Kroger did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
