events.title: Hiyd is a health tracker that attaches to the watch you already wear
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. If you’re a watch enthusiast, you probably don’t want to exchange your prized timepiece for a bulky fitness tracker. But Hiyd founder Salah Batroukh doesn’t think people should have to sacrifice fashion for function. “We don’t think that health tracking needs to be this overly conscious decision where you have to change something about the way you look,” Batroukh told TechCrunch. “That’s the ethos of the entire company. Our plan is to build out this product ecosystem of invisible health tracking.” Hiyd’s first device to make health tracking look cooler is a small, slim disc that attaches to the back of your watch via microsuction , a material technology that allows the sensor to sit flush under your watch without magnets or adhesive. That way, it won’t leave any residue or mess with the mechanics of watches that keep time using magnets. “Microsuction is essentially a textured silicone, with hundreds of tiny pockets per square inch molded into a pliable sheet. So when you press on it, it pushes air out of all those pockets, and you end up with a vacuum — just like traditional suction cups but scaled down incredibly,” Batroukh explained. “It works incredibly at stopping shear forces, but a little bit of prying allows it to pop right off, which is ideal for us. It’s also incredibly thin at just 0.3 mm with our manufacturing processes.” According to Batroukh, the sensor, which measures 2.7 mm thick and weighs 7 grams, collects biometrics similar to those of leading wearables, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep staging, movement, calories burned, and VO2 max estimations, then syncs to an iOS or Android app. In order to fine-tune the sensor, Hiyd’s team is filming themselves doing various activities, then labeling those datasets to train its AI. “We go for a walk and say, ‘This is somebody walking, this is somebody jogging, this is somebody running,’” he said. “The one thing that AI is really good at is data analysis, so we can basically fit a lot of heuristic analysis into our sets really quickly.” On its app, Hiyd is also working to incorporate nutrition tracking. The goal isn’t to count calories, but rather to help users glean insights about how their eating habits impact their sleep quality or workout performance. “What we will do is say like, ‘Hey, on days where you work out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m., your sleep quality is actually worse,’ and that’ll be specific to you,” he said. “Or it’ll say, ‘Hey, we think you had a less deep sleep last night because you had a slice of cake before you went to bed, and the sugar affected it.’” Batroukh spent about seven years as a manufacturing design engineer at Apple, a company synonymous with iconic hardware. But he wanted to know if he could design something great without the support of a global brand and a multitrillion-dollar market cap. “One of the reasons I left Apple was a lot of the products became a little bit more about being an Apple product, rather than being something for the customer,” he said. “[Hiyd] gives me the opportunity to do the exact opposite.” Batroukh is joined by fellow founders Omar Shakir, an experienced mechanical engineer who is the startup’s CTO, and Mahamad Charawi, who is its head of software. (Charawi previously co-led the Y Combinator-backed startup Laudspeaker through its sale .) Hiyd is bringing its tiny sensor to the big stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where the company is competing as one of the top 20 companies at Startup Battlefield on Wednesday. ( Don’t miss out on the action .) In November, the company plans to launch a Kickstarter. So far, over 16,000 people have made deposits to secure Hiyd’s first units. events.title: Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan? The OpenAI employee the FBI arrested is also a Saudi investor
events.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan has a glowing LinkedIn profile, more of a natural fit for a future CEO than someone arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), as he was on Oct. 9. It lists nine awards, five volunteer experiences, an enthusiastic recommendation from a coworker, a healthcare-related patent, degrees from two top-tier U.S. universities, and positions at well-known companies such as SAP , Microsoft , Meta , and, of course, OpenAI. The federal complaint charging him with secretly placing a recording device in an executive conference room does not allege a motive. But since his arrest, the internet has done what it does best: dug up details about his past. Venture partner at a Saudi-based firm Alfozan is a Saudi national who has been a legal permanent resident of the U.S. since Sept. 2020, according to court documents. He has a 15-year professional and educational history in the states, beginning with his enrollment at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2011. While most of his work history since then has been U.S.-focused, in 2025 he became one of 20 venture partners at the Saudi Arabia-based RAED Ventures. He is still pictured on their website, but RAED has not responded to Fortune’s requests for comment on whether he is still associated with the firm. Also at the firm, pictured in the screenshot below of RAED’s site is Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud, a member of the Saudi royal family. He joined RAED as a partner on Feb. 6, 2025, two days before RAED announced Alfozan joined the firm on Feb. 8, 2025. Alfozan didn’t join OpenAI until July 2025, the company told Fortune in a statement, while Alfozan’s personal LinkedIn says he joined the company in Sept. 2025. OpenAI did not respond to a question about the discrepancy. It’s unclear whether OpenAI allowed Alfozan to hold an outside investing role at RAED while he worked there. The company declined to respond to Fortune’s request for its conflict-of-interest policy. Abdulrahman Alfozan was still listed on RAED’s website after news of his arrest surfaced. RAED The complaint does not charge him with stealing trade secrets, nor does it allege that he acted for a foreign government. OpenAI said in a post on X that it had “no indications” he inappropriately accessed or exfiltrated model weights, source code or customer data. Alfozan has been “charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications,” the DOJ said . A trial attorney from the department’s National Security Division, in its Counterintelligence and Export Control Section, is assisting the prosecution. The government of Saudi Arabia has demonstrated interest in U.S. AI companies. In 2025, AI chip startup Groq secured a $1.5 billion commitment from the kingdom, Reuters reported . Saudi Arabia also has a state-backed artificial intelligence company, HUMAIN, which in 2025, led a $900 million funding round for the media production startup Luma AI that year, Semafor reported . HUMAIN also partnered with U.S.-based AI coding platform Replit in 2025. OpenAI reportedly held talks with Saudi Arabian investors in 2025, which The Information reported at the time. In Jan. 2026, the company returned to the Middle East and was in talks with sovereign wealth funds, CNBC reported at the time. Nothing in the court filings connects Alfozan to any of these investments. A one-way ticket out of the U.S. Starting Aug. 17, Alfozan allegedly asked a productivity agent about OpenAI’s conference room capacities and which meetings were held in them, the complaint says. OpenAI told Fortune the alleged agent was an internal tool. He also asked how to send USPS packages to the building. Then, starting on Sept. 24, Alfozan allegedly used a chatbot account associated with his wife to submit prompts about building a continuous audio recorder, encrypting its memory card and adding live listening, according to the complaint. OpenAI told Fortune the alleged chatbot was ChatGPT. He is then alleged to have planted the device on or about Sept. 28. Sources told Fortune OpenAI found the device during a routine sweep on Sept. 30. That’s when the company alerted the federal government. A camera was then placed behind the TV in the conference room where the device was located, and Alfozan was subsequently seen on the camera on Oct. 5. The company terminated Alfozan on Oct. 9, the same day the FBI arrested him. That’s three days before Alfozan, his wife and a third family member had booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia, via Istanbul, for Oct. 12, according to a motion to seal the case. Court documents don’t say why the family booked the trip. Prosecutors cited it in asking a judge to keep the complaint sealed until this week. “The defendant has the means—and will have an incentive—to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested,” the motion reads. Alfozan first appeared in federal court on Oct. 13, and he will return again on Oct. 19. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Construction firm BESIX Watpac has won the tender to construct Hobart's Macquarie Point Stadium, the ABC understands. An official announcement is expected today. The Australian-based firm was one of two shortlisted bidders vying for the stadium contract and has edged out a rival consortium headed by Italian firm WeBuild to progress to the second and final stage of the tender process. A fixed-price contract to build the stadium is expected to be signed before Christmas. But a final cost is still yet to be determined and haggling over the price is set to continue as part of detailed, exclusive contract negotiations over the next two months. The project has a $1.13 billion budget, but that number has not been publicly updated since late last year, and before an escalation of conflict in the Middle East which has contributed to a spike in fuel and diesel prices. That build is slated to cost about $3.6 billion. Site works at Macquarie Point began in July, but the stadium is not expected to be complete until December 2030. Its construction is a requirement of the Tasmania Devils' entry into the AFL and AFLW from 2028.

events.title: Hailey Bieber sold Rhode to e.l.f. Beauty after she and co-founder Lauren Ratner addressed their main fear in an acquisition
events.summary: Hailey Bieber had heard the horror stories before she ever sat down with e.l.f. Beauty.  “I’ve heard a lot of stories from founders that had gone through acquisitions and had regrets and were not super happy with where their brand went,” Bieber said onstage at Fortune’s Most Powerful Women Summit on Wednesday. “I went into it with a mindset of really wanting to know that Rhode was going to be safe where it was going.” Bieber and Rater launched Rhode in 2022 and three years later e.l.f. Beauty agreed to buy the brand in a deal worth up to $1 billion , one of the buzziest beauty acquisitions in recent years. Bieber has since stayed on to lead creative and product innovation alongside Lauren Ratner, Rhode’s co-founder, president and chief brand officer. For Bieber, the deciding factor wasn’t the price. In fact, Bieber said discussions about profit margins hate to see her coming, she told Fortune’s Ellie Austin. And in deciding to sell the brand she launched, Bieber said she wanted to know that she would still have a major role in the company she helped build. “That was my one fear, really—that I would sell my company and then they were gonna say, ‘OK, we’re gonna put this person in and this person in,’ and then we want to make the team bigger around product development, and that I would start feeling like I didn’t have as much say,” she said. “It’s my baby, it’s our baby. We’ve grown it from literally day zero, ground up.” ‘We’re not going to fix what’s not broken ‘ Bieber said she laid out every concern to e.l.f. from the beginning, including that she couldn’t imagine stepping back from the business. Their response was a happy surprise. “They were like, ‘Oh my gosh, we want you to be more involved if you want to,’” Bieber recalled. “I feel like you never hear that from an acquirer—that they want you to be as in it as you were before, if not even more.” Ratner said the pair worried an acquirer might start “meddling in the business,” dictating how Rhode should move forward. Instead, she said, e.l.f. was explicit about its intentions. “E.l.f. was very clear: ‘We’re not going to fix what’s not broken. You guys are doing an incredible job. You have a secret, special sauce,’” Ratner said. “‘We just want to supercharge the back end and let you guys do what you do best.’” Bieber said e.l.f. walked her through, in detail, how it had supported the founders of every brand it had previously acquired. “They told me, ‘We don’t want to come in, we don’t want to change anything. We really want you to continue operating exactly how you are,’” she said. “You have to trust that, and you have to follow your instinct.” More than a year after the deal, Bieber says e.l.f. has kept its word. When Austin asked her which decisions remain exclusively hers, she didn’t hesitate. “Pretty much all of them,” Bieber said. “Everything that they said before we were acquired, they have stuck to 100%. They have really just let us fly and let us continue to make every decision.” If anything, her role has grown, she added. Bieber now holds the title of chief creative officer at Rhode and serves as a strategic advisor to e.l.f. Beauty as a whole, weighing in on the parent company’s products. “Any question they have for me, they can come to me and ask me, ‘Hey, what do you think about this product? Will you test this for us?’” she said. “It really has been genuinely the dream scenario.” Why sell at all? Rhode was growing quickly on its own, and Bieber and Ratner said a sale wasn’t on their immediate agenda. “I don’t think we at that moment were thinking, ‘This is what we’re going to do right now,’” Bieber said, adding that the opportunity “took us a little bit by surprise.” She declined to say who approached whom. Timing mattered. Rhode was preparing to launch in Sephora, and Bieber wanted a partner that had done it before. Ratner said the brand’s lean team had reached its limits. “We had a small, mighty, nimble team, and we felt like we had taken it as far as we could with that team,” Ratner said. “We really needed the infrastructure of a bigger partner to scale globally.” Bieber said she, Ratner, and Ratner’s husband—Rhode’s third co-founder—reached the decision together. “When you have the synergy of all feeling good about it, it also makes the decision seem even more right,” she said. The bet appears to be paying off. Rhode generated roughly $390 million in net sales in fiscal 2026, an 80% increase from the year before, and the company has said it wants to pass $1 billion. Getting there depends on retail. Rhode, which built its business selling direct to consumers, entered Sephora in the U.S. last September. Ratner said Rhode is now the No. 1 brand in every retail market it operates in, including Sephora U.S., Sephora U.K., and Mecca in Australia. A couple of weeks ago, the brand launched with Sephora in Europe across 19 new markets and more than 500 doors. “Our first day of online sales for Rhode with Sephora EU actually surpassed the total Sephora EU Black Friday sales for the year prior,” Ratner said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: DOJ gave California a voter list, a 48-hour deadline — and a threat of court action
events.summary: The Trump administration is threatening emergency court action unless California officials investigate potential ineligible voters within 48 hours and set aside ballots from anyone whose citizenship they cannot verify, according to two letters sent to state officials from the Justice Department. Why it matters: With voting already underway, President Trump 's DOJ could delay ballots from eligible Californians mistakenly flagged as noncitizens and set up a court fight just three weeks before Election Day. Driving the news: Acting Deputy Attorney General R. Trent McCotter sent a letter Tuesday to Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan along with a thumb drive of "likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot," according to a copy of the letter shared with Axios. McCotter asks local officials to investigate their citizenship status by noon October 15. The letter did not say how many people are on the list. For anyone whose status can't be confirmed, DOJ asks the officials to "segregate—not cancel" those ballots and suspend signature verification or counting of any ballots already returned. DOJ also asks officials to withhold ballots from people on the list unless their citizenship has been confirmed. California Secretary of State Shirley Weber received a similar letter . Friction point: McCotter closed his letter with a threat: "If you cannot implement this process by then, given the ongoing federal election, the United States will have no choice but to seek emergency relief." What they're saying: "This should not be controversial, as the criminal statute is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. It is a federal crime for noncitizens to vote in U.S. elections, and the DOJ is asking California to ensure that is not occurring," a DOJ spokesperson said in a statement. The California secretary of state's office and the Los Angeles County office did not respond to request for comment. The other side: "One must question why the Justice Department would violate its own rules about investigating elections so close to Election Day, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors," said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research, in a statement. Becker added that the administration could have investigated California's voter rolls long before mail-in ballots began going out Oct. 5. The big picture: The demand escalates the administration's push to uncover suspected noncitizen voters. In July, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin alleged more than 190,000 voters were erroneously registered in California, a claim state officials disputed. ICE investigators, FBI agents and DOJ prosecutors have dedicated significant resources to ramp up the number of cases and charges against illegal voting, with about 1,600 on-going cases as of mid-September. Yes, but: The administration's sweeping claims of mass illegal registrations and noncitizen voting have quickly deflated after inspection. After alleging 16,000 illegal registrations in Nevada, a review from state election officials saw that number dwindle to potentially 185, according to the New York Times . In Pennsylvania, DHS officials conceded it had varying degrees of confidence in the flags it made on about 14,000 voters, according to Votebeat . DHS also claimed that New Jersey had 35,000 noncitizen voters. Gov. Mike Sherril (D-NJ) did admit to mistake registrations from a software error, but the number was a fraction of DHS' claim: about 6,600 . Flashback: There have been software errors leading to registrations problems before , particularly for people using DMV services like getting a driver's license. But election experts note actual voting by noncitizens remains rare.

events.title: Treasury says largest U.S. banks let politics influence who received banking services
events.summary: The Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found the nine largest banks serving the U.S. used reputation-risk policies that could let political and social considerations shape banking decisions. The review examined nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. The findings may bolster President Trump’s push against alleged political "debanking" as regulators also examine whether anti-money-laundering rules contributed to the practice. The Treasury Department's Office of the Comptroller of the Currency found some of the largest banks serving the U.S. allowed political considerations, public pressure and social concerns to influence decisions about who received banking services, according to a sweeping report released Wednesday. The OCC said it reviewed the nine largest national banks under its supervision, examining nearly 100,000 complaints and about 420,000 pages of documents. It found that all nine had used "reputation risk" policies that lacked "clear," "objective" standards and could disadvantage customers because of their political or religious views or lawful business activities. "Banks should make decisions based on financial risk, not the political or social preferences of their employees or executives," Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould said, according to a transcript of his in remarks Wednesday in Lexington, Kentucky. The findings may lend new regulatory weight to a grievance President Donald Trump has pressed since returning to office. Trump has repeatedly accused and sued major banks for discriminating against conservatives and has said he was personally " debanked " after the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol insurrection , claims banks have denied . The report lands a day after the OCC and other Treasury regulators imposed more than $1.2 billion in penalties on Bank of America over separate anti-money-laundering failures . At the same time, the OCC said it is examining whether banks' efforts to comply with anti-money-laundering rules have themselves contributed to debanking. The review covered JPMorgan Chase , Bank of America, Citibank , Wells Fargo , U.S. Bank , Capital One , PNC Bank , TD Bank and BMO Bank , which together held a majority of assets at OCC-supervised commercial banks when the probe began last year under a Trump executive order . The OCC stopped short of announcing fines or sanctions Wednesday, but said it is considering additional rules aimed at preventing political or religious discrimination. Among the cases it highlighted: JPMorgan subsidiary WePay closed accounts belonging to merchants selling Trump and conservative merchandise. An internal screening list included terms such as "MAGA," "Make America Great" and "America First," even though the OCC found neither WePay nor JPMorgan had formal written standards for deciding when flagged material amounted to prohibited hate or violence. JPMorgan told CNBC its policies prohibit discrimination based on political or religious views and said WePay's process "did not meet our expectations." The bank said it fixed the issue and has since shut down the business. "We are not forcing these banks to serve every customer," Gould said. "Instead, banks should evaluate every customer on objective, risk-based criteria." Citi declined to comment. The other banks did not immediately respond to request for comment. The Bank Policy Institute, which represents large U.S. and foreign banks, said in a statement that the industry supports "clear and consistent standards that promote access while maintaining sound risk management," adding that political or religious beliefs should not affect access to banking services. The report also found examples cutting the other way politically. Capital One declined relationships with an abortion-rights group after noting that about 95% of its political contributions went to Democrats , and with a public education group whose political arm endorsed only Democratic candidates. It also passed on a gun-rights group over concerns that banking it could look like an endorsement. The practices extended beyond overtly political groups too, the report indicates. The OCC found restrictions affecting firearms, fossil fuels, private prisons, tobacco and cryptocurrency , and said some banks' appetite for those businesses shifted with the political climate — risking a "whipsaw" effect between administrations. All nine banks told the OCC they have since revised or consolidated policies aimed at ensuring fair access. But the regulator said none has fully acknowledged past debanking decisions or created a comprehensive program to remediate affected customers.

events.title: Alaska LNG project becomes $54bn flashpoint for would-be Asian buyers
events.summary: A massive liquefied natural gas project in Alaska has emerged as an unlikely focal point in purported foreign investment, as Asian buyers rush to diversify their supply imports amid disruptions from the Iran war. On Tuesday in Wasilla, a town 70km north of Anchorage, US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 per cent of the LNG from the long-planned Alaska LNG project. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Taiwan had committed to investing $4.4 billion to develop the pipeline. The terms of the deal were not immediately clear. Last week, Mr Trump announced a $54 billion South Korea investment in Alaska LNG as part of a $200 billion energy package and $350 billion trade deal the two sides struck last year to lower tariffs on Korean imports. South Korea has rejected the claim, saying it has given no firm commitment on the project. “There's no investors other than the US government, and there are no buyers who have committed to signing any sales and purchase agreements,” said Ira Joseph, a global fellow at the Centre on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University. The project hopes to make a final investment decision on the pipeline this year, with a separate one on the export terminal in 2027. One of the dominant factors in the publicly promoted claims are the November 3 midterm elections . Alaska has become a battleground state for control of the US Senate. Mr Trump’s appearance in Wasilla on Tuesday underscored the race’s importance as he seeks to promote energy exports and foreign investment. At the same time, the Alaska LNG project holds big promises, as South-East Asian buyers are seeking to diversify their energy supplies as the Iran war cut off shipments from the region . If Alaska LNG becomes operational, it would drastically reduce the time for delivery of LNG shipments. The journey from Alaska to Japan is more than 9,600km shorter than from the US Gulf Coast, the project's developer said in a 2023 report. Theory v practicality For all the promise that Alaska LNG holds, it remains a far-off venture. Development is expected to begin in phases, with targets for the first exports in 2031. Glenfarne Group estimates the project will cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion. That means about $2.2 billion to $2.7 billion a tonne a year of capacity, according to a Reuters analysis. “This is an expensive project that's going to take at best a lot of years to sort of come to fruition,” said Rachel Ziemba, founder of risk advisory firm Ziemba Insights. Another possible sticking point is the about 106cm-diameter pipeline that would stretch 1,300km from Alaska’s North Slope to Nikiski, south of Anchorage, running parallel to the existing Trans Alaska Pipeline System for oil. LNG sites in Nikiski would produce 20 million tonnes a year for export and hold a daily capacity of 3.3 billion cubic feet. The pipeline itself – Phase One – is likely to cost between $13.2 billion and $16.9 billion, according to company estimates. “If the gas is sitting right next to the LNG facility, this thing would have been built 40 or 50 years ago, but it's not, and … that's the difference maker in this project,” Mr Joseph said. Investors remain cautious. As of January this year, only six non-binding offtake agreements have been signed totalling 13 million tonnes a year. Another point of friction is competition, with LNG projects in Canada and in America's Gulf Coast also attracting attention. Major players in the Middle East have continued to increase their interest in LNG, but through the Gulf Coast. This summer, Adnoc's XRG boosted its stake in NextDecade's LNG site in Rio Grande, Texas. QatarEnergy began LNG exports from its joint venture with Exxon at the Golden Pass project in March. “It is notable to me that at a time where you know Trump is looking for all the finance he can for this project, that he's not turning to these sources of capital,” Ms Ziemba said.

events.title: XBOX Nano Controller brings full-size controls to a pocket-friendly design
events.summary: Multiple Adventures Await as Stories: The Path of Destinies Arrives on Xbox One Coming to XBOX Game Pass: Battlefield 6, Valor Mortis, Forever Ago, and More Upcoming Changes to XBOX Cloud Gaming Go All in on All-Out Warfare in Battlefield 6 with EA Play Today, we’re introducing the XBOX Nano Controller, designed to fit nearly every pocket and budget. Its compact design offers a great option for younger players, smaller hands, or anyone seeking something portable for play on the go. The XBOX Nano Controller, at a little over 5 inches in length and just 3.5 ounces, is our smallest controller, lighter and shorter than most modern smartphones. It includes all 18 standard gameplay inputs, delivering a familiar controller layout players already love. At $49.99, the XBOX Nano Controller gives players a new, approachable option for jumping in and sharing the fun. It’s an easier way to be ready for games the whole family can play together, like Minecraft Dungeons II , where up to four heroes can team up for local co-op in the living room or online . The pocketable design also makes it easy to slip into a bag or bring along for the day, giving you a convenient way to play whether you’re traveling, visiting friends and family, or simply taking games like Forza Horizon 6 beyond the living room. The XBOX Nano controller includes a rechargeable battery and a programmable Action Button that can be customized for features like screenshots, gameplay capture, and other frequently used shortcuts. With XBOX Wireless and Bluetooth support, it connects across a range of compatible devices with ease. Players can pre-order the XBOX Nano Controller beginning today for $49.99 USD. It will be available beginning in November in Argentina, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Canada, China, Colombia, Czechia, Denmark, Dominican Republic, Finland, France, Germany, Guatemala, Hong Kong SAR, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Japan, Korea, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Norway, Panama, Peru, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Spain, Switzerland, Taiwan, Trinidad & Tobago, the United Kingdom, and the United States, with additional markets to follow. Pricing and availability vary by country. Visit your local Microsoft Store or authorized retailer for more information. To make it easy to get started, we’re teaming up with Samsung, to introduce a special XBOX Nano Controller and 2-months of Game Pass Ultimate offer (for new members) in the US with the purchase of select Samsung TVs this holiday season. With the XBOX app available through the Gaming Hub built into Samsung TVs, players in select regions can use their monthly cloud playtime to play hundreds of XBOX Game Pass titles by simply connecting their controller. We’re also working with Meta on a holiday offer in the US that includes an XBOX Nano Controller and a 2-month Game Pass Ultimate subscription for new members with the purchase of a Meta Quest.

events.title: Unpaid toll? Missed delivery? Microsoft moves to disrupt a global cybercrime marketplace
events.summary: Disrupting the service economy behind transnational cybercrime operations Oct 14, 2026 | Steven Masada - Associate General Counsel and General Manager, Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit Most people have opened their messages to find a suspicious alert urgently telling them that a package cannot be delivered, a toll remains unpaid, a bank account needs attention, or a tax bill is overdue. The details may change, but the goal is the same: to get someone to click, share personal information, or pay. These messages are relentless. Delete and block one, and another takes its place. Ignore them, and more will follow. Fall for one, and the floodgates open. What appears to be a simple scam message is often the visible end of a much larger transnational cybercriminal operation. When Microsoft and Japan’s National Police Agency (NPA) followed a wave of fraud and scam activity targeting people and businesses in Japan, they expected to find individual campaigns. Instead, they found themselves inside a sprawling Chinese-language cybercrime marketplace where criminals could buy accounts, hosting services and tools used to create fake websites and online identities. The investigation expanded globally, involving the Japan Cybercrime Control Center (JC3), Resecurity , Cloudflare, Oracle , Proofpoint and TRM Labs to uncover the businesses sustaining this criminal ecosystem. Today, Microsoft and Health-ISAC , a global non-profit that helps health sector organizations share cyber threat information and collaborate to improve operational resilience, are moving to dismantle three components of this criminal marketplace: YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man. Since January 2026, YAM Store, CoGUI and Iron Man have collectively enabled more than one billion malicious messages targeting over 75,000 organizations worldwide, including more than 750 million messages geared toward Microsoft customers alone. These messages have been used to target consumers, healthcare organizations, financial institutions, and other businesses in more than 150 countries, generating tens of millions of dollars for their operators. Tracing the businesses behind the scams The investigation began in late 2025 after Japan’s NPA alerted Microsoft to malicious messaging campaigns targeting people in Japan. NPA continued providing intelligence and investigative support as the partners traced those campaigns back to the businesses supplying criminals around the world. The trail led investigators deep into a Chinese-language cybercrime ecosystem that was difficult for non-native-speaking investigators to penetrate. There, they gained access to CoGUI, which supplied criminals with ready-made websites and messages impersonating companies, financial institutions, government agencies, and other trusted organizations. Instead of creating fraudulent websites themselves, criminals could quickly deploy pages designed to steal passwords, payment information, and other personal data. As Microsoft’s investigation expanded, intelligence from JC3 helped confirm the scale of the activity affecting Japanese organizations and their customers. Drawing on information collected across its network of more than 130 member organizations, JC3 connected what appeared to be separate incidents to a broader pattern of scams targeting Japanese companies and financial institutions, including efforts to defraud consumers and to steal credentials and other sensitive information. One name that kept appearing throughout the investigation was YAM Store. YAM Store operated much like an online shop. Customers could browse products, compare prices and purchase fraudulent Microsoft and Google accounts and other ready-made tools used to carry out scams, including credential theft. Controlled purchases conducted by Microsoft helped confirm how it worked. In some cases, operators acquired internet domains that legitimate organizations had allowed to expire, often targeting certain sectors, such as non-profits and education, with specialized product offerings. They then rebuilt the websites to make those organizations appear active, allowing them to fraudulently obtain Microsoft 365 accounts that could later be sold through YAM Store. YAM Store provided criminal infrastructure that was frequently paired with tools and services such as CoGUI. As investigators dug deeper, they found that the marketplace was already evolving. CoGUI had become one of the most widely used offerings in the ecosystem, particularly targeting victims in Japan and the United States but by mid-2026 it was increasingly being replaced by a newer offering known as Iron Man. Iron Man expanded the model by giving criminals access to thousands of ready-made templates designed to impersonate trusted organizations. Criminals could then quickly deploy email, text and web content tailored to specific brands, industries and countries. Through test purchases and work with Re s ecurity , investigators gained access to Iron Man and identified more than 2,300 templates impersonating banks, retailers, healthcare providers, transportation authorities, police departments , government agencies , a n d o t he r or g an iz a t ions a c r o s s more than 1 5 0 c ou nt r i e s w o r l d w i d e . Some were designed for government impersonation scams , using the appearance of official authority to pressure victims into making payments or disclosing sensitive personal information . Others impersonated organizations across industries, countries , and languages, from banks and airlines to telecommunications companies, retailers , and parcel delivery services. Examples of these impersonation templates are below. Importantly, the presence of an organization or government entity in these templates does not indicate that its systems were compromised. A blog from Microsoft Threat Intelligence shares more details on the network, as well as steps customers can take to protect themselves. No single organization saw the full picture. Japan’s NPA played a critical role throughout the investigation, providing intelligence, investigative support and collaboration that helped uncover how the operation worked. JC3 helped establish the scale of the activity affecting Japanese organizations and consumers. Health-ISAC provided insight into impacts affecting healthcare organizations, while Resecurity, Cloudflare, Oracle, Proofpoint and TRM Labs contributed intelligence and investigative support. Working together, an d wi th th e a s si s t a n ce o f A I t o o l s , we connected accounts, websites , and infrastructure that initially appeared unrelated, helping expose the broader criminal marketplace behind them. Microsoft also worked closely and shared intelligence with U.S. Secret Service and international law enforcement partners.

events.title: Israel’s former security chief sues Netanyahu for October 7 defamation
events.summary: Ronen Bar accuses Netanyahu of being warned before Hamas attacks, as elections loom. The former head of Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet has sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation over claims of his responsibility in the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack. Coming just before Israel’s close-fought October 27 election in which Netanyahu is fighting for his political life, the case filed on Wednesday is set to ramp up the country’s political drama. Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, accused Netanyahu of “lying to cover himself” and said it was slanderous of the prime minister to have accused him of “criminal failures” over the attack, in a 134-page court document. Bar said he telephoned the prime minister’s military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack became apparent, but that he did not have Netanyahu’s direct number. Netanyahu has said he was not alerted by Bar on the morning of the Hamas-led assault, insisting that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet’s then-director or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack. Bar’s lawsuit says Netanyahu made accusations “that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of October 7”. Instead, it was Netanyahu’s policies over several years that had “increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza”, it said. On Wednesday, Netanyahu responded to Bar’s accusations in a statement issued by his Likud party saying, “Ronen, are you serious?” “You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do,” Netanyahu asked, adding, “How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?” Bar resigned as head of Shin Bet in June 2025 amid recriminations over the deadliest attack in Israel’s history, while insisting he had informed Netanyahu of the threat in advance. He is seeking three million shekels (about $968,500) in damages from Netanyahu. The allegations in Bar’s lawsuit come days after Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, told Israel’s Channel 12 that the prime minister’s office had “falsified records related to October 7, 2023”, including altering the recorded time of a key phone call. Gil, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary from July 2021 to May 2024, said a stenographer in the prime minister’s office approached him in January 2024 with instructions from Netanyahu’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6:40am local time (03:40GMT) to 6:29am (03:29 GMT). “She told me, I’m not allowed to change it,” said Gil, accusing the head of Netanyahu’s office of manipulating telephone records, adding, “Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them.” Last month, the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu had been warned of the attack by Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel. In a rare move, Kamel reportedly phoned the prime minister just days before the attack, underscoring previous warnings in September 2023, when he is said to have flown to Israel to warn security officials in person that Hamas was planning an attack. Polls show Netanyahu is in a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 election, after being hammered by former staff and government officials as well as the opposition for failing to prevent the bloodshed. At least 1,221 Israelis were killed on October 7, 2023, after Hamas broke through the fence separating Israel and Gaza, according to Israeli official figures. Also, 251 Israelis were taken captive, including the bodies of 44 Israelis killed that day. In the three years since, Israel has killed more than 74,300 people in Gaza, according to the Health Ministry in the enclave. More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed in Israeli attacks since a tentative “ceasefire” backed by the US was reached last year.

events.title: A dietitian says GLP-1s aren't 'a free lunch' — you need a plan when you stop taking them. Here are her 3 best tips.
events.summary: Dr. Linia Patel is a registered dietitian and author of "Life After Weight-Loss Medication." Liudmila Pokrychuk Dr. Linia Patel is a registered dietitian and author of "Life After Weight-Loss Medication." Patel said GLP-1s can be great tools, but require a game plan when you stop taking them. She shared her tips for staying full and fighting food noise once you're off GLP-1s. For those with positive experiences on GLP-1s , the benefits are enormous. They might report feeling physically better, having more confidence, or improved relationships with their spouses. It's the moment when some people go off the medications that can cause stress, especially if they don't have a plan for maintaining their new weight. "Weight loss is the short-term part, and then the forever bit is the weight maintenance part," Dr. Linia Patel, a registered dietitian in the UK and author of "Life After Weight-Loss Medication," told Business Insider. One review published in March 2026 found that around 60% of the weight lost will be regained after one year off a GLP-1 such as Ozempic, Wegovy, or Mounjaro . It also projected a 75% weight regain in the long term. When stopping a GLP-1, weight regain, specifically fat, can also feel quicker. It's why medical professionals often encourage incorporating strength training and eating enough protein while on the medication; otherwise, you might lose too much muscle, which is crucial for weight maintenance. While Patel said the medications can be an enormous help, they should be seen as a piece of the puzzle, not a magic bullet. Without a workout routine in place or a mindful approach to meals, she said it's easy to yo-yo. "There's no such thing as a free lunch," she said, noting that weight management after GLP-1s requires intentionality. "Somewhere along the line, you're going to have to get on the lifestyle factors." Patel shared a few tips to stay full longer and silence food noise, the two dietary keys to weight maintenance . 'Satiety stack' with high-protein and high-fiber foods Patel said avocado toast with egg has protein, fiber, and healthy fats to keep you fuller for longer. DronG/Getty Images GLP-1s work by keeping you feeling full for longer. By that logic, "what you want to do when you come off the medications is to eat in a way that feels filling and satisfying," Patel said. She calls it "satiety stacking": building meals around protein, fiber, and healthy fats, which can help control appetite by triggering the release of hormones that signal fullness to your brain. Patel recommends aiming for about 25 to 30 grams of protein per meal, obtained from foods such as meat, fish, eggs, tofu, and Greek yogurt. Ideally, you'll pair it with fiber-rich foods like vegetables, oats, legumes, and whole grains, as well as healthy fats such as olive oil, nuts, seeds, or avocado. The idea is to find combinations you actively enjoy, she said, which will help you stay consistent. Delay overeating with high volume and crunchiness Starter salads can take up lots of space in your stomach and also take longer to chew, making it harder to overeat. Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images Patel has two other tips for staying full longer. One is to focus on high-volume foods — ones that "physically take up a lot of space and don't give you as many calories." Starting a meal with miso soup or a side salad can help you avoid overeating a calorie-dense main course, such as noodles or pizza. It's also a great rule for your main meal, such as focusing on leafy greens and grains like quinoa for a hearty salad. The other tip is to prioritize crunchy, high-fiber foods that take longer to chew. Think: carrots, nuts, or seeds. "The more you slow down how you're eating, the more you're going to allow your body that time for it to start doing its signaling from your stomach to your brain that you're actually full," she said, leading to less calorie intake. Hush your food noise Stir-fries are satiating and easy to customize, helping with food noise. LauriPatterson/Getty Images One of the most talked-about effects of GLP-1s is their ability to remove " food noise ." For many people taking them, the desire to eat or overeat ultraprocessed foods simply vanishes — only to return once they go off the medication. "What I would say is not to try and fight your appetite, but to rebuild the trust between your brain and your body," Patel said. She has a three-pronged approach to tackling food noise. The first is physiological. Besides eating satiating foods, other lifestyle factors, like proper sleep , good hydration, and stress management, can also help you fend off cravings. The next approach is psychological. Patel said it's important to be aware of when you're emotionally eating. She calls it a "HALT-B" check-in: Are you hungry, angry, anxious, lonely, tired, or bored? "How can you create a pause that is literally five seconds that allows you to make an intentional choice versus that autopilot mode?" she said. The final step is examining your own relationship with diet culture , such as labeling certain foods as "bad" or "cheat" foods, which can make you want them more. "It's not a moral test," Patel said. "Approaching food with this idea of curiosity instead of guilt creates that space for flexibility and enjoyment and a healthier relationship with eating." events.title: Tina Knowles launched hair care line Cécred with daughter Beyonce after years of mixing custom hair treatments
events.summary: Years before she was the matriarch for one of music’s most famous families, Tina Knowles started a business catering to professional women who needed their hair styled—and quickly. Speaking on Wednesday at the Fortune Most Powerful Women’s Summit in Santa Barbara, Calif., Knowles said Cécred, the hair-care line she launched with her daughter Beyoncé Knowles Carter in February 2024, is the product of four decades in business, fashion, and entertainment. In the Houston hair salon where the Knowles matriarch started her career, she relied on products that had human hair ground into them to add protein to strands. Knowles would whip up butter and hot olive oil treatments to bring more moisture and balance to her clients’ hair, including her daughters. Knowles said both Knowles Carter and actress and singer-songwriter Solange Knowles worked in her salon. “The dream has always been to create a product that had everything that you need in one product and one step,” Knowles told Fortune senior writer Sheryl Estrada. “And Beyonce had that dream as well—because I was doing all those things to her hair.” Knowles said Knowles Carter decided to fund the hair-care line herself rather than working with outside investors because the two were so focused on research and development. Investors balked at the costs. Knowles said they wanted a product that wouldn’t merely lay on top of strands to make it feel smooth, but instead they wanted a product that could penetrate the pores of all types of hair textures. “Our customers have done the marketing for us because it’s really a quality product,” said Knowles. The line is a family story, Knowles told Estrada. Her daughters first worked sweeping Knowles’s Headliners salon, and Knowles said she worked with plenty of entrepreneurial women there. Blockbuster musical group Destiny’s Child got its start performing for salon customers. Knowles started the Headliners hair salon business after her marriage ended and she needed to support her children. She told Estrada she decided at the time she would never be dependent again. Her own salon visits would take hours, so she made Headliners a go-to spot for professional women short on time. Clients were seen within 15 minutes or they would get their money back. Knowles, who published her best-selling memoir Matriarch last year, said that while writing she learned that the women in her family had a history of working and designing clothing as seamstresses, going back to her great- and great-great grandmothers, who were enslaved. She later styled Destiny’s Child through its rise and co-founded a fashion label. Since launching two years ago, Cécred has posted the most successful prestige hair-care debut in Ulta Beauty’s history, won 89 beauty industry awards, and expanded into the U.K. The team behind the brand tests its styling and restoring serums and conditioners in three countries to try to reach every hair texture. Despite the success, Knowles was candid about how two divorces in her past have shaped her. When she divorced at 59, she thought her life was over. But Knowles picked herself up and made it a turning point. She went back to museums, she said, and picked up art books and prioritized herself again. For years, she had remained low key in order to avoid embarrassing her children, she said. “I didn’t take credit for a lot of the work that I did as a woman,” said Knowles. “We just do it because it needs to be done.” At 70, she found herself going through a second divorce, which also left its mark. “There’s something about those divorces that make you take a look at yourself,” she added. That’s when she started writing, partly to set an accurate record down about her family, which strangers narrate on a daily basis on social media. Writing it down, she said, became therapeutic. It made her a best-selling author at 71. Now at 72, Knowles’ passion has shifted to philanthropy, which she wants to move it full time in the next few years. She chairs BeyGOOD, Beyonce’s charitable foundation, on top of Cecred. She also has her own charity, Waco (Where Art Can Occur) which she started with her ex-husband. The group mentors girls from Los Angeles communities and exposes then to art museums, travel, etiquette, and life skills they wouldn’t get otherwise. Next up, she plans to work on the Vision Theatre in Los Angeles’ Leimert Park. Actress Marla Gibbs invested in the theater and planned to turn it into a performing arts center, but lost the building after riots. The city has since poured millions into its restoration and Knowles plans to follow Gibbs’ lead and make it a community arts center. Knowles noted that after about five career pivots, she goes into new ventures with no fear. Her advice to the younger generation is to give it your all and if it doesn’t work, bring what you learned into the next thing you do. A strong work ethic matters, she said, along with never feeling entitled to anything. “Just be authentically yourself,” said Knowles. “That’s my mantra.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: OpenAI says it's 'very concerned' that its trade secrets could help Apple's push into AI-enabled devices
events.summary: OpenAI alleged that a former employee briefed top Apple executives about the products its developing. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images OpenAI alleges that a former employee took information about an unreleased device to Apple. In a legal filing, OpenAI said it is "very concerned" that the information could help Apple's upcoming products. On Tuesday, Apple announced a family of AI-enabled smart home products. OpenAI is escalating its trade-secrets fight with Apple on the heels of Apple announcing a family of smart home-focused devices. The AI company alleged in a new legal filing that an unnamed former employee sent themselves "a hundred highly confidential files" on their last day with OpenAI in June. The files contained information about at least one unreleased device OpenAI is developing, the filing said. The AI company said the former employee worked at Apple for six months before joining OpenAI, and he is now back at Apple. OpenAI said it's the company's understanding that the unnamed employee later briefed "Apple's senior leadership, including Apple's vice president of operations in Asia" about the AI company's product plans. "That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products," OpenAI's lawyers wrote in the filing. In a statement, Apple said it has found nothing to support OpenAI's claims. It said the filing on Wednesday is an attempt to distract from its own claims about own former OpenAI employees have stolen Apple's trade secrets. The files, OpenAI said, contained "highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s)" and "supplier information and project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports regarding coating and sealing of hardware components." In July, Apple sued OpenAI, alleging that the AI company engaged in "a coordinated pattern of misconduct at an institutional level" to steal its trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and said it is not interested in Apple's trade secrets. In an August blog post, OpenAI blasted the "careless, aggressive and oddly personal lawsuit sadly doesn't live up to that reputation." In a legal filing, OpenAI poked at Apple's perceived struggles amid the AI talent war. On Tuesday, Apple announced HomeView , a $299 display and the company's first smart home device, which is powered by Siri AI. Apple also announced a host of smart home products it developed alongside LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's announcement highlighted how its AI systems could add to the devices, allowing a user to do everything from summarizing what's happening in footage captured by an outdoor camera to automatically adjusting a thermostat when they enter a room. OpenAI said it is worried that the information the employee took could be used by Apple. "OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple," the company's lawyers wrote, "where Apple engineers can shape Apple's upcoming products based on OpenAI's confidential and innovative work." In referencing Apple's ambitions, OpenAI's lawyers linked in a footnote to the tech giant's collection of new devices, including HomeView. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: YouTube Music launches new labels as AI-generated music floods streaming platforms
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. YouTube Music announced Wednesday the rollout of a new labeling system aimed at improving transparency around songs created with the help of generative AI. Now listeners will be able to easily identify tracks created using AI, including those involved in composition and vocals. The label will appear on the player page. Clicking on this label provides additional information about the specific role of AI in the track’s creation. Notably, these labels will also extend to the main YouTube app. YouTube said it collaborated with various music partners and deployed its own detection tools to identify AI-generated music. According to its help page , partners using YouTube can declare their work’s use of generative AI through one of three designations: Fully Gen AI, Partly Gen AI, or No Gen AI. “Fully Gen AI” applies to tracks that are entirely generated by AI, while “Partly Gen AI” refers to works where artists may have incorporated AI-generated components but added their own live elements. Tracks edited using pitch-correction tools such as Auto-Tune fall under the “No Gen AI” category. The move comes as AI-generated music rapidly expands across streaming services, and many platforms are adopting their own approaches. For instance, Apple Music has plans to introduce “Made With AI” labels as part of its AI Transparency Tags later this year. Spotify also has AI labels, as well as a music spam filter. Deezer has taken one of the stricter stances, reporting in July that it was receiving nearly 90,000 fully AI-generated tracks daily. The platform labels detected AI-generated music and excludes it from algorithmic recommendations and editorial playlists, while also withholding royalties from fraudulent streams. The company is also working on an option to let users filter out AI-generated music . TIDAL also labels recordings it identifies as entirely AI-generated, allows listeners to disable them, and excludes these recordings from royalty attribution. YouTube, by contrast, is focusing on disclosure rather than blanket restrictions. Its new labels are intended to inform listeners about AI’s role in music creation, but AI involvement alone doesn’t make a track ineligible for monetization. YouTube even experiments with AI-powered music creation, including its tool Dream Track , which lets select creators generate soundtracks featuring AI-generated versions of participating artists’ voices. events.title: Meet a 23-year-old millionaire who canceled his plan to move to San Francisco because of a billionaire tax he might never have to pay
events.summary: At 23, Emil Barr is already a millionaire building a business in Columbus, Ohio. But San Francisco’s investors and AI scene caught his eye—enough that the Flashpass founder told Fortune he signed a lease to move there about a year ago. He changed his mind after looking more closely at California’s regulatory and tax environment, including its proposed billionaire wealth tax, which helped persuade him to cancel the move entirely. He wouldn’t owe the tax under the current proposal, but fears it could pave the way for taxes on millionaires like him. “I think it was less of a matter of immediate finances,” Barr told Fortune . Instead, he pointed to what he described as California’s “anti-entrepreneurial” political rhetoric. His decision raises the question dividing California: would taxing its biggest fortunes help pay for essential services, or make the state a less attractive place to build a business? Barr sees it as a warning sign, but supporters see a way to protect healthcare without sacrificing the talent and investment that draw businesses there. The debate has national stakes too. States invest in the public services that help businesses grow, but can lose the chance to tax some of that wealth when residents move before cashing out.  Billionaire flight gets the attention, but wealth can leave in quieter ways. Founders like Barr can choose where to build before their fortunes are big enough to tax, and residents who already have them can move before cashing out. States invest in the public services that help businesses grow, but can lose the chance to tax that wealth when it moves. The debate has national stakes, too. Proposition 40 , on the Nov. 3 ballot, would impose a one-time 5% tax on qualifying billionaires who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026. It would tax accumulated wealth rather than annual income, with most of the revenue going toward healthcare. The measure has drawn support from six Nobel Prize-winning economists, including Joseph Stiglitz, Paul Krugman, and Daron Acemoglu. In a September letter , they argued that the tax would be modest compared with billionaires’ wealth gains and would help replace lost federal healthcare funding while supporting public services important ot California’s economic growth. A billionaire tax, a millionaire’s cold feet Flashpass builds technology that helps government agencies connect people with work, including people displaced by AI, Barr said. He moved to Columbus because Ohio was the first state to use its software.  San Francisco initially appealed to Barr as the place to be because it’s closer to investors and AI companies. He hadn’t decided whether to move Flashpass’s headquarters there, but planned to relocate himself—until California’s regulatory and tax climate changed his mind. “I’m not 100% sure I’m going to stay in Ohio and keep building the business in Ohio,” Barr said. “But I am 100% sure that I wouldn’t build a business in California.” He argues that political hostility toward entrepreneurs could discourage them from building businesses beyond California too. “If we keep villainizing entrepreneurs, entrepreneurs aren’t just going to leave California; they’re going to leave America,” Barr said. His decision hasn’t ended his company’s California ties altogether, though. He says Flashpass still has employees and investors there, and he continues traveling to the state. He also leaves room for higher taxes, while arguing that the approach matters. “Maybe the solution is paying higher taxes and updating the tax code, but it needs to be done in a more nuanced, progressive way,” he said, without offering a specific alternative. Barr isn’t alone in opposing it. Gov. Gavin Newsom opposes the measure, and Google cofounder Sergey Brin has helped fund the opposition. Why supporters dispute the investment threat Not every billionaire sees the proposal as a reason to reconsider California as a whole. In a January Bloomberg podcast, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he was “perfectly fine” with the proposed tax, pointing to Silicon Valley’s talent pool as the reason the company works there. Debru Carthan, vice president of SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the union backing the measure, rejected concerns that the proposal would drive away wealthy residents or investment. The campaign argues the tax would help replace roughly $100 billion in federal healthcare funding it says California will lose over five years. “This scare tactic just doesn’t stand up to scrutiny,” she said in a statement to Fortune . “There’s more money and investors coming into California now, not less.” Carthan pointed to Massachusetts and Washington, arguing that their taxes on wealthy residents have raised billions for public services while their high-income populations have continued to grow. Those policies differ from California’s proposed one-time wealth tax, but the union presents them as evidence against predictions of an exodus. She argued that the more immediate threat is the loss of federal healthcare funding. “That’s the real crisis our state is facing,” she said, warning that without additional funding, clinics would close, hospitals would lay off workers, and Californians could lose coverage or face higher premiums. The measure would direct 90% of its revenue to healthcare. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates it would raise tens of billions of dollars over several years. It also expects taxpayer responses, including some departures, could reduce ongoing income-tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually.  What migration research can—and can’t—tell us Cornell sociologist Cristobal Young , who has spent nearly two decades studying how taxes affect migration among high earners, says fears of wealthy people fleeing higher taxes are often exaggerated. “The more money you make, the less likely you are to move,” Young told Fortune. Successful high earners tend to live where they built their careers, with business partners, professional networks, and family ties that make moving costly. “All of a sudden, you’re in a new professional environment, and now you’re more of an outsider,” he said. Young also said that people’s objections to a state’s taxes do not always explain where they actually live or start a business. Their existing roots, business partners, and customers can matter more. He began studying tax migration using New Jersey tax returns after its 2004 income-tax increase on high earners. Even with lower-tax Pennsylvania nearby, he said, the research did not find the departure pattern critics feared. A 2016 study he coauthored , examining 45 million tax records over 13 years, likewise found limited millionaire tax flight. But Young said those findings don’t necessarily predict what would happen in California. A large tax on accumulated wealth differs from adding a few percentage points to annual income taxes. “We haven’t passed a tax like this before in the U.S.,” he said.&nb

events.title: AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
events.summary: Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence . Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI. As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down. “Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson. Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun , a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them. Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online. The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry. Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes , which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress. OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI , warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer. As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way. Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science , and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound. “We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.” This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter . events.title: Real Madrid’s Vinicius banned for Clasico after hair-pull red card
events.summary: Vinicius will miss El Clasico on October 25, the first of his four-match ban for pulling Saliba’s hair in La Liga. Real Madrid’s Vinicius Junior will miss the upcoming match against Barcelona in the Spanish league after being issued a four-match suspension for pulling an opponent’s hair during a La Liga game last week. The Brazilian forward will miss Madrid’s next four league fixtures, including the highly anticipated October 25 El Clasico against fierce rivals and league champions Barcelona. The Spanish federation’s disciplinary committee announced the ban on Wednesday after Vinicius received the red card against Villarreal last week. The number seven thought he had scored Real’s second goal in the match on Saturday, but his effort was disallowed after a video assistant referee (VAR) review found he should be dismissed for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair in the build-up. The Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee confirmed the Brazilian will be banned for several matches, including the visit to face league leaders Barca, because of both the red card and his subsequent protests. After the match, Vinicius, ⁠⁠⁠⁠who came on in the ⁠⁠⁠⁠52nd minute and was red-carded 20 minutes later, posted on social media, saying, “sorry to the team and the ⁠⁠⁠⁠fans”. Vinicius was celebrating after scoring when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera was called by the VAR to review the moments before his goal. The referee waved off the goal and pulled out a red card for Vinicius, who also goes by his nickname Vini Jr. When he thought Vinicius had doubled the lead, Real manager Jose Mourinho ran to join the celebrations with his players. But moments later, Vinicius was left livid by the referee’s decision. He screamed at Diaz de Mera while his teammates tried to calm him down as he left the field.

events.title: Nvidia CEO Huang says society shouldn’t tolerate AI cyber incidents, says AI doomers “ought to stop working on” the technology
events.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the AI industry shouldn’t tolerate any cybersecurity incidents caused by the technology, putting him at odds with OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who has recently said that some hacks and scams may be a necessary trade-off for AI’s benefits. “I’m willing to accept no incidents of cybersecurity. We should not accept any of them,” he told Fortune in an interview in London. “We should do everything we can to avoid them.” Earlier this month, Altman said in an interview with Vanity Fair that the world may have to accept “some bad things happening” in return for AI’s benefits, including major hacks, misuse and scams, because people will do “orders of magnitude” more good than harm with the technology. In a subsequent interview with Politico’s “Decoded” podcast, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models, months after a swarm of OpenAI’s own agents escaped their training sandbox and hacked into the Hugging Face website. Huang told Fortune that the incidents so far could all have been avoided with stronger containment and monitoring of AI agents. He compared the problem to the early consumer internet, when clicking on a website could infect a PC with a virus. The fix was for browsers to run websites in isolation, so they couldn’t touch the rest of the computer. Huang says AI agents need the same treatment and should be sealed inside a secure container where they can’t do damage beyond what they’re allowed to. Huang also shrugged off warnings of existential risks from AI that have come from many within the leading AI companies, including executives such as Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, telling Fortune the technology was “completely in our control.” “I don’t know why anybody would want to support the advancement of a technology that’s going to result, you know, in the end of human civilization as we know it. And so, if they believe that, they really ought to stop working on it,” he said. Huang is in London as part of a European tour that kicked off in Paris on Tuesday, where he told the audience that “Europe needs to get in the race” on AI. Huang said Nvidia would announce $2 billion in new European investments within the next week. That comes on top of the $8 billion the chipmaker has already committed to the continent. The tour also includes Berlin, where Nvidia’s GTC conference will be hosted later in the month. The region still trails at the frontier, but Huang has pitched open-source models as Europe’s best route to catching up with the U.S. Nvidia is already a major backer of Mistral, the French open-weight developer that recently released its Large 4 model, trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs. The sovereignty pitch also suits Nvidia. Open-weight models lower costs for the companies building them, but the hardware spending still goes to the chipmaker. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com
