events.title: Lisa Cook lawyer doubts Trump committee's fairness as president calls her 'automatic no vote'
events.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook's lawyer sharply questioned the objectivity and fairness of President Donald Trump's committee investigating the central bank official. The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said a scheduled White House hearing in the probe would have to be delayed until at least December. Committee member Kevin Hassett has already prejudged the case, Lowell suggested, pointing to his prior comment that Trump has "cause" to fire Cook. Trump recently slammed Cook as an "automatic no vote," apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates. An attorney for Lisa Cook voiced strong doubts that President Donald Trump 's committee investigating mortgage fraud allegations against the Federal Reserve governor would be fair and objective. The lawyer, Abbe Lowell, said the committee is plagued by issues that undermine the appearance of the Fed's independence, including "demonstrably biased members" and "unspecified additional allegations" against Cook. Those and other issues "would have to be addressed before a hearing could occur" in the probe, Lowell wrote in a letter sent Tuesday to Will Scharf, Trump's aide and counsel. No such hearing could take place until at least December, weeks later than the initially scheduled date, Lowell insisted. The letter came three days after Trump slammed Cook as "dishonest" and griped that she was an "automatic no vote" — apparently referring to her opposition to cutting interest rates, which the president strongly desires. Cook last voted to cut rates in December 2025, siding with the majority. The Fed unanimously voted to raise rates after its most recent meeting in September. "She shouldn't be in an important position," Trump said of Cook in those remarks to reporters after returning from a rally in Tennessee on Saturday. White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said in response to Lowell's letter that Trump "is performing his constitutional duty in evaluating Lisa Cook's conduct and eligibility to continue serving as a governor on the Federal Reserve." "The Constitution charges the President with ensuring that the laws are faithfully executed and that the conduct of members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is above reproach," Middleton said in a statement. An in-person hearing at the White House is currently scheduled for Nov. 5, according to Trump's Oct. 7 presidential memo establishing the "committee of inquiry" into Cook. Cook's lawyers did not immediately rule out participating in that hearing, and in fact said the Fed governor "welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name," despite their concerns. But in Tuesday's letter, Lowell said Cook cannot attend a hearing on Nov. 5 because she "will be executing her official duties as Governor at financial and monetary policy meetings in Europe." After that, Cook will immediately start preparing for the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee in early December, Lowell said. The White House did not immediately respond when asked by CNBC if the scheduled hearing would be moved in light of Cook's alleged scheduling conflicts. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' Lowell also said he needs time to speak with Cook about issues raised by the White House's most recent correspondence, as well as to prepare her for any possible hearing, "which, because of her being in Asia on Federal Reserve duties, cannot be done until she returns." "With all of that (and court hearings I have scheduled in November), the earliest date for any hearing would need to be in December following the FOMC meeting," Lowell wrote Scharf. Trump established the three-member committee two months after reviving his long-running effort to fire Cook , an appointee of former President Joe Biden , from the central bank's board of governors. The Supreme Court in late June blocked Trump's first attempt to remove Cook, ruling that she was not given sufficient due process under federal law. But that decision did not stop Trump from trying again. Middleton said in his statement, "The President is going beyond what the Supreme Court required by offering Lisa Cook an in-person hearing that will be conducted in a fair and open process." But Lowell wrote Tuesday, "We have significant concerns regarding the objectivity and fitness of the committee," which comprises three executive branch officials, including top Trump economic aide Kevin Hassett. Hassett "already has publicly insinuated that the President has 'cause' to fire Governor Cook," Lowell noted, citing the economic advisor's comments from August 2025 .

events.title: IEEE Continues Preparations for the Realignment of Its Regions
events.summary: Progress continues in restructuring IEEE’s geographic regions, as outlined in The Institute’s February 2023 article “ IEEE Is Realigning Its Geographic Regions .” The “Region 1” designation will no longer be used. The new Region 2 will merge what is currently Region 1 (Northeastern U.S.) with the current Region 2 (Eastern U.S.). It will be called Region 2 (Northeastern and Eastern U.S.). The current Region 10 (Asia Pacific) will be divided into two separate regions. The new Region 10 will encompass North Asia, and the new Region 11 will cover South Asia and the Pacific. The restructuring is defined in the image of the redrawn map in this article. What’s underway Although the new regional alignment will not officially take place until 1 January 2028, several activities have begun within IEEE Member and Geographic Activities (MGA) and across other IEEE organizational units. Within MGA, volunteers and staff have been actively addressing system enhancements, director/director-elect elections , governance updates, communications, and regional finances and offerings. No changes to membership Work will continue from now until the effective date of realignment in 2028. The change will not affect your IEEE membership, nor will it change either your local IEEE section or chapter. If you have any questions regarding the realignment, contact Reg-Realignment@ieee.org .

events.title: Apate sends AI agents undercover to get scammed so they can gather fraud intelligence
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or to speed up workflows. Apate.ai sends them undercover to get scammed. Founded in 2024 on the basis of research done in Macquarie University in Sydney, the Australian startup deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, sporting different ages, genders, and accents, and speak various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful. The company says its fleet of agents has so far wasted 17 years of scammers’ time across 2.5 million conversations. More importantly for Apate’s customer base of banks, telecom companies, government agencies, and utilities, the undercover agents try to get scammers to reveal things about themselves that are usually learned only after a victim has been scammed: bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites, the brands they’re impersonating, and other details about the scams they’re running. Apate, one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, then feeds that information to its customers, who use it to inform their anti-fraud measures and initiatives. (The company will pitch a panel of VC judges at Disrupt , which is taking place this week at Moscone West in San Francisco through Thursday, October 15.) It’s a curious evolution of scam-baiting, but it’s not so surprising given how much AI has empowered scammers and hackers. The FBI received more than 22,000 complaints of AI-related crimes in 2025, which resulted in about $893 million in losses. More than $632 million of that came from investment scams, in which the FBI says fraudsters use AI to run conversations, and deepfake the voices and appearances of celebrities, executives, and trusted figures. For a long time, people have made a hobby out of deliberately stringing scammers along — sometimes hilariously, like getting scammers to read aloud entire books , or even to get ridiculous tattoos . Now, with AI growing increasingly capable, the tables are turning. Curiously, the idea behind Apate was sparked by a real scam call. Several years ago, Apate’s founder and CEO Dali Kaafar was at a family picnic when he got a call from an unknown number. Realizing it was a scammer on the line, he decided to play dumb for the benefit of his kids and managed to keep the call going for 44 minutes. Everyone had a laugh, but Kaafar noticed that those were 44 minutes the scammer had not spent calling a real victim. It was also 44 minutes of his wasted time, which led him to wonder: Could he automate it, and in the process, learn something useful? That idea eventually led to research work at his job at Macquarie University, where Kaafar and his colleagues used machine learning and natural language processing to uncover the content of scam calls, and develop better ways to detect and prevent scams. “Most of the industry works after the fact. Telcos block numbers, but scammers just get new ones. Banks watch transactions, but by then the scammer has already reached the customer. We go to the scammer directly and get the information before anyone gets hurt,” Brad Joffe, co-founder and chief commercial officer, told TechCrunch. “Our AI agents talk to tens of thousands of scammers every day across calls, messages, email, and the web. What we offer our customers is what comes out of those conversations, and what they can do with it.” Joffe said Apate uses both frontier models and its own fine-tuned models to power its agents and analysis. The company trains its models on conversations its agents have had with scammers, as well as the research Kaafar did at Macquarie. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get access to an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more. Customers can even assign these agents particular missions, such as obtaining a bank account number or crypto-wallet address. Its text agents can search forums, investment groups, and social platforms for potential scam activity, and can then enter conversations with a fabricated identity to surface scammers’ details. The startup’s customers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia, TPG Telecom, as well as other utilities, telcos, and government agencies. Joffe said TPG has diverted nearly 590,000 calls to Apate’s agents, Commonwealth has seen a 76% drop in publicly reported scam losses, and an unnamed Australian bank the startup works with has used its outbound agents to disrupt 22 scam campaigns.

events.title: This strange sea animal is on menus, but it is disappearing from our reefs
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sea cucumbers can live 100 years, but may not survive our hunger Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry The Great Barrier Reef's colourful array of sea cucumber species were the subject of this 1893 William Saville Kent illustration (which has been edited by ABC). ( Biodiversity Heritage Library: William Saville Kent ) The alien-looking sea cucumber is a delicacy eaten in soups or consumed for its perceived health and libido benefits. But a boom in demand since the 1980s has led to overfishing and population collapses in parts of the world, including the Pacific. Entire species are disappearing from remote Australian reefs, with illegal fishing pointed to as a key culprit. And there are now concerns that regulators for Australia's legal sea cucumber fisheries are underestimating how long it takes fished stocks to recover. A new "first-of-its-kind" genetic study, published in iScience , indicates at least one sought-after sea cucumber species lives longer than we thought. Study lead author and molecular ecologist Sven Uthicke, from the Australian Institute of Marine Science, said the black teatfish ( Holothuria whitmaei ) could reach 100 years of age. Black teatfish are a sought-after sea cucumber species in international markets. ( iNaturalist: brendonh / black teatfish / CC BY-NC 4.0 ) It was assumed the species, found in Australia's tropical waters but less so in other Pacific countries, only lived five to 20 years in the wild. Dr Uthicke said the finding meant fishery management needed to revise whether current catch limits were sustainable. The age a marine species reaches is a major factor for calculating a fishery's environmental sustainability. Dr Uthicke said the sustainable catch limit for black teatfish and similar species might be lower than we thought. Sea cucumbers are part of a large group of "spiny skin" animals that includes starfish and sea urchins. Colours and patterns of their leathery skin range from plain browns to vibrant reds and yellows. Sometimes they have alien-like mouth tendrils, which are actually modified "feet". Some species like the black sea cucumber (Holothuria leucospilota) have branch-like tendrils. ( iNaturalist: R Kabakoff/black sea cucumber/CC BY-NC 4.0 ) Sea cucumbers are believed to benefit the health of coral and seagrass meadows. "We don't necessarily understand all the ecological services that sea cucumbers provide, but we do know that they are very important in aerating sediment," CSIRO marine ecologist John Keesing said. Much is still unknown about these weird animals, with few studies into basic biology like how long they can live. In the new study, Dr Uthicke revisited a no-fishing zone near Lizard Island in the Great Barrier Reef 24 years after another study he did into the growth rates of black teatfish. He was surprised to find 31 out of the 76 sea cucumbers from his earlier fieldwork in 2000. "We still don't know how fast they grow because the individuals in my study basically did not grow at all over the entire 25 years … and we didn't find any small ones." As the research was only conducted in one location, Dr Uthicke said other locations and species could be looked at. But, he said, regulators could use the current findings to manage stocks more conservatively. Black teatfish stocks have previously collapsed at the Great Barrier Reef and Zenadh Kes (Torres Strait). As black teatfish are considered globally endangered, the federal environment department has to sign off on any fishing regimes occurring in Australia. The species is not caught in the regulated Western Australia or Northern Territory sea cucumber fisheries, but it is caught in Queensland fisheries . A Queensland Department of Primary Industries spokesperson said a recent stock assessment for black teatfish indicated the species was being fished at sustainable levels. "Future stock assessments will consider all new, relevant information." An 1839 fishing camp in the Northern Territory illustrates the connection between First Nations people and Indonesia, as well as the centuries-long sea cucumber trade in Australia. ( Library & Archives NT: Voyage au Pôle Sud et dans l'Océanie ) An Australian Fisheries Management Authority spokesperson said the new research would be considered when advice was developed for future management settings in the Torres Strait. They said a past CSIRO survey in 2019–20 found the black teatfish had significantly recovered from historic overfishing and was safe to be fished under a strict harvest strategy.

( Reuters: Hollie Adams ) The stock exchange operator says market participation is at a record high among Australians. An ASX survey found 54 per cent of Australian adults hold investments outside their super and primary home. The ASX estimates 950,000 Australians who do not currently invest plan to start within the next 12 months. A record 11.5 million Australian adults now hold investments outside their superannuation and their main home, a new survey by the stock exchange operator finds. The ASX Australian Investor Study 2026 has revealed an estimated 2.5 million Australians have joined the investor population since 2020. Investors, the survey showed, now represent 54 per cent of the adult population. "Australia is a nation of investors," ASX chief executive Anthony Attia said. Market participation in Australia is at a record high, the ASX says. ( ABC News: Darryl Torpy ) Most investors were middle-income earners and middle-aged, with a median gross income of $110,000 and an average age of 46. Younger people, aged 18–29, made up 21 per cent of investors. For the first time, the ASX survey looked at how investors were using AI tools for investment information and advice. The bourse said investors continued to use professional advisers, brokers, online investment platforms, family and friends, social media, podcasts and other digital sources. It found AI uptake was strongest among younger investors, used by 14 per cent of investors aged 18 to 29. Mr Attia said Australia's public participation in share trading was among the highest in developed markets. Anthony Attia took over the top job at the ASX last month. ( Supplied ) The survey, which polled roughly 4,500 people in January and February this year, found shares were the most widely held assets, followed by residential property, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), term deposits and cryptocurrency. "Almost 1 million more Australians are looking to start investing. "The rapid growth of ETFs, with ownership more than doubling since 2020, shows how innovation is opening new opportunities for investors." Australian ETF monthly inflows hit $7 billion for the first time in August, says Betashares. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration ) ETF boom as money pours into stocks Since the ASX survey, money has continued to increasingly flow into ETFs. Data from investment firm Betashares showed the Australian ETF industry experienced $7 billion in cash flowing in during September after monthly inflows surpassed $7 billion for the first time in August. The industry hit a record $388 billion in assets under management. Keen to invest but don't know where to start? If you've avoided investing because you've found the terminology intimidating, you're not alone. Recent tax changes appear to be behind the enthusiasm for stocks in general, but ETFs in particular. The government announced in the May budget that it planned to replace the current 50 per cent capital gains tax (CGT) discount with a discount based on the actual rate of inflation. It also said it would introduce a minimum 30 per cent tax on gains from July 1, 2027. Forager Funds chief investment officer Steve Johnson said ETFs were popular under the new settings as net gains and losses were contained inside the investment, so a surge in an individual company that might attract capital gains tax could be offset by another loss-making stock. Betashares agreed investors had paid more attention to the relative tax effectiveness of index-based investment strategies and ETFs following the CGT changes. The firm also said the continued fall in Australian house prices was giving investors more reason to look at other asset classes like shares, bonds and commodities. Global X ETFs senior strategist Marc Jocum said the scale of investing over the past quarter had been "significant". "Australian ETFs have just delivered a record $21 billion quarter, demonstrating that they are becoming a core building block in Australian portfolios," Mr Jocum said. events.title: Social Security Administration announces 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027
events.summary: The cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, provides an annual inflation adjustment to both Social Security and Supplemental Security Income, or SSI, benefits. With a 3.6% COLA for 2027, Social Security retirement benefits will go up by $75 per month, on average, the agency said. The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. The Social Security cost-of-living adjustment will be 3.6% in 2027, the Social Security Administration said Wednesday. Social Security retirement benefits will increase by $75 per month on average, the agency said. "Social Security will implement this cost-of-living adjustment for 76 million Americans, giving them greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano said in a statement. Around 72 million Social Security recipients will see the benefit increases in January, according to SSA. About 7.3 million SSI beneficiaries will receive higher payments starting Dec. 31, the agency said. The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is in line with Social Security experts' projections , which last month forecast an increase of 3.5% to 3.6%. Bigger COLA comes amid higher inflation The 3.6% COLA for 2027 is the largest increase to benefits since 2023. That year, beneficiaries received an 8.7% benefit boost — the highest in four decades — in response to rising inflation. New government inflation data released Wednesday shows consumer price increases are accelerating. The consumer price index rose 3.7% over the past 12 months, as gas prices jumped. About 40% of Social Security beneficiaries ages 65 and over rely on the program for at least half of their income, according to AARP . A recent AARP survey found 76% of respondents said a 3.5% COLA would not be enough . CNBC's No. 1 financial advisor takes a family-office approach Trump Accounts hit 70 million enrolled and can now accept stock donations Thousands of homeowners face ARM resets — and much higher payments CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The Social Security COLA is "critically important" because it helps millions of Americans cover rising everyday costs, including groceries, routine bills and health care, AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a statement. "There's a lot on the line financially right now for older Americans: one in five have no retirement savings, and more people feel financially insecure this year than last," Minter-Jordan said. How to calculate your 3.6% benefit increase Beneficiaries can multiply their current monthly benefit amount by 3.6%, or 0.036, to estimate the increase to their checks for 2027. However, keep in mind that increases to Medicare Part B or Part D premiums for 2027 — which may be deducted directly from benefit checks — can affect the size of beneficiaries' monthly payments. Standard monthly premiums for Medicare Part B are projected to be $209.50 in 2027 , up from $202.90 in 2026, according to a report from Medicare trustees. Some beneficiaries may pay extra surcharges, known as Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amounts, or IRMAAs, if they have higher incomes. Medicare Part B covers medically necessary and preventive services. Meanwhile, Medicare Part D prescription drug plans may see modest premium increases in 2027, according to an analysis by KFF , a nonpartisan health policy research group. The Social Security Administration will send beneficiaries notices about the COLA changes. The notices will include specific information about their 2027 benefits, including exact payment dates and dollar amounts as well as any deductions. Individuals who have created online My Social Security accounts can access that information starting in late November, according to the agency. Beneficiaries without an online account who want to see their COLA notice online must create an account and opt into paperless notices by Nov. 18. Beneficiaries who have not signed up to receive online notices will get mailed COLA statements in December. Those individuals should make sure the address the agency has on file is up to date, according to SSA. Medicare premium amounts for 2027 will also be available online through the My Social Security message center starting in late November, the agency said. How the Social Security COLA is calculated The COLA is based on the percentage increase of one specific government inflation measure — the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, or CPI-W — from the third quarter of the previous year to the third quarter of the current year. The CPI-W is a subset of the consumer price index that tracks the average change in prices for goods and services purchased by urban households. The CPI-W rose 3.9% over the past 12 months, according to September data the Bureau of Labor Statistics released Wednesday. Policymakers and advocates have proposed alternatives to the CPI-W for calculating the annual COLA.

events.title: The AI era will redefine business
events.summary: Reed’s view One of the most profound takeaways from my interview with Reflection AI co-founder and CTO Ioannis Antonoglou this week on Semafor’s Future Proof is his declaration that the AI era will force us to redefine what each business actually does and rebuild it from the ground up, using AI as scaffolding. And that is going to take decades, a lot longer than most people in Silicon Valley project. Right now, we are thinking about data all wrong. Today, businesses mostly capture data that’s measurable or the result of some kind of work product. What’s usually not captured is the work itself — the difficult-to-define causal link that connects all of the actions that a company takes. “A lot of the context is like, ‘we jump on a call, or someone shared something or said something’” Antonoglou told me. I’ve been thinking about that challenge with my own work. How can a journalist capture gut feelings about what might make a good story? (It’s a bit like that famous 1960s US Supreme Court case on pornography, “you know it when you see it.“) What about capturing how reporters decide who to call first, or what questions to ask to get the most revealing answers? In the AI era, Antonoglou told me, companies have to throw out what they’ve done for decades and come up with new ways to measure and carry out their work. That’s part of what Antonoglou is trying to help customers do with his company’s open-weight models. “It will take maybe a decade or two decades before people really rethink how things are done and how they can just do them with AI in mind,” he said. It won’t happen in every industry at the same time — probably a good thing for the economy’s stability — but it does provide another new entry for startups that move faster than incumbents to spring ahead. Notable Nvidia is in early talks to acquire Reflection AI , Financial Times reported.

events.title: Drop-off charges at UK airports to be reviewed after sharp increase
events.summary: Airport drop-off charges are to be reviewed by the government following sharp price increases in recent years. Prices at major UK airports have risen by a third since the summer of 2025 on average, according to one analysis, with Gatwick and Stansted drop-off charges found to be the most expensive, jumping from £7 to £10. Such charges at Edinburgh Airport have risen from £6 to £8.50, while fees at Bournemouth increased from £5 to £8, the same price as Leeds Bradford and London City. The Department for Transport confirmed it had committed to a review, saying it was "vital to ensure travel remains accessible and that passengers are treated fairly". The government added it hoped airports would "exercise restraint on rises, particularly where there are limited public transport alternatives". The RAC, which conducted the analysis in July this year, has campaigned against increases in drop-off charges. It said a review of "kiss and fly" fees would be "music to the ears to drivers". "We know airport drop-off charges are a growing source of anger and frustration," said Rod Dennis, senior policy officer at the RAC. "Four-in-five drivers we've surveyed believe they are a 'rip-off', with just one-in-10 understanding why airports charge what they do." The RAC's research found London City Airport, which only introduced charges in 2026, was the most expensive on a per-minute basis. Its £8 charge for five minutes works out at £1.60 per minute. Belfast International Airport now charges £5 for 10 minutes in the drop-off zone, up £2 on last year. None of the top 10 airports in the European Union charge for drop-offs, according to the RAC. It argues that international airports should not charge for dropping off passengers, however, the industry said the charges were a neccesary part of the business model of airports. Airport drop-off fees up by a third - here are the priciest Published 23 July Supporters of such charges also say they encourage travellers to use of more environmentally friendly modes of transport. "Airports outside the UK are typically publicly owned and in receipt of state subsidies and tax exemptions, while UK airports are generally privately owned and subject to the full array of commercial rates of taxation," said Karen Dee, chief executive of Airports UK, which represents airports. She added airports offered a "range of options for those travelling to terminals, including free drop off points" and that "any review" by the government would find airports make "excellent use of a variety of ways to manage traffic and air pollution". The Aviation Environment Federation campaign group has previously defended the fees, arguing they help reduce congestion and air pollution around airports. Earlier this month, the government announced extra charges for parents sitting with their children when flying would be scrapped in time for next year's summer holidays. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the changes were part of a series of "everyday fixes" to ease cost of living pressures on households. Have you been affected by issues covered in this story? events.title: ICE says no to automatic body-cams
events.summary: ICE is rejecting a Government Accountability Office recommendation for technology that automatically activates body cameras when weapons are drawn and safeguards to ensure agents record arrests, searches and detentions when required. Why it matters: The GAO warns that ICE risks losing crucial evidence on what happened during incidents involving force amid growing distrust over agent accountability in the wake of multiple fatal ICE shootings . The big picture: The GAO report found both CBP and ICE are struggling to manage their body-camera programs amid shifting deployment plans. CBP and ICE haven't updated their camera plans since 2022 and 2024, respectively. The plans fail to account for funding changes, expanded deployment needs and pauses in camera rollouts following one of Trump's executive orders that rescinded a Biden-era federal body-camera mandate. ICE's camera activation dispute is the central flashpoint in the GAO review, as DHS accepted all six other recommendations. CBP uses technology that automatically activates body cameras when officers draw firearms or turn on emergency lights, but ICE doesn't. Zoom in: At six of the 10 locations GAO reviewed, CBP and ICE personnel said they were unsure when they had to turn on their cameras. Some said camera use is "not mandated," "up to interpretation," and "has gray areas." Agents specifically reported uncertainty about whether they should record during "subpoena issuance, in-custody interviews, vehicle searches, undercover operations, and detainee transports." At five sites, people said they weren't sure how to use a newer camera model. The other side: DHS rejected the recommendation, arguing that automatic activation "presents significant operational risks, including inadvertent or false activations during routine movement." DHS warned that accidental activation could expose sensitive interactions with informants and victims or record people engaged in protected First Amendment activities. GAO pushed back, noting that DHS offered no alternative safeguards despite the risks of critical encounters going unrecorded. DHS didn't respond to Axios' request for comment. Worth noting: ICE issued no written reprimands for failing to comply with camera policies from the program's launch through September 2025. CBP issued just one. The bottom line: Both CBP and ICE say their body-camera programs are meant to improve public trust, officer safety and accountability. But without clear standards, the agencies can't determine whether their programs are meeting those goals, GAO found. Go deeper: ICE says all its offices will have body cams in 60 days

events.title: I paid $975 for Amtrak's business-class and then a first-class roomette on a 32-hour trip. Only one upgrade was worth it.
events.summary: I took Amtrak's business class and a private roomette on a 32-hour trip in June. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Prolonged delays added 10 hours to my travel time during a recent New York to Chicago Amtrak trip. The perks of a first-class private roomette made the trip very enjoyable despite the delays. I found the business-class seat to be identical to a cheaper coach ticket. I'm no stranger to long-distance train travel aboard Amtrak. Recently, it has been my preferred mode of travel as jet fuel costs push airfares to unpredictable heights. During a recent trip from New York to Chicago in mid-June, I chose to book a two-leg Amtrak trip to compare the business-class seats from New York to Washington, DC, and the first-class private roomette from Washington, DC, to Chicago. I chose the longer two-leg option over booking a direct trip so I could compare both the upgrades on a single trip. My Amtrak ticket, priced at $975 total, included a business-class seat from New York to Washington, DC, and a private roomette for the longer 18-hour section of the trip from Washington, DC, to Chicago. I found that one of the two upgrades was worth the extra cost, much more than the other. See the best perks that came along with my nearly $1,000-ticket. My journey to Chicago began bright and early in New York's Moynihan Penn Station. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider I started my travel morning in the sun-lit halls of New York Penn Station's Moynihan Train Hall. My private roomette booking gave me access to the Amtrak Metropolitan Lounges. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider While business class passengers do not usually have access to the Amtrak Metropolitan Lounge unless they purchase a $35 day pass (priced at $50 for the flagship New York lounge I went to) and have a same-day Amtrak ticket, first-class private room passengers have access to the lounges prior to their departure at no additional cost. The lounge truly wowed me. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider As soon as I stepped into the Metropolitan Lounge, my ticket paid for itself. I found the space, which opened in 2021, nicer than some airport lounges I have been in, and regretted not arriving earlier to spend more time there. I quickly grabbed my complimentary breakfast at the lounge. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Nearly as soon as I got to the lounge, I started looking for the complimentary food . The menu had a few options, including sandwiches, pastries, fruit, and yogurt. Additionally, the café also had various coffee and espresso options, soft drinks, juices, and teas. I found a perfectly relaxing spot in the lounge. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Arriving at the lounge during the not-so-crowded early mid-morning, I was able to claim what felt like a luxurious space for one. With more than enough sitting room and even a screen showing the current status of departing trains, the space, which was visually separate from the rest of the lounge by sheer curtains, was the perfect quiet spot to relax before my trip. My breakfast far exceeded my expectations. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider I went with a warm egg-and-cheese sandwich on a croissant and a pumpkin doughnut for my breakfast. The sandwich was cheesy, buttery, and tasty, and felt much more elevated than I had expected. The doughnut was similarly elevated and tasty, with nut toppings that added a nice artisanal quality. The latte was silky and smooth, and the coffee quality was beyond what I expected. The lounge has lockers to store belongings. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Shortly after getting to the lounge, I noticed the lockers where passengers could store their belongings. While I would've preferred the spaces had a way to lock them for extra protection, I trusted the lounge crowd enough to leave some of my less valuable luggage while exploring the space. The very private and spacious restrooms were also nicer than I expected. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Going into the lounge's restrooms, I expected a typical public-bathroom experience. Instead, I was greeted by a much more spacious and private space. I felt comfortable in the restroom, where I had some privacy and space to do my skincare and fix my hair before my long trip. I also noticed that the restroom had a lockable door leading to a small, separate nursing room, which felt like a thoughtful detail for mothers traveling on Amtrak. Having access to the lounge was the standout perk of my trip — and made the price worth it. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider As I walked to my train, I began plotting how I'd book my next trip to ensure I got access to the lounge again. I boarded the first leg of my trip after a refreshing morning. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider The first section of my trip was the 3-hour trek to Washington, DC. I felt very refreshed and ready for the trip after my time in the lounge. I was let down by the business class seat. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider When I boarded the business class car, I struggled to see the difference between coach class and the upgrade. The seat looked nearly identical to the cheaper seats I had traveled in before. The "extra" legroom was negligible. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Amtrak's business class promises extra legroom compared to their coach seats, but I struggled to feel any difference at all. Additionally, unlike coach class seats , business class lacked the legrest that extends from the bottom of the seat, resulting in a less comfortable experience than coach class. The restrooms were identical between the business and the coach, though one was cleaner. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Just like the coach cars, the business-class car featured two restrooms. In my experience, I did not notice any differences between the coach and business-class restrooms, although the latter were overall cleaner than I've found coach restrooms to be and had a better supply of soap and paper towels. Overall, I thought I could've been better off in the cheaper coach seat. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider Other than the ability to reserve a seat, I didn't see any major perks to the upgrade. I probably won't book a business-class seat again for my future trips. Amtrak's website says its business class includes "extra legroom, a wide, comfortable seat, and a complimentary non-alcoholic beverage," as well as "a more seamless boarding" and bonus rewards points, although "specific features vary by route." The Metropolitan Lounge in Washington, DC, wasn't as big or lavish as New York's. Kristine Villarroel/Business Insider After arriving in Washington, DC, I went to the station's Metropolitan Lounge, which I also had access to thanks to my private roomette booking. While not as lavish as New York's, the lounge provided free packaged snacks and drinks, a quiet space to sit, and a secure place to store my belongings during my originally two-and-a-half-hour layover. events.title: Exclusive: White House probes claims of missing Kennedy Center money in "MAGA blood feud"
events.summary: President Trump has directed his White House counsel to examine explosive allegations dropped on him Friday in the Oval Office: Former Trump attorney Alina Habba told the president that another one of his top advisers — former Kennedy Center leader Ric Grenell — failed to deposit a multimillion-dollar donation that her billionaire husband made to the center a year ago, according to four senior administration officials and three insiders briefed on the controversy. Grenell denied the accusations as "absurd" and a "lie." Habba and her husband, Turhan Mildon, declined to comment through a spokesperson. Why it matters: The extraordinary row between the two top-tier presidential advisers and former allies provides a rare and acrimonious behind-the-scenes glimpse into the intersection of power, influence and money in Trump's Washington. The total value of the contribution in question: nearly $6 million, White House sources said Habba told them. A senior administration official cautioned that "these are only allegations. We don't know if they're true. This could be a misunderstanding." Said another: "POTUS doesn't want to deal with this. Of course, he's concerned. But if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem." Just a few months ago , Grenell was friends with Mildon and Habba. But he was notably absent from their $10 million wedding that was attended by Trump world officials, power brokers and luminaries last month. "This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud," said one Trump world insider with knowledge of the conflict. Zoom in: The dispute grew out of a friendship between Grenell and Mildon, sources familiar with the conflict say. The men had mutual interests in Venezuela in early 2025, immediately after Trump returned to the White House. Grenell, as a Trump special envoy, was advocating for normalizing U.S. relations with Venezuela's leader at the time, Nicolas Maduro. Mildon, a Turkish national, had extensive Venezuelan business interests that were threatened by Secretary of State Marco Rubio's hardline pressure campaign targeting Maduro. The intrigue: In the spring of 2025, Grenell persuaded Mildon to include a multimillion-dollar Kennedy Center donation in a lump-sum $17.6 million payment for a business deal involving a U.S. company, Habba told the president and White House staffers, two sources said. Habba's attorneys plan to give the White House documentation — reviewed by Axios — to support her allegations about Grenell soliciting a Kennedy Center donation from Mildon to go to a private company in the spring of 2025. "The White House counsel has asked for documents and proof. None has come so far," a White House official said. Grenell called the statements from Habba to Trump "Absurd. I've never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I've never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations." When Habba initially leveled her accusations against Grenell, she said the total amount of the Kennedy Center contribution was $17 million, the sources said. But as she learned of the specifics from her husband, she said the amount of the contribution in question was $5.6 million. "This has been hard to track because numbers have changed," the White House official said. After making his alleged contribution , Mildon never checked to see if it was deposited. He believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center, where he met Habba in late 2025 before their whirlwind romance and marriage, those sources said. Friction point: Mildon and Habba, the sources said, discovered the issue after their business relationship frayed with Grenell, who lost an internal administration power struggle with Rubio that culminated in the U.S. seizing Maduro on Jan. 3 and taking him to New York City to face narcotics charges. In June, Maduro's successor, Delcy Rodriguez, issued an order revoking one of Mildon's company contracts to operate state-owned cement plants in Venezuela, the New York Times reported Monday. A source familiar with the situation told Axios this summer that her action was partly due to the U.S. government's prodding. Rodriguez then reversed herself, the Times reported, after learning of Mildon's new relationship with Habba because the Venezuelan leader believed Mildon therefore had Trump's backing. Amid the Times' reporting into Mildon's contract, Habba discovered that Mildon's supposed donation never made it to the Kennedy Center, the sources said. Inside the room: Habba then headed to the White House last Friday to tell the president about the situation. "Alina hit the roof" when her husband told her that he hadn't donated the money directly to the Kennedy Center, whose records indicate that Mildon actually owed a $270,000 pledged donation. There was no record of Mildon giving anything close to $5.6 million, officials said. Mildon on Tuesday paid the $270,000, records show, to the Kennedy Center. In partial confirmation of Habba's story , Kennedy Center staff reported that late last year there was a search for Mildon's contribution — then thought to be $6 million — but that it couldn't be found, an official said. But Lisa Dale, who handled finances for the Kennedy Center then, said the only record in her books connected to Mildon showed he owed $270,000. "There was nothing about $6 million," she told Axios. "I would have heard about that." Context: Habba and Grenell trace their roots to Trump's first administration. Grenell was Trump's ambassador to Germany and then his acting director of national intelligence. Habba was Trump's private attorney and briefly was U.S. attorney in New Jersey during this term. Between the lines: The Kennedy Center has been an ongoing sore spot for Trump, beset by controversy over his efforts to put his name on the building and fundraising woes. If Habba's allegations of missing money are true, it could prove particularly galling to Trump, who views the center and its fundraising personally. Those who know the president's thinking say he is particularly disapproving of people who use his name or misuse positions he has given them. His dismissal Tuesday of Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle was the latest reminder of that. Two top Trump world figures being engaged in such a bitter feud adds to the complexity. "Nobody wants to get in the middle of Alina Habba and Ric Grenell going to war," one official said.

A British court has handed a former army chef a nearly four-year jail term for possessing weapons for “terrorist purposes”. Mark Broadhurst, 28, was given the sentence on Wednesday at Sheffield Crown Court in England, two years after police uncovered online messages in which he expressed racist views and an intention to sell homemade firearms to right-wing groups. list 1 of 3 UK PM Andy Burnham vows to renegotiate post-Brexit trade deal with EU list 2 of 3 UK PM Andy Burnham met Man City chairman during time as Manchester mayor list 3 of 3 UK spy chief says Iran is stepping up targeting of military bases Police found a stockpile of weapons at Broadhurst’s home address when they took him into custody in September 2024, including knives and crossbows, black powder, ammunition, air pistols and what officials described as “an improvised homemade cannon”. events.title: OpenAI’s Sachin Katti to leave infrastructure role, stay on as advisor
events.summary: Sachin Katti, OpenAI's infrastructure and compute lead, announced he is departing his role and will continue supporting the company as an advisor. Uday Ruddarraju, OpenAI's CTO of compute, will replace Katti and lead the company's overall compute organization, according to a spokesperson. Katti said in a post on LinkedIn that he "decided to move on to build something new." OpenAI's infrastructure lead, Sachin Katti, announced on Wednesday that he is departing his role after roughly a year at the artificial intelligence company. Katti said in a post on LinkedIn that he "decided to move on to build something new," and he'll continue to support OpenAI as an advisor after his last day on Nov. 15. Uday Ruddarraju, who has been serving as OpenAI's CTO of compute, will replace Katti and lead the company's overall compute organization, according to a spokesperson. "Building AI infrastructure at this scale has given me an incredible view into every dimension of the compute world, from silicon and systems to datacenters, energy, supply chains, financing, and the economics of AI," Katti wrote. "I'm enormously proud of what our teams accomplished together and grateful to the partners who helped make it possible." OpenAI's compute organization is crucial to its overall strategy; it's tasked with developing the company's infrastructure roadmap and ensuring that it can train and serve its models. OpenAI is targeting roughly $600 billion in total compute spend by 2030, and it's involved with massive, multi-billion-dollar data center projects in states like Ohio , Texas and Georgia . The latest leadership shakeup lands during a tense moment for AI infrastructure in the U.S., where backlash against data centers has mounted over concerns about noise, electricity rates and water consumption. The issue has become a flashpoint in the upcoming midterm elections, where both Republican and Democratic candidates have campaigned against the facilities. "I'm proud of what we've built and have total confidence in Uday and the team to carry it forward," Katti said in a statement. "I'm a builder at heart, and I'm looking forward to building something new." Ruddarraju joined OpenAI in July of last year, according to his LinkedIn. He previously served as the head of infrastructure engineering at Elon Musk's xAI, which was acquired by SpaceX earlier this year. Katti's exit is the latest in a string of executive departures at OpenAI this year. In July, Fidji Simo , OpenAI's product and business chief, said she would move into an advisory role to focus on recovery after a "severe exacerbation of a chronic illness." The following month, Brad Lightcap , a longtime OpenAI executive, and Denise Dresser , who served as revenue chief, also left the company. OpenAI President Greg Brockman told CNBC at the time that he doesn't believe the wave of departures is atypical for a young company. He said since OpenAI is in the spotlight, "every departure gets scrutinized in a way that it doesn't otherwise." "There have been different eras where we have different sets of, of leaders in place," Brockman said. "I'm a constant, Sam [Altman] is a constant, and I think that we are stronger because of that resilience and diversity." events.title: The steel stock that has the shorts and options traders on edge
events.summary: Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me. That seems to be the refrain for Cleveland-Cliffs investors as the steel giant prepares to report earnings. Cleveland-Cliffs steps into the earnings spotlight on Oct.19, and options traders are bracing for impact. After a massive, nearly 16% one-day price jump following its July quarterly report — nearly double its long-term historical average move of slightly over 8% — short-term implied volatility (IV) has been aggressively bid up as traders fear a repeat. And who could blame them? Short interest is running close to 14%, and the CEO is famous for fighting the naysayers, noting that he likes boil them "like frogs" and that they are "messing with the wrong guy." With rhetoric like that, it's little wonder options traders are bracing for big moves. For strategic premium sellers, this inflated near-term fear creates a compelling opportunity to deploy what I call a "strangle-swap." You'll sometimes see traders or strategists refer to this as a "double-diagonal" spread. This structure allows traders to capitalize on the anticipated post-earnings decline in implied volatility (aka "vol crush") without taking on the unlimited risk of a naked short strangle. To execute this strangle-swap, you sell a shorter-dated strangle and buy a longer-dated strangle to define your risk. Net Cost: $24 per spread (recall each contract represents 100 shares) The key to this trade is the differential in IV decay between the shorter-dated November expirations being sold and the longer-dated January options being purchased. Traders are heavily bidding November options on concerns that the sharp move from the last quarterly earnings release may repeat. Whether it does or doesn't, that binary uncertainty vanishes after CLF reports on the 19th, causing November implied volatility (IV) to collapse, a phenomenon commonly known as "vol crush." Because the January options have significantly more days to expiration, they are less sensitive to this immediate IV crush and suffer much slower time decay (theta). This trade is most profitable if CLF stays between $11 and $17 after the report. In this scenario, the November short strangle rapidly bleeds value. A trader can then buy back the short legs for a fraction of the $0.80 initially collected, or let them expire worthless. This leaves the trader holding a long January 10/18 strangle for virtually nothing, providing "free" exposure to future price swings through year-end. This strategy loses money if CLF repeats or exceeds its explosive July fireworks. Because the short strikes (11/17) are narrower than the long strikes (10/18), a massive directional move will cause the short options' intrinsic value to expand faster than the long options can offset it in the short term. However, the risk/reward profile is highly asymmetrical. The long January wings strictly define catastrophic risk. Maximum Downside Risk: The width of the put spread ($1.00) plus the net debit ($0.24) = $1.24 ($124 per contract). Maximum Upside Risk: The width of the call spread ($1.00) plus the net debit ($0.24) = $1.24 ($124 per contract). By risking up to ~$124 to capture elevated front-month premium, the double-diagonal offers a cheap, defined-risk vehicle to fade the market's recent earnings trauma while maintaining long-term optionality. events.title: How high inflation became a 'fact of life' in the U.S.
events.summary: U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest streaks of elevated inflation levels on record, according to a CNBC data analysis. Some are beginning to act like high inflation is a new normal, which can cripple the power of the Federal Reserve's monetary policy tools. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said it's concerning that consumers are starting to view high inflation as a "fact of life." U.S. consumers are in the midst of one of the longest stretches of elevated inflation of the past century. Some are beginning to act like it's a new normal, raising alarm bells for members of the Federal Reserve . Wednesday's consumer price index release showed a 3.7% increase year over year in September. CPI has now registered around 65 months — that's more than five years — of consecutive annual readings above 2%, a widely accepted target for inflation in the U.S. This yearslong spell of high inflation has cast a dark cloud over everyday Americans' view of the economy, and could shape everything from how they budget to how they vote in next month's midterm elections. At the Fed, leaders are left questioning whether consumers' inflationary expectations are becoming too entrenched to rein in. "They're starting to accept high inflation as just a fact of life," Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wrote in a social media post last week. "That's concerning." The current streak of stubborn inflation ranks among the most persistent in modern U.S. history. The uninterrupted string of above-2% monthly CPI readings is the longest of the 21st century, according to a CNBC analysis of data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The U.S. has seen longer periods on only two other occasions going back to the late 1940s. Since inflation started running above 2% in early 2021, the average CPI reading has sat around 4.5%. The last time a streak had a mean reading that high was during a period ending in the 1980s . Consumers are expecting inflation to accelerate. The one-year inflation outlook in September rose three-tenths of a percentage point to 3.9%, its highest reading in more than three years, according to the New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations released last week. One of the main worries of central bankers is that businesses and consumers may start permanently adjusting their behaviors to account for high prices. That can have ripple effects through the economy. Businesses anticipating rising costs can preemptively hike prices for consumers. Workers expecting sticky inflation will ask for steeper pay raises to get ahead of any sticker shock. All of this can make inflation a self-fulfilling prophecy, rendering the monetary policy tools at the Fed's disposal less effective in slowing price growth. "Inflation expectations have to be anchored for monetary policy to affect the economy in an effective and predictable manner," said Gary Richardson, an economist and former historian at the Fed. "That's got to be number-one goal of any central bank." At this juncture, Fed officials are closely watching to see if and how consumers respond to inflationary pressures. During an event last month, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari said he heard from a labor union leader that inflation was "worse" than a recession for their members. Kashkari said that conversation influenced how he views the trade-off within the Fed's so-called dual mandate, which calls for stability in prices and maximum employment. At a gathering of economists in Ohio this week, Hammack told the audience that she did not take the fact that long-run inflation expectations have stayed anchored "for granted." With each month that inflation comes in high, she warned that the risk grows of an "inflationary mindset" getting entrenched. Economists widely view interest rate hikes as the Fed's main mechanism for slowing demand and, in turn, putting downward pressure on the annual pace of price growth. After hiking interest rates in September , Fed funds futures traders anticipate the central bank will raise borrowing costs further in December and in 2027. In the long run, Diane Swonk, chief economist at consultancy KPMG, said interest rate hikes can benefit consumers by getting inflation under control. But in the near term, Swonk said consumers can feel more pressure due to higher borrowing costs. "Inflation is like a cancer, and if you let it metastasize and go further, it's even worse," Swonk said. "Even when the cure hurts, it's better than letting it metastasize." In Hammack's district, the Cleveland Fed chief said via social media that she's found evidence that residents are "choosing" rather than "trading down." For instance, she said they need to pick whether to pay for groceries or essential bills. Consumers have lamented the cumulative price increases they now see in everyday life after the years-long run of high inflation.

events.title: Prediction market users are already betting on how long Trump's new press secretary will last
events.summary: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia during her inaugural press briefing on Tuesday. Win McNamee/Getty Images Prediction markets bettors are wagering on Katie Zacharia's tenure as White House press secretary. Zacharia, who has described herself as an attorney, had her first media briefing on Tuesday. She has since faced scrutiny over her legal qualifications. President Donald Trump's new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia , got off to a somewhat rocky start with her 14-minute debut media briefing on Tuesday. And now bettors on prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi are putting money down on how long the conservative commentator will last in the high-profile job. On Kalshi, bettors gave Zacharia a 38% chance of being out as White House press secretary before January 1 in a wager that had more than $313,000 in trading volume as of early afternoon Wednesday. Kalshi traders were more bearish over the longer term, putting the chance of Zacharia's departure before July 1 at 60% and before July 1, 2028 at 96%. The wager's trading volume indicated meaningful interest in the tenure of the newly appointed press secretary, though it remained well below Kalshi's biggest political markets. A market on whether Defense Secretary Pete Hegeseth will be out of a job, for example, had drawn more than $1.4 million in volume. Polymarket's site has a similar market about Zacharia, asking whether she would be out as press secretary by the end of the year or by the end of October. Bettors gave a 38% chance of an announcement by October 31 and a 51% chance by December 31. When asked for comment on Wednesday, White House communications director Steven Cheung told Business Insider: "Katie is a fabulous and wonderful addition to the team." "She is uniquely qualified and whip smart to help inform the American people about all the great things President Trump and his Administration have been doing, and she will do an incredible job as Press Secretary," Cheung said. Beyond the hiccups in her first press briefing, Zacharia — who has repeatedly described herself as an attorney — faced scrutiny over her legal qualifications. When asked what state she passed the bar exam in, Zacharia told reporters, "When I moved to China." State bar exams are generally administered in person within the jurisdiction. Zacharia told Business Insider in a statement Tuesday that she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials," without detailing where she may have passed the bar. The State Bar of California told Business Insider it didn't have any records showing that Zacharia, who has lived and worked in the state, was ever licensed to practice law there. A spokesperson said, "The State Bar of California has no record of Kate Sharon Zacharia or Kate Sharon Black having been licensed to practice law in California." events.title: Iran says it’s ‘counting the moments’ until it can strike U.S. warships; Saudi Aramco facilities attacked
events.summary: Iran Revolutionary Guard chief Ali Ozmaei said Wednesday that Tehran is "counting the moments" until it can sink American warships, according to Iranian state-affiliated media. U.S. President Donald Trump said American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm elections in early November. Saudi officials said Wednesday that Saudi Aramco facilities had been targeted overnight. Saudi officials said Wednesday that an administrative building belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco was targeted overnight, as the Tehran-backed Houthi militants step up their attacks on the kingdom. The strike caused a fire, but no injuries were reported at the site in the city of Dhahran on the country's eastern coast, according to a statement from the Saudi Ministry of Energy. The Houthis, a Yemen-based militia group backed by Iran, have launched a series of strikes on Saudi targets over the past week. Airport attacks in the capital city of Riyadh led to multiple fatalities, flight cancellations and property damage. Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport remains closed until Saturday. Yemen's civil war has returned to full-scale fighting between the Houthis and the country's internationally recognized government amid a wider regional escalation linked to the U.S.-Iran war. Iran 'counting the moments' until it can attack U.S. ships "If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships," Ozmaei reportedly said in a televised interview. "We are waiting for U.S. warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens." CNBC has reached out to the White House for comment. The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the Islamic Republic has been strengthening defenses around sensitive locations like nuclear sites, and telling regional officials that Tehran will respond to any new U.S. strikes with retaliatory measures across the Middle East as it prepares its population for renewed war in the coming weeks. U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election, which will take place on Nov. 3. On Wednesday, reports emerged that a cargo ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a naval mine as it attempted to transit the waterway. CNBC was not able to independently verify the reports. Later on Wednesday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre — a Royal Navy-sponsored maritime security organization — said a "verified source" reported that a container ship had been struck by an "unknown projectile." In a post on X overnight, U.S. Central Command refuted Iranian claims that the strait is under Iran's control. "IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz," Centcom said. "Just yesterday U.S. forces assisted Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait." Correction: U.S. President Donald Trump said Thursday that American forces would not attack Iran before the midterm election. An earlier version misstated the day.

events.title: FBI says an OpenAI engineer used his wife’s ChatGPT account to figure out how to plant a secret recording device at the office
events.summary: The ChatGPT prompts read like a to-do list. Build “a continuous audio recorder.” Add “live listening” and “downloading/deleting recordings.” Encrypt the SD card. Make the USB output “power-only.” Develop “a second unit and speech-triggered recording,” then “a third unit.” Finally, “apply final protection and silence boot output.” According to court documents unsealed Tuesday, the prompts were sent between Sept. 24 and Sept. 30 from a ChatGPT account linked to the wife of Abdulrahman Alfozan, an OpenAI engineer, a Saudi national who has been a U.S. legal resident since Sept. 2020. Prosecutors say that on or about Sept. 28, Alfozan hid a recording device behind a television in an executive conference room in one of the company’s San Francisco buildings after prompting an AI chatbot associated with his wife to build it. The complaint does not charge his wife. The federal complaint against Alfozan does not list which chatbot Alfozan is alleged to have used to make such prompts, but OpenAI confirmed to Fortune that the chatbot was the company’s own ChatGPT. The chatbot referenced Alfozan’s personal AI chatbot account and shared unique identifiers and IP usage. But his wife’s account isn’t the only chatbot Alfozan is alleged to have used in this recording incident : about six weeks earlier, court documents say Alfozan used a productivity agent internal to OpenAI to determine which meeting rooms had a capacity for six or more people, and which rooms would host high-powered meetings. “How about external partners, where would those usually meet with,” Alfozan is said to have prompted the productivity agent at OpenAI, according to court documents. OpenAI has not yet responded to Fortune ‘s request for comment on whether the company was alerted to Alfozan’s prompts before discovering the recording device. According to the FBI agent’s affidavit in court documents, Alfozan is said to have chosen this specific conference room, after prompting the productivity agent, because meetings there would “frequently involve discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities.” The affidavit also reads that the room “typically is used for internal leadership meetings…as well as external briefings with government officials and business counterparts.” Alfozan did not have access to the conference room; only executives and their assistants could reserve it. Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan and what did he do? Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, was arrested Oct. 9, according to the Justice Department . He faces one count under the federal Wiretap Act, which carries up to five years in prison. The affidavit says he used a device to intercept oral communications, but it is still unknown whether the device actually captured a conversation. When OpenAI made a forensic copy of the memory card, “none of the files on it could be recovered or decrypted,” the agent wrote. OpenAI and the Justice Department have described the contents as encrypted; the affidavit says they “may have been.” The rest of the case runs on cameras and logs. OpenAI had no camera in the room when the device went in. CCTV inside the company’s offices placed Alfozan near the room on 10 different days in September. On Sept. 28, the day the device’s firmware was compiled, he was there from 2:18 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Staff found the device on Sept. 30, wrapped in toilet paper, tucked behind a TV in the room during a routine sweep, OpenAI told Fortune . It was a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, a thumb-sized board with a microphone and microSD storage, made by a Shenzhen-based company. This prompted cooperation between OpenAI and the FBI, and by Oct. 5, a camera had been placed in the room. In the photo in the complaint (and above), Alfozan was caught in the video at 1:20:47 p.m. that day, checking behind the TV. That same day, court documents say he left a bag in a printer room. Security went through the bag and found his wallet, his ID, and a second Seeed recording board inside—which security removed from his bag. After he told the company he had lost the bag and picked it up from lost and found around noon the next day, he sent a written update inquiring about what he characterized as “stolen” items. “A few items were stolen: one credit card, cash (~$500), 2 AirPods, 1 headphone, sunglasses, power bank.” He didn’t ask about either device. CCTV then showed him that day moving items into a Target shopping bag. According to the motion, Alfozan, his wife and a third family member had booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia, via Istanbul, for Oct. 12. Prosecutors wrote that he “has the means—and will have an incentive—to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested.” He was arrested on Oct.9, three days before his one-way flight. What are the consequences? The government’s cover sheet asks for no bail and lists “deportation” among possible penalties. The complaint doesn’t charge trade-secret theft or economic espionage, and it doesn’t allege a foreign tie. But a trial attorney from the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section is assisting the prosecution, according to the Justice Department. The sealing motion also asked to let prosecutors share the files with “any other law enforcement and intelligence agencies as may be necessary for investigative purposes.” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the intelligence community is committed to protecting American intellectual property “from foreign threats.” FBI Director Kash Patel called protecting “American SI innovation” one of the bureau’s “highest counterintelligence priorities.” OpenAI said in a post on X that it had “no indications” he took model weights, source code or customer data. Under the Speedy Trial Act, prosecutors have 30 days from his arrest to indict him, and a grand jury can add charges. Alfozan made his initial appearance Tuesday and is due back in court Oct. 19 for a detention hearing. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Saudi tennis ‘slam’ with Alcaraz, Djokovic postponed amid Houthi attacks
events.summary: The Six Kings Slam exhibition tournament has been pushed from October to December by Saudi organisers. An exhibition tennis tournament featuring the world’s top men’s players has been postponed for two months by the organisers in Saudi Arabia as the country reels from a spate of attacks by Yemen’s Houthis . Turki al-Sheikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority (GEA), said on Wednesday that the exhibition Six Kings Slam tennis tournament had been postponed due to “organisational and logistical challenges”. The announcement came shortly after the Saudi Pro League postponed three fixtures , including one involving Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr, for “logistical considerations, taking into account the mandatory minimum rest period between matches”. The Six Kings Slam was due to hold its third edition later this month, with tennis stars including Carlos Alcaraz, Novak Djokovic and Alexander Zverev due to take part alongside Taylor Fritz, Learner Tien and Alex de Minaur. The event, originally scheduled for October 21-24 and to be streamed live by Netflix, will now take place from December 27-30. “The Six Kings Slam tournament has been postponed due to logistical reasons and will now take place on December 27,” al-Sheikh said on X, sharing a statement from the Riyadh Season entertainment programme. Earlier on Wednesday, the three SPL matches involving teams based in Saudi capital Riyadh were postponed. The meeting between league leaders Al Hilal and Al Riyadh and the match between Al Ittihad and Al Shabab have been postponed to December 19, while the clash between Al Ahli and Ronaldo’s Al-Nassr has been rescheduled for March 6, 2027. The SPL added, however, that the other matchweek nine fixtures “will be played according to the previously announced schedule with no changes”. The move comes two days after al-Sheikh promised that boxing’s world title fight featuring Saul “Canelo” ‌‌Alvarez and Christian M’billi will go ahead this month. Alvarez vs M’billi is scheduled for October 31 in the Saudi capital, which has repeatedly come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, but al-Sheikh sought to allay the doubts over the bout on Sunday. “Canelo reached out ⁠⁠and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” al-Sheikh wrote in a social media post. “He [Alvarez] fears nothing.” On Monday, Al-Nassr’s AFC Champions League match against Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana in Riyadh was delayed by an hour after the coalition announced it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive in Yemen to retake coastal territory from the Houthis in recent days, with missile strikes on airports and energy facilities across the kingdom. Saudi Arabia’s sporting programme has been heavily hit since the outbreak of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran in late February. The Formula One Saudi Arabian Grand Prix slated for April in Jeddah was cancelled. The WTA Finals were also scheduled to be held in Riyadh next month, but will instead take place at Indian Wells in the US.

events.title: Morgan Stanley tops estimates as equities trading revenue beats expectations by $909 million
events.summary: Morgan Stanley topped expectations on the top and bottom lines for the third quarter. Results were powered by equities trading, which exceeded revenue expectations by $909 million. Still, the results were good, not great, as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, according to Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo. Morgan Stanley posted third-quarter results that beat expectations on blockbuster results in its equities trading franchise. Earnings per share: $3.03 vs. $2.91 LSEG estimate Revenue: $20.34 billion vs. $19.95 billion LSEG estimate The company said profit climbed 6.5% to $4.91 billion, or $3.03 a share. Revenue rose 12% to $20.34 billion. The firm's equities trading division, long a marquee business for Morgan Stanley, posted a 41% increase in revenue to $5.8 billion, exceeding the StreetAccount estimate by about $909 million. Morgan Stanley noted widespread strength across its equities products and regions, but cited Asia as a source of particular strength in the quarter. The gains in that business helped offset disappointments elsewhere. Fixed income trading revenue fell 7% to $2.01 billion, driven by declines in credit and commodities, which is roughly $260 million below expectations. Investment banking revenue edged 2% higher to $2.16 billion, about $110 million below expectations. The bank cited an increase in advisory revenue on more completed mergers, but declines in equity underwriting on lower initial public offerings and a drop in fixed income underwriting. Still, the results were "good, but not great," as some business metrics showed slower improvement in the quarter, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo said Wednesday in a note. Morgan Stanley shares declined about 3% in midday trading. The economy is subject to two key forces right now: the boost from the artificial intelligence build-out and the drag from geopolitical strife, Morgan Stanley CEO Ted Pick told CNBC's Leslie Picker on Wednesday. Starting in early September, concerns with overseas conflict, inflation and surging yields slowed activity across Wall Street, Pick noted. "The interaction of the AI phenomenon and geopolitics has been the dominant reality the whole year," Pick said. "It's really two very different stories, and I'd like to think that we are going to have the first narrative, the positive narrative, if we can get some control over the geopolitics." Pick is "cautiously optimistic" about markets in the fourth quarter, he added.
