events.title: Kenya’s Health Ministry confirms second Ebola case
events.summary: A relative of the first case, 39-year-old man’s infection raises concerns of a cross-border spread. Kenya has reported a second Ebola infection, about a week after confirming its first-ever case of the disease when a citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) travelled to Kenya and died two days later at a Nairobi hospital. The second patient, a 39-year-old man who is a close family member of the first case, fell ill on Tuesday and was already in quarantine when he came down with symptoms of fever, fatigue and joint pain, the Ministry of Health said in a statement Wednesday. Last week’s case raised concerns about deficiencies in border screening systems in the region after the patient drove from the DRC to Uganda and flew to Nairobi from there. list 1 of 3 Kenya confirms first Ebola case as man dies in Nairobi after DRC return list 2 of 3 Kenya on high alert amid concern over screening after first Ebola death list 3 of 3 Why single Ebola death in Kenya has prompted fears of wider African spread Given the closure of the border between the DRC and Uganda since May because of the outbreak of the virus, it is not clear how he was able to enter the country. Alan Kasujja, executive director of the Ugandan government’s media centre, questioned how Kenya allowed the man to enter via its airport. “Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here,” he wrote on X. When asked how the patient was able to travel through three countries undetected, Kenya’s Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said last week that a meeting was scheduled with officials from the DRC and Uganda and the Africa CDC to investigate. Kenya has intensified its national response to the disease since the country recorded the first case. At the time, Kenya traced everyone who came in contact with the patient and reported at least 57 people, with 10 immediately quarantined, Health Minister Aden Duale told journalists on October 7. Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record globally with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths. Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year but was declared Ebola-free in August. A doctor who returned to France in June from the DRC tested positive, but there was no further spread of the virus. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. The second patient is currently at a designated treatment centre, where he is receiving the appropriate care, the Health Ministry said. It will continue to share information on his progress, the ministry added.

Ukrainian officials have accused SpaceX of throttling Starlink satellite services, disrupting its ability to carry out military operations and leaving Kyiv vulnerable to deadly attacks. An adviser to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that without warning, services had been limited for terminals travelling over 100mph overnight on Wednesday – effectively limiting Ukraine’s ability to launch drones, which use satellite internet to pilot the craft. list 1 of 4 Will Ukraine survive the winter? list 2 of 4 Russia and Ukraine trade strikes amid doubt over ‘energy ceasefire’ list 3 of 4 ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan? list 4 of 4 ‘Massive’ Russian attack on Ukraine kills at least 9, damages power sites Writing on Telegram, defence technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said Ukraine was “deprived of one of the few chances to defend itself from Shahed drones”. He later said, “No matter how much I disagree with the Ukraine policy, Starlink will never turn off its terminals … We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.” The slowdown comes after Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv for the second night in a row, killing at least nine people and damaging electricity and heating infrastructure. Beskrestnov warned that the slowdown “cannot be a coincidence” after Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel – despite international sanctions to isolate Moscow. Speaking to AFP, another Ukrainian official accused Washington of throttling Starlink and helping Russia. On Saturday, Trump suggested Zelenskyy had not done enough to end the war with Russia, blaming him for high diesel prices in the US.

events.title: Mosqitter is turning its mosquito traps into an AI-powered surveillance network
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Mosquitoes and the diseases they carry are expanding into new territory. Rising temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, and global travel are reshaping where disease-carrying mosquitoes can thrive, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Cases of dengue, a viral illness spread by mosquito bites, more than doubled in a year, from 6.5 million reported globally in 2023 to a record 14.6 million in 2024, the WHO says. A 30-person, Pennsylvania-based startup, Mosqitter , thinks fighting that problem requires more than killing mosquitoes. The company started by building chemical-free devices that lure and trap female mosquitoes by mimicking the heat, scent, and breathing cues of humans. Anastasiia Romanova, co-founder and CEO of Mosqitter, told TechCrunch that the company set out to bring more sustainable mosquito-control products to a market still heavily reliant on chemicals. Romanova says it now has more than 5,000 devices operating across five continents, up from just over 250 when TechCrunch last covered the company in 2022. The startup now wants to turn its traps into an AI-powered monitoring network that can identify mosquito species, track changes in their numbers, and give earlier warnings about emerging disease risks. Mosqitter began its R&D in Ukraine in 2019 and launched business operations in 2021, which the company considers its official go-to-market year. The company started by examining mosquito behavior. Female mosquitoes, the only ones that bite, seek blood before laying eggs. They lay eggs on a roughly three-week cycle, typically 100 to 200 at a time. “We saw an opportunity: If we could catch the female mosquito at the point when she is about to lay eggs, we could potentially reduce the mosquito population and prevent it from growing,” Romanova said. “That’s why we combined elements such as heat, similar to the temperature of human skin; scent that imitates human skin odor; and light. In the Grand model,” which is the company’s highest-end offering, “we also use CO 2 to imitate human breathing.” Mosqitter, presenting Wednesday as part of TechCrunch’s storied Startup Battlefield competition happening this week in downtown San Francisco, is using AI to identify the mosquitoes its devices catch. Its computer-vision system analyzes biological characteristics to distinguish between species, Romanova told TechCrunch. To identify a mosquito, Mosqitter runs an image through its neural network, checks the result against external datasets, and has entomologists validate the findings. It then assigns a confidence score based on how closely those assessments align. “You can think about it as three judges analyzing a case and producing a verdict,” Romanova said. Mosqitter also feeds environmental data, including weather, wind, and humidity, into its system. The company says that as it collects more data, it plans to use those inputs to forecast changes in mosquito populations and potential health risks. Mosqitter’s product portfolio currently centers on two devices. Mosqitter Grand, its flagship product, is designed for larger areas and public spaces, while Mosqitter Mini targets smaller residential spaces and can also be deployed as a portable monitoring device. The startup plans to officially introduce its Febris Monitoring System next month, adding a data layer to monitor mosquito populations and assess the potential spread of mosquito-borne diseases. “It’s very important to understand that Febris does not diagnose disease,” Romanova said. “We can’t say with certainty that a particular mosquito carries dengue. What we can say is that a particular mosquito species is present, and knowing that can help indicate an increased potential risk associated with diseases that species can transmit.” The company is looking for B2B partners globally, particularly distributors with established sales networks and relationships with governments and retailers, Olga Diachuk, COO and co-founder of Mosqitter, said. Unlike Mosqitter’s hardware products, Febris targets institutional customers, including governments, public-health and mosquito-control agencies, airports, municipalities, and universities that need continuous mosquito monitoring. Brazil, which has a high burden of dengue , is one example of Mosqitter’s expansion. Mosqitter has built local manufacturing and sales operations there, according to the co-founders. The startup also considers the U.S., Greece, India, Ukraine, and Nigeria key markets, and it uses a different sales approach in each. In Greece, Mosqitter works with a long-established pest-control company. In the U.S., it sells its Mini device directly to consumers through Amazon and its own website. The company is also working with the U.K.

events.title: I've spent 154 hours on Amtrak trains in 5 different classes, from coach to bedrooms. The best deal was a premium cabin.
events.summary: The reporter has sampled five Amtrak booking types — coach, business class, first class, roomettes, and bedrooms. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I've spent enough time on Amtrak trains to know that more expensive doesn't always mean better. And the best deal isn't always the cheapest. I figured out which upgrade is most worth it. I travel by train every chance I get. Over the past five years, I've spent roughly 154 hours crisscrossing the US on Amtrak trains , and each time, I've had a different experience. I've lounged on a couch in a private bedroom with a full bathroom, transformed two seats into a bunk in a 20-square-foot cabin called a roomette, and received complimentary meals in the dining car on overnight trains . I've also saved money in coach and upgraded to business and first class on shorter rides. In total, I've sampled five different booking types on 10 trains from the Northeast to the Southwest. One premium seat offers the best value for the upgrade. I spent $50 on a four-hour ride in coach, the most basic seating car. Joey Hadden/Business Insider In May 2025, I took the Amtrak Cascades train from Vancouver , British Columbia , to Seattle. For the four-hour ride, I rode in coach, where seating was first-come, first-served. Coach has the smallest seat of all the classes, but it's still pretty big and comfy, especially compared to a basic economy flight . Like on a plane, the seats reclined, and the seat backs had tray tables and storage pouches. Each row also had power outlets and overhead reading lights. I've taken three business-class Amtrak rides. Joey Hadden/Business Insider In 2022, I spent $120 on a two-and-a-half-hour ride in business class on Amtrak's Acela train from Baltimore to New York City. Unlike regular Amtrak trains with several coach train cars, the Acela fleet has only business and first-class seating. The Acela is also faster than Amtrak regional trains. My trip from Baltimore to NYC was 20 minutes shorter than it would have been on a regular Amtrak train. A few months later, I booked a 10-hour ride on an Amtrak Maple Leaf train from NYC to Niagara Falls, New York . I paid $168 for a business-class seat, which was $100 more than a coach booking on the same train. Three years later, I paid $180 for a business-class seat from NYC to Washington, DC, on the new NextGen Acela train that launched in August 2025. All of them included a roomy seat and a complimentary drink. Joey Hadden/Business Insider A representative of the train line told Business Insider that business-class perks on all Amtrak trains also include fully refundable rides if they're canceled before departure and a 25% point bonus on Amtrak Guest Rewards. The business-class seats were wider than the ones in coach, but they weren't significantly more comfortable on the first two rides, in my opinion. The seat on the NextGen Acela was wider and much cozier than the others. None of the tickets included a meal or in-seat service like the higher-tier cars. Overall, the bookings didn't have as many perks as I expected in a premium cabin. While I wouldn't upgrade to business class on most Amtrak trains, I would still book a seat on the Amtrak Acela train again. I think it's worth paying a little extra to save time and arrive at my destination sooner than I would on a regional train. I've booked two first-class seats on Amtrak trains. First-class seats on the Nextgen Acela train. Joey Hadden/Business Insider The Acela is Amtrak's only train with first-class cars . I first experienced it in 2022 on a two-and-a-half-hour trip from NYC to Baltimore that cost $270. I rode in first class again on Amtrak's NextGen Acela train in 2025. My ticket cost $450 when the fleet was just weeks into service. More recent pricing shows $275 for the same booking three weeks in advance. Both included a meal, access to station lounges, and an even larger chair. Joey Hadden/Business Insider As a New Yorker, part of the allure of a first-class ticket for me was having access to Penn Station's Metropolitan Lounge , a quiet waiting area for select Amtrak customers with comfortable seats and free snacks. First-class passengers and those traveling in roomette and bedroom accommodations get in for free on the day of their trip, while other passengers can pay $50 to access the club. Anyone traveling from Philadelphia, Boston's South Station, and Washington, DC, also has access to a lounge. But 10 other stops on the Amtrak Acela don't offer this perk. On both trains, the first-class seats were larger than those in business class, but I didn't find them significantly more comfortable. First-class tickets also come with a complimentary meal and in-seat service. I found that the food was significantly better on the second ride. Although first class had more perks than business class, comfort on the ride is the most important thing for me when traveling by train. And while the first-class seats were larger than the business-class seats, they weren't upgraded enough to justify the price, in my opinion. However, I couldn't help thinking that splitting a private roomette with a friend might be even cheaper (more on that later). I've taken two overnight rides in Amtrak's roomette accommodation — a private cabin that's around 20 square feet. Joey Hadden/Business Insider In my experience, Amtrak's greatest value is the roomette, which sleeps two and includes a private room with two beds and complimentary meals. My first roomette experience was a 30-hour ride on an Amtrak Viewliner train from NYC to Miami in 2021. I paid $500 to stay in a roughly 20-square-foot private cabin with two beds, a table, two chairs, a sink, and a toilet. Then in 2025, I booked another roomette on an Amtrak Superliner . The 15-hour train ride from Denver to Salt Lake City cost $400. This roomette was similar to the first, except it didn't include a toilet or sink and had been freshly updated with new seat cushions and lining. Amtrak is also working on interior updates for sleeper cars on the Viewliner fleet, which will be available in 2026, Amtrak spokesman Marc Magliari told Business Insider. Each had two chairs facing each other that folded out into a bed, and another bed pulled down from the ceiling. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Both rooms also had a small closet and a mirror. All roomette passengers have access to a bathroom and shower in the sleeper car. The roomettes made great use of a small space, with clever storage features that reminded me of a tiny home . I was pleasantly surprised that I could control the temperature inside each roomette with a dial and air conditioning vents. On both rides, the bed and sheets were comfortable enough for one night, though the updated cushions on the Superliner ride were cozier. For a long-haul train ride, I think the roomette's price tag is worth it for the private space, temperature control, and a lie-flat bed. I've also slept in two Amtrak bedrooms. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I

events.title: Suspected Israeli online operations cause alarm in Iran and Lebanon
events.summary: Suspected online espionage triggers intense security crackdowns and counter-intelligence measures in Iran and Lebanon. Israeli intelligence services are believed to be turning to social media to gather information and recruit potential informants in Lebanon and Iran, according to security experts, using online advertisements and appeals tailored to local audiences. One Instagram account, presenting itself as belonging to Israel’s foreign intelligence agency Mossad, has published Arabic-language messages encouraging people to make contact through confidential channels. list 1 of 3 Iran targets Starlink as ‘tool of war’ with hints of more internet curbs list 2 of 3 Iran steps up Hormuz surveillance: Attacks soar, oil flows crash again list 3 of 3 How Israel’s ‘Yellow Line’ is reshaping southern Lebanon The account, which is verified and operates under the handle @themossad_official, has posted recruitment appeals in colloquial Lebanese Arabic, including inviting people to explore new opportunities by initiating a private conversation. The profile prominently features pinned highlight reels with Arabic titles such as “Lebanon” displaying a photo of fighters, “Israel”, “Mossad wants you!”, “Protection”, and “Think about your future”. In August 2025, Lebanon’s General Security Directorate warned residents against interacting with the Instagram account. In Lebanon, where years of economic turmoil have left many residents facing financial hardship, security officials have warned of suspected Israeli intelligence recruitment efforts involving social media. In January 2025, the Lebanese newspaper Al Akhbar reported that Israeli intelligence operatives were attempting to recruit Lebanese citizens through fake job advertisements offering high salaries, and through direct outreach on WhatsApp. Retired Brigadier General Mounir Chehade told the newspaper that the recruitment efforts targeted areas with significant support for Hezbollah, including Beirut’s southern suburbs, southern Lebanon and the Bekaa Valley. Also in January 2025, Lebanon’s General Security Directorate warned against interacting with a Facebook page called SAWA, which it suspected was a Mossad front aimed at recruiting Lebanese citizens. Similarly, in December 2025, another Lebanese newspaper L’Orient Today reported that the security agency had warned residents against interacting with a social media page calling itself “Unit 504”. The page claimed to represent the Israeli military’s human intelligence unit and said it was looking for individuals interested in joining its ranks. The concerns have been accompanied by arrests of people accused of passing sensitive information to Israel. Lebanese authorities were reported in October 2025 to have previously arrested 32 people suspected of giving information to Israel that was used to target Hezbollah leaders. Academic and political researcher Wissam Nassif Yassin told Al Jazeera that Israeli intelligence uses colloquial Lebanese Arabic on these platforms to avoid arousing suspicion and to facilitate communication. “The Israeli side focuses on all segments of society because it considers that every person can be penetrated from their own angle, based on the fact that Hezbollah in Lebanon is integrated into the core of Lebanese society,” Yassin said. “It focuses on the party’s members primarily, then on the resistance environment secondarily, and on the environment surrounding it thirdly.” While Israel has had notable sucesses in its intelligence operations in Lebanon – including in gathering information leading to attacks on Hezbollah leaders and members, Yassin argued that collaboration with Israel remained widely rejected in Lebanon. He also pointed to Hezbollah’s own counterintelligence capabilities, arguing that the group has a long history of identifying and disrupting Israeli intelligence activity. Yassin pointed to the case of Elhanan Tannenbaum , an alleged Israeli spy who was captured in 2000 after being lured abroad, and was released in 2004 in a prisoner exchange deal. The use of digital platforms to recruit potential informants also forms part of the longstanding intelligence war between Israel and Iran, which has intensified alongside the military conflict between the two countries. Hassan Ahmadian, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Tehran, described the current situation as one of the most intense periods in decades-long espionage between the two countries. “This is an intelligence war. The confrontation between Iran and Israel has continued for decades, but in recent years it has reached its peak,” Ahmadian told Al Jazeera. “Both sides are engaged in intelligence operations. It is an intense conflict that has never stopped.” Ahmadian said that Israeli recruitment efforts in Iran were sometimes carried out through openly advertised opportunities on social media. “Israel certainly uses online advertising to recruit people,” he said.

events.title: Bank of America shares drop 8% after third-quarter revenue miss and regulatory penalty
events.summary: Bank of America's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Revenue was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading. Misses in fixed income and equities trading revenue totaled roughly $750 million. The trading disappointment comes after CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts last month that trading revenue would be roughly flat; instead the combined bond and stock trading results fell by 5%. Bank of America on Wednesday posted a sharp profit decline after being hit with a $1.2 billion penalty by U.S. regulators, while revenue also disappointed after trading operations generated about $750 million less than expected. Earnings per share: 91 cents, may not compare with $1.10 expected by LSEG Revenue: $30.12 billion vs. $30.69 billion expected by LSEG The bank's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.93 billion, or 91 cents a share. Excluding the penalty, which sapped income by 17 cents, EPS would've been $1.08 a share. Companywide revenue rose 3.2% to $30.12 billion in the quarter, on an FTE basis, but that was below expectations by about $570 million, largely on misses from Wall Street trading operations. Fixed income trading revenue dropped 17% to $2.55 billion on weakness in mortgages, municipals and credit activity. That is roughly $450 million below the StreetAccount estimate. Equities trading revenue climbed 10% to $2.51 billion, but that was also below analysts' expectations, by nearly $300 million. Investment banking revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion, roughly in line with expectations and Moynihan's September guidance. Net interest income, a key profitability driver watched closely by Bank of America investors, rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion, slightly edging out the $16.53 billion StreetAccount estimate. In a research note published Wednesday, Wells Fargo analyst Mike Mayo called the firm's capital markets results "easily worst in class" for the quarter. The Treasury episode, in which U.S. regulators said the company failed to report billions of dollars in suspicious transactions, sparked questions as to whether Moynihan has a handle on controls at the second-biggest U.S. bank by assets. On the company's earnings call Wednesday, several analysts remarked on the sharp decline in Bank of America shares and pressed Moynihan about earlier guidance that compliance costs would be contained. "Clearly you've had a huge charge this morning," JPMorgan analyst Vivek Juneja said. "It's not that you can't absorb a billion. … But obviously it's a reputational and confidence issue." Other analysts questioned management on the pace of future share repurchases and asked about the bank's underperformance in trading. Management blamed the firm's bond trading results on the sharp rise in interest rates during the period. "It just happens when rates go up 85 basis points in a quarter, that tends not to be good for" credit and mortgage trading businesses, CFO Alastair Borthwick said. Later Wednesday in an interview with CNBC's Leslie Picker , Moynihan didn't commit to a timeline on the resolution of regulatory issues. "We got to do the work, and then the regulators look at it," Moynihan said. "So I don't want to speculate about the precise timeline." The CEO added that he was "confident that we are on the right course to remediate everything." Moynihan took the helm in 2010 and spent the early years of his tenure making amends for mortgage-related abuses in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. The Treasury fine, announced on Tuesday, added 11th-hour intrigue to what was an otherwise fairly routine bank earnings week. On Tuesday, JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and Wells Fargo posted mixed results, with JPMorgan missing EPS and revenue estimates for the first time in years. Correction: Bank of America reported third-quarter revenue on an FTE basis of $30.12 billion compared with LSEG estimates of $30.69 billion. An earlier version misstated the comparison.

events.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 16:51 BST Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals. The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce. Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to". The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers. In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation". Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount . Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". TV series Below, starring Josh Hartnett, is one of Netflix's most popular shows The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October. Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series. It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films. However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer. He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau. "Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said. The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. Are you affected by issues covered in this story? events.title: Trump's diesel dilemma — by the numbers
events.summary: The cut in global supply from the wars in Ukraine and Iran have made wholesale diesel prices more than double since the beginning of 2026. Last week, President Donald Trump lifted restrictions on Russian diesel to ease global shortages. Experts agree that bringing more Russian diesel to market is unlikely to sway near-term prices. Diesel prices are surging as midterms approach – and they are likely to stay high in the near future, according to analysts. The International Energy Agency's monthly report for October, released Wednesday, was the latest to predict that constraints on the diesel market will likely keep prices elevated into next year. The group warned that even if refineries step up production of diesel into the year-end, inventories will likely remain strained until the second half of 2027. Last Friday, President Donald Trump unexpectedly paused sanctions on Russian diesel fuel and announced that he reached a deal with President Vladimir Putin in which the Kremlin would release 4.8 million metric tons of diesel , or nearly 36 million barrels, to the global market. Over the weekend, he took to Truth Social to announce an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine , but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later accused Russia of attacking the country's energy facilities . The foreign policy developments come as rising fuel prices — particularly skyrocketing diesel — have become a major flashpoint ahead of this year's midterm election. But releasing Russian diesel to the global market is unlikely to drop prices in the near term. A note from Goldman Sachs last week even predicted that diesel prices will remain high through 2027 as refineries struggle to meet demand. Here's what the numbers tell us so far: Wholesale diesel prices have more than doubled since the beginning of 2026 through the end of September as both the war in Iran and Russia's war in Ukraine have dramatically cut global supply. Trump has insisted that the war in Ukraine is to blame for high diesel prices. On July 8, Russia banned diesel exports after Ukraine struck its refineries. In the U.S., the price of a gallon of diesel rose nearly 40% between July 6 and Sept. 22. However, the price of diesel had already jumped after the Iran war started and was still 20% above its prewar level when Russia instituted its export ban, making that tightening of supply feel that much more acute. Indeed, both conflicts have created major ripple effects across global energy markets causing major swings, sometimes daily.

events.title: The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’
events.summary: There are many reasons to reject this affordability ‘solution’, not least it being complex and fiddly. Just keep things simple ‘M y mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not. That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” So said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, recently , bracing for the hike in energy bills that looks inevitable in January. Industry projections suggest £400-ish on an annual basis is on the way, with “stubbornly high” levels for the rest of decade even if wholesale gas prices cool down. So, yes, one can understand why “affordability” is Fahnbulleh’s “top priority”. And, as this newspaper reported last week , there is likely to be an intervention in that direction in chancellor John Healey’s budget this month: £1bn of extra support for poorer households this winter. But the chat in energy-land is about what comes after that – and what Fahnbulleh’s other remarks about covering the costs of the energy system in a “fairer” way seem to be hinting at. Will the government finally get round to designing a co-called “social tariff” for energy – a way to get financial support to the most needy on a more targeted basis than the clunky warm homes discount, the mechanism Healey will be obliged to use? Will Healey, after chopping VAT from electricity for six months, do so permanently and then shift more green levies and other “hidden taxes” of energy transition into general taxation? And is Fahnbulleh also contemplating something very different? Welcome to the idea of the “rising block tariff” (RBT), the unwieldy name for the proposal to give every household an initial block, or allowance, of cheaper gas and electricity to cover “essential” use and then make subsequent blocks more expensive. In other words, heavier energy consumers would pay higher rates for their extra units. Fahnbulleh has got officials in her department to explore an RBT model. And, note, the New Economics Foundation, the thinktank she used to lead, is a proponent . The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is another backer: in its version , the government could fund an RBT with, say, £5bn of public money, allowing bills to fall for most households – but, critically, the biggest savings would flow to light users, who tend to be low-income households. “An RBT would produce greater reductions in bills lower down the income distribution,” it says. What’s not to like? Plenty. There are at least three reasons why an RBT has few fans elsewhere, not even among charities and thinktanks that focus on fuel poverty. First, Citizens Advice regards low energy use as a poor proxy for low income in practice. Traditional electric heaters, with high electricity usage, “are more common in social or private rented homes, where people can’t change their heating system”, it argues . Quite: a progressive-sounding policy could end up being nothing of the sort, especially if second-home owners, by spreading their usage, are winners. If the reply is that an incomes overlay could address tricky cases in both directions, why not just do the data modelling work to design a proper social tariff in the first place? Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Second, a rigid RBT would be an awkward fit with a renewables-heavy system where the most interesting innovations are “flex” tariffs to exploit very windy or sunny hours when wholesale power prices are dirt cheap. There is a danger of baffling consumers by making them mix their blocks with their flexes. Third, a core aim of the energy transition is to drive take-up of electric vehicles, heat pumps and so on. That becomes harder if the message to consumers is that “the more electricity you use, the more you’ll be charged per unit”. Lobby group Electrify Britain calls block tariffs “hugely counterproductive” for electrification: “You can’t ask families to go electric and then pursue a policy that would charge them more for doing so.” That feels the killer point: an RBT model cuts across too many other goals. Fahnbulleh should keep things simple: go for a serious social tariff or discount scheme that effectively identifies “vulnerable” energy users. That idea has enjoyed wide support for years. Block tariffs are too complicated and fiddly to administer.

events.title: 21 details you may have missed in 'The Cabin in the Woods'
events.summary: The cast and crew of "The Cabin In The Woods." Eric Charbonneau/WireImage/Getty Images "The Cabin in the Woods" was released in 2012, a whopping 14 years ago. The slasher satire is full of references, Easter eggs, and tributes to many horror films. Here are 21 details you might've missed in the film. Warning: spoilers ahead. October, for many of us, means horror movie marathons. But did you know there's an underrated classic waiting for you out there that rewards your years of service toiling away in the scary movie mines? It's true. And it's called "The Cabin in the Woods." Every frame of this movie is chock-full of jokes, Easter eggs, and references to the horror classics that any self-respecting horror fan would get. But if you're not interested in watching your Halloween faves with a magnifying glass and a tab on your computer opened to Fangoria, we've got you covered. Here are our favorite little details in "The Cabin in the Woods." "The Cabin in the Woods" was released on April 13, 2012. If you need a quick refresher on the plot, keep reading ... "The Cabin in the Woods." Lionsgate To get away for the weekend, five college students (Dana, Curt, Holden, Jules, and Marty) travel to Curt's family cabin. Things start getting ... weird ... after Dana reads Latin incantations from an old diary in the basement. Specifically, zombies start attacking them. Simultaneously, two engineers, Sitterson and Hadley, have been orchestrating these horrifying events on behalf of a shadowy organization at a site known only as the Facility, led by the Director. Over the course of the film, it's revealed that the Facility sacrifices five classic slasher-movie archetypes (the virgin, scholar, fool, jock, and the promiscuous one) annually to keep a group of ancient monsters, the Ancient Ones, from destroying the Earth. Spoiler: Instead of killing her friend Marty, Dana (the "virgin") decides to let the world end, because humanity's not worth saving. The Easter eggs start right at the beginning. The film's jump-scare title-card drop is just like the one in the horror classic "Funny Games." "Funny Games" and "The Cabin in the Woods." Concorde-Castle Rock/Turner; Lionsgate In "Funny Games," the title card comes on screen, accompanied by screaming heavy metal, right after a seemingly very normal scene of a family taking a road trip. "Cabin's" title card is almost the same, down to the bright-red font. It appears (along with some screams) after a mundane conversation between two Facility employees. The movie's title itself is a reference to the horror classic "The Evil Dead," which follows a group of friends staying at a cabin in the woods. "The Evil Dead." New Line Cinema In addition to the name and setting, a later reference on a whiteboard pays homage to a rather infamous scene in "Evil Dead" in which one of the five main characters is sexually assaulted by a tree. The characters also inadvertently summon the zombies using a diary filled with Latin phrases, eerily similar to "Evil Dead's" Necronomicon. While most of the monsters in the film are famous mythological figures or pop-culture staples, you can see a shot of some real-life monsters, the KKK, in one of the cells. "The Cabin in the Woods." Lionsgate The Facility is populated by plenty of classic monsters — you'll learn more about them later — but in a brief shot, you can see a crew of people wearing white hoods, an obvious nod to monsters that exist in the real world: the Ku Klux Klan. You can also see some zombies from the popular "Left 4 Dead" video game series. "The Cabin in the Woods" and "Left 4 Dead." Lionsgate; Valve "Left 4 Dead" and "Left 4 Dead 2" are popular zombie video games that were released in 2008 and 2009. It might be hard to tell in this photo, but an eagle-eyed Redditor found at least three zombies from the games in the cells of the Facility, including Boomer, the Witch, and Tank. Director Drew Goddard shared in a Reddit thread that there were plans for a "Cabin in the Woods" downloadable level for "Left 4 Dead 2," but money issues held up the collab. "We were actually going to do a downloadable 'L4D2' pack, where you'd fight in the 'Cabin' world, but then MGM went bankrupt so the delay squashed it," Goddard wrote. "But the people at Valve were still cool enough to let us use some of their monsters to fill the cubes in the background." The film was written by Joss Whedon, so, predictably, he threw a few nods to his work in the film, like a Reaver from his sci-fi cult classic series "Firefly." "The Cabin in the Woods." Lionsgate Whedon, the now-controversial screenwriter and director , cowrote "Cabin" with director Drew Goddard. As a former patron saint for nerds everywhere, Whedon threw in a reference to "Firefly," his space Western TV series. In "Firefly," Reavers were a group of cannibalistic humans who traveled throughout space and antagonized the main characters. A Reaver can be spotted wandering the halls of the Facility, as one Redditor pointed out. Two of Whedon's frequent collaborators, Amy Acker and Tom Lenk, also have small roles, while another Whedon favorite, Fran Kranz, stars. "The Cabin in the Woods." Lionsgate Kranz has the biggest role of the three, as he plays one of the five college students who is targeted by the Facility. He also starred in Whedon's series "Dollhouse" as Topher Brink. Acker played Fred in four seasons of the "Buffy" spin-off, "Angel," from 2001 to 2004. She also recurred on "Dollhouse," playing Dr. Claire Saunders. In "Cabin," she plays Wendy, a technician inside the Facility. After "Cabin," she worked with Whedon and his brother on their series "Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D." Lastly, Lenk has a small (but funny) role as an intern at the Facility in "Cabin." But fans know him best as Andrew Wells from across the "Buffy"-verse, in both "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" and "Angel." Acker, Kranz, and Lenk also appeared in Whedon's 2013 film adaptation of Shakespeare's "Much Ado About Nothing." A shot of an elevator bay covered in blood is a nod to an iconic scene from "The Shining." "The Cabin in the Woods." Lionsgate The trailer for the 1980 horror classic "The Shining" is simply a long shot of an elevator opening and dousing the lobby in blood. The scene later appears in the film, too, in a shorter version. This shot of a bay of elevators covered in blood is an obvious nod to the iconic scene. You can also spot a pair of creepy twins holding hands, just like in "The Shining." "The Cabin in the Woods." Lionsgate One of the creepiest aspects of "The Shining" is the twins who beckon young Danny Torrance to come play with them. events.title: Tehran municipality accused of ‘overstep’ after launching welfare projects
events.summary: Tehran’s municipality has launched new welfare initiatives to combat inflation, drawing intense scrutiny over funding sources, institutional overlap, and transparency. Tehran municipality has launched a series of welfare initiatives to help residents cope with soaring living costs, but the measures have raised questions about their financing and effectiveness, as well as whether the local authority is taking on responsibilities better handled by Iran’s national government. The local authority has launched four projects it says are aimed at protecting citizens, including a housing project, freezes on the prices of 12 basic goods , and a maternity package. list 1 of 3 US sanctions 10 entities for allegedly supporting Iran’s military list 2 of 3 ‘Better deal’: What’s behind Trump’s rejection of Iran’s truce offer? list 3 of 3 Trump made the right decision to reject Iran’s offer Questions have been raised about how they will be funded and whether the municipality is overstepping its traditional functions. In Iran, municipalities are responsible for local services and urban management, while the national government oversees broader economic policy, including efforts to control inflation. Iranian law does give municipalities some responsibilites beyond conventional urban services, but Article 55 of Iran’s Municipal Law does call for municipalities to provide for public food markets, make certain essential goods more affordable, and provide social welfare facilities and low-cost housing. The dispute is therefore less about whether Tehran municipality can provide the services, and more about their scale and financing. The municipality’s price-freezing initiative, dubbed the “Zero Inflation” project, has been the most controversial. It comes as year-on-year inflation reached nearly 90 percent last month, while annual food inflation hit 108.8 percent. Doubts have been raised about how the project will be funded and its effectiveness. Others believe that the measures could fuel inequality between the capital and other cities. They are viewed as steps to address the huge economic challenges faced by Tehran residents, worsened since the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28. Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani said the municipality had recently guaranteed prices ranging between 5 percent and 50 percent below market rates for the next six months. Yousef Akandeh, a political activist, told Al Jazeera that freezing the prices of some goods or providing free services will not reduce inflation to zero alone. “Even if we assume that the Tehran municipality succeeded in stabilising the prices of 12 basic goods, what about the rise in rents, medicines, transportation prices, and the rest of living expenses,” Akandeh asked. Real steps to tackle inflation, Akandeh said, would have to begin with controlling liquidity growth and monetary discipline, which he said are nearly impossible amid the ongoing war. The municipality has also introduced a maternity support programme offering mothers of children born this year monthly credits worth up to 40 million rials ($15) for two years for each newborn. Akandeh raised the issue of institutional overlap, noting that a similar national scheme already exists. “The government implements a similar package and provides monthly financial amounts for all newborns across the country and not just in Tehran, and if the municipality’s package is independent of it, the Tehrani family may benefit from the national and municipal programme simultaneously,” Akandeh said. Receiving support from both programmes would not, in itself, indicate wrongdoing. But critics are instead raising the question of whether it is an appropriate use of Tehran’s municipal resources, particularly when the city faces competing spending demands. Amir Dabiri Mehr, a former adviser in the Tehran municipality, told Al Jazeera that although supporting the homeless falls under the municipality’s social responsibilities, the problem lies in a lack of transparency. The municipality is funded by taxes and building density licences. “The people have the right to know what the municipality spends within the framework of its original tasks, and in tasks it has chosen for itself, and where it gets its resources from?” Dabiri Mehr said. The municipality-affiliated Hamshahri newspaper said that the “Zero Inflation” project is not funded by municipal budget subsidies, but through direct purchases from producers and reducing commercial profit margins in council-run stores. The biggest crisis facing Tehran’s residents is housing, which is the national government’s responsibility, Mehr said. Food and living expenses are the national government’s responsibility. “If the goal is to solve the people’s problems, it seems that the biggest problem facing the residents of Tehran today is the housing crisis, and this dilemma cannot be solved by building an apartment building consisting of a few residential units,” he said.

events.title: Aldar to launch major Dubai villa and townhouse project by end of year
events.summary: Aldar plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. The new project, whose value is not disclosed, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London. It will be the fourth project in Dubai for Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, following the launches of the Haven, Athlon and The Wilds. “It’s another partnership with Dubai Holding , and it's a very large villa community [with] townhouses and also sits above the Blue Line extension,” Mr Emery said. In February, Aldar and Dubai Holding expanded their joint venture announced in 2023 by adding two plots in Dubai to deliver almost 14,000 new homes with a combined gross development value of more than Dh38 billion. The first plot of four million square metres, is along Dubai’s eastern growth corridor opposite Nad Al Sheba. The second plot, on Palm Jebel Ali, will be an ultra-luxury waterfront development of branded and non-branded residences. The new developments are coming even as buyers become cautious due to regional uncertainty driven by the Iran war. Transaction volumes and values fell in the third quarter. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year, while the number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, according to the latest report from Cavendish Maxwell. “The customers are still there for the right product. Now, clearly, the international side of the market is the one that's just slowed a little bit. There’s uncertainty and people are taking their time to have a look. But we still believe in the fundamentals … the products that we have brought to the market have all done really well,” Mr Emery said. Aldar, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, will hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company's launch. The deliveries will go up to 4,500 next year, he said. Among the projects that are expected to be delivered this year are the Sustainable City on Yas Island, and the Grove and Louvre Abu Dhabi residences on Saadiyat Island. The Abu Dhabi-listed company will also hand over its first homes in Dubai next year, at its Haven project near Dubailand. New partnerships In September, Aldar and Sharjah-based Arada announced a partnership to build housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, with a combined value of about Dh15 billion. The partnership involves a master plan joint venture to create a large-scale mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah on the Abu Dhabi-Dubai border and Arada’s acquisition of three residential plots on Yas Island. Aldar will continue to look for new partnerships with established developers, Mr Emery said. “Partnerships is a way that we believe we can diversify the customer offer, because you know if we pick the right partner that has a great proposition, maybe they have a great following with their customers … then it’s good to be able to introduce that to our customers as well,” he said.

events.title: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters
events.summary: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Axios Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey. The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism. By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup. That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974. The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions. Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005. Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup. State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%). The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media. Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels. Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

events.title: Trump returns to Ohio as Democrats try to claw back his advantage
events.summary: David’s view YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Toward the end of Monday night’s MAGA rally, after Jon Husted heard Donald Trump compliment his jawline and his “ass,” he thanked the president for making Ohio so much easier for Republicans to win. “The Youngstown area, for decades, used to vote Democrat,” the Republican senator said. “And then you ran for office in 2016, and flipped it red forever.” For a decade after that, Youngstown has become the first stop on what media critics derided as “Trump voter safaris,” journeys into the working-class counties that never voted Republican until he showed up. Husted’s claim of a permanently red state, however, isn’t adding up for Democrats: As soon as I arrived this week, they insisted that MAGA’s advance was over. This isn’t because Democrats have snapped back to the image and values they ran on in the 1970s, when they had a lock on this state. No, the party insists that Republicans are in charge, making voters angry with their handling of the economy and the Middle East, so the culture-war politicking that worked for a decade won’t be as potent in November. “People aren’t buying that again because they’ve realized you can’t deposit culture war into your bank account,” said Chris Anderson, the chairman of the Mahoning County Democrats, who’d spent years trying to limit their losses and defections. “You can’t fill your gas tank with it.” Campaigns have a queasy rhythm to them — hype followed by panic followed by hype. We’ve reached the time in the cycle where the party that built a post-Labor Day polling lead begins to question its own confidence. “They’re undersampling Republicans,” Speaker Mike Johnson told the faithful in South Texas on Tuesday, a part of that state that seemed to be following the same rightward march as northeast Ohio — and before that, Appalachia. Republicans around Youngstown expected the trend of underestimating their vote to hold this year, but not accelerate. They agreed that Democrats would at least be competitive. Rep. Michael Rulli, who represents the Mahoning Valley in Congress, said that the GOP got an opening when “Clinton came in and lied about NAFTA,” which made local Democrats thrash around in search of a populist alternative. “When Trump came around, the people just took to it, and so they’re giving us a shot,” Rulli added. “This area will not always stay Republican or Democrat.” This year’s Democrats are making hard plays for northeast Ohio, at least to trim the GOP margins. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost the five most Democratic counties east of Cleveland for the first time in 2024, has painted Husted as a “Big Tech” shill, captured by the next industry that’ll threaten working-class jobs. Amy Acton, the party’s gubernatorial nominee, takes every chance to talk about her Youngstown roots; her ads often portray Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire GOP nominee, playing tennis as he daydreams about cutting Medicare and Social Security. “I know what it’s like to not have the heat on, or live in a tent in the winter and experience a lot of neglect and abuse,” Acton told me on Tuesday, when I asked her to respond to the president rallying in Youngstown — specifically, about him telling voters they’d get rebate checks and energy bill relief only if Republicans won. “And I can also tell you that I wouldn’t be here today if it wasn’t for the institutions that gave me a chance.” A Democratic comeback in Ohio is unlikely to look like the winning maps of Barack Obama’s campaigns, much less Bill Clinton’s. While losing to Bernie Moreno two years ago, Brown ran stronger in the suburbs of Cleveland and Cincinnati than he had in elections he actually won. On Monday, the standard Trump rally scene of MAGA-hatted voters in line and liberals yelling at them from free speech zones showed how the coalitions had changed. The protesters skewed older; the younger they were, the more profanity they were comfortable putting on cardboard. A “progress pride” flag was hoisted on a pole, right under an American flag. Any Trump fan who objected got an earful about the “pedophile president” they were lined up for. Trump, at this point, was not the rebel candidate who first showed up in Youngstown 10 years ago, with rally speeches about the threat of mass Muslim immigration. He was the party leader every Republican wanted to borrow some aura from, by communing with his superfans. Ramaswamy posed for selfies a few steps away from MAGA activist Vince Fusca . Blake Marnell , who wears a brick-patterned suit to every Trump rally, got a seat near the main stage. Both men were at the 2024 Trump rally in Butler, Pa., where a failed assassin’s bullet clipped his ear; neither needed convincing that he was saving eastern Ohio, where they didn’t live, from neoliberalism. The Covelli Centre, where Trump had rallied before, was a bit more than half-full when the president got onstage. Like Democrats used to, he described all the investments he was bringing to the region. Submarine construction was coming to Cleveland; nearby Warren was getting a new ​​Kimberly-Clark plant ; he would figure out how to save the local heating utility company. The applause thinned out when he talked about how he’d rebranded artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” Notable David Skolnick covered the rally for the Youngstown Vindicator. Richard Cowan went to Warren, Ohio, for Reuters, to take the temperature of its Obama-Trump voters: “We ⁠believe our Christian ​values are more than gas prices.”

events.summary: Netflix plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce as part of wider organizational changes CHICAGO -- CHICAGO (AP) — Netflix plans to lay off about 6% of its workforce, amounting to nearly 1,000 positions, as the streaming giant makes wider “organizational changes.” Co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos announced the job cuts in a memo to employees Wednesday. They said the company's product, tech, legal and human resources teams would be the most impacted. "Decisions like these are never easy, and we don’t take them lightly," Peters and Sarandos wrote in the memo, which was obtained by The Associated Press. They maintained business was strong — but that Netflix needed to be “disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources" as it invests in future growth and “high impact areas to improve our service.” Beyond the memo from its chief executives, Netflix declined to comment further about Wednesday's cuts. Between membership signups and price increases, Netflix’s profit has grown this year. In its second financial quarter , the company earned $3.4 billion and racked up revenue of $12.56 billion — up 9% and 13%, respectively, from the same period last year. Still, Netflix’s forecast for the third quarter fell below Wall Street's expectations. The company plans to report those earnings next week. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Competition in the streaming space is growing more crowded overall. Netflix continues to be a dominant player (accounting for 19% of the market per the latest data from streaming guide JustWatch), but rivals like Amazon's Prime Video and Disney+ are close behind. HBO Max and Paramount+ are also now under the same roof — Skydance — after Paramount's $81 billion buyout of Warner Bros. Discovery closed last week. The new Hollywood giant plans to unify its streaming products “into a single service over time.” Netflix initially inked a deal to buy Warner's studio and streaming business late last year, but walked away from that offer back in February. At the end of 2025, per regulatory filings, Netflix had about 16,000 full-time employees worldwide. The layoffs announced Wednesday mark the biggest round of cuts the California-based company has rolled out in years. The Wall Street Journal first reported Wednesday's news of the layoffs. events.title: Fire erupts at Albania’s Education Ministry as protests enter third day
events.summary: At least 16 additional protesters have been arrested after clashing with riot police. Protesters started a blaze at Albania’s Education Ministry overnight after a second day of student protests in the country’s capital Tirana that continue unabated. Demonstrators broke in overnight on Tuesday and lit a fire inside of the building, according to police, adding that the violence resulted in 16 arrests. list 1 of 3 Activist Greta Thunberg joins French student protests list 2 of 3 Presidential hopeful Melenchon joins France school protest march list 3 of 3 India’s ‘Cockroach’ leaders jailed after entering ‘banned’ protest site Protesters continued to rally on Wednesday. Hundreds of students gathered and slung rocks at the ministry, as they demanded better university conditions and the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. In an attempt to break up the crowds, riot police responded with tear gas and water cannons. Demonstrators also ripped out nearby fencing and used it to block the street. Hundreds of people rallied on Tuesday in front of the Education Ministry, after fierce protests broke out in Tirana on Monday. “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used as an excuse for violence, city destruction or ugly fighting in the middle of the road,” Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu said on Facebook. “I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: Distance yourself from violence and vandalism!” Besar Likmeta, editor at the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network in Albania, told Al Jazeera that “this protest came on the back of four months of daily rallies on the main streets of the capital”, known as the “ Flamingo Revolution “. The movement started in protest of a resort project in a protected area of southern Albania linked to the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, Jared Kushner . The project fuelled anger over alleged corruption and a lack of transparency, with protesters demanding Rama’s resignation. “But then they, they spread into wider demands about better, better opportunities and anti-corruption, lack of opportunities for youth, and particularly a sign of growing disenfranchisement among this younger generation of Albanians,” Likmeta added. Students told local media that the protests were against university conditions, tuition fees and a lack of support for young people.

events.title: At least two security officials killed near Iran’s critical Chabahar port
events.summary: Iran says ‘terrorist groups’ supported from outside the country are targeting security forces. At least two Iranian security personnel have been killed in separate incidents along the country’s eastern border with Pakistan, adding to a string of attacks near the critical Chabahar port over the past few weeks. An officer commanding a women’s unit in Iran’s Basij paramilitary force – part of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IGRC) – has been shot and killed outside her home in the Mehrestan district of Sistan-Baluchestan province on Wednesday, according to Tasnim news agency. Another officer was killed in a separate attack on a police vehicle, also in Mehrestan, which lies close to Iran’s border with Pakistan. On Wednesday, Haalvash, a rights group focusing on the region’s Baluch ethnic minority in the province, said military helicopters were circling over the city of Iranshahr, adding that the security situation remained tense in several locations. Iran’s Sistan-Baluchestan province houses the critical Chabahar port on the country’s eastern flank, where US forces carried out air strikes targeting infrastructure and naval control facilities in July. In recent months, the region has seen multiple attacks staged by groups that Iran’s government says are “terrorist outfits” being funded and supported from outside the country. Last week, gunmen killed one person and injured three others while attacking a minibus transporting security personnel from a division stationed along the Makran coast, according to the official IRNA news agency. In a separate incident, IRNA reported that “several terrorists” killed a police officer after attacking a convoy patrolling the area. Earlier this month, IRGC’s Al Quds Force said it killed at least two suspected attackers and destroyed an alleged “terrorist cell” in an operation near Chabahar port. The IRGC statement said it had launched the operation after the group killed a member of Iran’s security forces at a checkpoint near the city of Rasak. IRGC said it had recovered a Starlink device, along with a large quantity of weapons, in the group’s mountainous hideout.

events.title: I thought Napa was the gold standard for wine trips. Then, a city in Washington changed what I look for in a vacation.
events.summary: The Walla Walla Valley region is famous for its wine, and I loved visiting. Wirestock/Getty Images I celebrated my 30th in Napa Valley and loved it, but the cost made it tough to justify returning. Later, I found Walla Walla, Washington, which had great wine, dining, and vineyard stays for less. I was able to have the kind of wine vacation I loved without a hefty price tag or packed itinerary. When I turned 30, I wanted to do something different as I exited my 20s. Since I had recently developed an interest in champagne, I looked into wine destinations . I quickly settled on Napa in Northern California since it was the only one I'd heard of, and I found out the area offered sparkling wine tours. With stunning vineyard views, ideal weather, tours and tastings, and, of course, incredible food and wine, the destination was nothing short of magical. My husband and I stayed at a Vrbo called "The Casa," a little house we had all to ourselves, surrounded by vineyards and an adorable farm with chickens visiting our yard throughout the trip. As memorable as this getaway was, it came with a high price tag. The tours, tastings, meals, and Vrbo added up quickly, making our wine excursion an unlikely recurrence. That is, until I discovered Walla Walla. This smaller city in southeastern Washington is home to a thriving wine region and is only a short plane ride from our home in Seattle. I decided to visit with my husband for my 33rd birthday, hoping to recreate my Napa experience. During our three-day trip, I realized that Walla Walla offered me the kind of wine vacation I'd loved in Napa, with more spontaneity, fewer crowds, and a lower price tag. The food and drink scene was even better than I expected Walla Walla Valley is organized into six different wine districts. don51/Getty Images There are well over 100 wineries in this little valley, with more than 30 walkable tasting rooms in downtown Walla Walla alone and five other wine districts to explore in the surrounding area. We spent most of our time on Main Street during our trip since it was our first visit, and we weren't yet familiar with the surrounding wine pockets. We spent most of our time in downtown Walla Walla. Cheyenne Elwell Like Napa Valley, Walla Walla is known for its Bordeaux-style reds , including cabernet sauvignon and merlot. We also tried white wines like chardonnay and viognier, along with sparkling options. Dossier, cofounded by former NFL player Sidney Rice, is one of the newer wineries in the area, and we happened upon it while exploring downtown. We stopped in for a flight. We also visited Pursued by Bear, founded by actor Kyle MacLachlan. As a "Twin Peaks" fan, that was a must for me (unfortunately, Agent Dale Cooper wasn't in that day). Throughout the trip, we experienced different tasting rooms and wineries. Cheyenne Elwell At Grosgrain, we tried some less-conventional wines and sipped them while overlooking the vineyard right outside the tasting room. I also wasn't sure what to expect from Walla Walla's food scene, but I was pleasantly surprised. At The Walls Vineyards, we were able to pair our wine tasting with food, including a hummus plate and wood-fired pizzas curated by its sister restaurant Passatempo Taverna, which multiple people recommended to us during our trip. At some places, we paired wine with small plates. Cheyenne Elwell We made reservations at a couple of restaurants based on ratings and recommendations, and ended up having two really nice dinners at The Marc, right on the main drag, and Saffron Mediterranean Kitchen. Both had great wine and cocktail lists, too. And, as an avid coffee drinker, I always seek out the best coffee shops wherever I go. I wasn't expecting much of a specialty coffee scene in a city this size, so I was pleasantly surprised when I stumbled upon Carte Coffee, which offers specially curated beans. They even offer cupping classes, where you learn about brewing and tasting coffee, something I hadn't come across at my usual Seattle coffee spots. I enjoyed vineyard and waterfront views for less than I paid in Napa We got the kind of scenic stay in Walla Walla that we'd loved in Napa, but it cost us much less. Cheyenne Elwell We opted to stay at Eritage Resort, a quieter property about 10 minutes from downtown, hoping to recreate the vineyard setting we'd loved in Napa. Our private bungalow offered exactly that. Each morning, we woke up to views of the lake and vineyards beyond it. The resort also offered activities like wine tasting at its restaurant, biking through the vineyards, and canoeing or kayaking on the lake. We ended up simply walking through the vineyards and along the lake since there was so much else we wanted to explore in the area. Our Walla Walla bungalow cost about $296 a night before taxes, a deal compared to the $410 nightly rate we'd paid for our Napa rental three years earlier in 2023. Each place has a range of accommodation options at different price points, and this is just what we chose to book. Ultimately, we got the kind of scenic stay we'd loved in Napa, but at a price that felt much easier to justify. The slower pace and sense of community made me want to come back I love the vibes of Walla Walla. Cheyenne Elwell Before our visit to Walla Walla, I scheduled most of our tastings in advance, just as I'd done in Napa Valley to secure our spots at some of the popular wineries. But when we arrived in this smaller city, we found that we had more freedom. Walla Walla never felt too crowded, and reservations were not required for every meal and tasting (at least not during our April visit). We were able to enjoy our vacation the way I love most — making discoveries along the way that led to memorable moments. That alone made this trip all the better. I also liked feeling a noticeable sense of community among the people working in the hospitality industry. All of the hosts at the places we visited offered local recommendations for restaurants, wineries, and experiences. They also all seemed to know one another when we mentioned which places we'd already visited, making the city feel that much more connected. While trying to recreate my unforgettable  Napa Valley trip , I realized that what I wanted from a vacation had changed. Instead of cramming everything into a packed schedule and trying to snag reservations at the most well-known wineries and restaurants, I found myself enjoying the freedom to explore at my own pace. Walla Walla offered the incredible wine, hospitality, and beautiful setting I'd loved in Napa, but with fewer crowds and more opportunities for spontaneous discoveries. I'd gone hoping to recreate Napa, but Walla Walla gave me a new appreciation for small-town travel . Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Everything we know about the suspected plague case in Russia so far
events.summary: Pneumonic plague is nearly always fatal unless treated quickly with antibiotics. buboes On October 2, an Irkutsk lab employee died from pneumonia. There's confusion over what illness the woman died from, with conflicting reports out of the region. The World Health Organization says the US is at "very low risk" of being exposed to the plague. After a technician at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia died, Russian officials are attempting to calm global concerns. Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died on October 2 after being hospitalized days earlier for pneumonia in Shelekhov, a nearby town . The World Health Organization told the Associated Press on October 6 that the plague presents a "very low" risk to the broader European region. That doesn't mean we know everything — or really, much of anything — as of now. While there's no confirmation of a plague outbreak so far, conflicting reports about how Shipilova got infected, whether she was infected at work, and Russia's current safety protocols have given some medical experts pause. On October 7, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization had requested more information from Russian health authorities. "It's an odd situation that needs more transparency and requires more information for clarity," Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, the founding director of the Boston University Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases, told Business Insider. Here's everything we know so far. What happened to Darya Shipilova? Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said that Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology." A friend told CNN that she died on October 2. WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said Wednesday that the health agency doesn't know how Shipilova and urged Russian officials to provide more information. People of Baikal , an independent regional news outlet, reported that Shipilova was "deeply anxious about ever infecting anyone if something happened," according to one of her colleagues at the institute. Other colleagues called her "responsible" and described the anti-plague institute as "a serious facility" in terms of safety measures. Did she die of pneumonic plague? Reports from Russian exiled publications — ones forced to operate outside Russia or use decentralized reporting methods — speculate whether Shipilova died from the pneumonic plague. The Moscow Times , an independent publication located in Amsterdam, reported unconfirmed claims that Shipilova may have broken a test tube containing plague bacteria at the institute before she fell ill. It also reported, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash, that she was hospitalized with pneumonia symptoms and placed on a ventilator before her death. A maintenance worker walks out of the headquarters of Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor in Moscow on October 5, 2026. (Photo by Igor IVANKO / AFP via Getty Images) Igor IVANKO / AFP via Getty Images Why has Shipilova's case raised alarm? Reports from Russian state media and independent publications have often clashed, leading to more questions than answers. "The scenario, to me, doesn't fit together," Bhadelia said. If the reports of a broken test tube were true, an anti-plague institute should have several safety measures in place, such as protective equipment, ventilation, and clear treatment protocols. "She needs to have broken a test tube, have a breach in her personal protective equipment, not reported the incident, not gotten the antibiotic prophylaxis, just gone home under no one's observation, shown up at a local district hospital, and exposed 200 people," Bhadelia added. That explanation, however, is at odds with another report from the People of Baikal. Rospotrebnadzor said authorities identified and monitored 197 people who had contact with Shipilova. By October 8, the agency said it had completed the health checks, and nearly 5,000 laboratory tests found no dangerous pathogens. It had previously reported two COVID-19 cases and two rhinovirus cases among those tested. "It could be that we just don't have the perfect information, that there might be some media sensationalism in the regional media, or there may be something else going on that we don't know," Bhadelia said. Still, the current risk is nowhere near a COVID-19-level threat. What is pneumonic plague — and how does it spread? Yersinia pestis, or plague , is a bacterial infection that progresses very quickly, Bhadelia said. Patients with pneumonic plague can sometimes develop symptoms in under 24 hours. It can be fatal if left untreated. Luckily, when caught early, treatment is also pretty straightforward: A course of antibiotics. In July 2025, an Arizona man contracted pneumonic plague from two ill cats. He was medically evaluated after two days of abdominal pain, chest pain, and dry cough. He died eight hours after admission. However, all 46 people exposed to him recovered after taking antibiotics. Bhadelia said it points to one of the biggest mysteries of the Russia case so far: If Shipilova was reportedly experienced, knew she was exposed, and reported it, why wouldn't she be under quarantine and quickly treated with medication? "Early identification and post-exposure prophylaxis is one of the ways that this could be avoided," she said. Is there any risk to people in the US? The WHO says the risk outside Russia is "very low," and there is no evidence of cases in the US or beyond the Irkutsk area. Still, US officials are seeking more information. At a press conference in Iceland on October 6, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, "It's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world." President Donald Trump also said he had expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of pneumonic plague, but the Kremlin said a call hadn't been scheduled yet. When asked if he thought the incident was somehow connected to Russia developing a bioweapon, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, "We hope not," and "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so." President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House on October 05, 2026, in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images How are other countries reacting? Despite WHO advising against blanket travel or trade restrictions, parts of mainland China have taken some precautionary steps. Specifically, officials in the northeastern region, including Manzhouli along the Russian border, said they plan to strengthen surveillance with port and customs authorities. Hulunbuir, a city 130 miles south and which Manzhouli is administratively a part of, also released a risk-prevention notice for those who recently traveled to Russia. Hong Kong's health officials have started screening visitors flying from Russia, such as conducting temperature checks at airport
