events.title: US Social Security benefits to rise by 3.6 percent in 2027
events.summary: Retired Americans will see a $75 boost in monthly cheques as benefits rise amid widespread inflation challenges. United States Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent beginning in 2027, marking one of the largest cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) of the decade. On Wednesday, the Social Security Administration announced the hike after the Bureau of Labor Statistics published the Consumer Price Index for September. The alteration represents a four-year high, boosting average monthly cheques by $75 for older adults and people with disabilities. list 1 of 3 Tens of thousands protest in Spain after failed housing reforms list 2 of 3 Libyan teachers’ strike escalates as union demands major education reforms list 3 of 3 France protests: What we know as schools face nationwide action The benefit bump will roll out in January for 72 million Social Security recipients, and on December 31, for nearly 73 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) beneficiaries. Starting in 2027, the maximum limit for a taxable wage base, or income cap, is slated to increase to $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026. The social security programme is the largest federal social insurance framework in the country. The entitlement programme provides financial support for older adults and disabled people, as well as benefits for survivors of families of workers who have passed away. Funded through dedicated payroll taxes, it serves primarily as a federal pension system that replaces a portion of an individual’s pre-retirement income upon leaving the workforce. The agency bases the annual increase, closely watched by retirees and others receiving benefits, on the ‌average of the annual increase in the CPI for urban wage earners and clerical workers, also known as the CPI-W index. That index rose 3.9 percent in September and averaged about 3.6 percent for the three months of July, August and September. For 2026, the increase was 2.8 percent. The announcement comes as high US inflation continues to remain a persistent economic headwind, fuelled primarily by energy shocks from the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have caused global energy market turmoil that has sent crude oil prices above $100 a barrel. More recently, refined petroleum products like diesel fuel have climbed to ‌record highs and have contributed to a widening of inflationary pressures. Most older adults in the US believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5 percent COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.

events.title: NVIDIA and Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI Across Chip Design and Manufacturing for AI-Defined Fabs
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA introduces cuPotential, a new NVIDIA CUDA-X library developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact, accelerating already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x in early-access testing. NanoVDB, an open source library for working with 3D data, accelerates chipmaking simulation for AI-defined fabs, helping Lam Research achieve 30x faster simulation. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, accelerates chipmaking inspection for AI-defined fabs, helping KLA accelerate inspection. Applied Materials, Cadence, KLA, Lam Research, Siemens, Synopsys and other semiconductor leaders are using NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI stack across chip design, manufacturing and testing, helping drive faster development, better yield and greater production capacity. NVIDIA today announced semiconductor leaders are adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ libraries — including the new NVIDIA cuPotential library, which developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact — to advance AI-defined fabs. AI-defined fabs are semiconductor factories where AI helps engineers optimize processes, solve production issues and improve production efficiency. As demand for advanced chips rises, such fabs must expand production while managing increasingly complex manufacturing processes. Engineers need new ways to model materials, analyze inspection data and test process changes in digital twins before applying them in production. The expanded CUDA-X portfolio gives AI agents and engineering applications accelerated tools for semiconductor simulation, 3D data processing and image analysis, helping automate more engineering work across chip design and manufacturing so fabs can predict process behavior and improve yield. “The semiconductor industry made the AI revolution possible. Now, AI is transforming how chips are built,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “As fabs race to meet demand for advanced chips, NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries give AI agents accelerated simulation and inspection tools to help engineers manage complexity, improve yield and advance AI-defined fabs.” NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates How Researchers Model Atomic Interactions Understanding how atoms and molecules interact is critical to modeling semiconductor materials and manufacturing processes, but these calculations can take significant amounts of time, even in software already optimized for GPUs. NVIDIA cuPotential accelerates atomic-scale simulation with specialized GPU-accelerated functions developers can add to existing software. It helps researchers model electrical forces and other interactions across large numbers of atoms to test and refine simulations faster. Synopsys is among the early adopters using cuPotential to accelerate materials simulations. By making these modeling capabilities available to AI agents, cuPotential helps agents run, evaluate and iterate on advanced molecular simulations. In early-access testing, the library accelerated already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x. Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI-Defined Fabs With NVIDIA CUDA-X AI-defined fabs require faster ways to model chip designs, materials behavior and manufacturing processes before changes reach production. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries — including NVIDIA cuPotential for simulating atomic interactions, NVIDIA cuEST for modeling electronic behavior and NVIDIA cuDSS for solving complex engineering simulations — accelerate these workloads to help make fabs more autonomous. Synopsys is using cuPotential, cuEST and cuDSS to accelerate semiconductor simulations, with early QuantumATK results showing a potential 30x speedup using cuEST, and S-Device benchmarks showing a 12x speedup using cuDSS. The company’s AgentEngineer solutions interoperate with NVIDIA Nemotron ™ open models and NVIDIA NeMo ™ to support AI agents for chip design and verification. Cadence is using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Nemotron open models and CUDA-X libraries to bring agentic AI to the design and simulation of electromechanical systems — from semiconductors to advanced packaging and printed circuit boards. Examples include Cadence AuraStack AI Super Agent optimizing advanced packages for heat and stress 8x faster using cuDSS with Cadence Celsius, and Nemotron with ChipStack AI Super Agent for semiconductor design and verification. COMSOL is accelerating semiconductor multiphysics simulations with NVIDIA cuDSS, delivering up to 10x faster simulations to help engineers optimize equipment and processes. Its upcoming COMSOL MCP Server will use the NVIDIA Nemotron Ultra open model to enable AI-assisted modeling and design exploration. Voltai accelerates advanced chip packaging with Voltaire, its agentic multiphysics platform for 3D-IC design and simulation. Voltaire combines AI agents with GPU-accelerated solvers powered by NVIDIA cuDSS and CUDA-X libraries, compressing complex electro-thermal-mechanical simulation workflows from months to a day. ChipAgents uses NVIDIA AI infrastructure and NVIDIA model-training and optimization software to develop specialized AI models for chip design. The company is also working with NVIDIA to develop Build-A-Chip Bench , a new AI benchmark that evaluates agents across end-to-end workflows from specification to graphic data system. The benchmark gives the industry a comprehensive measure of progress toward fully autonomous semiconductor engineering. NVIDIA Open Libraries Help Prepare and Optimize Manufacturing Workflows Fabs depend on thousands of process steps that must be modeled, refined and validated before production. The NVIDIA cuLitho library accelerates calculations for printing chip patterns; NanoVDB — an open source library for working with 3D data — accelerates chipmaking simulations; and the open NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo ™ framework helps train physics AI models to predict how physical systems behave. Siemens is using cuLitho to speed up Calibre software for chip-pattern refinement and mask preparation. Its Solido team is also developing agent-driven characterization workflows with Nemotron open models and NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Lam Research intends to integrate NanoVDB into its advanced semiconductor process modeling platform SEMulator3D , part of the company’s Semiverse Solutions family of virtual products. The addition of NanoVDB is expected to accelerate select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x, while using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo has been demonstrated to assist in reducing plasma-prediction simulation time to as little as milliseconds instead of days. Luminary is applying NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo to semiconductor package design, training physics AI models to predict temperature, pressure drop and thermal stress across package configurations —

events.title: Palantir and Sadiq Khan drop legal battle over Met contract
events.summary: Dispute related to claims London mayor blocked US tech firm from £50m police deal because of concerns over its values Palantir and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, have called off their legal fight over claims the Labour mayor was blocking the US tech company from signing a contract with the Metropolitan police because of its values and ethics. Palantir and the mayor’s office for policing and crime (Mopac) announced on Wednesday they had withdrawn allegations against each other, heading off a high court trial scheduled for January. Palantir sued Mopac in June after Khan stepped in to block it from awarding Palantir a two-year, £50m deal for Scotland Yard to use AI to process intelligence in criminal investigations in a system called unified operational analytics (UOA), citing a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules. With Palantir also working for the Israeli military and for the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, Khan has previously said Londoners only wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”. Louis Mosley, who heads Palantir in the UK and Europe, responded by accusing Khan of politicising procurement and said he was “putting politics above public safety”. He said: “What Londoners value is not being mugged, not being raped by a serving police officer.” The agreement to drop the claims against each other comes a month after Palantir hired Tom Watson , the former Labour party deputy leader, as a full-time lobbyist. The firm was concerned that if public authorities were able to block it from winning contracts due to objections over the values of its senior leadership, it would undermine its ability to operate in the UK. Palantir is facing a battle to retain its £330m NHS medical data contract amid a vociferous campaign from parts of the public and some MPs for it to be replaced by a less controversial company. Palantir and Mopac said in a joint statement that Mopac’s decision in May to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company”. “Mopac recognises Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision,” it said. “Mopac’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners.” Khan said: “London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond.” Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Watson said: “The mayor and his team have recognised their actions could have created the impression that the decision to block the UOA contract was based on Palantir’s values. I’m very pleased that they have today corrected any such impression, and that even in the face of extreme provocation from highly organised pressure groups, decisions about deploying technology can still be made on their merits and in the public interest.” A new procurement process for the £50m police tech deal is under way and Mopac has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it bids, as expected. Equally, Mopac is not bound to agree to Palantir’s appointment. Each side is covering its own legal costs, no admissions of liability are made and no damages have been paid.

events.title: Netflix has a problem layoffs can't solve
events.summary: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos has guided the streamer through growth concerns before. Can he pull it off again? Bloomberg/Getty Images Netflix has responded to a slumping stock price by cutting 6% of its staff. The streamer has dealt with growth concerns before and bounced back. This time around could be different: Netflix's big worry isn't other streamers like HBO, but mega tech platforms like YouTube and TikTok. The good news for Netflix: It's been here before. In 2022, after years of breakneck growth and go-go spending, the streamer suddenly lost subscribers. Cue layoffs, a hasty pivot to an ad model it had always criticized, and tons of industry schadenfreude . But it turned out that Netflix's growth problems were overstated. Or at least, that its growth problems weren't a sign of opportunity for its streaming rivals. Years later, Netflix's position at the top of paid streaming services remains unchanged . Meanwhile, Wall Street has grown tired of watching would-be competitors like Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery struggle to make headway — which is why both of those companies are now owned by the Ellison family . The bad news for Netflix: The levers it pulled four years ago no longer seem available. It has already done the ads thing, and the live sports thing — another move they had previously sworn off. A foray into video games doesn't seem to have produced much at all. Meanwhile there has been a steady series of reports indicating that not only is Netflix's subscriber and revenue growth slowing, but its existing subscribers are finding the service less  engaging  than in the past. Netflix responded to that one by arguing that its engagement was just fine, really — and then announced it would make it harder to understand its performance by cutting back on the audience data it provides to the outside world . Most concerning: Wall Street and the rest of the media industry have started catching up to the fact that Netflix's competition isn't just other paid streamers, but giant platforms — YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok. Those companies may not have the next "Stranger Things," but they don't have to. They have unlimited content that costs them either nothing (Instagram and TikTok) or nothing upfront (YouTube). And they provide it to consumers for free, in a never-ending river of clips. It's very hard to compete with that, though you can see Netflix trying: YouTube has a lot of video podcasts, so now Netflix is doing that, too . None of that has convinced Wall Street, which is why Netflix stock is down 43% over the last year. Some of that was a reaction to the company's pursuit of HBO and Warner Bros. — an uncharacteristic mega M&A swing that investors hated. But after Netflix bailed on that one, shareholders remain skeptical. That may be why Netflix stock isn't moving on Wednesday, after the company announced it is laying off 6% of its workforce . Cutting heads can cut Netflix's costs and improve its margins. But it doesn't help the company grow — or help it compete with ruthless Big Tech platforms. events.title: New inflation warning sign
events.summary: America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy . Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further. What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note. The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote. By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month. Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%. The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening. Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge. Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs. "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months. The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December. The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report. Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch. What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike. But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated. Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component." Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures. The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated. The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

events.title: Exclusive: Koch’s venture arm backs a16z-backed Emanate’s push to bring AI to industrial sales
events.summary: In much of industrial America, a sale still starts with a spec sheet, an inbox, and a rep who has worked the account for 20 years. Emanate wants AI to do that job, and now it has one of the country’s largest private companies in its corner. Koch Disruptive Technologies , the venture arm of Koch Inc ., is making a strategic investment in the San Francisco–based startup, Emanate told Fortune exclusively. Neither side would say how much. Koch is private, and Emanate said it doesn’t disclose investment size. Koch, the second-largest private company in the U.S., runs refineries, factories, and farm-to-market supply chains, as well as software and logistics businesses. Koch said it generates more than $125 billion in annual revenue and employs about 120,000 people in more than 50 countries. “While much of the conversation around AI has centered on efficiency and cost reduction, we believe some of the biggest opportunities lie in helping companies accelerate growth,” Jon Chisholm, managing director at Koch Disruptive Technologies, said in a statement. The 20-year rep Emanate’s bet is that speed wins. An industrial buyer can usually get the same part from multiple suppliers, so whoever answers first, with a better read on price, gets the order. The company says its software sits on top of systems suppliers already use and pulls that scattered knowledge into one place. “Doing nothing isn’t neutral in this market,” Emanate founder and CEO Kiara Nirghin said in a statement. Fortune previously wrote about Emanate in February, when it came out of stealth with backing from a16z, Peter Thiel, and Reddit cofounder Alexis Ohanian. Nirghin is a Thiel Fellow, a former Google Grand Prize winner, and the youngest board member of the Google Impact Fund. “Before Emanate, customer accounts were handled per account, by whoever owned them, with whatever that person remembered and had time for,” Nirghin told Fortune in written responses. “Now they’re handled 24/7, with a full knowledge graph of every single interaction on the account.” She doesn’t call the product a chatbot or an agent. She calls it an engine. “You point it at a business metric, and the engine figures out the rest.” Emanate wouldn’t name a customer, citing confidentiality agreements. It didn’t share revenue or margin figures for any customer. In February, the company said its product could lift customer revenue by 60% to 80%. Nirghin said Emanate measures results by giving the engine to one group of accounts and comparing it with the rest of the customer’s business over the same stretch. Both groups face the same prices and demand, so the gap should be the engine’s doing. Nirghin said the engine can autonomously reactivate, manage, price, and expand accounts. But it doesn’t start out that way. “Our model is earned autonomy,” she said. “The engine starts with a human in the loop and earns the right to act on its own, step by step, as it proves itself on an outcome.” Asked about the worst mistake the engine has made, Nirghin said there hasn’t been one. “Because autonomy is earned and we deploy incredibly intelligently, it has never happened,” Nirghin said. events.title: Prismm helps banks keep inherited money in-house
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Meet Prismm , a startup that helps banks keep families’ money in-house after an account holder dies. It does this by building beneficiary and estate planning into accounts from day one, which makes the transfer of assets to heirs less complicated. Prismm is presenting its mission today on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 . Prismm was founded in 2020 by sisters Martha Underwood and Shella Sylla, who each have decades of experience in banking and finance. The pair came up with the idea for Prismm based on their own experience of seeing firsthand how difficult it can be to manage a family’s affairs in an emergency. Their father was hospitalized in 2017 after he fell while helping clear a tree from a neighbor’s roof following Hurricane Irma in Miami. Their mother, who had always relied on him to handle the family’s finances and paperwork, didn’t know where all the important documents and financial information were, and neither did they. Their father recovered, but the experience of not knowing how to access critical information stuck with them. That was the starting point for Prismm, but the idea really took shape three years later, when Underwood was working at a bank during the COVID-19 pandemic. She saw families come in after a loved one had died, scrambling to find accounts, understand bills, and figure out how to support the surviving spouse. “That’s when it hit us that this is an infrastructure problem, and as I started to dig deeper, we’ve created all of these platforms for wealth growth and tracking, but almost nothing for transition,” Underwood said in an interview with TechCrunch. “It’s still very much all manual. And that’s when we said, ‘We can digitize this process.’ We were like, ‘We can solve it because we see that there’s other families that are going to have this issue,’ and that’s when we really doubled down.” With Prismm, account holders can give designated family members access to their accounts and documents ahead of time. When the account holder dies, the designated person can log in, see the assets and documents in one place, and start eligible beneficiary transfers digitally. Because identity, consent, and supporting documents are all already on file, the process can be completed remotely, even when family members live in different states. “What’s on the market is consumer-based,” Underwood said. “What we found is when you’re asking the consumer to do something with everything else on their list, that’s going to be the last thing they do, especially women. Women are the ones that are typically going to be handling these issues when there’s a death. We’re typically the caregivers, and so asking me to manage the documents for my mom and dad while I take care of my kids, my husband, everyone else, it just becomes too much. And so, this needs to be built as infrastructure, and there needs to be as little friction as possible to allow people to get to the information that they need to execute on a decision, and so that’s why we integrate directly into bank cores.” The company has two central products, with a third in development. The first, Prismm Designate, lets banks offer customers a simple, digital way to update their own beneficiaries. The goal is to make keeping beneficiaries up to date faster and easier for both customers and banks. The second, Prismm Anchor, gives account holders a secure place to keep track of their accounts, documents, property, and other assets across multiple institutions, with controlled access for designated people. It’s offered through financial institutions, so users can manage everything without needing a separate consumer app. The third product, Prismm Continuity, is coming soon. It will guide staff and families through the transfer process step by step. The startup says this will keep the hardest part of the process within the institution rather than putting the burden on families. Underwood and Sylla describe Prismm as infrastructure that helps banks handle what happens when a customer dies. They say financial institutions lose billions in deposits to “estate attrition” every year, which is when heirs move inherited money to other institutions, because banks have no system for managing the transition of accounts after a death. Instead of losing those accounts, banks can use beneficiary information and simpler inheritance processes to keep assets, and potentially the next generation of customers, within their institution. “We will be the infrastructure that financial institutions use to move money to the next generation, because we don’t only understand that you execute on the back end,” Underwood said. “We understand that you need to be proactive and build relationships with the next generation of consumers on the front end.

events.title: 'It's rough out here': Americans struggle with rising inflation
events.summary: Kathryn Vaughn works many odd jobs to supplement her teacher's salary Kathryn Vaughn returned to work at a rural West Tennessee elementary school this autumn with a lot more stress on her plate than in previous years. The 46-year-old, like many Americans, is juggling how to provide for her family with rising costs of, as she described it, "everything". She spends her days working three different jobs to support her family of four, including as a primary school art teacher, as US inflation continues to rise . Inflation in September was above forecasts. Over the past 12 months, prices rose by 3.7% - up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August, according to officials numbers released on Wednesday. High energy prices have driven up the cost of living in America as diesel prices have hit record highs and the price of gasoline has risen too, and all of this has landed on the shoulders of everyday Americans. Once school finishes, Vaughn heads to her second job as a facilitator at an after-school programme for at-risk youth. Her five-year-old son can join too, reducing the need and cost of after-school care for Vaughn's family. "I have done some incredibly unhinged things to survive," she said. "I hand-modeled for a local jewelry store, I sell everything that sits longer than ten minutes at my house on Facebook swap sites, I resell clothes on ThredUp and Poshmark." Vaughn even writes obituaries for people who have died to make extra money. And it is still not enough to support her family. Vaughn said she had to cancel a trip to see her parents because she couldn't afford gas Punal Bhavsar thought 2026 was going to be the year he saved enough money to purchase a home. "I was thinking the interest rates would decrease and then I'd be able to purchase a house, but I don't think that's likely now," he said. The 39-year-old said the rise in the cost of goods has made saving money difficult. And the biggest burden for Bhavsar has become the price of gasoline. "I drive a car that takes premium gas, and unfortunately, in California and the area that I live in, it's almost $6 (£4.5)," he said. Come November, when midterm elections happen and the economic tumult is bound to be on voters' minds, Bhavsar said he may become a single-issue voter: "For me, it's just like gas prices have got to be under control." Punal Bhavsar says he can't afford a home with interest rates as high as they are He described the current economic outlook as bleak, and the numbers back him up. The Gallup Economic Confidence Index summarizes Americans' assessments of current economic conditions and economic outlook and puts them on a scale of -100 to +100. In September, Americans put that number at -40. A summer survey from the Guardian showed a staggering 95% of respondents think the US is in an affordability crisis. This fall, across the US, people are finding ways to cope with that. When Caitlin Green first moved to Utah seven years ago, her mom moved her into her new home and left her with some wisdom: "If you ever need a cheap, easy meal, always get ground beef." As prices have increased, Green has struggled to follow that guidance. She remembers paying $2 a pound for ground beef; now she is paying $8, she said. Caitlin Green says she's had to get creative with recipes because of the high cost of beef Instead, Green and her husband sometimes choose alternatives, opting for ground turkey or ground chicken. "[Ground beef] is almost ...not a luxury like steak... but it's just to the point where it's become a luxury; we have to think about it if we're going to purchase it," she said. Green and her husband have gone from spending some $200 a month on groceries to $400 a month. "I understand inflation is a thing, but I just feel like in my lifetime, I've never seen inflation hit so quickly and so drastically." For Vaughn, the Tennessee school teacher, the difficult choices keep coming. She was gobsmacked as her children returned to school, at the $130 bill she faced for her five-year-old son's school supplies. Vaughn made the call to have her son purchase lunch at school each day, rather than take homemade lunches, as the cost of groceries continues to rise and she calculated it would be a cheaper choice. The family has even made the call to forgo a trip to Florida this autumn to see Vaughn's parents because the price of gasoline is too much. "It's rough out here," she says. "The cost of everything is insane. Gas to get to work, my insurance costs have gone up, feeding two children and a husband. It's a lot." events.title: There's only one B-2 stealth bomber on public display in the world. Here's where I saw it.
events.summary: A wider look at the B-2. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The National Museum of the US Air Force in Ohio has the only permanent public exhibition of a B-2. B-2 planes are known for their stealth technology, long flight range, and nuclear capability. The plane on display at the museum bears remnants of the ground-based testing it underwent. I never thought I'd get to see a B-2 Spirit stealth bomber in person. The advanced warplanes, which cost around $2 billion each, can evade radar detection and drop tens of thousands of pounds of nuclear or conventional weapons. They were deployed in Operation Epic Fury , the US and Israel's joint operation targeting Iran, in March. US Air Force Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said that B-2s dropped "precision penetrating munitions on Iranian underground facilities." B-2s also dropped 30,000-pound bunker-buster bombs on Iran's nuclear facilities during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025. They also participate in occasional ceremonial flyovers, such as celebrations for America's 250th anniversary in July and Chinese leader Xi Jinping's state visit in September. All 19 of the US Air Force's operational B-2 planes are housed at Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri, where access is strictly limited. However, there is one place in the world where a B-2 is on permanent public display: the National Museum of the US Air Force in Dayton, Ohio. I visited the museum in August 2025 to see the one-of-a-kind exhibit. The B-2 Spirit stealth bomber is one of the most fearsome warplanes in the world. A US Air Force B-2 Spirit bomber, deployed to RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, flies over the English countryside near Dover, August 29, 2019. Royal Air Force The Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit entered development during the Cold War, and the first plane became operational in 1993. B-2s were used in Operation Allied Force in Serbia in 1999, as well as in Afghanistan and Iraq during Operation Enduring Freedom and Operation Iraqi Freedom in the early 2000s. With advanced stealth technologies that make it extremely difficult to detect by radar, a capacity to deploy nuclear and conventional weapons, and an ability to refuel midair for flight times that can exceed 30 hours, the B-2 is one of the most powerful warplanes in the world , and it has a very long reach. No other country operates anything comparable in combat power and capability to the B-2 bomber. The National Museum of the US Air Force added a B-2 to its collection in 2003. The National Museum of the United States Air Force. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The aircraft was shipped to the National Museum of the US Air Force in pieces in seven separate shipments. Reassembling it took restoration staff three years. At the 2003 dedication ceremony, then-museum director Charles D. Metcalf called it "one of the world's largest jigsaw puzzles." With a wingspan of 172 feet, it's one of the most prominent displays in the museum's Cold War gallery. A B-2 at the National Museum of the US Air Force. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Even with the wide-angle camera setting on my iPhone, I could barely capture the entire plane in frame. The B-2 housed at the museum never flew — it was one of two that Northrop Grumman built for ground-based testing. A wider look at the B-2. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Northrop Grumman built two test planes with the exact same specifications as the operational B-2s but without engines or instruments. A museum volunteer showed me metal patches on the aircraft, which were used to repair one of the wings after it snapped during fatigue testing. Patches under the wing. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Fatigue testing uses hydraulic plates to simulate flying conditions and test an aircraft's durability. "Whatever the maximum load is, the plane has to take 150% of that to pass the test," the volunteer said. "This one actually passed, though, at 161%, but you can see where it failed." A nose landing gear panel featured artwork added by the service members who conducted temperature testing. Artwork and signatures on the nose landing gear panel. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Technicians conducted over 1,000 hours of temperature testing at McKinley Climatic Laboratory at Eglin Air Force Base in Florida and found that the B-2 could withstand temperatures ranging from -65 degrees to 120 degrees Fahrenheit. To commemorate their work, the technicians painted a decorative "Fire & Ice" decal on the nose landing gear panel and signed their names. Nose art was popular during World War II, when pilots and crew members would often personalize their planes with cartoons, pin-ups, or tallies of their missions. It's not as common on bombers in active service today. The plane's exterior featured the emblem of the Air Combat Command. The seal of the Air Combat Command. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider Air Combat Command prepares and equips Air Force teams to provide fighter power, intelligence, cyber operations, and support for combat missions around the world. The shield-shaped emblem shows a downward-facing sword with wings spread on either side. Wording on one of the landing gear doors indicated the plane's name: "Spirit of Freedom." "Spirit of Freedom" was written on one of the landing gear doors. Talia Lakritz/Business Insider The "509th" and "Follow us" reference the origins of the modern 509th Bomb Wing, which operates B-2 planes. During World War II, the historic 509th Composite Group was responsible for deploying nuclear weapons. The B-29 Superfortress bombers that dropped the first atomic bombs on Japan were part of this unit. Their motto was "Follow Us, Follow Us, as we usher in the Nuclear Age," according to the US Air Force's official website . The 509th was instrumental in the formation of Strategic Air Command and continues to support US nuclear deterrence. I found the B-2 to be one of the most memorable exhibits at the museum. The B-2 on display. US Air Force photo by Ty Greenlees The National Museum of the US Air Force features around 350 planes and missiles over 19 acres of exhibit space. Exhibits include an Air Force One used by eight US presidents, Titan and Minuteman intercontinental ballistic missiles , and the B-29 that dropped the atomic bomb on Nagasaki. But seeing one of the world's most advanced warplanes up close was a memorable experience. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I grew up with strict parents and a fear of bad grades. I'm raising my son differently.
events.summary: The author (not pictured) said that she feared near-daily grade checks from her mother. She's choosing to do things differently with her son. Pressmaster/Getty Images I grew up with near-daily grade checks and believed anything less than perfection meant I had failed. It took me nearly 30 years to let go of the perfectionism I learned as a teen. When I check my son's grades, I make sure to focus on his effort instead of the score. Sophomore year of high school, I recall sitting at my desk in chemistry class , head down, working unsuccessfully to hold back tears. I'd done poorly on a quiz in the previous class, and I knew there'd be hell to pay when I got home. My mom checked my homework and quiz results every day, and anything less than an A or a B meant trouble. Decades later, I don't remember the grade from that day or even the subject, only the dread I felt. And the nagging question I kept to myself: Why do we treat a daily quiz as if it's my final grade ? The author said that the mindset around grades while growing up led her to chase perfection. Courtesy of Karin Crompton. I believed anything short of perfect meant I had failed As someone who loves a good sports metaphor, I can also see the situation from another perspective. What's a quiz if not practice? You go hard every practice . Even more, you aim for flawlessness. "Practice doesn't make perfect," my mother, a brilliantly successful high school softball coach (four state titles, National High School Softball Coach of the Year), would tell our team. "Perfect practice makes perfect." She had a point. She was hard on me, and I understand now it was probably the "Because I know you can do better" approach. And the pressure to perform was as much self-imposed as it was external. One basketball game, my disgust after missing a shot must have been scorchingly obvious because a teammate's father called teasingly from the stands, "You can't make 'em all," and I heard a few parents chuckle. The author, shown in high school after winning the state championship with her team, chooses to focus on effort when encouraging her son. Courtesy of Karin Crompton. He meant it in a "You'll get the next one, take it easy on yourself" way, but I wasn't thinking of the next one. I staked my worth on being a perfectionist . I saw everything as a win or a loss It would take me nearly 30 years to learn that perfectionism is a fool's errand. The aha moment came when I discovered psychologist Carol Dweck's research on fixed mindset versus growth mindset: the difference between believing your abilities are set in stone and believing they grow with effort After reading her book, "Mindset," I realized how rigid, how black-and-white, the thinking in my teen years and much of my adulthood had been. Win or lose. Success or failure. A grades were rewarded; C grades were punished. And a D? It happened just once, in the spring of my freshman year, and the fallout was nuclear. No fall sports . My son and I review his grades together, and he isn't nervous about it My son is a sophomore in high school, and we do things differently. I check his quizzes, his homework, and his projects, but I don't focus on the grade in isolation. I look at effort. My son's not afraid when I log into PowerSchool or Google Classroom to check his progress. He stands next to me at the kitchen table, watching over my shoulder. "What's going on here?" I asked recently, pointing to a few late assignments. I always start with questions, not accusations. He was ready with a reasonable answer. Some were glitches in the system, and some were teachers who hadn't updated grades yet. A couple of items were due to his confusion about steps in the process. The conversation was easy, and we were both fine. I want my son to hold himself to high standards without fearing failure His biggest challenge has been speaking up, and we've been troubleshooting ways for him to do that. How can he approach the teacher to ask for help? How can he make sure to speak up sooner rather than later? I make it clear those are his responsibilities. I've told my son something my mother never would have told me: the grade matters less to me than the effort behind it. I want him to go hard in that metaphorical practice every day, and it seems to be working. He gets good grades — including making all A's once, which I never did — doesn't procrastinate on homework, and has good rapport with his teachers. When he struggled in a couple of subjects a few years ago, we worked together. No tears. I'm raising a son with high standards, not a perfectionist. If and when something goes poorly, I want him to be resilient. I didn't do well with that as a kid and as a young adult, but so far, he's got it. Maybe that's what perfect practice is all about. events.title: What we learned from watching the Kelly Clarkson toy store security cam footage — and one question we still have
events.summary: Security footage shows Kelly Clarkson browsing inside Brooklyn toy store Art of Play during the visit that sparked her public dispute with the business. The video has no audio. : Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Video has emerged of Kelly Clarkson's viral attempt to buy an animatronic bird in a Brooklyn toy store. It sheds more light on the incident, which has made global headlines, but doesn't have sound. With no audio, the dispute’s key unanswered question remains: what was actually said? Kelly Clarkson’s feud with the Brooklyn toy store Art of Play has produced dueling accounts, social-media pile-ons, and now security footage. The spat began when the singer named and shamed the store in an X post on Sunday, saying she was given the "Pretty Woman" treatment during her visit. In return, Art of Play disputed Clarkson's account, saying she tried to buy something that wasn't for sale, and then promptly left the store when this was explained to her. Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn’t afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me. Wow, dude. You’re an idiot and just lost a… — Kelly Clarkson (@kellyclarkson) October 10, 2026 What has followed is several days of he-said, she-said accounts and a global media frenzy — all over a $15,000 (or maybe even priceless) animatronic bird. Exactly what happened remains somewhat unclear, but on Tuesday, journalist Pablo Torre made a break in the case when he shared what he said was security footage from Clarkson’s visit on his YouTube channel. Business Insider has not independently verified the footage's authenticity, but key details match what reporter Ben Shimkus found during his visit to the store on Tuesday. Shimkus filmed the store’s interior and spoke with staff during his visit. At least two products visible in the security footage match items shown in his video. The man behind the counter in the footage also appears to be one of the staff members Shimkus spoke with. You can watch the footage here: Although the CCTV footage has no audio, it establishes a few things. First, Clarkson’s visit was short. She was in the store for less than five minutes. The footage begins with her browsing and picking up several items as she walks around the shop. She then stops, most likely near the bird, and appears to speak with a store employee. The exchange is brief. Clarkson appears to point at something on the wall, while the employee gestures at the same area. The camera’s angle is partly blocked, making it difficult to see exactly what they are indicating. The employee is leaning against a surface while holding a cup of coffee as he interacts with her. Clarkson walks away shortly afterward and continues looking at other merchandise. The employee stays near the display for a moment. He later gestures toward another part of the store while looking in Clarkson’s direction. But Clarkson is facing away, looking at another display, and does not visibly react. The employee then appears to turn his attention to another customer. Clarkson eventually puts back the items she had been carrying and heads toward the exit without making a purchase. That is where the footage appears to show its most tense moment. Clarkson pauses near the counter and speaks to another employee. Her hand gestures are more animated than they were during the earlier interaction near the bird. A few customers standing nearby seem to look toward her before she leaves the store. In an interview with Curbed, the store's owner seemed to confirm a tense moment, saying, "Nothing happened in this shop to justify her scolding our shopkeeper on the way out." The video then shows Clarkson exiting and pulling out her phone. The timestamps shown in Torre’s footage indicate that her original post about the experience was published about 15 minutes later. While the video footage gives us a good sense of what happened at Art of Play between Clarkson and staff, what it doesn't give is any sense of what was actually said. With no sound on the CCTV, there is no clear sense of the tone, wording, or context of the conversations. Unless we get footage with audio, or more eyewitness accounts, we may never know exactly what happened in the Brooklyn toy store. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: I shopped at Aldi and Lidl. After comparing prices and experience, I found my winning budget grocery chain.
events.summary: Although Aldi had slightly lower prices for most items on my list, I really enjoyed my shopping experience at Lidl. Elliott Harrell I visited my local Aldi and Lidl to compare shopping experiences and prices for my grocery staples. Prices may vary, but Aldi's prices were marginally lower on most of the items I checked. Both budget grocery chains were solid, but I preferred my shopping experience at Lidl. Life feels especially expensive these days as inflation and rising costs of many essentials stretch household budgets. However, we still need to eat. Two of my biggest money-saving strategies right now include cooking more meals at home and seeking out cheaper groceries for my family of four. Luckily, a lot of grocery chains are betting on price cuts to attract shoppers right now — and the discount grocers Aldi and Lidl are especially on my radar. Both German-owned retailers primarily stock their own private-label products, which allows them to cut out the middlemen and offer lower prices to customers. Since I have both a Lidl and an Aldi within a 10-minute drive of my house, I decided to visit each to compare the selections, shopping experience, and prices to find the better store for me. I didn't love that I needed a quarter to use Aldi's carts. Elliott Harrell At Aldi, shoppers must insert a quarter into a special slot in order to use a shopping cart. They get their quarter back when they return it. It sounds like a smart strategy to incentivize people to put carts back and keep the parking lot clean. Many fans of the retailer have even embraced this by carrying special keychains that hold their " Aldi quarters ." However, I don't always have a quarter with me and didn't love this extra step. In comparison, my local Lidl had carts available to borrow, no quarter needed, which I like a lot better. From the start, Lidl felt more welcoming. Elliott Harrell The two chains originated in Germany, but Aldi has been in the United States longer. Its first US location opened in 1976, while Lidl didn't arrive until 2017. That said, the Lidl I visited opened in 2017, and the Aldi in 2007 — a decade prior, which could explain why it felt a bit more dated. This Aldi felt like a typical discount chain to me when I walked in — the lighting seemed surprisingly dim, the floor tiles didn't look very clean, and some areas felt cluttered, with product haphazardly strewn about on some of the shelves. First impressions count, and it really started my shopping on a sour note. My local Lidl felt more welcoming to me with its higher ceilings, shiny flooring, and much brighter lighting. Everything looked clean, and I didn't necessarily feel like I was walking into a bargain store. At both chains, most items were displayed in the ready-to-shelve boxes they're shipped in. This differs from traditional grocery stores and is another money-saving move — it makes products quicker to stock. Both stores had a great selection of ready-made meals. Aldi (left) and Lidl (right) both had ready-made meals available for under $10. Elliott Harrell I was impressed by both stores' selections of ready-made meals , most of which were private-label. There were a number of meals my family would eat, like the chicken fajitas from Aldi and the pulled chicken from Lidl. The prices were generally similar, typically between $5.99 and $6.99, though Aldi beat Lidl in several side-by-side comparisons. For example, Aldi's 16-ounce pork carnitas were $5.99 compared to Lidl's for $6.59. Both stores had a ton of cereal options. Both Aldi (left) and Lidl (right) had a decent selection of cereal. Elliott Harrell The cereal selections seemed similar and broad at both Lidl and Aldi . Both stores had a mix of name-brand offerings like Fruity Pebbles, Honey Nut Cheerios, and Lucky Charms, plus private-label options that seemed like dupes for popular cereals like Reese's Puffs and Honey Bunches of Oats. However, Aldi's cereal section impressed me just a little more. Elliott Harrell The cereals at both stores were mostly comparable in price, ranging from just under $2 for private-label options to about $5 for name-brand boxes. However, in a few side-by-side price comparisons, Aldi just slightly came out on top. For example, Aldi had a 16.8-ounce box of Cinnamon Toast Crunch for $3.99, or $0.24 an ounce, while Lidl had an 18.8-ounce box for $4.97, or $0.26 an ounce. On this trip, bread and milk were slightly cheaper at Aldi. Elliott Harrell As I shopped, I noticed that both stores carried similar product assortments across several categories, and the price differences were often in Aldi's favor, though typically only by a few cents. On this trip, a gallon of whole milk was $0.06 cheaper at Aldi. Both retailers had 27-ounce bags of organic seeded bread in packaging that seemed nearly identical (and resembled the packaging for the popular Dave's Killer Bread ). A loaf of Aldi's bread was $4.19, and Lidl's rang in at $4.59. Lidl's displays continued to win me over in the produce section. Bananas were a bit cheaper at Aldi (left) than Lidl (right). Elliott Harrell All in all, the fruit seemed priced similarly between the stores, with a few price differences here and there. Seedless green grapes were both $1.25 a pound across stores. A 3-pound bag of Mandarin oranges, one of my family's other favorites, was $0.04 cheaper at Aldi. Lidl's 1-pound container of organic strawberries was $4.29, and Aldi's was $4.65. Aldi's bananas were $0.02 cheaper per pound, but they were in a large box on a wooden pallet near the ground. It made me feel like I was in a budget store. At Lidl, there was a nicer, eye-level display that felt more akin to how a traditional grocery store would display bananas. Although the cost of food is important, presentation does matter to me. In terms of displays, Lidl's appealed to me more — especially in the produce section. I found applesauce and name-brand chips for the same price at both retailers. Elliott Harrell With a new kindergartener, I needed to stock up on lunchbox snacks . I was pleased to see that the same mixed 18-pack of Frito-Lay chips, with varieties like Cheetos and Doritos, cost $8.97 in both stores. Plus, a 12-pack of 3.2-ounce squeezable private-label applesauce pouches was $6.49 at both Aldi and Lidl. When comparing pizzas, the chains felt fairly evenly matched. Elliott Harrell This Lidl had a much wider selection of pizzas and more of them in stock than my local Aldi. Aldi's inventory seemed so low, I'd be worried about not being able to snag one on future shopping trips. However, I could have also visited the store right before a restock. (And Aldi's premade pizzas do get rave reviews — maybe that's why so many were missing.) Prices were generally comparable, but for the variety I wanted, Aldi's prices were slightly better. events.title: Characterization of HBM Power Consumption (ETH Zurich, NYU)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at ETH Zürich and New York University published a technical paper titled “Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips.” “We perform the first comprehensive experimental characterization of power consumed by real HBM2 DRAM chips. Our extensive characterization yields 1) the empirical basis for developing new, accurate HBM power models or validating existing power models and 2) key insights into structural and data-pattern-dependent variation of power in HBM2 chips. Out of our 13 new findings and 6 key takeaway messages, we highlight: 1) a read operation consumes significantly higher current than any other operation and 2) the toggled data bus signals in a data transfer burst significantly affect current draw where toggling all HBM2-internal bank group bus signals causes 29.4% higher power consumption than keeping them constant. events.title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 13:47 BST US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month. The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August. Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran. The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US. Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%. Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI). It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy. The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change. There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise. If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example. Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices. Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel. Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100. What is the current rate of inflation? Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices. Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months. In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics. Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year. Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher. At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%. Will the inflation hike change Social Security payments? Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027. The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month. The cost of living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72m people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December. How have tariffs affected inflation? Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world. While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them. Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. US President Donald Trump raised tariffs Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost. In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax. Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas. Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year. While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.

events.title: Deezer will soon let you filter out AI-generated music
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Streaming platform Deezer remains steadfast in its intent to help users avoid listening to AI-generated music: The company on Tuesday said it is working on a new toggle that lets users filter out AI-generated music uploaded to its platform. The feature is expected to be available before the end of the year. Deezer said turning on the toggle will stop you from seeing AI-generated tracks, albums, and related artists in search results. “We’ve seen clear user demand for the ability to filter out AI-generated music, and we are now giving everyone the option to remove this content completely from their streaming experience on Deezer, and focus only on human creators and creations, if they wish,” Deezer CEO Alexis Lanternier said in a statement. He added that the explosion of AI music on the platform was one of the catalysts for the toggle-based features. The company cited a survey from last year, which noted that around 45% of Deezer customers wanted a way to remove AI music from their feeds. Deezer added AI-detection tooling last year and has been reporting on the number of tracks being uploaded to the platform ever since. At that time, AI-generated tracks represented 10% of daily uploads . In July, the company said that more than 50% of daily uploads to its platform were AI-generated tracks , with an average of 90,000 tracks per day. Other music streaming services have also created their own policies in relation to AI music. Bandcamp has completely banned AI tracks, while Tidal cut off monetization for people uploading AI music. Spotify has taken a leaner stance, only tagging AI tracks and artists more prominently on its platform. In August, Variety reported that Apple Music was looking to label AI tracks by the end of the year. Besides platform-based tagging, users are also turning to independent tracking systems to identify AI music. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Netflix to lay off about 1,000 employees in biggest cuts since 2022
events.summary: Streaming company faces ⁠tough competition for viewers and engagement ⁠from legacy rivals ​and YouTube Netflix is laying off 6% of its workforce, ⁠or roughly 1,000 employees, in its biggest cuts since 2022, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters, as the streaming pioneer faces ⁠tough competition for viewers ⁠from legacy rivals ​and YouTube. The bulk of the job cuts would be in Netflix’s product, tech, legal and human-resources teams, the email co-CEOs Greg Peters and ⁠Ted Sarandos sent to employees on Wednesday showed. “Our mission – to entertain the world – is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined ⁠about where we prioritize our people and resources,” they said in the memo. “Our business is ​strong and growing, and we remain on ‌track to deliver our full-year ‌forecast.” Netflix shares, down about 25% so far this year, rose 0.7% on Wednesday. The company ‌had about 16,000 employees at the end of last year. This year, the streaming company faced doubts about its ability to sustain the growth that disrupted the US media industry by putting pressure on cable TV businesses. Engagement, or the amount of time users spend on Netflix, has become a key concern for investors as platforms such as YouTube and TikTok ‌attract viewers with free-to-watch, user-generated content that gives them a cost advantage over Netflix. A failed pursuit of Warner Bros Discovery’s streaming and studio assets earlier this year ​deepened doubts about Netflix’s strategy. Paramount completed its $110bn Warner Bros acquisition earlier this month to form Skydance. “They haven’t been able to find like another line of major revenue,” said Ross Benes, a senior analyst at eMarketer, adding the company remained reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a ceiling. “Eventually, ⁠because they’ve kind of nearing a ceiling with that, they’ll need another ​revenue stream to diversify, ​and that’s where it’s been more of ​a struggle.“ Netflix has been trying to expand beyond its subscription business by ​investing in an ad ‌tier, live programming ​and gaming. Its last major ​round of layoffs came in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs in two rounds after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday’s memo.

events.title: Zenzap raises $44M for its AI chat app that aims to replace WhatsApp in the workplace
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Many businesses around the world use consumer-facing chat apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, or iMessage to talk and coordinate with staff, and exchange documents or data. Guy Weiss is building Zenzap , a private messenger with AI that wants to help companies communicate with their staff and arm them with their organization’s context while staying in line with IT and security rules. The company has raised $44 million in funding from investors including Bessemer, Lightspeed, and The Garage, as well as individual investors Wix president Nir Zohar and former GM of EY, Yoram Tietz. The fundraise is interesting because Weiss is raising money for the first time in his career. In 2012, he bootstrapped e-commerce marketing platform StuccoMedia, and sold it to Market Group in 2015. After that, he became an investor for a few years. In 2022, he founded Zenzap after meeting Bessemer partner Adam Fisher and noodling on different ideas along with his current co-founders Noam Neumann and Jonatan Bien. Weiss said he initially bootstrapped the app and worked out of Bessemer’s office. “I didn’t want to raise capital. The only thing I had to lose was my name, and I was super afraid to do a second round as a founder and become a failure, because my first round was very successful. I didn’t need to work for money. So, when I met Adam, I actually started my idea with my own capital,” he told TechCrunch. Weiss said Fisher convinced him that Zenzap should be a venture-backed business, as the company would need capital to scale. He said that the idea was to build a messaging app for a wide range of businesses, ranging from hospitality and construction, to healthcare and fast food. “You can’t use WhatsApp or iMessage within a workplace with the AI agent on top of it because it doesn’t comply with IT. So that’s off the table. You can’t implement Slack and Microsoft Teams because they were not built for this day-to-day use case for mobile-first that is meant for average users,” Weiss said. Zenzap offers usual chat features on its free tier, including group chats and direct messages, task management, calendar integration, and schedule management, as well as AI-powered voice chat and search. Organizations can pay for plans starting from $51 per month for up to 20 users to unlock voice and video calls, smart task sorting, task templates, and higher limits on file storage. The paid tier also lets you use the AI search across the workspace and turn messages into tasks. The company also offers AI agents for workflow automation as well as AI-aided voice note and call transcriptions. For these features, it has a credit-based pricing system. At the moment, Zenzap lists organizations like FedEx, Dollar General, Taco Bell, Starbucks, Casey’s, and Regal as clients. Weiss added that branches of fast food chains like IHOP and McDonald’s often coordinate shifts and talk about supply on its platform. “Each vertical has its own use case and workflows, which they self-serve with AI, but they all share something in common,” he said. The startup has 50 staff in the U.S., Tel Aviv, and Europe. In the near future, the company wants to hire in its product and R&D departments. Bessemer’s Fisher said Zenzap’s focus on catering to a broad range of people could work in its favor. He said that even the venture firm is using the messenger within its investment team to discuss and manage deal flows, showing that it can cater to different kinds of audiences. “The only work platform with any allegiance is Slack, and that’s almost entirely among the developer community. Zenzap is not focused on developers, but on the other 99% of employees using personal messaging apps and waiting for an agent of their own. People desperately want a clear separation of work from their personal lives, and the adoption of personal and work agents makes it imperative that separation happen now,” he told TechCrunch in an emailed statement. Elisabetta Trevisan - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images In May 2025, Pope Leo XIV was elected as the current pope. Hailing from Chicago, he has been outspoken about the impact of AI on society during his papacy. Pope Leo XIV was recently diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery. Pope Leo XIV was elected pope in May 2025. Born Robert Francis Prevost, Pope Leo XIV has since made his mark on the papacy, writing his first encyclical about the impact of artificial intelligence on society and making key appointments to the Vatican. He's the first pope from the US and the 267th pope overall. Most recently, Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Here's what you need to know about Pope Leo XIV. Robert Prevost was born in Chicago in 1955. US Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost attends the funeral of Pope Francis in 2025. Franco Origlia/Getty Images He's 71 years old and was ordained to the priesthood in 1982. He has two brothers. He's also a citizen of Peru , where he was first assigned in 1985, and later served as the Bishop of Chiclayo. He has a doctorate and is multilingual. Pope Leo XIV, Robert Francis Prevost, celebrates a Mass in 2025. Franco Origlia/Getty Images He studied at Villanova University and the Catholic Theological Union of Chicago. In 1984, he obtained his Canon Law licentiate, and in 1985, he defended  his doctoral dissertation  at the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas. Pope Leo XIV speaks English , Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French. Pope Francis appointed him to one of the Vatican's most influential positions. Pope Francis and Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost in 2023. Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images In 2023, the then-pope appointed then- Bishop Prevost as Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, which plays a key role in bishop nominations. In 2024, Pope Leo said in an interview with Vatican News that a "bishop is not supposed to be a little prince sitting in his kingdom, but rather called authentically to be humble, to be close to the people he serves, to walk with them and to suffer with them." A group of 133 cardinals elected him during the May 2025 conclave. Cardinals of the Catholic Church at the papal conclave in 2005. Arturo Mari - Vatican Pool/ Getty Images The process is known as the conclave . It took two days and four rounds of voting for the cardinals to agree on a new pope, per the AP . Before the conclave, the National Catholic Reporter wrote that it was unlikely the US cardinal would become pope because of political implications. Yet Cardinal Prevost was considered a contender by others, especially as the week went on, ABC News reported. Pope Leo XIV gave his first message on May 8, 2025. Pope Leo XIV, Robert Prevost, addresses the crowd from the balcony of the St Peter's Basilica in 2025. TIZIANA FABI/AFP via Getty Images Speaking from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Leo XIV said, "Peace be with all of you" in his first words in his new role. He spoke in Italian and then Spanish. "My experience of Cardinal Prevost was that he's not a showboat," Father Mark R. Francis, who worked with Pope Leo in the past, told CBS News in 2025. "He's very calm, but extremely intelligent, and extremely compassionate." Since becoming pope, he has begun putting his stamp on the Church. TOPSHOT - Pope Leo XIV is welcomed by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Presidential Palace in Ankara on November 27, 2025. (Photo by Andreas SOLARO / AFP via Getty Images) Andreas SOLARO / AFP via Getty Images He canonized Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati in September 2025, and made his first foreign trip to Turkey and Lebanon in November and December of that year. His first encyclical, a letter written by the Pope for guidance, addressed AI. Pope Leo XIV attends the presentation of his first Encyclical Letter, "Magnifica Humanitas," on May 25, 2026. Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty Images Business Insider's Joshua Nelken-Zitser identified  three main takeaways  from the encyclical: the power of AI should not be monopolized by a small group; AI developers should ensure that what they are cultivating "is a genuine good"; and warnings that AI could lead to mass unemployment. In addition to the encyclical, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about AI multiple times, including  a recent address  to artists and curators in which he said, "We urgently need to distinguish human art from what is produced by machines." Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer on October 13, 2026. Pope Leo XIV arriving at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital ahead of his surgery. Isabella Bonotto/Anadolu via Getty Images The pope underwent an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, the Holy See press office said in October. It added that the surgery was successful with no complications. The operation confirmed a previously suspected lung cancer diagnosis. On Wednesday, the Holy See press office said the "night passed calmly" for the pope . Read the original article on Business Insider
