events.title: Floqer’s AI agents research sales prospects so teams don’t have to
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Floqer is an autonomous customer knowledge platform that provides business-to-business sales and marketing teams with an AI-powered database designed to continuously collect, organize, and update the information used to understand their customers. Floqer is pitching Wednesday on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 . The startup told TechCrunch ahead of the presentation that it plans to open-source the technology behind its autonomous customer knowledge database. It’s targeting early 2027 for the release, pending security reviews. Floqer also says it has surpassed $1.2 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), and that its overall revenue has grown roughly tenfold over the past year. The startup was founded by Shivam Mahajan, the CEO, and Zaaheda Islam, who met at university. Before Floqer, Mahajan worked as a software engineer at Kyndryl, and Islam worked as a senior data scientist at Axis Capital. Floqer’s first product looked nothing like its current one. “We started with a Chrome extension, which is called ‘Super Chat,’” Mahajan told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this month. “Anybody can go and log in with their ChatGPT account and then understand [information] and take notes.” The founders soon noticed that enterprise companies were using the extension to clean up data in their customer relationship management (CRM) systems. Conversations with those companies showed that keeping CRM data clean was mostly manual work, with few established processes for keeping customer records up to date. “When we spoke with them, they told us that it’s super manual for them to clean their CRM data, and there were no established processes around that,” Mahajan said. “So that was insightful for us, and then we pivoted from there to build Floqer.” The problem Floqer is trying to solve is familiar to anyone who has worked in sales or revenue operations. Finding potential customers takes hours of searching Google, LinkedIn, company websites, job boards, and other sources to identify companies that fit a particular profile, then tracking down the right people and their contact information. Floqer aims to automate much of that research. Users can describe what they are looking for, and its AI agents search across different sources to build lists of relevant companies and contacts. The company says its system can enrich accounts, or add detail about the companies a sales team is targeting, using more than 100 third-party data sources. When it needs a verified email address or phone number, Floqer uses a “waterfall” approach, checking one data provider after another until it finds usable information. The system also continuously monitors the web for changes. If a prospect changes jobs, gets promoted, or works at a company that raises new funding, those updates can be reflected in the user’s customer records. Floqer describes the technology as a fleet of AI agents that continuously research companies, people, and customer interactions, so team members don’t have to perform that work manually. According to the company, customers have reported cutting prospecting time by as much as 70%. “Our autonomous customer knowledge database is only available to a limited audience, mostly due to how much demand our team can actually serve properly,” Mahajan said. “But open-sourcing it will help us fix that.” The decision comes partly in response to customer demand. Mahajan said some companies want to host their own data rather than keep it inside a vendor’s proprietary platform. Others want to modify the technology or build on top of it. “Our mission is to really enable every team to build their central source of growth,” Mahajan said. Before releasing the database publicly, Floqer is conducting security reviews because the database can contain sensitive customer information and large companies already use it. Floqer was founded in 2024 and has raised $2 million in pre-seed funding, with participation from investors such as Perplexity’s F7 Fund, N49P, Tidal Venture Partners, and Perplexity co-founder Denis Yarats. It says it now has eight employees and more than 1,000 customers, including Perplexity, Wise, and AngelList. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Why one spoiler candidate is now trying to replicate his work nationwide
events.summary: The News Aaron Day’s third-party campaign cost Republican Kelly Ayotte her Senate reelection bid in 2016. Now he’s trying to take his spoiler project national. With several Senate races tight enough for an alternate candidate to make a real difference, whether they’re Libertarian or another third party, Day is looking to spend as much as $2.5 million — or perhaps less, if his effort works as designed — to cost the GOP the Senate. Day’s strategy is simple: Use his Stark Freedom PAC to spend relatively small amounts on online ads made with AI that boost name ID for spoiler candidates, figuring he can do just enough to hand those races to the Democrats. Republican leaders are highly skeptical of Day’s efforts, but he sees a real chance at disrupting races across the country. What’s more remarkable is how open he is about his goal of ending the Senate Republican majority. “You call it a spoiler campaign, I call it holding Republicans accountable,” Day told Semafor in an interview. His website is equally explicit: “We fund the margin. It costs the GOP the Senate.” Day is targeting eight states where he’s deduced that boosting third-party candidates would hurt the Republican nominee: Texas, Iowa, New Hampshire, Minnesota, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, and Kansas. It’s a “Moneyball” theory of modern politics, banking on a relatively small amount of cash to mess up the margins in close contests. Nudging a third candidate’s vote share up by a couple of percentage points higher, as he explained, takes a lot less money than the obscene amount needed to actually win a race. “People are going to be shocked after the fact at how effective this is,” Day said. “Most voters don’t know that the third-party option exists, and a lot of these candidates don’t actually have money, and they’re not allowed to participate in the debates.” In addition to Ayotte’s 2016 New Hampshire campaign , Libertarian candidates’ support boosted former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester in his 2006 and 2012 Montana races. The effect was clear in Nevada’s 2024 Senate race, which Democrats narrowly won as nearly 5 percent of voters picked a candidate outside the two major parties. And no one can forget Jill Stein’s Green Party spoiler effect on Hillary Clinton’s presidential chances in 2016. It’s hard to see how giving Democrats the Senate helps advance Day’s causes — which include concerns over centralized digital currencies and government surveillance via cryptocurrency legislation. But Day says he wants to check President Donald Trump through “gridlock” and that with Democrats in charge, the crypto market structure bill and other legislation he dislikes will continue to stall. Several Republican groups, including the National Republican Senatorial Committee and Senate Leadership Fund, declined comment. While third-party hopefuls appreciate his support, their goals are different. Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate in Texas, said he’s running to win, not to cost Republicans Senate control. “I’m running to defeat the corrupt two-party system,” Brown told Semafor. “But I would say this, if the Republicans lose the Senate on November 3: The good news is, the Republicans lost control of the Senate. The bad news is, the Democrats won control of the Senate.” Day said his model would be replicable to punish a Democratic majority in the future as well, by boosting Green Party candidates to eat into their candidates’ margins: “I actually view this, if it works, as something that can be used to hold both major parties accountable.” Know More So, why do this? Day was originally planning to be a candidate himself this fall, even fighting to get ballot access in New Hampshire to take out former Sen. John Sununu, R-N.H. But he said he didn’t run, in part because he was in negotiations with Republicans and the Trump administration over a list of demands that weren’t fulfilled: “I was told something definitive was going to happen, and it did not.” He declined to go into further detail; the White House did not comment. After the schism, he threw his support behind Edmond Laplante, a Constitution Party candidate in New Hampshire. He then decided to “duplicate” his 2016 bid against Ayotte by boosting anti-war candidates to reach the small percentage of “disaffected voters in these swing states.” “People do not want to vote for the Republican, but a lot of people still don’t want to vote for the Democrat,” Day said. “Texas is in play, Kansas is in play, South Carolina is potentially in play. I mean, who would have ever thought? But it’s true, and this really could make the difference.” Day’s ads are unique to each race, but most have peppy AI music critiquing the GOP candidate. They knock Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., for her pro-war votes and boost Libertarian Kasie Whitener; in New Hampshire, they hit Sununu for supporting the Wall Street bailout; in Texas, they whack state attorney general Ken Paxton for being a “mouthpiece for DC” and dub Brown the “voice of Texas.” Republicans are more worried about Day’s machinations in New Hampshire and don’t believe he’ll be effective anywhere else. Burgess’s view I’m a skeptic, and so naturally lean a bit bearish on the idea of a national spoiler campaign funded by the political equivalent of spare change. I watched a bunch of Day’s ads, as well, and found them somewhat tedious but also relentlessly on-message in driving the name ID of these somewhat obscure candidates. (It’s possible that AI-generated music just isn’t for me.) But Day is onto something with the spoiler effect, whether it’s induced by him or not. It’s undeniable that disaffected Republicans who cast primary votes for, say, Sen. John Cornyn in Texas or Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina may struggle with voting for Paxton and Graham — but not want to support their Democratic counterparts either. It just won’t be clear until Election Day how big of a threat these candidates are. The percentages they are drawing in polls are small enough to be a rounding error; given how tight the polls are, a rounding error still could cost Republicans multiple Senate seats. Notable Brown is courting jilted Cornyn voters , Houston Public Media reported earlier this year.

events.title: Netflix to lay off 1,000 staff amid intensifying competition for user attention
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Netflix is laying off about 6% of its employee base, or close to 1,000 staff, the company confirmed to TechCrunch. The streaming giant said most of the cuts would affect its product, tech, legal, and human resources departments. The company said it will “continue to invest aggressively in high impact areas” to improve its service, and stated it is on track to deliver its full-year forecast. Netflix had 16,000 full-time employees as of the end of last year, according to its annual filing with regulators. The Wall Street Journal first reported the news, citing an internal memo sent to employees. “Our mission—to entertain the world—is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” the Journal cited the company’s co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters as writing in the memo. The layoffs come in the wake of a protracted bidding war for Warner Bros. Discovery’s streaming and studio businesses that Netflix lost to Paramount Skydance earlier this year. Netflix ostensibly saw great potential in Warner Bros.’ assets, which include its studios, HBO, streaming platforms, games, and TV networks such as CNN and HGTV. Long the dominant TV app, Netflix has in recent years faced intensifying competition from the likes of YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and other social apps to attract and keep users’ eyes. According to reports from various market research firms, social apps like TikTok are catching up to Netflix when it comes to user engagement, and YouTube is said to have surpassed Netflix in average daily viewing in 2025. The streaming giant has been trying extensively to extract more value from its subscribers, raising prices , expanding its ad-supported tier, and investing in live events and sports , gaming, and children’s programming to increase user engagement. It has also bet on AI-supported features , gaming , and video podcasts , and has dabbled in short-form video content alongside redesigning its mobile app to compete for users’ attention with social media platforms. events.title: US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms
events.summary: Final inflation report before voters go to polls comes amid widespread anger over cost of living under Trump Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday. US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living. Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%. Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually. Price increases this year have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record high last month. September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990. The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans more than $1,020 per household, according to Brown University , and a total of $133bn for all US consumers. Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump. In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest inflation report. On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections. “They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote. Later on Tuesday, Trump defended his record on the economy during a rally in Wasilla, Alaska, saying that his support for families has been “substantial”. “Every time they want to try and get me, they say ‘affordability’,” he said. Heightened inflation will put more pressure on the Federal Reserve to increase interest rates, its tool to cool prices. Last month, the Fed raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated prices. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%. “Inflation in the US has come in higher than expected, in a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, in a statement. “The president has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.”

events.title: US mortgage rates reach 7.5%; home-buying slump hits sixth week
events.summary: The contract rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage ticked up one basis point to 7.50%. US mortgage rates rose to 7.50%, the highest since November 2023, and home-buying activity fell for a sixth straight week. The Mortgage Bankers Association said purchase applications dropped 4%, while refinance demand hit its lowest level since early 2025. Experts warned the fourth quarter could see fewer closings, as Redfin reported September contract signings fell 4%, the biggest drop in more than three years. WASHINGTON – US mortgage rates continue to rise, pushing down home purchasing activity for a sixth straight week. The contract rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage ticked up one basis point to 7.5% in the week ended Oct 9, still the highest level since November 2023, according to Mortgage Bankers Association data released on Oct 14. Rates are up nearly one percentage point since the end of June. The MBA’s purchase index, which measures loan applications, dropped 4%, marking the sixth straight weekly decline – the longest such stretch since July-August 2023. The gauge stands at the lowest level since early 2025. Home sales had shown signs of stabilising prior to the recent run-up in mortgage rates. Data out on Oct 13 from the National Association of Realtors showed a slight increase in purchases of previously owned homes. However, those data are based on contract closings and mainly reflected contract signings prior to the latest surge in borrowing costs. “The fourth-quarter outlook for closing activity will clearly be down, maybe even measurably down,” because of higher rates, said Lawrence Yun, NAR chief economist. Data released this week from brokerage Redfin Corp showed contract signings plunged 4% in September from a month earlier. That was the biggest decline in more than three years, according to Redfin’s figures. Meanwhile, MBA’s refinance gauge fell for an eighth straight week, to the lowest level since early 2025. The overall market index fell 2.7%, a sixth straight decline. The MBA survey, which has been conducted weekly since 1990, uses responses from mortgage bankers, commercial banks and thrifts. The data cover more than 75% of all retail residential mortgage applications in the US. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Diesel shortage to persist into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA warns
events.summary: The global diesel shortage triggered by the Iran war is set to persist well into next year, with depleted inventories unlikely to recover until the second half of 2027, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday. Supplies of gas oil, which contains diesel and heating oil, will fall short of demand in the fourth quarter, even as refineries increase output towards the yea's end, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly oil market report. Without a recovery in refined-product exports from the Middle East, further cuts in consumption and the “heavy economic costs these will entail” may be needed to balance the market, it warned. Wholesale diesel prices surged to record highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US last month and exceeded $200 in Singapore. Prices have since eased but remain nearly double crude benchmarks and prewar levels. US diesel pump prices topped $6 a gallon for the first time in September, up about 70 per cent since the Iran war began, the IEA said. The shortage reflects a sharp decline in shipments from two major suppliers. Combined net gas oil exports from the Middle East and Russia plunged more than 60 per cent annually to 820,000 barrels per day last month, a loss of 1.3 million bpd. Gulf export routes remain constrained, while Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged Russian oil refineries. Higher shipments from the US and China have failed to offset the losses. Inventories offer little relief ahead of winter. US diesel stocks ended September at a 14-year seasonal low, while European commercial gas oil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July. On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflict. Gulf rebound Gulf crude exports rebounded sharply last month, rising by 4.4 million bpd to 13.9 million bpd, more than three quarters of prewar levels. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz climbed to 10.9 million bpd, supported by increased ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. However, refined products and liquefied petroleum gas shipments have recovered much more slowly, remaining below half their prewar volumes. The IEA warned that the recovery remains fragile following the bombing of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline on September 11 and an escalation in Houthi attacks on regional energy infrastructure and shipping throughout this month. North Sea Dated crude, a physical oil benchmark, was trading near $134 a barrel when the report was prepared, reflecting mounting supply risks and record freight costs. Global observed oil inventories stood 509 million barrels below prewar levels at the end of September, leaving markets increasingly exposed to more disruption. Demand outlook cut The IEA cut its 2027 oil demand forecast by 630,000 bpd and downgraded its global economic growth outlook by 0.4 percentage points to 3 per cent, as central banks raise interest rates to contain war-driven inflation. Global oil consumption is now expected to rebound by two million bpd next year, but remain 620,000 bpd below 2025 levels. For 2026, demand is forecast to fall by 2.6 million bpd to 102.4 million bpd, with diesel accounting for about a quarter of the decline. The agency also trimmed its global supply forecast for this year by 60,000 bpd to 100.7 million bpd, a decline of 5.8 million bpd from 2025. Output is projected to rebound by 7.7 million bpd in 2027, although recovery remains vulnerable to renewed disruption in the Gulf.

events.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
events.summary: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus , a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions. Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders. On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay , TokenSpot , and the Tsunami Payments service . As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “ How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks ,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “ Heleket ” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations. The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy. “Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.” The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions. In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations. TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing. Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible. “A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn . “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.” As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said. Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction. Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation. Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation , which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara . That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara. The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

events.title: UAE-backed GlobalFoundries to run two chip plants under $21bn US-Japan deal
events.summary: Japan is set to invest up to $21 billion in two chip-production plants in New York state that will be operated jointly by GlobalFoundries and the US government, the semiconductor manufacturer said on Wednesday. In a separate agreement, the Commerce Department will take a 4 per cent equity stake in the company, bringing the US government's stake to 7 per cent, chief executive Tim Breen told Reuters. The company is majority owned by Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company. The move is part of a deal struck last year, under which US tariffs on Japanese imports were lowered from 25 per cent to 15 per cent while Japan will invest $550 billion in the US economy . “This is a bold new initiative for semiconductor manufacturing, bringing together the United States and Japan with GF’s differentiated technology and decades of manufacturing expertise to accelerate trusted capacity in New York,” Mr Breen said. Shares in GlobalFoundries were trading 4.9 per cent higher at $48.99 each as of 10am ET. Under the agreement, Japan will provide all the capital while GlobalFoundries will input its technological and manufacturing expertise, and operational capacities. The company makes integrated circuits on silicon wafers designed to help support AI and high-performance computing, communications infrastructure, and applications for aerospace and defence. The deal comes with an initial investment of about $10 billion to boost the construction of a new 300mm semiconductor manufacturing plant – or “fab” – expected to come online in 2029, with an additional $10 billion to fund a second fab. The company said the first fab will add about 900,000 of the 300mm wafers to annual US manufacturing capacity when fully operational, with a second factory adding about the same. GlobalFoundries also agreed with the Commerce Department to amend its existing award under the Chips Act to reallocate $955 million and accelerate investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium and advanced packaging at its sites in the US states of New York and Vermont. The announcement comes about a week after GlobalFoundries announced a $2 billion manufacturing agreement with TSMC.

events.title: English and Welsh water firms could be forced to return £107m via lower bills
events.summary: Yorkshire and Thames among providers facing penalties for missing performance targets, but bills could rise elsewhere Thames Water, Yorkshire Water and other providers could be forced to cut tens of millions of pounds from household bills after the regulator said they had missed performance targets. Customer bills at Yorkshire Water could fall by £27 on average, while those at Thames could decrease by £7, according to estimates by Ofwat, the regulator of the privatised industry in England and Wales. The water industry has faced growing criticism in recent years amid rising bills , scrutiny over sewage pollution , high levels of debt and underinvestment in ageing infrastructure. As water customers cannot switch away from their provider if it underperforms, Ofwat instead has an “outcome delivery incentive” (ODI) system of automatic payments or penalties based on agreed targets. Yorkshire and Thames will have to return £75.1m and £45.8m, respectively, after missing targets in 2025-26, Ofwat said. The payments will add to the financial pressures on the companies, although Thames has been allowed to delay some of the penalties by a year. Yorkshire is among the companies subject to enhanced monitoring by Ofwat over its financial resilience, while the government is considering whether to bring Thames Water under public control after years-long negotiations to reduce its crippling debts. The other companies that must return money to customers include: Dŵr Cymru (or Welsh Water), at £16.7m; South West Water, at £16m; and United Utilities in north-west England, at £13.4m. However, some companies will receive a reward payment because they met their targets – covered by higher bills. Severn Trent, which serves the Midlands, south-west England and parts of Wales , and Northumbrian Water are in line to receive an extra £41.8m and £35.9m respectively, Ofwat said. Northumbrian customers’ bills could rise by an average of £21, the regulator said. Severn Trent customers could pay £8 more per year. Overall, the industry is expected to cut its bills by a net £240m for failures during 2025-26. Of this, £107m is expected to be returned to customers via lower bills in 2027-28. Ofwat said at this stage the figures were still at the draft stage and not every household would receive the same change. Bills are “affected by a range of factors and the effect will vary by company and customer type”, the regulator said. It will make its final decision on the payments by 15 December, which will take effect on bills from 1 April 2027. Ofwat recently announced that water companies could increase annual tariffs by an extra £3.4bn, on top of the 36% average rise agreed over five years to 2030. Customer bills are rising to pay for long-overdue investments to fix leaking pipes and treatment works, as well as to pay for new assets such as reservoirs. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Andy Burnham last month said the government would pave the way for public ownership of water firms and promised a 10-year path to a “very different water system in the UK”. The comments suggested the prime minister might opt for a temporary nationalisation of debt-laden Thames Water as the government seeks to make a decision on a £10bn rescue takeover put forward by lenders for the UK’s biggest water supplier. Ofwat’s announcement came after Burnham said customers must not be “treated as a blank cheque” and after the regulator said in August it planned to allow yet more bill increases on top of those already agreed. A government spokesperson said: “This government won’t allow customers to be treated as a blank cheque, and we are committed to protecting households from cost-of-living pressures. We will always challenge water companies where they seek to pass unnecessary costs on to households. “We will deliver a strengthened water bill that puts people first, ensuring affordable access to clean water, driving down pollution, and strengthening public control.” A Yorkshire Water spokesperson said: “We recognise that our performance last year fell short of the standards we and our customers expect in some areas, and we remain focused on improving. “We are already delivering Yorkshire’s largest ever environmental investment programme and with the help of over 1,000 new colleagues, we’ve completed improvements at almost 300 locations across the county.” A Thames Water spokesperson said: “To help smooth customer bills, Ofwat has agreed to defer the timing of some ODI penalties by one year. This does not remove or reduce the penalties. Customers still receive the full benefit, and Thames Water does not gain financially. We recognise these penalties reflect areas where our performance fell short. The deferral will prevent sharp year-on-year bill movements, which research shows our customers want us to avoid.”

events.title: Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief
events.summary: Trump's diesel deal with Russia unlikely to bring down fuel prices As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that. With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon. That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin . "The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne. The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said. Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined." Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler. But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war. Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars. "If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said. Trump expects prices to fall at record speed In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel. He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps. Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets." Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel. But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on. Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky. Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home. The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports. At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries. Debates over export restrictions continue Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan. "There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again." Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions . "An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski. "Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added. Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact. According to calculations by the platform The World Data , the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels. Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand. "I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

events.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
events.summary: Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment. Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter. That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month. The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax. How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment. Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January. However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years. The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

events.title: Merry squishmas: £10 squeezy banana on list of top festive season toys
events.summary: Social media-driven craze puts ‘squishies’ up there with evergreen favourites such as Lego and Barbie, Hamleys says A cartoonish banana so addictively squidgy that it is “really difficult to put down” is tipped to be among the must-have toys this Christmas , according to expert buyers at Hamleys. The £10 “slow-rise, squeezable, sensory” fruit taps into the “squishies” craze that is fuelling a high street boom in toy sales. In the coming weeks, Hamleys expects to sell thousands of the Big Squij toys, which come in a variety of food and animal shapes filled with a flour-based compound. Their popularity has been supercharged by social media and a growing army of child and adult collectors. There are more than 260,000 TikTok posts and more than 600,000 on Instagram tagged #squishies. The most popular official brand, NeeDoh, has 1.1m TikTok followers. Victoria Kay, the head of buying and merchandising at Hamleys, said the “squishy craze is only really just getting going”. “The demand is huge. There is a wonderful simplicity to their power whether you are a young child or an adult . Literally once you squeeze one, it’s really difficult to put it down.” Squishies are the biggest toy trend of the year, according to Andrew Murphy, who runs The Entertainer, the UK’s largest chain of toy shops. Some theories suggest their viral success is because of their stress-relieving powers or simplicity, but he suggests the “degree of fanaticism from kids under 10 for these products is not explainable in any rational way. It’s just a real, deep desire”. The squishies craze is good news for independent toy shops, he said: “It will be increasing sales in total by minimum of 30%. Most of their costs are fixed so they’ll probably be doubling the profit for the year.” The craze has been a shot in the arm for UK toy sales this year, which by the end of August were up 13% by value and 19% by volume, according the market research company Circana. Sales of toys that cost under £10 are growing fastest, with an extra £100m worth of these so-called “pocket money” items sold during the period thanks to the clamour for World Cup stickers and squishies. As for Christmas – still 72 days away – Hamleys says this week is when shopping for the festive season “officially” starts, according to a poll of consumers. With that in mind it has produced its annual shortlist of toys to please toddlers through to teenagers and older. At £10, the Big Squij toys are the cheapest. while the remote-controlled flying Thunder Unicorn” is the most expensive at £75. The list of 15 items includes evergreen favourites such as Lego, Barbie, Peppa Pig and PlayDoh. With the upcoming Marvel superhero extravaganza Avengers: Doomsday on the horizon it features two Doctor Doom toys – a £45 Lego bust and a £30 action figure. There is also something for J-Pop fans with a collectible figurine of the computer-generated pop-star Hatsune Miku . The 16-year-old vocaloid – her “voice” comes from music software – is playing London’s O2 arena next month. events.title: NTangible bets it can predict how athletes will perform under pressure
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When collegiate sports programs recruit athletes, they can measure concrete metrics like a player’s sprint speed, throwing velocity, and physical strength. But there has never been a clear way to quantify the mental aspects of sports — how well will this athlete perform in high-pressure situations? Will they stay calm, focus, and give it their best shot? Or will they panic in the spotlight and mess up? NTangible co-founder and CEO Dan Connerty thinks he’s unlocked the secret to measuring if a player will execute in the most important moments. “We really wanted to hyper focus on this idea of clutch performance,” Connerty, a professional baseball player turned sports-tech entrepreneur, told TechCrunch. “Cognitive [science] itself is just this black box that nobody’s wanted to touch, because nobody’s had the ability to measure it accurately prior.” Alongside psychologist Dr. Ed Levine, a professor emeritus at the University of South Florida, Connerty developed a psychological assessment that he says can predict how likely an athlete is to perform under pressure. The Clutch Factor assessment is inspired by the Thematic Apperception Test, a psychological examination in which people are presented with photos of ambiguous situations and describe what they see happening, who they imagine themselves to be in the scene, and what they think might happen next. “There’s no right or wrong answers,” Connerty said. “The key words that you use, the way in which you use those words, and the semantic phrasing associated with it get scored against the neurolinguistic scoring guide that psychologists created, and it shoots out your clutch factor score.” The score is between 0 and 1,000 and, according to Connerty, an athlete who scores over a 750 is twice as likely to commit to a Division I school. “What we’ve been able to do is leverage this analysis, where we can show the predictive ability,” he said. “This number can be heavily used in rankings, leaderboards, recruiting conversations, NIL conversations, and scholarship conversations, especially in the crazy wild west that is collegiate sports right now, where we’re writing $4 million checks to quarterbacks.” A possible flaw in the product, however, could be that athletes seeking to impress coaches and recruiters may answer the questions dishonestly to get a higher clutch score. When I took the quiz and answered honestly, I got a below-average score of 584, which didn’t surprise me — I dreaded high-leverage situations when I played high school sports. When I took the quiz a second time, answering as I imagined a very level-headed, clutch, top recruit might respond, I scored 802. Perhaps the platform would work better as a way for coaches to learn more about their athletes and help them improve in weaker areas. Connerty thinks that “clutch” is a skill that can be trained. While he isn’t positioning NTangible as a training platform, he worked with former MLB sports psychologist Howie Schwartz to create a list of exercises that athletes can use as a starting point for upping their mental game. While Connerty’s background is in baseball, NTangible now supports testing for nine sports. He also has ambitions to expand the clutch test to apply to corporate settings, so that HR departments can evaluate employees’ strengths and weaknesses under pressure. The NTerpret assessment translates more directly to the workplace — the respondent answers questions about how they best respond to coaching and feedback, giving management data on how that employee processes instructions and acts on information. NTangible’s most viable business model seems to be selling to sports organizations and companies directly, rather than to individual athletes. The company will elaborate on its strategy onstage on Wednesday at TechCrunch Disrupt, where it’s currently among the top 20 companies dueling for the grand prize at Startup Battlefield. You can check out the rest of the field, and the investors who will decide the winner, by joining us in person this week at Disrupt, happening Tuesday through Thursday, October 13 to 15, in downtown San Francisco. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. events.title: Closer EU trade ties greater prize for UK than making separate deals, minister says
events.summary: Exclusive: Douglas Alexander, on trade delegation to India, talks up economic benefits of joint trading arrangements with Europe Britain will benefit from much closer trading relations with the EU even if that means giving up its ability to negotiate free trade agreements, the Scotland secretary has said. Douglas Alexander helped negotiate deals with India and the US when he was a trade minister under Keir Starmer. But he has told the Guardian he thinks joint trading arrangements with the EU – whether under a customs union or full membership – would be a bigger economic prize, not least because the EU has now negotiated its own similar deal with India . When Starmer was prime minister, ministers would argue against rejoining the EU because it would mean having to abandon trade agreements with other countries. Alexander’s comments show how much Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham, who called this week for a “serious dialogue” on the UK’s relations with the EU, including possible re-entry, has shifted the government’s position. Speaking to the Guardian from a trade delegation to India, Alexander welcomed the progress made since the Indian agreement came into force earlier this year, since when the price of scotch whisky in India has fallen by 10-15%. But he said the economic benefits of trading agreements with the EU would be greater. “In trade policy, geography still matters,” he said. “The Channel is just 21 miles wide. Our largest trading partner is and will remain the European Union in the years to come. We trade almost twice the amount with the European Union that we do with the United States, the largest single-country trading partner.” He said: “It’s no secret that I was not a supporter of leaving the European Union, and I called out early as trade minister what I described as the ‘post-imperial delusions’ of the Brexiteers. Back in 2016, they promised a world of Britain as a buccaneering free trade nation in a world where barriers were coming down. Sadly, what we’ve witnessed in the year since is a more protectionist, more regionalised world in which barriers have been going up. “At the time we joined the Pacific trade grouping, the CPTPP [Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership] – which undoubtedly makes a lot of sense geopolitically for the UK – our own analysis made clear that the long-term boost to UK GDP from membership is less than a tenth of 1%. If you compare that with estimates of the structural damage to the UK economy from Brexit , you get a sense of just how important Europe remains to our future trade and prosperity. “We’re already paying a real economic price for putting up new barriers to our European neighbours who, with almost half of total UK trade, remain easily our largest trading partners.” Alexander was speaking in Mumbai, where he was joined by the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, and the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, as well as a group of mayors from northern England. He made it clear he did not support any particular method of achieving closer relations with the EU. The ministers spent much of their time in meetings with Indian officials as they attempt to iron out what they say have been “teething problems” with the early implementation, especially for smaller businesses. “There are always teething problems,” Alexander said. “We’re also having a conversation at the level of regulation to see how do we overcome non-tariff barriers that can prove to be an inhibitor to the kind of progress we want to see unless they’re addressed.” Many in the government say a bigger prize will be to reach an agreement at next month’s EU summit, where Burnham hopes to sign new trading deals for emissions, electricity and agricultural products. One hurdle to delivering that is the UK’s desire to discuss the protectionist “Made in Europe” policy , which British manufacturers fear will shut them out of a key market. EU leaders say they are willing to discuss British entry into that scheme, though they are also pushing for the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, without which they fear the UK will become a back door into the European market. Reynolds told the Guardian this week he would not impose tariffs simply because of pressure from Brussels.

events.title: Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
events.summary: Ola Källenius says it will ‘weaken the industry on both sides’ ahead of act intended to counter non-EU competition Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said. Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”. He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU. The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU. It is mainly aimed at China , which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland. “It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry. “We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added. Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France. The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December. Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors. But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK. “We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director. The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car. Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year. The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time. The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently. Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years. One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

events.title: Driving test waits fall to two-year low - but still average 20 weeks
events.summary: Waiting times for driving tests have dropped below 20 weeks for the first time since November 2024, according to official figures. But learner drivers in September still had to wait an average of 19.7 weeks, or around five months, for a practical test. The Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) has been trying to cut waiting times and clear a backlog which began during the Covid pandemic in 2020. Commenting on the agency's progress, one driving instructor told the BBC: "I don't think this is anything to boast about." The DVSA initially had hoped to reduce the average waiting time to seven weeks by the end of last year. Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander pushed the target back to summer 2026, but subsequently admitted even that would not be possible - with waits not expected to fall to seven weeks until next autumn . The DVSA conducted 191,682 practical driving tests in September, with more than half of those passing. Learner drivers have repeatedly told the BBC how a lack of access to driving tests has limited their freedom, education and job prospects. Until earlier this year, many learner drivers chose to pay inflated prices to access driving tests being resold by third party providers who'd used automated programmes, or bots, to block book tests before learners could access them. But a number of changes were made to the test booking system earlier this year by the DVSA to stop the system being exploited. Now, only the learner driver is able to book their driving test. Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, previously showed the BBC hundreds of driving tests being offered for sale by resellers on messaging groups Sophie Stuchfield, a driving instructor in Watford, told the BBC: "Whilst the re-selling of tests does seem to have stopped, which is a massive positive, they've still failed to recruit enough examiners to cope with demand." She didn't believe that the slight fall in numbers for waiting times "is anything to boast about", adding that in many areas the wait for a driving test when booking is 21 weeks. "On many occasions, my drivers wake up at 5.45am on a Monday, only to not end up with a test as when they click on something, by the time they put their details in, they are told the test has already been taken." Sophie added that the waiting time to get a test meant that many learner drivers "who haven't even started driving lessons will book a test knowing it's 5 months away", putting themselves and the instructor under a lot of pressure. Justin Madders, the minister for roads, said the government "inherited record waiting times and a significant backlog". "While driving test waiting times are still not where we want them to be, these figures show real progress is being made," he added. A DVSA spokesperson said the agency was "committed to reducing waiting times" and that "examiner numbers are at their highest level since November 2017". "But we know there's more to do and we won't stop until every learner can get a test slot when they need one, wherever they're learning to drive," the spokesperson added. events.title: US inflation heats up in September; Fed rate hike in October back on table
events.summary: Petrol prices above US$6 a gallon at a gas station in Emeryville, California, on Oct 12. US consumer prices rose 0.6% in September and 3.7% over the year, driven by a 7.1% jump in petrol costs, Reuters reported. Core CPI also firmed, rising 0.3% in the month and 2.6% yearly, keeping inflation pressure on the US Federal Reserve and rate rise fears alive. The report hurt Trump politically and will help set 2027 Social Security COLA, with seniors expecting about a 3.5% rise, or US$67.90 a month. WASHINGTON – US consumer prices accelerated in September amid a surge in fuel costs, dealing another blow to President Donald Trump and his Republican Party ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections and putting an interest rate increase later in October back on the radar. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Oct 14 showed a broadening of price pressures beyond energy, raising concerns among economists that underlying inflation could be getting sticky. Financial markets now see the Federal Reserve’s interest rate decision in October as a closer call than before the data was released. The report added to surveys in October that showed a further deterioration in consumer sentiment and a plunge in Trump’s approval rating, driven by angst over the rising cost of living. A Reuters/Ipsos poll showed about 78% of Americans blamed Trump’s policies, including tariffs on imports and the Middle East conflict, for rising prices, which are outpacing wages. “The last mile back to target could remain bumpy and keep interest rates elevated,” said Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial. “The report complicates the Fed’s decision in October , as the road back to price stability is looking increasingly difficult to navigate.” The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.6% in September after climbing 0.4% in August, the Labour Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics said. The increase in the CPI was in line with economists’ expectations. A 9.1% surge in petrol prices accounted for more than half of the increase in the CPI over September . The US-Israeli war with Iran is driving up energy prices. Diesel prices have vaulted to record highs and there are fears that those costs will soon feed through to higher prices at the supermarket. Food prices were unchanged after gaining 0.1% in both July and August. Grocery store prices dipped 0.1% over the month, but rose 1.8% on a year-over-year basis. Beef prices dropped 1% in September and the cost of dairy and related products eased 0.9%. But prices for non-alcoholic beverages surged 0.9%, while fruits and vegetables cost 0.5% more. In the 12 months till September, the CPI advanced 3.7% after rising 3.4% in the year ended August. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI gained 0.3% in September, matching the gain in August. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the so-called core CPI would rise 0.2%. The core CPI was lifted by a 0.4% increase in the cost of shelter, including hotel and motel rooms. Owners’ equivalent rent rose 0.3%. There were increases in the costs of recreation and education. Prices for used cars and trucks increased 0.7%, while airline fares rose 1.2% amid higher jet fuel prices. Apparel prices climbed 0.3%. In the 12 months through September, core CPI inflation increased 2.6% after advancing 2.4% in the year to August. The US central bank tracks the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index for its 2% inflation target. The core CPI measure is lagging behind core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation, which increased 3% in August, because of the different weights assigned to the components in the baskets. Financial markets raised the chances of a rate hike at the Fed’s Oct 27-28 policy meeting to roughly 52% from about 22% prior to the CPI report, CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed. The odds of a rate increase in October had diminished following underwhelming payroll gains in September as well as cooler-than-expected PCE inflation readings for July and August. US Treasury yields were mostly higher while the dollar advanced versus a basket of currencies. US stocks opened lower. The central bank in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4% range, the first hike in three years , and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. Economists had expected the Fed to raise rates in December. The September CPI inflation report was keenly awaited by millions of retirees and other Social Security recipients trying to figure out how much their benefits will increase in 2027. The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security and Supplemental Security Income benefits for 2027. The programmes benefit older Americans who have retired as well as the disabled and certain widows, widowers and children. REUTERS

events.title: Turkish authorities raid TV channel as press freedom groups warn of a crackdown
events.summary: Authorities have raided Halk TV, one of Turkey's few independent broadcasters, and appointed a trustee manager as part of a corruption investigation ISTANBUL -- Authorities on Wednesday raided the headquarters of one of Turkey ’s few broadcasters not aligned with the government, and appointed a trustee manager to oversee the popular news channel as part of an investigation into alleged corruption. Press freedom groups and opposition parties, however, denounced the move against Halk TV, calling it yet another step by the government to silence opposition voices. Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index. A statement from the Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said an investigation was launched into Halk TV chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over allegations of bid rigging, bribery and money laundering. Detention warrants were issued against 17 suspects and 11 of them were taken into custody, the statement said. Trustees were also appointed to run other companies owned by Mahiroglu. The channel’s broadcasts were temporarily halted. Police surrounded the station’s headquarters while financial crimes investigation teams conducted searches inside, media reports said. The raid on the channel came as Istanbul's imprisoned mayor, Ekrem Imamoglu , was due to appear in court to defend himself against allegations of widespread corruption in a case that critics also see as a politically motivated move against the opposition. Imamoglu, who has been behind bars for more than a year, was considered the main challenger to Erdogan. Halk TV has reported extensively on the trial and other cases against Imamoglu. In a video message posted on X, Mahiroglu condemned the appointment of a trustee for the channel, calling it a politically motivated move and a “dark day for Turkey.” Mahiroglu, who lives abroad, denied the allegations against him as “baseless” and said seven of his relatives were detained. The Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against the channel. “The appointment of a trustee to Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression,” the group said. “This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public’s right to access information, is unacceptable.” Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid amounted to an abuse of power by the government. “Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit,” he wrote on X. “Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country.” Amnesty International urged Turkish authorities to "immediately restore Halk TV’s independent operations and end their attacks on media freedom.” Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship. Last week, two journalists were arrested and two others were placed under house arrest for alleged misleading reports on a recent Turkish investment fund scandal — which has implicated a senior figure from Erdogan’s ruling party. On Monday, international and Turkish human rights groups urged social media platforms, including X, to resist court orders blocking hundreds of accounts belonging to journalists and activists. They also called on the Turkish government to stop issuing orders to block the accounts. The government has cited public safety concerns to justify the restrictions. events.title: Qatar’s wealth fund keeps spending as war slashes government revenue
events.summary: The News Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund isn’t slowing its dealmaking, a senior executive said, even as the Iran war gutted the state’s revenue by 42% in the first half of the year. The war “hasn’t impacted our progress,” Mohsin Pirzada, head of funds at Qatar Investment Authority, told Semafor. “We continue to invest, we continue to deploy.” “We’re obviously very mindful that we manage the surplus wealth for the state of Qatar, and that is largely derived by LNG exports,” Pirzada said. The sovereign fund has remained an active investor, with its funds division deploying billions of dollars already this year. QIA announced a $20 billion investment partnership with JPMorgan last month, following a $25 billion agreement with Goldman Sachs just before the Iran war began. While no new fund deals are “on the radar” now, Pirzada said, QIA “will have a handful of strategic platform arrangements with managers or institutions like JPMorgan, or like Goldman Sachs,” focused on firms that the fund has had long-standing relationships with.” Know More Before the war, QIA said it planned to invest $500 billion in the US alone over the next decade. The fund had expected to nearly double in size, boosted by an 85% expansion of its liquefied natural gas (LNG) output by 2030. That gas expansion has now been delayed — an Iranian attack on the Ras Laffan complex knocked out about 17% of its existing capacity. Qatar’s economy is expected to contract 15.6% this year , and the government will likely post a deficit. QIA, with around $580 billion in assets, is a significant backer of Wall Street firms and US technology. Its appetite mirrors that of its Gulf peers: with the exception of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, all are on track for one of their most active years of dealmaking ever, according to fund tracker GlobalSWF. Qatar has been one of the most impacted Gulf countries by the US-Iran war. Unlike some of its neighbors, it has no export routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, and has been reluctant to move LNG tankers — which are more flammable and expensive than crude carriers — through the strait. Despite the disruptions, there are signs of recovery. QatarEnergy Chief Executive Saad al-Kaabi said last month that the expansion project is expected to begin production in the first half of 2027. Meanwhile, an LNG export facility in Texas, majority owned by QatarEnergy in a joint venture with ExxonMobil, shipped its first cargoes in April. Notable Qatar cut government department budgets by around a third and funding for overseas aid by about 85% to cope with the financial strain of the war , the Financial Times reported. A “dinosaur” gas tanker is one part of an ambitious effort to revive Qatari energy shipments , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: More expensive gas, semiconductors likely pushed up inflation last month
events.summary: U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas, clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections WASHINGTON -- U.S. inflation accelerated last month as gas , clothes, and air fares got more expensive, evidence that rising prices remain an economic challenge just a few weeks before the midterm elections that have focused heavily on issues related to affordability. The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year ago, the Labor Department said Wednesday , up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, costs jumped 0.6% from August to September, the biggest gain in five months, up from a 0.4% increase the previous month. The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on gas prices and the stubborn persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but this year has ticked higher since the war began in late February. The rise isn't all linked to gas prices, as surging investment in data centers and AI has also pushed up prices for computer chips and the consumer electronics that also use them. Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and is a challenge for the Federal Reserve, which is required by Congress to seek stable prices. Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% in September from a year ago, up from 2.4% the previous month. And they climbed 0.3% from August to September, an elevated pace that, if it continued for a year, would run well above the Fed's 2% target. Ongoing inflation has taken a toll on Trump’s standing with U.S. voters. A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of U.S. adults approve of his handling of the cost of living issue. And only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low. Federal Reserve officials are watching inflation data closely to determine whether they need to raise their short-term interest rate further, and by how much. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said last month that inflation isn't moving quickly enough back to the central bank's target, causing the Fed to hike rates for the first time in three years, to about 3.9%. Yet some key Fed officials have suggested the central bank can wait before increasing rates again. The Fed has a policy meeting Oct. 27-28, but most Wall Street investors expect it to hold rates then, and potentially implement another hike in December. Fed officials have penciled in just one more rate hike this year. By raising borrowing costs, the Fed hopes to slow spending and growth and cool price increases. Yet much of the current inflation comes from supply shocks, such as the Iran war's disruption to oil and gas supplies, and higher interest rates can't address those bottlenecks. It's already pushed up the price of air fares about 22% from a year ago. Gas prices jumped more than 9% from August to September, Wednesday's report said. Rising gas costs are a highly visible sign of inflation and often drive down measures of consumer sentiment about the economy. Prices at the pump have ticked lower in the past two weeks to a nationwide average of $4.33 a gallon, according to AAA, though they remain higher than a month ago. Those costs raise shipping and other expenses for many large and small businesses, some of which are forced to pass the cost to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said that it will raise prices for its snack foods, including Doritos, Ruffles, Sun Chips, and some sodas to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminum, and food ingredients. The artificial intelligence buildout has also sharply elevated the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment, and electrical components, which have been passed on to consumers in the form of more expensive electronics such as gaming devices, laptops, and smartphones. Goldman Sachs estimated in a report Tuesday that the AI buildout has added about a half-percentage point to the annual inflation rate, according to the Fed's preferred inflation gauge. On September 1, Nintendo increased the price for its Switch 2 gaming system by 11% to $499.99. And Apple's newest iPhone, the iPhone 17, cost about 10% more than its previous upgrade , though some of that likely reflects greater capabilities.
