events.title: Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in Manchester
events.summary: Company hails first step in rolling out technology across UK as first autonomous vehicles take to city’s streets Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK. The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe’s first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb. Uber said it was “excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK”. In social media posts, Verne said it had “started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester”, while Pony said there were “plans to bring robotaxis to the city” and that testing was under way. The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers. Limited passenger services started last month in London , but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London’s licensing rules for private hire vehicles. The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital’s politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected. A critical report from London assembly’s transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. It said there was “considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far. A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it wanted the city’s taxis to be the safest in the country. events.title: What does the historic Bank of America fine mean for US-China capital streams?
events.summary: Analysts say penalties signal tighter scrutiny over cross-border financial flows As the US Treasury imposed historic fines on Bank of America over compliance failures involving Chinese money-laundering networks, analysts see the action as a signal that could prompt Western banks to tighten scrutiny of Chinese clients and cross-border transactions. The penalties, announced on Tuesday and totalling more than US$1.21 billion, included what the US Treasury described as its third-largest penalty on record and the largest in the history of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. Bank of America had failed to report more than US$5 billion in suspicious transactions in a timely manner, including more than US$1 billion involving national security-related and other priority risks such as “suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese money-laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money-laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border”, according to a Treasury statement. The bank had also processed millions of dollars in payments “in apparent violation of sanctions programmes”, including those targeting Russia, Iran and narcotics and global terrorism networks, the Treasury added.

events.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
events.summary: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said. That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August. Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month. Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices. Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August. Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month. Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country . President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies. Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices. What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday. The increase will take effect in January. The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again , with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation. In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices. Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month. New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027. The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month. Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data. The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

events.title: A former Ukrainian officer goes on trial over sabotage of Nord Stream pipelines
events.summary: Defense lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial HAMBURG, Germany -- Defense lawyers for a former Ukrainian army officer charged with damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines in blasts four years ago have called for the dismissal of charges in the first day of his trial. The trial that opened Wednesday in Hamburg centers on undersea explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany in what is considered one of Europe’s biggest acts of sabotage since World War II. Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, faces charges of causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure. His lawyers, making the motion for dismissal, argued that Kuznietsov was still an active duty soldier and as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for reasons of secrecy linked to national security. As the proceedings got underway at the Hanseatic Higher Regional Court, Kuznietsov, dressed in a gray suit and dark tie, kept a calm expression as he sat between two lawyers in black robes. From the dock, Kuznietsov glanced over to a packed visitors area and exchanged smiles with two people. He did not speak during Wednesday’s proceedings, which lasted about two hours, and listened to simultaneous translation from German into Ukrainian through white headphones. After the charges were read out, a judge asked whether Kuznietsov wanted to comment, and his defense lawyers said he did not. They went on to request that all the charges be dismissed. Kuznietsov’s legal team said allegations of war crimes would be better targeted against the Russian forces acting on orders from President Vladimir Putin during the 4-1/2-year-war, citing examples like atrocities in the Ukrainian town of Bucha and the kidnapping of Ukrainian children . The defense team also disputed the accusation that the attack was sabotage of civilian infrastructure, with defense lawyer Nicola Canestrini saying the pipelines “were a weapon in the hand of the Russians.” But the crux of their call for dismissal was that Kuznietsov had to keep quiet as a Ukrainian officer. “He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers,” defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court, adding that under German law: “Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted.” Meyer-Lohkamp also decried the detention conditions of his client, likening them to solitary confinement: “He is brave, but he is locked up for 23 hours a day and suffers because of it. He has no opportunity to participate in social life.” The trial of the suspect , who is alleged to be the ringleader of the attack, is being held under strict security measures. While international observers initially blamed Moscow for the blasts, investigators later found suggestions that Ukrainian state security agencies may have been involved — even though Ukraine counts Germany as one of its closest allies. More than 100 media representatives from around the world, including Britain, China, France, Ukraine and Russia, have been accredited to cover the case, according to the court. Pro-Ukraine protesters gathered outside the courthouse as attendees filed into the building, holding up placards and signs that carried messages including “Russia is a Terrorist” written in red. Ivan Kuritsyn of Citizens’ Initiative Vilni De Ua, a nonprofit formed by Ukrainians displaced by the war, said the demonstrators were on hand “to show our solidarity with Serhii Kuznietsov and to support him.” Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded “I want to emphasize here that we in no way question the court’s decision, because only the court can decide whether Serhii is guilty or not, but we must support him regardless,” Kuritsyn added. According to the charges, the defendant was allegedly involved in causing the Sept. 26, 2022, explosions that damaged pipelines built to carry Russian natural gas to Germany under the Baltic Sea. At the time, European countries were moving to wean themselves off Russian energy sources, following the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 . Prosecutors say the aim of the plot was to permanently disrupt gas deliveries and prevent Russia from using the revenues to finance its military operations. The defendant and others allegedly used a yacht that departed from the German port of Rostock. It had been rented from a German company using forged IDs and with the help of intermediaries. Kuznietsov’s lawyers argued that his fingerprints were not on the yacht and no witnesses spotted him on it.

events.title: Rwanda confirms it will host F1 Grand Prix
events.summary: Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in more than three decades with a Grand Prix in Rwanda in the early 2030s, the sport’s governing body confirmed. The FIA, which has committed to a 10-year race deal, linked the move to expanding the global reach of F1, highlighting the “exciting growth opportunities” of the continent’s young fan base. After Rwanda beat South Africa to the honor of hosting a Grand Prix, President Paul Kagame said at the launch in the capital, Kigali, that “today belongs to Africa.” The race forms a significant addition to Rwanda’s growing portfolio of international events as it raises its global investment and tourism profile. But rights group Amnesty International has accused the FIA of handing the country a “sportwashing prize.” It accuses the authorities of arbitrary detention and torture of opponents, as well as stoking conflict in neighboring DR Congo — all of which Kigali denies. — Damian Zane

events.title: Malawi launches black market fuel crackdown as prices soar
events.summary: Malawi launched a nationwide crackdown on fuel hoarders and black market sellers as the nation struggles with shortages that have left truckers queuing for up to a week and bus fares doubling on some routes. Diesel and petrol have been scarce for weeks because the country lacks the hard currency to buy fuel supplies, sparking a scramble for dollars that has seen the central bank sell off gold to pay suppliers and the government return to the IMF for a bailout. Malawi, which has among the highest fuel pump prices in Africa at more than $3 a liter, highlights the impact of a $100-plus per barrel crude price on import-dependent economies with thin buffers. Unlicensed resellers face arrest , and stations caught hoarding can lose their license under the new measures. The IMF last week said it was making “ considerable progress ” in designing a “package of macroeconomic policies.” Its last program was a $175 million loan that expired in May last year, the latest in a string of support packages for one of the continent’s poorest countries, whose agriculture-based economy has been hit hard by extreme weather patterns. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
events.summary: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Challenging to shut down Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Former DR Congo president forms new rebel movement
events.summary: DR Congo’s former President Joseph Kabila has formed a new rebel movement incorporating Rwanda-backed forces, openly taking charge of the insurgency despite US sanctions against him. The move deepens the political and security threat to President Félix Tshisekedi’s government and challenges Washington’s efforts to end fighting and secure access to the country’s critical minerals. UN experts reported in June that Kabila’s growing prominence appeared intended to obscure Rwanda’s role by portraying the rebellion as a Congolese movement addressing a national problem. Rwanda has acknowledged defensive “security coordination” with the M23 insurgents, who have held large swaths of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo for more than a year. US sanctions against rebel leaders and Rwanda’s military, a Washington-brokered peace deal, and talks mediated by Qatar have so far failed to end the fighting. Insecurity has complicated DR Congo’s hopes of profiting from rising demand for copper, coltan, and cobalt used in digital infrastructure and the energy transition. Washington has paired its peace efforts with a bid to loosen China’s grip on mining in the world’s largest cobalt producer. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: IMF raises sub-Saharan Africa growth outlook
events.summary: The IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for sub-Saharan Africa to 4.5%, cementing its position as one of the world’s fastest growing regions. The IMF said the new projection, marginally higher than July’s 4.3%, “ masks substantial divergence, ” with oil-importing economies the most exposed to higher energy and food prices driven by Iran-war-related supply chain shocks. The IMF expects the continent’s biggest economy, South Africa, to grow more than four times slower than the region this year and next, as the higher oil prices hit its already fragile prospects. On the flip side, the fund raised its projected growth rate for Nigeria, Africa’s top crude oil producer, to 4.2%, citing a “favorable terms of trade effect.” Looking globally, the IMF named rising national debt as a growing risk to financial stability, “especially with high borrowing costs.” Last week, the World Bank said that nearly four-fifths of African countries spend more on interest payments than on health or education. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: IMF chief urges wealthy nations to rein in debt to ease global economic pressure
events.summary: The head of the International Monetary Fund says the United States and other wealthy nations must urgently tackle mounting global debt, which is weighing most heavily on low-income countries BANGKOK -- The U.S. and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing most heavily on low-income countries and straining the global financial system, the head of the International Monetary Fund said Wednesday. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other U.S. leaders recognize that the federal deficit and national debt are too high. But economic growth alone would not be enough to address the country’s more than $40 trillion in national debt, she said. Meanwhile, rising bond yields , reflecting higher premiums demanded by investors for taking on greater risk, have been disrupting financial markets. “We believe that growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. “There is no magic,” she said, adding that other measures would be needed. “You have to go in a direction of tightening, bringing it down, bringing the deficit down.” Rising debt levels and global inflation, partly resulting from high energy costs due to the Iran war , have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world’s poorest nations. Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call “fiscal consolidation” have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since. “Fiscal risks are rising, and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries,” said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs Department. “And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world.” “Among the world’s poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance,” the IMF's latest Fiscal Monitor said. That is forcing countries to make hard choices between supporting their most vulnerable people and meeting their debt repayment obligations. “The Global South is paying the price for rising interest rates in wealthier countries,” U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at an event on the sidelines of the IMF meetings. “We need a new deal on debt, a deal that supports countries to repay over longer time horizons and, crucially, refinancing with better rates to give developing countries precious fiscal space,” he said. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says The median developing country pays three times as much in interest as developed countries, said Alexander De Croo, former Belgian prime minister and administrator of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). On average, nearly 10% of government spending goes toward debt repayments. High fuel and fertilizer prices, the effects of the El Niño weather phenomenon and rising borrowing costs have left many low-income countries with little room to recover. “I mean, we don’t see really a light at the end of the tunnel,” De Croo told The Associated Press. Creating jobs is another top priority, particularly as the growing use of artificial intelligence threatens to make many traditional occupations obsolete. More than 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce over the next decade or so, while forecasts suggest only 400 million net new jobs will be created. The UNDP this week announced its “Jobs for Prosperity” initiative to bring together governments, development banks — such as the World Bank — and private businesses to encourage investment in sectors such as tourism, healthcare and food processing. The initiative and related efforts will help countries attract investment by strengthening governance and policies and developing pipelines of “investible projects,” De Croo said. “These are things that are feasible. It’s been proven that you can do it in many places of the world,” he added. Separately, the IMF, Bank of Thailand and World Bank Group announced a “Bangkok Blueprint” on Wednesday to combat cybercrime, financial fraud and online scams. The announcement came a day after cyberattacks caused refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France. events.title: ‘From liabilities to goldmines’: refineries eye record profits from diesel shortage
events.summary: Firms turning crude oil into the ‘workhorse’ fuel stand to gain most despite economic fallout from record prices D ays after Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US in an effort to lower soaring pump prices, the world’s energy watchdog has warned that the global fuel shortage will drag into 2027. Trump’s temporary sanctions reprieve was criticised for offering “too little, too late” to temper the sky high pump prices triggered by the shutdown of war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia – once the world’s second-largest diesel exporter behind the US. The International Energy Agency said on Wednesday that the shortage would stretch into the new year despite plans to ease trade sanctions or release emergency stockpiles, in a blow to the global economy. “Record diesel prices are already having broad economic consequences by raising the cost of goods and impacting real incomes, economic activity, and inflation,” the IEA added. Yet amid this gathering economic gloom some of the western refineries that turn crude oil into fuels are preparing to have their day. The global shortage that has led to high prices on UK forecourts is poised to hand them record profits. “I prefer the world of disruption to the peaceful world,” the boss of the French energy company TotalEnergies, Patrick Pouyanné, mused last week. He said the energy crisis ignited by almost eight months of war in the Middle East had provided “plenty of opportunities if you’re able to capture them”. For Pouyanné, the key to reaping the benefits of a global fuel crisis lies in owning a string of refineries across Europe that stand ready to cash in by selling diesel into a starved market. Diesel accounts for 10% of the world’s energy consumption, and is known as a “workhorse” fuel for its role powering the equipment vital for sectors ranging from agriculture, mining and manufacturing to shipping and logistics. But by last month supplies into the global market had fallen by about 1m barrels a day from their 2025 level, owing to a combination of damage to refineries in the Gulf and Russia , and export restrictions from China. The soaring costs for businesses and consumers have economists worried. They are already piling pressure on areas of the global economy from US farmers in the midwest corn belt to local bus operators in England. Many fear a broader impact, as fuel prices raise the cost of food, goods and transport across the economy. However, for some of the companies that turn crude into diesel this is a very lucrative crisis. “We’re doing really well by being integrated,” Pouyanné explained. “Integration means your refineries in Europe, which you thought were liabilities, are suddenly becoming goldmines.” These goldmines helped TotalEnergies to its strongest quarterly profits in three years this summer, after income from its refining and chemicals business more than quadrupled to $1.8bn (£1.35bn) between April and June. TotalEnergies is far from alone in its good fortune. The biggest windfalls are likely to come from refiners in the US, where exports of fuel products have climbed by more than 50% in the past year from about 1.25m barrels a day to an all-time high of 1.9m barrels a day over the summer, effectively offsetting the losses from Gulf refineries. The market value of three of the largest US oil refiners – Marathon Petroleum, Valero Energy and Phillips 66 – have more than doubled since the start of the crisis. The US listed stocks have climbed by a combined $215bn this year as their shares rose steadily to reach successive record highs. In the coming weeks these refineries are expected to reveal their largest-ever profits. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Europe’s largest oil and gas company, Shell, told investors last week it expects to make record profits from each barrel of fuel produced over the last three months after it reported its second highest quarterly profit ever over the summer. Shell’s refining margins are forecast to nearly double to $42 for each barrel of refined product sold in the July to September period, up sharply from $24 a barrel in the second quarter. The companies are benefiting from the price difference between a barrel of crude oil and the barrel of refined fuel. The Brent crude benchmark price has eased back to oscillate around the $100 a barrel level in recent weeks, helped by an uptick in cargoes leaving the Gulf region, although given recent fears about the Middle East conflict escalating it is back above the $106 mark. . Meanwhile, fuel exports have remained constrained and global stockpiles of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel have continued to shrink. The supply squeeze means that while oil prices are lower than feared at this point, the cost of diesel is far higher. Refiners that produce diesel and jet fuel have fared best in the crisis.

events.title: Companies may be held liable when AI harms their clients and customers
events.summary: When AI messes up on a tax return or in a court filing, it's no laughing matter. DigitalVision Vectors/Getty Images Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from a novelty on the job to a common workplace tool. Gallup found that 52% of U.S. employees and 68% of professional services workers were using AI by February 2026. Thomson Reuters similarly found in spring 2026 that 74% of professionals use AI several times a week for work. This widespread use shouldn’t surprise anyone. For accountants, attorneys, consultants and other professionals, AI can accelerate research , summarize complex information and assist with writing and other forms of communication. But its rapid adoption has a big downside – AI can produce information that sounds authoritative and looks polished while being completely wrong . And when AI generates mistakes, responsibility for those errors belongs to the professional or business relying on the AI output – not companies that develop AI systems. AI errors have led to lawsuits, court fines, financial consequences and public embarrassment from fabricated citations, nonexistent sources and inaccurate AI-generated information. These cases raise an increasingly important question: How can professionals benefit from AI without outsourcing the judgment their work requires? Fake citations We are two certified public accountants who research tax accounting . In the September 2026 issue of Journal of Accountancy, we examined what happened in Clinco v. Commissioner , a case before the U.S. Tax Court where an attorney submitted a brief to the court with allegedly fake citations. The Tax Court is a specialized federal court that resolves disputes between taxpayers and the IRS. This case involved a restaurant owner accused of underreporting more than US$2 million in business receipts and claiming unsupported depreciation deductions on rental properties. The main issue concerned Clinco’s accounting records used to determined how much of their income to tax. The taxpayers’ attorney, Abraham Wagner, cited four cases to support his argument that an IRS notice assessing additional taxes was invalid. The court determined that three of the citations appeared to be AI-generated hallucinations that cited nonexistent Tax Court cases. The court rejected the taxpayer’s argument and warned Wagner that submitting fake citations could lead to sanctions from the court, including financial penalties or disciplinary action against Wagner. Ultimately, the court did not sanction Wagner in the case, but the decision stands to put attorneys and other professionals in Tax Court on notice that AI hallucinations will not be tolerated. Using AI for audits and other professional work may save time but also poses some legal hazards. iStock/Getty Images Plus When AI gets it wrong AI errors made on behalf of clients are not limited to briefs drafted by attorneys. Nor are these mishaps limited to the United States. When Deloitte produced a 237-page report in 2025 for the Australian government examining its automated system for penalizing welfare recipients who failed to meet job-seeking requirements, it contained nonexistent academic citations and a fabricated quotation it attributed to a federal court judgment. The global consulting firm later issued a revised version of the error-ridden report. Deloitte blamed generative AI for the errors in the original and agreed to partially refund its fees. Like most airlines, Air Canada has a chatbot on its website to respond to its customers’ questions. The chatbot told a customer in November 2022 that he could buy a plane ticket under a bereavement policy and be reimbursed later. This was not company policy, and Air Canada refused to honor what the chatbot had told the customer. The customer sued the airline and won 812 Canadian dollars in damages. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada had failed to take reasonable care to ensure that its AI bot provided accurate information and agreed with the customer that the airline had negligently misrepresented the bereavement policy. AI lawsuits There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers. In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages. There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC , that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026 the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable. Hallucinations and ‘confabulations’ Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible. The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations” – the confident presentation of erroneous or false information. Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way. Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid. AI errors in the workplace A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency. Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use. As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work. AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops. The University of Dayton is an academic partner of The Conversation. Kaitlin Newkirk is affiliated with the Ohio Society of CPAs.

events.title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The US military’s race to make fake blood In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply. Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.  The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives. Discover how the military hopes to make blood last longer . —Andrew Rosenblum This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday, October 21!   10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges. Explore WeLion’s push to make safer, higher-capacity batteries . —You Xiaoying Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from geothermal power plants to carbon dioxide batteries .  MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process. Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins.  The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. events.title: Wayfair among firms fined millions for misleading sales tactics
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 10:24 BST Wayfair is among three firms which have been fined £6m in total by the competition watchdog for illegally using misleading sales tactics – with some customers set to receive refunds. The online furniture retailer was fined £4.8m for misleading customers with time-limited offers, while online electronics seller Appliances Direct was fined £1.2m for the same practice, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) said. Meanwhile, Gold's Gym has been fined £45,000 for not telling customers the total price of its memberships. It and Appliances Direct have been ordered to refund customers a total of £440,000. Wayfair and Appliances Direct said the CMA's fines were disproportionate. Gold's Gym has been contacted for comment. Thousands of Appliances Direct customers will receive refunds of £25 each on average while 726 Gold's Gym customers will get refunds of up to £50, according to the CMA. The watchdog said customers do not need to take any action and both companies will contact those affected customers about refunds. Appliances Direct has been told to pay refunds by 11 March, while Gold's Gym has been given a deadline of 29 March. The CMA said Wayfair, Appliances Direct, and Gold's Gym had "engaged constructively" with its investigation. They all admitted to breaking the law and agreed to settle the case early, it added. The watchdog said their co-operation reduced the firms' fines by 40%. The CMA's fines are the result of an investigation it launched last November into online pricing . Eight firms under investigation over online pricing Published 18 November 2025 AA and BSM ordered to refund learner drivers for hidden fees Published 15 April A Wayfair spokeswoman said the penalty was "excessive" but that "we take the CMA's findings seriously and we chose to settle so we can continue to focus on serving our customers". Nick Glynne, chief executive of Buy it Direct, which owns Appliances Direct and several other online retailers, accepted that its practices were wrong, but said the firm should have simply been given "a rap on the knuckles" instead. Glynne said the CMA's process for calculating the fine was a "black box" and that it only settled because appealing was too expensive, accusing the watchdog of pressure tactics. "When one body is investigator, prosecutor, judge and jury, it needs an exceptional commitment to fairness, restraint and proportionality. That is not what we experienced," he added. Hayley Fletcher, senior director for consumer protection at the CMA, said: "At a time when many households are carefully managing their budgets, people shouldn't lose out because of misleading sales tactics. "Businesses must treat their customers fairly and make sure they comply with the law - or risk hefty fines." Sue Davies, head of consumer rights policy at Which?, praised the CMA's response. "The refunds secured by the CMA are a much-needed win for consumers at a time when household budgets are under strain," she said. The CMA's investigation found that the three companies had misled customers in different ways. Wayfair had advertised products as if they would disappear the next day, through phrases like "Here Today, Gone Tomorrow" and countdown timers. However, the CMA said many products remained available at the same price or lower after the stated deadline, meaning the time-limited offer was false. Meanwhile, the regulator said Appliances Direct had automatically opted customers into services such as recycling old machines. Gold's Gym was fined for failing to include joining fees in the total price of gym memberships or not making its total price clear to customers, the CMA said. events.title: Sharjah turns to AI to identify foreign investment opportunities in seconds
events.summary: Sharjah is using artificial intelligence to help foreign investors identify investment opportunities within seconds, as the emirate seeks to attract more foreign direct investment despite mounting geopolitical uncertainty . A new AI-powered platform, called Najm, will initially help investors find sites for factories and warehouses across the emirate. It was launched by the emirate's investment promotion agency, the Sharjah FDI Office, also known as Invest in Sharjah. The AI agent is designed to help investors make “informed investment decisions”, Mohamed Al Mushrrakh, chief executive of Invest in Sharjah, said at the Sharjah Investment Forum on Wednesday. For the introductory phase, Invest in Sharjah has teamed up with property portals Bayut and Property Finder, as well as e-commerce platform Dubizzle . Najm will use commercial and industrial real estate data from the online portals and will provide instantaneous information to investors. “Investors could struggle to find information they need to make an investment decision, so we asked ourselves a simple question: how can we deliver the right information at the right moment, when they need it,” Mr Al Mushrrakh told delegates at the Sharjah Investment Forum. “Najm is the answer to that question. It is Invest in Sharjah's new tool for global investors.” The launch of the AI agent is driven by the need to cut the noise around the investment ecosystem in Sharjah and find new ways to bring foreign direct investment to the emirate. Sharjah, the third largest emirate in the UAE after Abu Dhabi and Dubai, is home to 33 industrial zones. Sharjah’s real estate sector recorded more than 16,000 transactions during the first half of this year, with the emirate’s Muwaileh commercial area accounting for the highest value and volume of deals in the first six months, according to Invest in Sharjah data. Sharjah received Dh7.74 billion in FDI last year, an 8.8 per cent increase on an annual basis. The count of projects in the emirate that received FDI also soared by 45 per cent year-on-year, to reach 142 developments, data showed. In the second phase, the Najm platform will expand its sector horizon to cover a broader range of assets and investment opportunities in the healthcare and education sectors, Mr Al Mushrrakh said. “What you have seen today is just the beginning ... Najm stands to cover investment opportunities across multiple sectors from industry to education and technology and beyond,” he said. “We will continue to invest in human capital, technology, infrastructure and partnerships between the public and private sectors. "Through these efforts, we can build a resilient economy, attract new investments into opportunities that we will build together."

events.title: Saudi set to drop plans for five 2034 World Cup stadiums
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund is preparing to inform organizers of the 2034 men’s soccer World Cup that it plans to drop five new stadiums it proposed to build to host the tournament, according to people familiar with the matter. Public Investment Fund will likely narrow its focus to three new stadiums as it cuts spending on some of its signature domestic investments, the people said. Dropping the five venues would leave the kingdom with 10 stadiums for World Cup matches. The changes are part of a revised plan the kingdom is preparing to submit to FIFA, the tournament’s organizers, the people said. PIF is looking to drop plans to develop stadiums in King Abdullah Economic City and Qiddiya Coast, both near Jeddah; Roshn and New Murabba in Riyadh; and NEOM, in the kingdom’s northwest. Several of the cancelled stadiums are attached to broader real estate projects that have been halted or where work has slowed. Saudi Arabian officials are still working on the updated proposals and the plans could change, the people said. PIF and the Saudi Ministry of Sport didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More Reuters earlier reported on the cancellation of the NEOM stadium, which was envisaged as being on the roof of The Line, a 500-meter-tall skyscraper. Work on The Line has effectively ground to a halt , and NEOM has not allocated any funding for the project until after at least 2030, Semafor previously reported. Saudi Arabia had also proposed a 45,000-seat stadium at Qiddiya Coast, a planned entertainment and tourism destination north of Jeddah. That development has also been put on hold. Another 45,000-capacity stadium in Riyadh’s New Murabba district is also set to be dropped. Work on the wider development has slowed after the departure of Chief Executive Michael Dyke and the suspension of work on the project’s centerpiece, a 400-meter-tall, cube-shaped skyscraper with screens lining its interior, similar to The Sphere concert venue in Las Vegas. The kingdom is still proceeding with plans for other new stadiums including one in Dhahran being developed by Saudi Aramco, and the King Salman International Stadium and Prince Mohammed bin Salman Stadium in Riyadh. The cuts could leave Saudi Arabia developing just six new stadiums and refurbishing four existing ones for the World Cup. Four of the stadiums it plans to use in 2034 are also due to host matches for the 2027 Asian Cup, which starts in January. The outlook for that contest going ahead in Saudi Arabia has been thrown into doubt by the kingdom’s involvement in the war in Yemen against Houthi militias. The group has launched multiple attacks against Saudi cities in recent weeks, shutting down the capital’s airport and killing at least 18 and injuring hundreds. Qatar also previously dropped four of the stadiums it had planned to build for the 2022 World Cup as it got closer to the tournament. Notable Saudi Arabia shelved plans for a World Cup stadium at the futuristic city of NEOM , Reuters reported earlier this month

Apollo’s dryly named “capital solutions” business, launched in 2024, was a bet that asset managers could cosplay as banks. Their money could go places that banks’ deposit funding couldn’t, especially after post-2008 regulations. Apollo has since made big loans to companies including Intel and Keurig Dr Pepper, notching $800 million from the business last year on its way to a $1 billion target . Two years ago, I wagered that BlackRock and Apollo would be the winners of the weird debt world that limped, then sprinted, out of the global financial crisis. events.title: Civil servant faked illness with make-up to juggle five jobs, court hears
events.summary: Kashim Chowdhury allegedly juggled five government jobs Published 14 October 2026, 12:40 BST A civil servant is accused of earning almost £350,000 by juggling five full-time public sector roles - using sick notes and working from home to cope with the workload. Kashim Chowdhury allegedly held multiple government jobs between February 2020 and September 2023, earning £350,000 overall. The jury at Southwark Crown Court has been told he wore white make-up during a video call with his boss to try to look ill, but the make-up began peeling off his skin. Chowdury, a 55-year-old from east London, is on trial accused of nine counts of fraud, which he denies. He denies acting dishonestly or intending to make a dishonest gain. The jury was told that Chowdhury got jobs by making ''false representations'' about his employment status whilst applying. Over three years he held overlapping jobs at Tower Hamlets Council in east London, the Home Office, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the UK Health Security Agency and the Department of Health and Social Care. The jury was told that in 2023 his manager at the Health Security Agency, Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him to discuss his sick leave. Ms Adams claims Chowdhury was wearing make-up on his face to appear ill - and that during the meeting the make-up started to separate on his forehead showing his real skin underneath. At the time of the call he is alleged to have been paid for five full time jobs. Lucy Organ, for the prosecution, told the court: "There could be no doubt about it, the defendant had applied make-up to his face for this Teams meeting to try and pretend to his line manager that he was unwell. "This almost laughable incident demonstrates, we say, quite how far the defendant was willing to go in his deceit." Prosecutors say Chowdhury "exploited" the work from home culture that began during the Covid pandemic. The court was told that Chowdhury had told his employers that he had to work from home to care for his "unwell" mother. But the prosecutor, Ms Organ, said his workload eventually became "too much to cope with" and his performance suffered. The court heard that he was signed off work from some jobs due to "mixed anxiety and a depressive disorder", but he did not hand his sick note to all his employers. Jurors heard that the alleged fraud came to light after the National Fraud Initiative alerted Defra to them. events.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn for money-laundering failures
events.summary: Third-largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings Bank of America (BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators for widespread failures to detect ‌potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings. The US treasury department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report more than $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, including $1bn that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks. “Financial institutions are on the ​front lines of protecting our economic and national security,” the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said in a statement. “When a bank of this size ​fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the ⁠entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.” The treasury said the bank “prioritized its revenues” in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries ​from outside parties such as law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. The consent order requires Bank of America to hire an ​independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that the bank failed to detect at the time and report those transactions to the treasury department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network. “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of ​employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised ​by our regulators.” The spokesperson added that the bank’s third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2bn, which will reduce quarterly net income ‌by approximately ⁠17 cents a share. Analysts have estimated adjusted earnings per share of $1.10, according to mean estimates compiled by LSEG, but that excludes one-offs like this fine. The penalty is likely to add to negative investor sentiment and raise concerns about higher expenses and whether Bank of America can maintain its roughly $6bn quarterly share buyback pace, the UBS analyst Erika Najarian said in a note. With earnings due ​on Wednesday, “we think shares likely underperforming at ​open”, she said. She noted there ⁠was no asset cap, a regulatory penalty that would limit how large the bank could grow. As part of the fine, the treasury department’s office of the comptroller of the currency levied a $750m civil ​penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money ​laundering programs that were ⁠identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog. The regulator said the bank’s compliance program was “deficient and ineffective”, and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions. In addition, the bank paid an $11.6m fine to the treasury department’s office of foreign ⁠assets control ​for more than 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The treasury said the bank mistakenly ​processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran. The fine comes days after American Express was also hit with a $350m penalty for similar anti-money ​laundering shortcomings.

events.title: These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.
events.summary: They were victims, not abusers. That’s what they told police officers, attorneys, visitors and anyone else who would listen. It didn’t matter. The women were all taken to a sprawling immigration detention center in the woods of west Michigan and handed thin jumpsuits — red, to mark them as a high security risk. Inside the North Lake Processing Center, they talked about the men whose calls to police landed them there. The boyfriends or husbands who threatened to get them deported and cut them off from their children. The men, or sometimes women, who hit them, pulled their hair or choked them, bruising their throats. They didn’t know where to go for help before, but now, in the confines of a cold cellblock in a former prison, the women helped one another. If one spoke to somebody on the outside who could connect them with advice, legal aid or money for the commissary, she’d pass around a tablet used for calls so others could tell their stories. Migladys Bermudez, an immigration attorney in southeast Michigan, remembers a call in May from a Peruvian woman detained at North Lake. Her name was Pilar, and she’d heard about Bermudez from a fellow detainee who had been a client. Pilar told Bermudez about the boyfriend she tried to escape before her arrest, when she used makeup to cover the marks she said he left on her face. But he had accused her of being the abuser, resulting in her arrest. Pilar handed the tablet to a Cuban woman named Leya. Over the echoes of the other detainees’ chatter, she described how her boyfriend insulted her, isolated her and gave her a black eye. Then, after grabbing him by the arm during an argument, she was the one behind bars, separated from their nursing daughter. On video calls, the girl didn’t seem to recognize her mother anymore. She stopped calling her “Mamá.” Bermudez was taken aback. All three women in that chain — the former client, Pilar and Leya — said they were trying to get out of abusive relationships when they were arrested by local police on domestic violence allegations. In all three cases, the charges were dropped or never filed at all. The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained the first woman during a routine check-in a few months after her charges were dropped. The others were handed over to ICE by local officials.  It’s long been intimidating for immigrants who suffered abuse to call 911, regardless of who was in the White House. They knew — and their abusers knew — that their immigration status made them vulnerable. But previous administrations treated victims as just that, people who needed help, not as targets for deportation. Bipartisan coalitions in Congress have long supported the Violence Against Women Act, which creates a pathway toward legal status for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence or other serious crimes. Now, under President Donald Trump, all bets are off. On inauguration day, his administration rescinded guidelines that largely prevented immigration agents from making arrests at sensitive locations — including domestic violence shelters and hospitals. About a week later, the administration eliminated key protections granted to VAWA applicants and other crime victims. For the first time in decades, immigration authorities could disregard those protections and more freely arrest, detain and deport immigrant victims. Life became more harrowing in other ways for immigrants who were victims of domestic violence. Federal immigration agents made arrests outside specialized domestic violence courts. And the administration persuaded more and more local police and jails to carry out the president’s mass deportation campaign, sweeping still more immigrants into custody.  Even communities without these so-called 287(g) agreements are helping the government round people up. In west Michigan’s Kent County, where Pilar and Leya were arrested, the county jail turned over more immigrants to ICE in the first six months of 2026 than it did during the entire Biden administration. Advocates across the country say they’re seeing signs of an alarming increase in the numbers of domestic violence victims who are detained and deported. And many immigrants are staying in abusive relationships, fearful of calling for help or even stepping outside their homes. “It’s just probably the most dangerous time for immigrant women right now who are victims of domestic violence,” said Bermudez, who took on Leya’s immigration case. The arrest and detention of domestic violence victims is, in part, an unanticipated consequence of an effort meant to keep them safe. In much of the country, law enforcement officers are encouraged — or even required — to make an arrest when they have probable cause to believe that a domestic violence assault has taken place. Sometimes victims are mistaken as the abuser and taken into custody. Then, if they’re immigrants, they can be turned over to ICE — even if they were never criminally charged. There’s no comprehensive way to track how often this happens or how many domestic violence victims have been detained by ICE or deported. But ProPublica spoke with a half-dozen alleged victims who were locked up together in a single facility, North Lake, and reviewed police records about others who were there, too. Their stories offer a picture of why Congress created programs like VAWA in the first place, and what’s at stake when those guardrails are taken away.  A coalition of immigrant survivors and advocates have sued the Trump administration, saying changes to how immigrant victims are treated not only undermined public safety, but also broke promises enshrined in federal law and policy. “We were seeing our clients be more scared, be systematically targeted, be arrested, and deported very quickly,” said Kathleen Rivas, supervising attorney of the survivors team at Public Counsel, a law firm that’s involved in the litigation. In May, a federal judge ordered the government to restore protections while the case played out. The Trump administration has appealed the order.  White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” But Leya, Pilar and other immigrants we interviewed have no criminal records. And advocates said communities are less safe now because immigrants are afraid to call police when their partners hurt them. events.title: Getty Images to go private under ‘pre-packaged’ bankruptcy
events.summary: Getty will continue to operate normally throughout the process, citing up to US$143 million (S$184 million) in financing from Koch, as well as cash from ongoing business. Getty Images will go private through a “pre-packaged Chapter 11 filing” after agreeing a debt restructuring with major lenders and new equity of up to US$533 million. The company says it will keep operating normally, with up to US$143 million from Koch and no expected impact on contributors, partners, customers or staff. The move follows a warning that its shares would be delisted from the New York Stock Exchange after falling below US$1, after a US$206.1 million loss in 2025. NEW YORK – US photography company Getty Images announced on Oct 12 it reached an agreement with major lenders to restructure its debt, take the company private and undertake a “pre-packaged” bankruptcy. Getty, which partners with AFP among numerous other media companies, said members of the Getty Family and affiliates of Koch Equity Development will invest up to US$533 million (S$683 million) o f new equity to pay down debt under a restructuring. Getty “reached agreement with all of its major financial stakeholder groups on the terms of a comprehensive restructuring,” the company said. Getty will continue to operate normally throughout the process, citing up to US$143 million in financing from Koch, as well as cash from ongoing business. “There is no anticipated impact on content contributors, partners, customers, or employees across the Company’s worldwide network,” Getty said. The company plans a “prepackaged Chapter 11 filing” to win court approval of the restructuring. “The requisite majority of creditors have committed to vote in favor of the Plan,” said Getty, which expects the restructuring to be complete by end 2026. The announcement came after Getty disclosed in a securities filing earlier in October that it had been notified of plans to delist its shares from the New York Stock Exchange because they had fallen below US$1. Getty reported a loss of US$206.1 million in 2025. AFP

events.title: Kenya clears path for Dangote refinery IPO investment
events.summary: The News Kenyan investors hoping to participate in the Dangote refinery initial public offering now have access through a financial instrument being used for cross-border African investment for the first time on Nairobi’s bourse. The use of global depositary receipts (GDRs), which allow backers to buy a stake in a foreign company without leaving their home market, bypasses regulatory barriers that have held up intra-African investment. The use of GDRs offers a template for exchanges across the continent to expand pan-African trade and broaden their investor bases. After an extension of the IPO period was announced on Monday, Kenyan individuals and institutional investors will have until Oct. 27 to buy into their country’s $300 million allocation of Africa’s largest public offering. The minimum entry price in Kenya was slashed from $824 to $4.12, matching what Nigerians were being offered. Announcing the extension, Dangote said he wanted greater African participation and highlighted the Kenyan arrangement that he hoped could be replicated. African policymakers are keen to deepen capital markets as a way to mobilize more of the continent’s domestic resources to fund infrastructure projects and reduce borrowing costs. Know More The refinery’s stock market debut was touted as a way for African investors to own a stake in the continent’s largest refining plant. But the prospectus for the $1.6 billion share shows it was not registered as a public offering outside Nigeria, Reuters reported. That has left investors relying on their own country’s regulations or finding workarounds using the few eligible online financial platforms. Reuters reported patchy take-up outside Nigeria , reflecting low levels of cross-border investment. The Nairobi Securities Exchange’s (NSE) approach is structured around Standard Bank’s Kenya subsidiary Stanbic, which will hold the shares and issue the GDRs. These will be traded on the NSE in Kenyan shillings, and Stanbic will manage the foreign exchange conversion and pay out dividends. Karimi Warui, vice president of investment banking at Renaissance Capital, which is overseeing the IPO in Kenya, told Semafor that the Dangote Group initially intended to pursue a conventional cross-listing approach to get on the NSE and other stock exchanges, but ultimately settled on GDRs for ease. Trying to deal with the rules and regulations of 10 different jurisdictions “became a bit onerous for them,” she added. She said this approach in Kenya could inspire others. “I wouldn’t be surprised if companies that are already listed like [Kenyan telecoms company] Safaricom pursue GDRs in the future to tap into markets like South Africa and Nigeria,” she said. “I actually think we will see more of this now,” saying the IPO would “show regulators the need to work with financiers and issuers” to accelerate growth and integration of Africa’s financial markets. Warui also emphasized the need for regulators to customize policies to fit African markets instead of copying Western regulators. The use of GDRs comes amid a significant push to enhance retail investing in the country. Safaricom this year rolled out NSE trading on the mobile money service M-Pesa, helping drive retail participation in the IPO of the state-run Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) . Warui told Semafor that Renaissance Capital was copying the KPC blueprint for the Dangote IPO — with an online platform for share purchases during the offer period, and trading on the M-Pesa platform expected once it is listed on the NSE. Besides Kenya, Uganda’s markets regulator has approved a restricted offer limiting participation to high net-worth individuals and professional investors. Botswana has been selected to host the southern African portion of the public offering, Bloomberg reported. Step Back Some analysts have cautioned that the GDRs could leave Kenyan investors exposed to FX risks as the GDR tracks the Lagos share price, which is in naira, meaning currency devaluation could significantly affect investors. Acknowledging the concerns, Warui noted that Dangote Refinery’s revenues were dollarized and that dividends could also be paid in dollars, mitigating the potential impact of naira devaluation. Previous GDR listings by African companies have been outward, where issuers list the underlying shares on exchanges outside the continent — mostly on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) to attract Western capital. Room for Disagreement Sultan Mwangi, a Nairobi-based investor and financial researcher, predicted that participation in the Dangote IPO among Kenyan investors would be far lower than expected, especially among retail investors. He attributed this to the handling of the IPO which he said had left investors “disappointed” despite initial excitement. Among issues he cited were inadequate investor education and a need to address concerns regarding the use of GDRs, especially over whether this will leave people exposed to fluctuations in the value of the naira. According to Mwangi, the extension of the IPO offer as well as lowering the minimum investment were a response to low uptake among retail investors. “People were not convinced, and the amount of time available to explain it has not been enough,” he told Semafor. Dangote Industries has yet to respond to enquiries from Semafor on whether the lowering of the minimum investment was a response to underwhelming participation among Kenyan retail investors. Notable African nations should turn to an estimated $4 trillion in capital held by domestic institutions, such as pension funds, to develop infrastructure, the Africa Finance Corporation has said.

events.title: It’s a different oil crisis, but Saudi Arabia will still pay
events.summary: Wael’s view In June 2008, I sat in a Jeddah Hilton conference room packed with ministers from more than 100 countries waiting for King Abdullah to arrive. Oil was closing in on a record price. Saudi Arabia’s message that day: The world had enough oil. It offered a modest increase in output and told governments to cut taxes and rein in speculators. Less than three weeks later, on July 11, crude hit about $147 a barrel. This week in Riyadh, another ministerial gathering took place. The man now leading the kingdom’s response, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, was an assistant oil minister two decades ago. This time the crisis is different — and so is his answer. Then, the argument was about speculation. Saudi officials said investors had pushed prices well past what supply and demand justified, and that financial trading in oil had grown many times larger than the physical market. Washington thought OPEC should pump more. Riyadh replied that it would not build capacity for buyers who did not exist. Now the argument is about geography. Gulf crude is trapped behind the Strait of Hormuz, and the kingdom’s answer is to build around it. Prince Abdulaziz told the World Petroleum Congress that Saudi Arabia may lift its East-West pipeline capacity from about 7 million barrels a day to 10 million within three years, and he wants more international involvement. His logic is that the more countries have a stake in the line, the better it is protected. Both responses share one feature. Saudi Arabia cannot solve the crisis alone, and it ends up paying for the attempt. In 2008 it built rarely used spare capacity and has carried its cost ever since. A new pipeline will follow the same pattern. When the war ends it will not run full, and Riyadh will keep it as insurance. The oil market has also shifted. In 2008, OPEC was dominant and no one else could add meaningful supply. Some consumers searched for substitutes, and ethanol was an answer then. Today, it’s the electric vehicle. But neither remedy has removed the need for fossil fuels and no price spike has changed the thirst for oil. The biggest difference is Washington. In 2008, the US relied on OPEC’s oil. Today, it has plenty of its own, a reality that may not be felt by Americans paying more at the pump. If America needed OPEC barrels as badly as it did in 2008, the politics of this current crisis would look very different. Geopolitical risk has been the main factor driving $100 oil this year, with shipping and insurance comprising more than a third of the price of the global crude benchmark. Even if Hormuz is opened tomorrow, the new logistics of moving crude will weigh on producers. It will also change the relationship between states: Iraq is planning to build a pipeline through Syria to the Mediterranean, while Kuwait and Qatar may lean on their Gulf neighbors to reach ports outside the strait. Ultimately, much of the bill will go to the same address: Riyadh. The kingdom has carried the cost of a largely idle pipeline for decades, and will soon have to revert to its role as the global swing producer, keeping prices fair to producers paying for new infrastructure, and consumers who won’t tolerate high prices forever. Notable Saudi Arabia’s oil supply could still be threatened even after the end of the war. This report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies looks at what options there are. Despite the oil shock, the Saudi economy can remain resilient, according to t his briefing from the Atlantic Council .

events.title: Job cuts could fund diesel price drop says deputy
events.summary: Prices at the petrol pump in Guernsey have reached record highs A Guernsey deputy has said leaders could fund a fuel price drop for drivers by cutting civil servant posts. Deputy Neil Inder said he plans to submit two amendments around the cost of fuel in relation to the upcoming States budget amid "exceptional circumstances due to global events". The proposed amendments are to freeze fuel duty and to also cut the cost at the pumps of white diesel - used by cars, trucks and buses - by 5p. Asked how the States would fund this, he added: "What the States needs to start looking at properly is reducing the size of the civil service." Deputy Neil Inder said rising fuel price rises were set to get worse amid global unrest In the 2027 budget, fuel duty is due to increase by inflation (4.3%) from 1 January 2027, increasing duty rates to 94.4p per litre. With the war continuing in the Middle East, fuel prices have increased across Europe, with diesel prices hitting an all-time high, according to the RAC motoring organisation. It comes as fuel prices recently hit record highs across Guernsey, and the price of diesel hit £2.00 per litre in the UK. White diesel, used for regular road vehicles, is subject to the standard fuel duty rate, while red diesel, used in industries including farming and fishing, is a rebated fuel that is duty-free or has a heavily reduced tax rate. "I think we've got to realise what's happened to the world diesel prices," said Inder. Listen to the latest news for Guernsey "There's been an unreasonable spike in diesel prices over the last three or four months and it really is set to get worse." He said this would inevitably impact the cost of living and added: "Whether we like it or not diesel really does make the world go round and the wheels turn in Guernsey." Inder said under "normal circumstances" he would probably go along with the P&R proposal to "up duty on the diesel", but said the global climate called for greater consideration. "In reality the biggest cost to the States is the amount of people we employ," he said. "Given the cost of the revenue they would gain, all that really is, is four or five civil servants - stop employing them, those that retire, don't replace them." "There's only one budget a year and this is the time to address it," added Inder. The BBC has asked the States for comment. events.title: Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget
events.summary: The managing director of the IMF, Kristalina Georgieva, has praised the UK's approach to debt reduction. Published 14 October 2026, 12:03 BST "Get your fiscal health in order," is a key message at the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) annual meeting here in Thailand. The IMF is worried about the debts of the world's biggest economies. It is doing its job as a watchdog, looking for and warning about financial vulnerabilities. In the meantime, the finance ministers of former crisis countries are boasting about how little their borrowing costs have gone up, compared to the world's biggest economies, such as the US. On three occasions in the past 24 hours, top IMF officials have praised the UK's plans to reduce its annual levels of borrowing, bucking the trend of the rest of the G7 group of countries, which includes Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US. The IMF clearly seeing the UK in a different light to these major economies is very interesting. "The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively and we see the UK in that sense enjoying a bit of a better growth prospect," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said earlier. Her comments followed those of the IMF's chief economist Silvana Tenreyro who told me that UK borrowing reductions "stand out". Three things we've learnt about the UK economy from the IMF Published 1 day ago UK growth forecast upgraded but higher energy prices to hit economy next year Published 1 day ago The IMF's twice-yearly assessment of global countries' economic prospects showed only the UK among the G7 having a serious plan for consolidation of its annual borrowing over the next few years, worth nearly 4% of the size of the economy. The US, Germany and Japan are increasing borrowing. Canada and Italy are keeping borrowing at the same level. It appears the UK is now the IMF's model pupil - at the top of the G7 table for reducing deficits. This matters because for the past half decade the UK has been on the bond market naughty step, often having the highest borrowing rates among the G7 since the Liz Truss mini budget, as political and economic crises afflicted different governments. While this is good news for the chancellor and the Treasury, it also points to the sort of Budget we will get in a fortnight's time. To keep its plans to reduce debt on track, John Healey is likely to have limited room for extra spending. He will want to marry this with limited tax rises. There could be a modest decrease in the margin for error around meeting debt rules - so-called headroom. If so that will be tied to providing a cushion against an expected rise in energy prices due to the ongoing Middle East conflict and the impact on the cost of living overall - the so called global inflation shock. This is likely to mean disappointment for many public services expecting cash injections to account for rising inflation, as suggested this week by think tank the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It will mean tough public sector pay discussions. It won't be "austerity" but the chancellor is likely to lean into the IMF framing of a government with austere plans, relative to other advanced countries. The initial prize is to avoid the direct gaze of the bond markets, whose full glare is on others, such as France now. The bigger prize could be lower relative borrowing costs for government and households. Ultimately forecasts mean nothing without the underpinning of solid plans. Those plans will be here for everyone to judge soon enough.
