events.title: Scimplify raises $25M to challenge China’s grip on critical materials with AI
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. As manufacturers across industries strive to reduce their reliance on Chinese suppliers, Indian startup Scimplify has raised $25 million to expand its AI-powered approach to producing specialty chemicals and critical materials, with semiconductors, defense, and energy emerging as key growth markets. The all-equity strategic round was led by Hitachi Ventures, with customers Henkel and Teknor Apex joining as new investors. Existing backers Accel India, Bertelsmann India Investments, Omnivore, and 3one4 Capital also participated. The round values the Bengaluru-based startup at $250 million after the investment, according to a person familiar with the transaction, up from $150 million after a $40 million Series B round in March 2025. The latest investment brings Scimplify’s total equity funding to $80 million, the startup said, though it declined to disclose its valuation. The growing adoption of AI and advanced computational tools has accelerated materials discovery and research. However, turning promising chemistry into commercially available products at scale remains a slow and complex process. Manufacturers need to develop production processes, qualify facilities, and meet stringent quality standards, all while navigating supply chains limited to a handful of countries. Scimplify is seeking to shorten that process. In some cases, the startup, founded in 2023, has gone from receiving a customer’s requirements to delivering the finished material in just two months, compared with the 12 to 18 months such work would typically take, co-founder Sachin Santhosh (pictured above) said in an interview. Once it receives an order, Scimplify develops chemical manufacturing processes at its research facilities in Bengaluru and Hyderabad and then transfers them to partner factories for commercial production. Its proprietary AI platform, Scinode, helps coordinate the work by identifying suitable production routes and manufacturing facilities, while tracking quality and regulatory requirements. The platform uses specialized AI agents for different functions, including research, manufacturing, and quality control, Santhosh told TechCrunch. “Each of these agents is basically solving for what [a customer] would want, working backward from the customer’s requirement,” Santhosh said. “This helps us move a lot faster and remember customer context even for future references.” Scimplify’s in-house team of scientists and engineers oversees production across a network of more than 500 manufacturing facilities. It helps customers establish alternative sources for materials whose supply is concentrated in China and a few other countries. About 90% of Scimplify’s manufacturing currently takes place in India. The startup, however, plans to expand its production network to the U.S. and Japan over the next year as it seeks to attract more customers in both markets, Santhosh said. The U.S. has emerged as a key growth market, with Scimplify’s annualized revenue run rate in the country rising sixfold to about $60 million from $10 million a year ago, according to Santhosh. The market now accounts for roughly 30% of its business, while customers outside India collectively contribute more than half of its revenue, compared with less than 5% about 18 months ago. Overall, Scimplify, which serves more than 1,000 customers and has delivered products to more than 40 countries, has reached an annualized revenue run rate of about $200 million, tripling from a year earlier, Santhosh told TechCrunch. The startup is targeting a $400 million annualized revenue run rate over the next year. Scimplify has also been EBITDA-positive for the past two months and expects to turn profitable after tax this month, he said. Energy, electronics, and defense now account for about 45% to 50% of Scimplify’s revenue, up from less than 15% a year ago, Santhosh stated. The growth comes as AI fuels demand for materials used in electronics and energy infrastructure, while ongoing wars drive demand from the defense industry. Scimplify is working on producing tungsten derivatives from scrap, offering customers an alternative source of materials whose supply is heavily concentrated in China. The startup is also working on rare-earth materials, another category where global supply chains remain heavily dependent on China. The startup works with customers including Japanese electronics manufacturer TDK, German chemicals group BASF, and Hitachi. Santhosh cited a project involving TDK as an example of how the startup can shorten the time needed to develop and deliver specialty materials. Timelines, he said, vary depending on the project. events.title: Dubai and Abu Dhabi among top destinations for next-generation wealth, Savills says
events.summary: Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tensions, according to Savills. Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, the London-based consultancy said in its Spotlight on Wealth Trends report on Wednesday. Next-generation wealth refers to individuals under 40 who have inherited significant wealth or have accumulated it through entrepreneurial success. Dubai and Abu Dhabi benefitted from a slew of government initiatives that support economic and societal growth, including favourable tax environments, business-friendly policies and significant infrastructure investment “with a sophisticated luxury offering”, Savills said. In particular, Dubai's entrepreneurial ecosystem, global connectivity and lifestyle appeal attract international talent and capital. Abu Dhabi complements this with its growing financial centre, a rising number of family offices, expanding economic opportunities and a high quality of life, the study said. Those are “reinforcing the UAE's position as a compelling destination for globally mobile wealth”, Kelcie Sellers, associate director for world research at Savills, wrote in the report. In the wider Gulf, “economic diversification and succession planning are becoming more prominent, with growing focus on family governance, next-generation involvement and the long-term deployment of capital within the region”, Ms Sellers said. Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and the flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country is a magnet for the ultra-wealthy , as well as for global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as institutional partners. Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East , a report this week by Boston Consulting Group found. In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report said. Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion. New York leads globally New York topped the Savills list, followed by Miami, London, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Singapore, Hong Kong and Monaco at ninth. Dubai and Abu Dhabi were the only Gulf cities on the list, which ranked more than 100 destinations worldwide. Cities in Europe, the Middle East and Africa accounted for 16 of the index’s top 30 locations, driven by lifestyle and sporting events, which include major golf and tennis tournaments and Formula One races. In terms of the number of sporting events, Dubai was number one in the Emea region, while Abu Dhabi, home of the season-ending F1 race, was sixth. “The defining characteristic of Emea is the diversity of its wealth proposition. Global business centres, leading educational institutions, major sporting and cultural events, coastal retreats and mountain resorts are all within reach,” Ms Sellers said. Global wealth continues to grow rapidly. Total personal wealth jumped by nearly 11 per cent in 2025 to create about one million more millionaires, according to industry tracker Altrata. More than 510,800 are now ultra-high net worth individuals, or those with a net worth of $30 million or more, holding around $60 trillion in combined wealth – which is greater than the combined economies of the US and China, Altrata said. “Location decisions are becoming a core component of wealth planning … at the same time, new fortunes generated by technology and artificial intelligence are reshaping global wealth hubs,” Ms Sellers said. “As a result, many wealthy families are adopting multi-jurisdictional lifestyles, balancing residence, education and wealth structures across multiple markets.”

events.title: Singapore marine fuel supplier Equatorial eyes higher LNG bunker demand from 2028
events.summary: Vessels including oil tankers in the Singapore Strait. The Republic is the world’s biggest refuelling hub for ships, supplying an average 4.7 million tonnes of bunker fuel monthly so far this year. Equatorial Marine Fuel Management plans to use part of its 2026 profits to expand into LNG bunkering, with demand expected to rise from 2028 as more LNG capacity and dual-fuel ships come online. The Singapore supplier won one of eight LNG bunker licences in July and is talking with LNG cargo suppliers and shipowners. Its first new LNG bunker barge should arrive in late Q3 2027. Singapore LNG bunker sales reached 487,100 tons in January to September 2026, up more than 21% year on year. Equatorial says demand is resilient, while biofuel demand has slowed because of delays to the IMO net-zero framework. SINGAPORE – Equatorial Marine Fuel Management, a top Singapore bunker supplier by volume, plans to channel part of its 2026 profits to fund its expansion into supplying liquefied natural gas (LNG) to ships as it positions for higher demand from 2028, its executives said. The company, which was one of eight suppliers awarded an LNG bunker licence in late July, is in discussions with LNG cargo suppliers and shipowners for collaboration, its executive director Choong Zhen Mao told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore International Bunkering conference (SIBCON) 2026. “The opportunity that we see in LNG still seems to be growing, even in this climate. I think that’s where we see the market moving,” he said, referring to the surge in LNG prices after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted exports from the Middle East. The company will be receiving its first new-built LNG bunker barge in the later part of the third quarter in 2027, he added. Singapore’s January-to-September 2026 LNG bunker sales totalled 487,100 tonnes, up more than 21% from a year earlier, data from the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore showed on Oct 14. Equatorial’s chief operating officer (COO), Choong Sheen Mao, expects a more notable increase in Singapore’s LNG bunker demand from 2028, as more LNG production capacity and dual-fuel vessels come online globally. Equatorial currently supplies about 10% of total bunker volumes at Singapore, the world’s biggest refuelling hub for ships, according to its executives. The city state has supplied an average 4.7 million tonnes of bunker fuel a month so far in 2026, official data show. The company’s year-to-date profits for 2026 have exceeded last year’s level, the executives said, though they did not disclose the figures. Bunker fuel prices surged after US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February drove oil prices higher, and have remained volatile since then. The ensuing disruption to shipping routes supported refuelling demand in key hubs including Singapore. “Demand looks to be resilient,” said executive director Choong. “When there is uncertainty, sometimes people tend to purchase a bit more, fill their tanks a bit more... people tend to break a voyage down into smaller trades these days to ensure availability and cargo security.” Equatorial owns eight fuel oil barges, seven marine diesel barges, as well as four chemical bunker tankers that meet the International Maritime Organization’s type 2 standard to carry methanol or biofuel blends up to 100% biofuel content. Some of the chemical bunker tankers have been repurposed to supply conventional fuel this year amid a slowdown in marine biofuel demand, COO Choong said. “Demand for biofuels has slowed this year because of the delay in the IMO’s net-zero framework, while current prices are not competitive,” he said. Depending on the blend and delivery window, biofuel blends command premiums of at least US$100 per tonne over conventional low-sulphur bunker fuel oil, according to industry sources. REUTERS

events.title: Mary Chia insolvency proceedings dismissed, but $350,000 loan dispute remains unresolved
events.summary: As part of court-given directions, Mary Chia transferred $651,498.97 to the court’s account on Oct 6. Mary Chia’s insolvency proceedings were dismissed after it paid $651,498.97 into court and $13,900 in costs, but a High Court dispute over two loans remains unresolved. The company still contests the claimed balance, including default interest, late payment interest and restructuring fees on loans with a combined principal of $350,000. Fullink had sought about $902,640. Mary Chia also plans to raise $1 million through share subscriptions for working capital and expansion, while five subsidiaries face separate CPF arrears cases worth $103,727. SINGAPORE – Insolvency proceedings brought against beauty and wellness group Mary Chia Holdings and three other parties have been dismissed, although a legal dispute over two loans totalling $350,000 remains unresolved. The Catalist-listed company announced on Oct 14 that the court had confirmed the dismissal of proceedings brought by Fullink Capital on Oct 13, following compliance with court directions issued on Sept 30. As part of these directions, Mary Chia transferred $651,498.97 to the court’s account on Oct 6. The amount had previously been placed with the company’s solicitors as security. It also paid $13,900 in court-ordered costs to Fullink’s solicitors on Oct 9, with receipt confirmed on Oct 12. The proceedings involved Mary Chia Holdings, Organica International Holdings, Mary Chia chief executive Ho Yow Ping and chief financial officer Su Jun Ming. Despite the dismissal, the $651,498.97 will remain with the court pending the outcome of an ongoing High Court case concerning amounts claimed by Fullink. Mary Chia stressed that placing the money with the court “does not constitute an admission of liability” in respect of the disputed amounts. The company had earlier paid $343,829 on July 21, representing the amount it acknowledged was due. It continues to contest the remaining sums claimed by Fullink, including disputed default interest, late payment interest and restructuring fees arising from two loans with a combined principal of $350,000. These issues have yet to be determined by the court. Fullink issued statutory demand seeking $902,640 The dispute dates back to March, when Fullink issued a statutory demand seeking about $902,640 over loans extended to Organica, a wholly owned Mary Chia subsidiary. Mary Chia had provided a corporate guarantee for the loans, while Ho and Su were personal guarantors. Fullink subsequently commenced winding-up proceedings against Mary Chia and Organica, as well as bankruptcy proceedings against the two executives. At a hearing on Sept 30, the High Court directed that the insolvency proceedings be dismissed once the secured sum of $651,498.97 was paid into court. Separately, Mary Chia said it had entered into subscription agreements on Oct 6 to raise $1 million in gross proceeds through a proposed share subscription. The funds are intended to strengthen the group’s financial position, with net proceeds earmarked for working capital and business expansion in China and Thailand. The proposed fund raising remains subject to shareholder approval at an extraordinary general meeting, regulatory approvals and other conditions. The latest development comes as five Mary Chia subsidiaries face separate court proceedings over unpaid Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions. In an Oct 9 filing responding to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation, the group disclosed that the five subsidiaries owed a combined $103,727 in CPF arrears , based on the CPF Board’s revised computation. Mary Chia also admitted that it had failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four subsidiaries in an earlier announcement, attributing the omission to shortcomings in its internal reporting and disclosure processes. In its Oct 14 media release, the group said it had worked with the CPF Board to establish a monthly payment arrangement for its outstanding contributions. It added that the first monthly instalment had been “paid in full”, and that the relevant subsidiaries would continue making payments according to the agreed schedule. The five CPF-related cases have been adjourned to Nov 12.

Nearly a quarter of Wall Street firms now link pay, bonuses or promotions to AI skills, the Selby Jennings survey found. Another 30% make staff report AI use in performance reviews, showing firms want clear proof of AI's value. The survey of 500 finance executives also found 42% use formal AI skill checks, and 30% have teams tracking AI returns. NEW YORK – AI skills are starting to count towards pay and promotion on Wall Street, with nearly a quarter of financial firms tying raises, bonuses or promotions to employees’ proficiency with the technology, a survey showed. Another 30% require employees to disclose their use of artificial intelligence tools in formal performance reviews, according to the survey by Selby Jennings, a financial-services recruitment firm. The findings point to a broader shift on Wall Street as firms seek tangible returns from their investment in the technology. “Companies are no longer just seeing if their employees are using AI tools but are also monitoring its impact on output and contribution to business results,” Dylan Gomez, executive director at Selby Jennings, told Reuters. “While currently there is no established formula on how much compensation is getting tied to AI usage and performance, we expect this to become more defined by next year,” Gomez added. The survey found that 42% of respondents had introduced formal criteria to evaluate employees’ AI skills, while 30% had created dedicated teams or roles focused on tracking whether their AI investments were delivering results. The firm polled 500 executives across the finance industry. REUTERS

events.title: Aldar's international unit plans to deliver 9,000 homes in next five years
events.summary: London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties , plans to deliver about 9,000 homes in the next five years in the UK capital with a total development value of £5 billion ($6.6 billion), as demand remains resilient. The homes will be built across about 30 sites, with the company targeting buyers in the affordable segment as well as international investors. More than 3,600 homes will be for sale, 1,538 will be for build-to-rent and another 3,575 will be in the affordable segment, in which government provides grants to registered developer to help it lease to tenants at affordable rental rate. London Square plans to start work on 12 sites this year with 65 per cent of those affordable, said chief executive Adam Lawrence. “There's always demand for affordable housing, it is a huge market and a huge need,” he told The National. There is also international demand from buyers in Turkey, Hong Kong and Middle East countries, he added. “Turkey is really strong at the moment. We've opened an office in Turkey, in Istanbul, recently, and we're seeing, within days of opening, we're into double-digit sales there. Hong Kong's been very quiet, but that looks like it's coming back.” The company, which was acquired by Aldar in 2023, has delivered 5,000 homes across 46 sites with a development value of £2.9 billion ($3.8 billion) since London Square was founded in 2010. “Under the Aldar banner, our sales have actually been better than they were historically and in the current market have been outperforming all of our peers,” said Scott Brown, chief financial officer of London Square. “Through our involvement with Aldar, we've not only been able to drive the capital but we've also been able to drive our sales.” London Square, which regenerates former industrial sites, is behind projects such as the Nine Elms development, which features more than 750 residential homes and 21,500 square feet of commercial and retail space. It is also transforming the former headquarters of Surrey County Council into a premium 292-home development, which includes the restoration of old structures. The company aims to complete 600 homes this year, up from 398 last year, with sales backlog to reach £1 billion by the end of 2026. “Most of this year will be on the affordable market rather than the build-to-sell market … about 30 per cent of what we're building is affordable,” Mr Brown told The National in London. He did not provide details on the total sales the company expects this year. London Square reported sales of £251 million for the first half of 2026, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf. Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity, says Naomi Minegishi, London Square international sales director. “International demand is being driven by investment opportunity, safe haven of their capital and a strong legal framework,” Ms Minegishi said. “Families also want to have a second home to spend time in summer, as well as to have a home to support their children as they enrol them in school or universities to study in London.” London's property market has been affected by geopolitical uncertainty that is pushing inflation higher. In the third quarter, the average home price in London grew modestly by 0.4 per cent annually to £529,720, as demand remained subdued amid higher borrowing costs, according to the Nationwide Building Society. However, fundamentals remain strong on higher investment activity, lifestyle vibrancy and a diverse population, said Sharief Ibrahim, executive director and head of residential agency at CBRE. “There is real cause for optimism. There are countless examples of schemes that are performing really well, many in the London Square portfolio in terms of the volume of apartments being sold and the value being achieved,” he said. “London is a resilient place. It's been through economic downturns, shocks to the economy and the system and the appeal of London has endured throughout that period. It's a global powerhouse and one of the, if not the most, successful city in terms of inward investment globally.” It projects home transaction volumes to be around 6,000 to 7,000 this year and 7,500 to 8,000 next year.

events.title: Diesel supplies to remain ‘tight’ into 2027: IEA
events.summary: The IEA predicted that refining capacity will recover and lead to a surplus on the diesel market in the first quarter of 2027. PARIS – Diesel supply disruptions in the Gulf stemming from the US war against Iran will keep the market tight into 2027, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Oct 14 , as it will take time to rebuild depleted stocks. “The gasoil market balance will remain tight well into 2027 and is dependent on a recovery of product supply from the Middle East,” the Paris-based agency said in its monthly energy markets report. Diesel prices have hit record highs across Europe and in the US in recent weeks, due to both reduced oil exports from the Gulf and damage to refineries in the region from retaliatory attacks by Iran. Governments have responded by reducing fuel taxes or providing subsidies, and by releasing strategic reserves that will need to be rebuilt. The IEA predicted that refining capacity will recover and lead to a surplus on the diesel market in the first quarter of 2027 , “lifting stocks broadly in line with normal seasonal patterns”. But that will not fully compensate for the deficit accumulated since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February, which sent energy prices soaring around the globe. And if Gulf supplies do not return to normal levels soon, “further demand reductions and the heavy economic costs these will entail may be needed to balance markets”, the IEA warned. AFP

events.title: Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research
events.summary: Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research. The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released. Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”. Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face , a tech startup. Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London. The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips. “The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.” Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”. On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access. The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year. “It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said. Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.

events.title: AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s how | Richard Wilson and Clara Long
events.summary: AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s how A fight over a datacentre in Utah has been a testing ground for citizens’ assemblies, paving the way to oversight What’s your “(p)doom” – the percentage chance that rogue AI will create an existential catastrophe? Judging by their recent warnings, it is rising among tech bosses. On 25 September, OpenAI paused training of its latest frontier models as reports of AI agents going rogue mounted. A day later, Australia’s Senate asked the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic to appear before an inquiry after rogue OpenAI agents broke into US government websites and an Australian health portal. Both declined. Bill Gates, meanwhile, has warned that AI in the wrong hands could “cause a billion deaths”. “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said. Days before, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, the chief executives of Anthropic and OpenAI, appeared before the UN security council . Amodei warned that AI could become “a risk to humanity as a whole”. Altman said that “if AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone”. Doomsday scenarios aside, AI is already disrupting schools, workplaces and public services, with the most marginalised often feeling the impacts harder and faster. If democracy is to matter in this era of tech power, surely we must try to democratise AI. But how? Utah offers a glimpse. Proposals for a datacentre more than twice the size of Manhattan provoked a furious backlash over energy use and the potential impact on the state’s stressed water supplies and Great Salt Lake ecosystem, all while people felt excluded from having a say. On 18 and 19 September, Utah Common Ground convened 38 residents selected by civic lottery to consider what role the public should have in shaping decisions about AI technology and infrastructure. Despite their political differences, participants overwhelmingly agreed on the need for greater public control. Their 10 recommendations included public hearings and independent environmental assessments for hyperscale datacentres, community-led AI literacy programmes and tighter transparency rules. Every recommendation received at least 82% support. In a polarised state, that is a mandate legislators should struggle to wave away. Globally, there have been more than 80 public participation projects focused on AI over the past five years, involving more than 200,000 people in more than 95 countries. In Switzerland, a citizens’ assembly demanded privacy, transparency and meaningful human control. A Belgian citizens’ panel called for AI that serves everyone and leaves nobody behind. At present, however, this work is fragmented and largely ignored by decision-makers in government and the labs. The Citizens’ Track on AI , a decentralised network of assemblies rooted in communities but connected to the institutions where consequential decisions about AI are being made, intends to change that. The Bloom Project , which helped convene the Utah assembly, is building one part of that network: a series of US local and state assemblies intended to feed into a national citizens’ assembly on AI in 2028. At the global level, the ambition is to connect assemblies across countries into the UN’s emerging processes for AI governance, while also creating direct lines of accountability to the AI companies. A bridge built by the powerful can be withdrawn by them. That is why Utah matters. Its forum was rooted in civic groups that will outlast the forum itself, though it has no guaranteed hearing yet. Durable civic power needs both: communities that keep convening and decision-makers who have to answer them. The same principle underpins proposals published last week for a standing global citizens’ assembly on AI : combining the independent moral authority of globally representative, self-governing citizens with legislated powers to hold AI companies accountable for their safety and alignment practices. None of this is easy. Yet deliberation need not be slow: Taiwan went from citizens’ panel to law in months in an effort to address scam advertising. It is also hard to buy: lobbyists can buy policy influence, not the outcome of a citizens’ assembly. Can any of this protect us against AI being used to launch a cyber-attack, develop a biological weapon or escape human control altogether? Not by itself. But how much risk society should accept isn’t an engineering question – it’s a political one. Citizens’ assemblies can give governments the mandate, and the cover, to impose the testing, red lines and stop buttons that companies won’t impose on themselves. The danger is not only that AI may escape human control. It is whether the humans controlling it are a tiny group of elite executives, investors and politicians vulnerable to corporate capture. Altman was right: decisions of this magnitude cannot remain inside laboratories in San Francisco.

events.title: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis | Anonymous
events.summary: I work for a major insurer. Much of my industry is fudging the numbers in the face of the climate crisis Insurers are taking on more risk than they should. If – or when – a major disaster hits, the catastrophe will have far-reaching consequences I work for a major insurer, assessing the risk posed by natural disasters on properties around the world, from family homes to schools, government offices and multibillion-dollar commercial centres. The world is facing greater risk than ever from extreme weather. We are not prepared – and that inaction could have profound consequences for the global financial system. In the face of ever more extreme and unpredictable climate risks, I am coming under pressure to cut my forecasts for the losses that disasters will cause in order to make insurance more affordable – and get my employer more business. In some instances, the questioning of our numbers and models is justified. But too often, it is not being done to produce more accurate models, but to artificially lower prices. If this is happening at my firm, which is struggling to compete with rivals’ prices, it’s happening elsewhere. Our sector is carrying more risk than we realise. The warming global climate has caused more frequent high-intensity storms, rising sea levels, flooding, wildfires and drought. While the immediate impact of these events is plain to see, the long-term effects will be compounded as insurers withdraw from affected areas, leaving the economy in freefall and people’s day-to-day lives in ruins. As a modeller, it is my job to look objectively and scientifically at the data to calculate an expected loss from a natural disaster, which affects the price of the premium for a given policy. Our industry says it holds those numbers as sacrosanct, but as my analysis shows higher and more volatile risk, the price rises with it and we lose customers. So modellers like me are coming under pressure to reduce their projected losses. In the most basic terms, we are collectively fudging the numbers and taking on more risk than we should for a lower price than the expected loss demands. Sometimes I will forecast losses that would normally be seen as much too risky for us to insure, but we offer the policies anyway. This will eventually lead to a sector built on “competitively priced” contracts that underestimate risk, leaving gaping holes in the safety net that insurance is supposed to provide. For example, if subsidence – which is made worse by drought – damages a number of homes in your area, insurers may exclude this from your policy, so you won’t be covered if subsidence then hits your house. When that happens to an entire community, businesses leave, investment dries up and the local economy tanks. Now imagine this happening in multiple towns around the country, at the same time. And subsidence is just one such issue, alongside wildfires, coastal erosion, wind and floods – and that’s just in the UK. I have respect for underwriters who are just doing their jobs, and I know that no single individual is responsible. My concern lies with the attitude of much of the industry towards modellers, actuaries and researchers: there is a sense that we are an inconvenience to the deal-making process, rather than an essential part of risk management. We are the failsafe that stops our industry from reckless gambling. At the largest scale, misquoted insurance can damage insurers, companies, their employees and the communities that rely on them. The upshot is that our customers are likely to be much more exposed to climate-related risks than they realise. People are not budgeting for a major increase in their insurance premiums or planning for their homes becoming uninsurable, but many of them absolutely should be. If the worst happens, the insurance industry may not have the money to pay every claim when a major disaster hits. That would have profound consequences for the economy as a whole – businesses could go bankrupt, the housing market could seize up and, if people couldn’t pay their mortgages, banks would fail. Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more As natural catastrophes continue to become less predictable and more severe, the foundations of our entire economy will only become more fragile. Our customers deserve to know. The writer is a modeller working in the insurance industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of their Secret Source series , a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

events.title: Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? | Arwa Mahdawi
events.summary: Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? Airports’ TSA staff have been stripped of their chairs in the name of ‘professionalism’. Most supermarket staff have never had them. Meanwhile, Donald Trump is seated at his desk – and apparently snoozing G reat news for everyone who is soon to fly via a US airport: the Trump administration has just elevated the travel experience. You still risk getting arrested by immigration agents and thrown into a detention centre, but never mind that! Instead, luxuriate in the fact that none of the poorly paid Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff with whom you interact will be sitting down. The government recently got rid of all the chairs at travel document checking stations, arguing that “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism” and strengthens “our security posture and … commitment to hospitality”. Funnily enough, border patrol and customs officers have not adopted the same policy. Perhaps because their job tends to involve being as inhospitable as possible. TSA agents aren’t the only US workers getting sore calf muscles during their shifts. Unlike their European and British counterparts, cashiers at US supermarkets have traditionally been forced to stand while working . The US’s upright obsession seems to be down to a Protestant work ethic and a lack of labour laws . Sitting apparently conveys laziness to the discerning American consumer. Over the years there have been numerous right-to-sit lawsuits pushing back on mandatory standing but, while things are shifting slightly, seated supermarket cashiers are still unusual. One exception is Aldi, which has been expanding aggressively in the US. Cashiers get chairs at Aldi because (surprise) it’s more efficient when your workers’ feet aren’t aching all the time. While seated cashiers and TSA agents may be looked down on by the US establishment, it’s a different story for high-flyers. Rather than “maintaining a standing posture” to “reinforce professionalism”, the US president often looks as if he is snoozing at his desk. Which, to be fair, is probably because he regularly stays up all night posting extremely important memes on the internet. Having their chairs seized isn’t the only indignity that TSA agents have faced recently: along with other federal employees, they had to work without pay for several weeks during government shutdowns in Trump’s second term. Members of Congress on the other hand? They could continue to collect their generous salaries during the shutdown unless they explicitly chose not to . Americans should not take this injustice sitting down. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? events.title: New Mexico and El Paso Spent Millions on Climate Plans. Three New Data Centers Could Undo Them.
events.summary: Meta is building a massive data center on the northeast edge of El Paso, Texas, on the New Mexico border. Paul Ratje for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.  Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.  Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.  A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso. The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters. The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months , as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune .  But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year. They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside.  “The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said. Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately. “We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.” The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.  Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not. A truck sprays water for dust suppression at the construction site of Project Jupiter in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.  Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said. “This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?” Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.  State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break , which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.  New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.  The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019 . (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)  “This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University. “This is a huge source.” Homes in Chaparral, New Mexico, sit adjacent to Meta’s data center, just over the state border in El Paso, Texas. events.title: 'It's definitely tight trying to budget on maternity leave'
events.summary: Sara Ody was among the first customers at a new community food pantry in Sheffield Published 14 October 2026, 10:59 BST Almost 50,000 households in Sheffield are struggling to make ends meet and cannot pay their bills, according to a new cost of living report by the council. Described as having a "negative budget", these people are unable to afford the necessary costs even after all benefit entitlements have been claimed and their outgoings have been reduced to the bare essentials. In the same week the report was published, a new food pantry opened in the Woodseats area of the city, offering low priced food for anyone struggling with the cost of living. Within the first hour 14 people called in, with 37-year-old Sara Ody among those through the door. "There's always a thought process, 'can we afford this? do we have to sacrifice this to be able to afford food, childcare and clothes?' It's definitely tough," she said. The Community Grocery pantry, run in partnership by The Message Trust and Ikon Church at Woodseats, offers membership for £1 per year, with food and household staples from just 50p. Sara said her finances were especially tight now she is on maternity leave from work. "There's four of us now, and I've got to the point in my maternity leave where there is not really any money coming in, so it's definitely tight trying to budget, especially in the run up to Christmas," she said. "It's frustrating because I saved up so much money while I was working to be able to still have opportunities and do things while on maternity leave, but you have to budget all the time. "We're finding food is so expensive and every week it seems the prices are going up and up so things like this are amazing. We can get definitely some staple bits to see us through winter." According to the report to Sheffield City Council , external , Citizens Advice estimates 47,500 people in Sheffield have negative budgets. It says that poverty in the city predates the cost-of-living crisis and reflects longer-term inequalities in income, employment, health, housing and opportunity. However, it says years of financial pressure have also left some households with depleted savings, debt and arrears, reducing their ability to absorb further shocks It adds that children are particularly affected, with approximately one in three children in Sheffield living in poverty, "substantially above" the national rate. John Lawson is from The Message Trust John Lawson is the regional lead for The Message Trust, which has 35 stores nationwide, and is based in Sheffield. He says community grocery stores can bridge the gap between food banks and supermarkets, as they offer a variety of food but at a fraction of the cost. "We opened here after seeing the need on the doorstep and the challenges that people are facing with the cost of living," he said. "Even a lot of the community who wouldn't necessarily have been struggling five years ago are now finding themselves living paycheck to paycheck." The store is open to everyone and there is no means testing. Lawson added: "We want to make it accessible for everyone, so if someone is passionate about saving food from landfill, they should shop here. If someone's in crisis and needs free food, they can come here. "Or if someone just wants to be in the community, in an amazing space like we've got here, they can come and hang out. "We want to create an opportunity and a resource where anyone can come and access healthy food and wraparound care so we can holistically look after the whole person with mental health support, debt advice, cookery courses or just simply offering a social space for people to come together." Another customer Debbie Schofield, 44, said she thought the pantry would help people realise they are not alone. "I think Woodseats needs this community hub where people can get some cheaper resources and have a chat somewhere warm," she said. "I like the concept of the community pantry. I think everybody's struggling with the cost of living, everything has gone up quite considerably, but I also feel like social media isolates us in our own homes. "I don't feel there's a sense of community like when I was growing up, like in the 1980s and 90s. It's really important for these pantries to exist because they bring neighbours together and then people in the wider community start to recognise each other.

events.title: Temasek Trust, World Bank Group tie up to advance initiatives in climate and energy
events.summary: Desmond Kuek, executive director and CEO of Temasek Trust, and Paschal Donohoe, managing director and chief knowledge officer of the World Bank Group, at the MOU signing. SINGAPORE – Temasek Trust and World Bank Group have inked a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to advance initiatives in areas such as agriculture, climate and energy. “By building shared knowledge and a repository of effective solutions, the parties aim to help translate promising pilots into replicable and scalable models that can advance impact outcomes,” said a Temasek Trust spokesperson. The spokesperson added that these sectors were chosen as Temasek Trust and World Bank Group have complementary strengths in them. Both parties will explore co-financing and innovative financing approaches to mobilise additional resource in these sectors. The MOU was signed on Oct 12, on the sidelines of the inaugural World Bank Group Philanthropy Forum in Bangkok. World Bank Group also launched the Philanthropy Hub, a platform to deepen collaboration with philanthropic organisations and other partners. As part of this, and under the MOU, Temasek Trust will launch a Knowledge Node at Temasek Shophouse by 2027. Through this, philanthropic partners will be able to access World Bank Group’s datasets, expertise and networks. “As development needs grow and resources come under pressure, partnership matters more than ever,” said Paschal Donohoe, managing director and chief knowledge officer of World Bank Group. “The Philanthropy Hub will connect ideas, resources and partners to take those solutions to scale, and to deliver for people and communities around the world.” Desmond Kuek, executive director and chief executive officer of Temasek Trust, added that the development challenges of today “do not fit neatly into silos – and neither can our response”. “Philanthropy can move early, take risks, and unlock the partnerships and capital needed to turn bold ideas into lasting impact,” he added. “Working in concert with the World Bank Group and its Philanthropy Hub, we can bridge systemic gaps, scale what works and forge new pathways for collective action.” THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.summary: President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s deal to deliver Russian diesel to global markets may be sending shockwaves through the GOP — but don’t expect it to do the same to prices. The planned imports will “have very little unnoticeable impact on domestic US diesel prices, even if it happens — and I think that’s a big if,” given legal complications and Russian constraints, Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations, told Semafor. events.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
events.summary: Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a...smart display? Why it matters : Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future. It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday. Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: Getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts. Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices. "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios. Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners. HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other, a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4. Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri. The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: Making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets. Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making . Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm , a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses. Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand. U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana. "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon. Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones. Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it remains unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market. "The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios. The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

events.title: Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI
events.summary: Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence . You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton? In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton. There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist. Compared to women , “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.) While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides. Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men. Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women. “Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says. Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did. In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty. “We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says. events.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
events.summary: Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond. Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action. U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study . Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat. Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap." The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next. "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study. State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models. Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here." Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions. The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings. Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans. Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes. Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions. She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning. One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a PhD student in Cornell's Information Science Department. What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions. AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said. That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said. The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

events.title: Former Cathay cinema operator mm2 Asia, subsidiary still owe over $219k in CPF arrears
events.summary: Cinema operator mm2 Asia formerly operated Cathay Cineplexes, which ceased operations in Singapore on Sept 1, 2025, after its four remaining outlets closed amid mounting financial difficulties. mm2 Asia and its subsidiary mm2 Entertainment still owe over S$219,000 in CPF arrears, while founder Melvin Ang says restructuring makes further repayments hard. The court heard mm2 Entertainment paid S$20,203.50 but still fell short, and it must pay at least S$80,000 before the next hearing on Nov 11. mm2 Asia’s restructuring plan includes a S$15 million share placement, a rights issue of up to S$10 million, and debt-for-equity conversion after Cathay Cineplexes closed in 2025. SINGAPORE – Former Cathay Cineplexes operator mm2 Asia and its subsidiary still owe more than $21 9,00 0 in Central Provident Fund (CPF) contributions, with their founder telling a court that demands for further repayments are difficult to meet while the companies undergo a restructuring . Th e St ate Courts heard on Oct 14 that mainboard-listed mm2 Asia owed $8,633.50 while its wholly owned subsidiary mm2 Entertainment had an outstanding amount of $210,843.50. Their founder, Melvin An g, who represented both companies in court, said mm2 Asia could settle its outstanding arrears in full by the next hearing on Nov 1 1. During the hearing for mm2 Entertainment, the prosecution said the company made a payment of $20, 203 .50 on Oct 13, but had fallen short of the $5 0,0 00 it was previously directed to pay. Ang said the company hoped to settle all its outstanding contributions by D ec 31, after completing its restructuring. However, when asked how much it could pay in four weeks, he said it hoped to make another $20 ,000 payment. $20k to $40k repayments will prolong the matter The prosecution said repayments of between $20,000 and $40,000 would prolong the matter, given the substantial amount still outstanding. The court subsequently directed mm2 Entertainment to pay at least $80,000 before its next hearing on Nov 11. Ang pointed out that the company had been granted a moratorium by the High Court and said there had been no staff complaints to the Ministry of Manpower over the CPF arrears. He said mm2 Entertainment would struggle to meet a court direction to pay at least $ 80, 000 by the next month , citing its financial difficulties and ongoing restructuring efforts . “Asking us to pay $80k by next month before the scheme of arrangement is completed is really difficult,” he said. Separately, during mm2 Asia’s hearing, Ang initially told the judge that the company had paid “everything” in full on Oct 13, after making an $11,000 payment. However, the prosecution said records showed that $10,438.50 had been paid, leaving a discrepancy of $561.50. The prosecution suggested that part of the payment might have gone towards other statutory obligations, including Skills Development Levy payments. Ang said the discrepancy could have been an error and undertook to settle the remaining $8,633.50 before the Nov 11 hearing. At an earlier hearing on Sept 16, the court was told that both companies owed about $213,000 in CPF contributions. Ang, who had also represented the company then, had cited financial difficulties and an ongoing scheme of arrangement when seeking more time to pay. “There is no fund in the company,” he had said then, adding that mm2 Entertainment proposed to begin repaying its arrears from January 2027. mm2 Asia faces three charges over unpaid CPF contributions for one employee between November 2025 and January 2026, while mm2 Entertainment faces eight charges involving four employees for November and December 2025. Both companies are seeking to restructure their debts through proposed schemes of arrangement , which allow financially distressed companies to negotiate repayment terms with creditors, subjected to creditor and court approval . What are some aspects of mm2 Asia’s proposed restructuring On Sept 18, the High Court granted both companies permission to convene creditors’ meetings to vote on their proposals. It also extended a moratorium protecting them from creditor enforcement proceedings by two months to Nov 21 , giving them more time to complete the restructuring . According to court documents filed on Sept 3 and seen by The Straits Times, mm2 Asia’s proposed restructuring includes a $15 million share placement to MMRA, a subsidiary of private equity fund Hildrics Asia Growth Fund. The proposed investment involves the issuances of approximately 16.34 billion new shares, alongside cash distributions and debt-for-equity conversion for creditors. The company also proposes a rights issue to raise up to $10 million. On Sept 22, mm2 Asia announced that the Securities Industry Council had granted MMRA a conditional waiver from making a mandatory general offer for its remaining shares, subject to conditions including independent shareholder approval.

events.title: Bank of England and IMF bosses warn of cyber threat to trust in financial system
events.summary: Kristalina Georgieva says online fraud could lead people to opt out of system and turn to ‘shoeboxes under their bed’ The heads of the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund have issued a stark warning that rising cyber-attacks risk undermining trust in the financial system. Speaking on a panel about online fraud at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, pointed to alarming headlines about self-replicating AI agents hijacking personal devices , and the French supermarket hack that heated fridges up to 50C . “If you try to say what’s at the heart of this debate about AI – for me, it’s about trust in technology and it’s about human control to achieve that trust in technology,” he said. Pointing to the key importance of technology in underpinning today’s financial system, he added: “If we don’t have trust in money, we don’t operate as a society.” Echoing his concerns, the IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva , said the toll of cyber-fraud was now so great that people could decide to opt out of the formal financial system altogether. “I was born and grew up on the other side of the iron curtain,” the Bulgarian economist said. “We didn’t trust the system. What did we do? I would have my dollars in a shoebox under my bed. “And I worry, today, that unless we figure out how to get ahead of this curve, given the speed, the scale and the cost of fraud growing up, we may end up with lots of people with shoeboxes under their beds.” She said this threat was particularly acute for people on the fringes of the financial system. “Imagine what would happen if trust disappears or is eroded to a point that people no more have the courage to be included,” she said. Her comments followed a warning from the IMF on Tuesday that the possibility of a big cyber-attack was one of the factors raising the global financial stability threat level to “elevated”, alongside higher borrowing costs and the risk of an AI share price crash. Bailey stressed that fraud was now frequently committed via social media platforms and apps, not just traditional financial channels – and urged big tech to take responsibility. He contrasted today’s environment with the legal status in the UK of outlets such as newspapers, which are responsible for the veracity of everything they publish. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Instead, the governor said: “We’ve moved into quite an extreme position of, well, these platforms are open to everybody and there’s no real liability to the provision of the platform to what’s on it. Guess what? Everything’s on it. You know, the good, the bad and the incredibly ugly and downright criminal and terrible.” He added: “I don’t go around pointing the finger at people and saying: ‘You’re bad.’ What I have said is: ‘Look, there is responsibility all around.’ And we need to evolve to a world where everybody understands this responsibility, and everybody is then a part of addressing the problem.” He added: “We must get the social media companies involved because a lot of this fraud is transmitted through those channels.” Bailey called for the same tools that are being used by cybercriminals to be put to work protecting the financial system. “I’m going to use a sporting metaphor: this technology is arming the offence but it can also arm the defence, and it must do.” The panel event at which the pair were speaking was to launch a new set of international principles for avoiding cyber-fraud in financial institutions, called the Bangkok blueprint.

events.title: NoonTalk needs continued financial support from CEO Dasmond Koh, auditors warn
events.summary: Auditors said NoonTalk will continue to require financial support from CEO and controlling shareholder Dasmond Koh to continue operating. NoonTalk Media faces serious financial trouble, with auditors warning it may not continue operating because of losses, cash outflows, and debts above assets. CEO and controlling shareholder Dasmond Koh has promised 12 months of financial support, including help from his listed shares and a $1.8 million loan conversion. The company hopes new China marketing income, cost cuts, and extra fundraising will improve cash flow, while it will keep quarterly reporting because of the uncertainty. SINGAPORE – NoonTalk Media’s financial difficulties appear to remain unsolved despite financial support from its chief executive and controlling shareholder Dasmond Koh. Auditors flagged significant uncertainty over the talent management, multimedia production and events firm’s ability to continue operating, citing its losses, cash outflows and liabilities exceeding assets. The warning was disclosed in an Oct 14 announcement on its audited financial statements for the year ended June 30. Koh has given a written undertaking to provide the necessary financial support for 12 months from Oct 14 to help the company meet its debts as they fall due, NoonTalk said in the statement. The support will come mainly from Koh’s holdings of Singapore-listed shares, which can be converted into cash when the company calls upon him. It follows Koh’s conversion of a $1.8 million loan to NoonTalk into company shares in July. This comes as the auditing team highlighted several factors that could cast significant doubt on NoonTalk’s ability to continue operating. The group reported a loss of $2.55 million for the financial year ended June 30, and used $2.16 million in cash in its operations. At the end of June, its total liabilities exceeded its assets by $2.93 million. Its short-term liabilities also exceeded its short-term assets by about $2.93 million. Short-term liabilities are obligations due within a year, while short-term assets include cash and other assets expected to be converted into cash or used within that period. The auditors added that the assumption that NoonTalk could continue operating depended on continued financial support from Koh. Besides Koh’s support, NoonTalk said it expected income from a new platform marketing business in China. Its subsidiary Ruiqi Zhongxin (Chengdu) Culture Technology has entered into a framework agreement with a third party to carry out promotional campaigns and place advertisements on ByteDance’s Ocean Qianchuan platform. The board said its cash flow forecast, which took account of potential income from the marketing services, and planned cost reductions, indicated that the group could generate positive operating cash flows. NoonTalk is also evaluating options to raise or obtain additional funds for its day-to-day operations. For now, the board said sufficient information had been disclosed for trading in NoonTalk’s shares to continue in an orderly manner. The Catalist-listed company will also continue reporting its financial results quarterly instead of twice a year because of the material uncertainty over its ability to continue operating.
