events.title: Is the modern economic system broken? These urban beekeepers think so – and this is their solution
events.summary: At Bybi in Copenhagen, a dedicated group of staff and volunteers have built a community for all centred on the production of honey – much of which is given away for nothing. Could it be replicated elsewhere? T he bees at Bybi, a collective of beekeepers in Copenhagen , live on the roof. Their home is a complex of Victorian buildings, right in the centre of the city, that looks like an idealised vision of the modern social enterprise, ennobled by the architecture of the past. It’s a place of cottage industry in concert with nature, where the marginalised are brought in from the fringes and corporations stand waiting to help, where jobs happen but a lot of the work is done by volunteers, and where – this bit is important – a lot of time is spent discussing ideas. Oliver Maxwell, Bybi’s 48-year-old founder, encourages me to examine the buildings more closely. They were once a prison, a workhouse and a hospital; their functions today – a homeless shelter, a young offender institution and, until recently, a job centre – are not so different. Denmark’s Victorian transformation, from “agricultural backwater to industrialised agriculture”, was reflected in how they treated people, Maxwell says. In the middle of it all is the collective, which looks like a lot of things – a commune, a kitchen-table business, an art space. Everything smells of honey. Long drapes in earthy colours frame the entrance to a space where volunteers jar honey by hand. Small pots are stacked against a window in what appears to be a random formation, but this turns out to be a stylistic map of the city: each jar is from a particular street, with its own shade and its own taste, thanks to “the flowers people planted, the weather, the bees’ own decisions and choices”, as Maxwell puts it. “Bybi is a constellation of time, work, money, community and connection, a place asking an open question: what would it take for bees, people and communities to thrive?” he says. Between 40 and 50 volunteers come in and out throughout the year, with a core team of 15 undertaking practical, honey-related tasks and events. They have 80 to 100 colonies, not just on this rooftop, but all over the city, on businesses and conference centres, schools, municipal buildings, restaurants. They produce between four and six tonnes of honey every year. How that turns into money really depends. Sometimes they give it away, at weddings and festivals. “Honey is an invitation,” Maxwell says. “It wants you to come in as a co-creator, with a joint responsibility for its health. We ask that you share it with someone you care for. And you plant a flower to help the bees.” Sometimes they sell it in the old-fashioned way, at a couple of boutique delicatessens around the city. Sometimes they ask people how much they want to pay; some are generous, some are not. Sometimes they discuss it in a reverse haggle, sitting in a group where they, as sellers, start low; the bidders tend to drive the price higher by thinking deeply about what went into the honey. Maxwell, an anthropologist, is originally from the UK. He spent time in Vietnam doing forest protection, some more in Brighton training social enterprises, then arrived in Denmark in 2007, setting up Bybi along similar lines in 2010. The plan was to employ homeless and other marginalised people, who would then be absorbed back into society. Honey would be made at the same time. Bybi also employed a social worker, “who was always a really nice person”. The problem is, “it just doesn’t work”, he says. “The bottom half of the jobs market has fallen out and everyone else has to run faster and faster. The moment you make contact with the market economy, everyone just melts. We’re sitting here with a crisis of community, a loneliness crisis , a crisis in the meaning and purpose of work. People need to do stuff – we’ll find stuff to do. But the labour theory of value, where you create worth with your time, your boss takes it and gives you some back that you can live on? That does not work.” They abandoned the “giving homeless people jobs” agenda. Now, people come because they want to, not because they’ve been forced to by the job centre. Five or so people are employed, with more in the summer; there are scores of volunteers, including disabled people who pack flower seeds. “They do it as slowly as they like and we give most of the seeds away for free,” Maxwell says. “It’s outside the logic of work.” And yet jobs are found. Maybe that, like the honey, is a byproduct of the bees. Back on the roof, 53-year-old Aref Haboo, the principal beekeeper, is looking for the queen amid sheets of honeycomb. The Syrian Kurd, who came to Denmark in 2014, finds her first time with an instinct gleaned from 18 years doing this job in the Afrin province of northern Syria, before he was displaced by Islamic State. Bees can recognise faces , apparently; they can also count and maybe even dream.

events.title: Trump plays Russian roulette on eve of midterms
events.summary: President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions. Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters. Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues. On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader. On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington. On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets. On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary." Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes. For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war. For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment , as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. For Republicans: With control of Congress hanging in the balance, Trump is embracing a dictator viewed unfavorably by 81% of his own 2024 voters, according to a January YouGov poll . The big picture: Trump's warm relationship with Putin has haunted his political career since 2016, when Russia interfered in the presidential election to help him defeat Hillary Clinton. From the Mueller investigation to the Helsinki summit , Trump's deference toward Putin has long divided Republicans and put him at odds with his own national security establishment. A decade of investigations, scandals and Washington outrage has done little to shake that affinity. If anything, the scrutiny appears to have hardened Trump's determination to defy the foreign-policy consensus. What they're saying: On Monday, Trump again suggested that Russia was more interested in ending the war than the country it invaded, telling reporters: "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky." "The President's diesel deal will help lower prices for farmers, truckers, and families across the nation as he simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement. The bottom line: Losing control of Congress could paralyze Trump's legislative agenda and expose his administration to years of investigations and subpoenas. But as polling alarms pile up , the president appears increasingly willing to follow his raw political instincts, regardless of the consequences for Republicans fighting to keep him in power. In a Truth Social post Tuesday, Trump made clear that he sees himself as personally immune from the results of the midterms, writing: "I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE."

events.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
events.summary: Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows. Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work. The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic. Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios. That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt. It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker backed AI safety group, which has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4). The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike. OpenAI President Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI. Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void. Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future. Eliosoff, an active participant in New York's effective altruism community, said he didn't want to see a repeat of 2024, where crypto industry funding had outsized influence on the regulatory positions of most candidates. "If politicians feel like they can't say anything because there's a very deep-pocketed and ruthless political entity that's going to go after them, that motivates me to step in," Eliosoff said. Between the lines: Eliosoff has donated to Democrats and Republicans who he says appear to be open to taking AI risks seriously and could be well positioned to pass regulation. Donors told Axios they are not primarily motivated by party affiliation or specific policy positions but by fears that industry spending will silence candidates on an unpopular technology. The other side: Leading the Future had retained more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has supported more than 15 Democrats and more than 25 Republicans. In a statement, the group said AI regulation will need 60 votes to pass in the Senate, so anyone serious about safety "and harnessing the benefits of AI for all Americans should be focused on building a broad coalition for action." What's next: This cycle will be a test of whether candidates who take AI industry money and oppose real regulation lose and whether that is clearly understood as a central factor in their loss, Guardrails Alliance Executive Director Shaunna Thomas said. "Republican leadership and the Trump administration are on the other side of the majority of Americans on AI," Thomas said. "That's a very important place for Democrats to be stepping into – boldly." Yes, but: Guardrails faces pushback from some Democrats who warn its strategy, which includes opposing some Democrats, could help elect Republicans less inclined to regulate AI. The bottom line: Trump allies have opened a new front against Anthropic and safety advocates affiliated with the EA movement, but their political giving — as well as the insistence of AI insiders — shows that the political clout of pro-safety AI advocacy is set to grow.

events.title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
events.summary: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight. Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off.  As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher. The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move. But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board. After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground. All seven crew members were killed.   Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back. It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer. Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide. A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it. The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons. Globally, that figure is likely in the millions .  One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem. Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline. But that’s an imperfect solution. The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less. Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation. Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says.  A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started. That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems. He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”). Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer. Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals.  KaloCyte techs use a device called a tangential flow filtration machine to process unencapsulated hemoglobin. MATT ROTH After processing, the hemoglobin is concentrated and then freeze-dried to make it shelf-stable. MATT ROTH With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has.  Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage. Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says. After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”   In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit. Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s. On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding. In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors. But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products. Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians.  As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success. Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles. The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets. The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale. Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic. Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane. For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible. Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage . It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict. events.title: Former Canadian official says Europe erred on Trump tariffs
events.summary: Europe made a “historic” blunder by caving to the Trump administration on tariffs during Trump’s second term, the former Canadian trade minister who helped negotiate the US-Mexico-Canada deal during the first Trump administration told Semafor. “A real problem for the Western alliance has been the decision by the UK and by the EU to give in to the Trump bullying on tariffs,” Chrystia Freeland said. “People thought appeasement would win a reprieve for us all.” The EU and UK have each negotiated with the administration following the imposition of unilateral tariffs, and the former agreed to a pact that went into effect this year. US trade relations with Canada, meanwhile, have broken down, and Ottawa has announced counter-tariffs following US pressure. Freeland, who is out with a new book , said it’s “possible” albeit difficult for the US and Canada to return to a constructive relationship. That might need to wait until Trump is out of office, though. “There would have to be a clear break because the problem is: How do you do a deal with someone who already broke the deal that you did with them?” she said.

events.title: AI task force readies for first meeting
events.summary: All eyes are on the first meeting of the White House’s AI task force this week as groups and members of Congress try to influence the newly formed body. Americans for Responsible Innovation, former Oklahoma Democratic Rep. Brad Carson’s nonprofit focused on federal AI safety regulation, is pushing the task force to “explore the need for Congress to develop new laws that provide for enforceable safety standards and public transparency” into AI development. Voluntary commitments will not be enough, the group argues, and the task force should make specific recommendations to Congress. Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., also wrote to the task force asking for more resources for the National Institute of Standards and Technology and its in-house testing lab. They also want the task force to ensure that the Energy Department’s National Labs can test AI independently and to mobilize the technology to guard against cybersecurity incidents. Meanwhile, the FBI arrested a Saudi national Tuesday for allegedly secretly recording conversations at the offices of his employer, OpenAI. It’s still not clear what exactly will be discussed at the task force’s first meeting, as the group scrambles to organize following its formation earlier this month. Industry watchers are awaiting any official guidelines for enforcement of its new directive, which may come from the Office of Director of National Intelligence (headed by task force chair Jay Clayton) and the Federal Trade Commission. — Ashley Gold

events.title: Trump mulls intelligence-sharing with Ukraine
events.summary: President Donald Trump is downplaying the idea of cutting off intelligence-sharing with Ukraine, telling reporters yesterday that the US is still sharing intelligence and that “we help them” — while emphasizing that his goal is to see an end to Russia’s years-long war on the country. But the idea is actively being discussed inside the White House, one Trump administration official told Semafor. And notably, there’s not yet consensus on what to do: CIA Director John Ratcliffe is said to be opposed to the idea. “Trump is pretty pissed off. He could order it,” the administration official said, suggesting that Trump should end its intelligence sharing specifically for targets inside Russia instead. Last year, Trump briefly suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine after a tense Oval Office meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said recently that Kyiv had received no intelligence from partners on a Russian missile attack. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: OpenAI employee and Saudi suspect ‘came to the US with a dream’, lawyer says
events.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and OpenAI employee, has been arrested over accusations that he hid a recording device at the company's offices in San Francisco. The Justice Department said Mr Alfozan hid the device – a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3, manufactured by a company in China – behind a television in a conference room. The device has a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and micro-SD storage”, the Justice Department said. Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said. California lawyer William Pernik said that he is still waiting to see what other evidence the government has against his client, and that he plans on presenting all appropriate defences in court. “Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream,” Mr Pernik told The National via email. “These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why.” He emphasised that his client has been charged with breaching a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent. “There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us,” he said. Mr Pernik implied that his client is already facing bias because he was not born in the US. “It is regretful that this is the one factor that seems to have caught the most attention,” he wrote. “Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origin is – and always should be – a protected status under our system of laws.” Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan? According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Alfozan has lived in California since 2015 and started working at OpenAI as a lead engineer in 2025. Before his years in California, he was an intern at Meta, Microsoft and SAP. Mr Alfozan received his undergraduate degree from MIT in 2016 and then earned his master's degree in 2025 from the University of California-Berkeley. According to the Justice Department, he was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications. He is scheduled to appear in court on October 19 for a detention hearing. “If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release,” a press release from the Justice Department reads. OpenAI has faced a barrage of criticism from employees amid allegations that it has disregarded the need for regulations when developing AI technology. American AI companies such as OpenAI also face stiff competition from China, as Washington and Beijing vie for dominance in the technology race. Companies have gone to great lengths to protect intellectual property and trade secrets.

events.title: Hongkong Land in talks with Ong Beng Seng’s HPL for stake in Orchard Road buildings: Sources
events.summary: The assets under discussion are (from left) the HPL-owned voco Orchard hotel, Forum The Shopping Mall and HPL House. Hongkong Land is in early talks with HPL to buy a majority stake in three Orchard Road properties, comprising voco Orchard, Forum mall and HPL House. The deal could value the assets at over $2 billion, but talks may still fail. HPL has faced pressure after Ong Beng Seng’s 2025 conviction and leadership changes. HPL plans to redevelop the site into a mixed project, but investors worry about high costs, lost income and the theatre's weak profits. Hongkong Land would strengthen its Singapore retail presence. SINGAPORE – Hongkong Land Holdings is in discussions with Ong Beng Seng’s Hotel Properties Ltd (HPL) to buy a majority stake in three buildings in the Republic’s Orchard Road shopping belt, according to people familiar with the matter. A potential deal could involve the developer, controlled by Hong Kong’s Jardine Matheson Holdings, investing in the three adjacent properties earmarked for development, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters. The assets comprise hotel voco Orchard, shopping mall Forum, and HPL House, which houses the group’s headquarters and Hard Rock Cafe. Discussions are still at an early stage and could conclude without a deal, the people said. A stake sale will likely value the assets at over $2 billion, although that is subject to change, they said. A Hongkong Land spokesperson declined to comment. Christopher Lim, HPL’s group executive director, declined to comment when contacted by phone. A successful transaction will mark a respite for HPL, which has faced challenges after its co-founder Ong was convicted in 2025 in a scandal that led to the imprisonment of a former senior politician in Singapore. The Malaysian tycoon, who controls the firm with his wife Christina through a roughly 60% stake, relinquished his decades-long tenure as managing director of the company, citing medical conditions. Ong, who was then 79, avoided a jail sentence as the judge exercised judicial mercy owing to his ill health and fined him the maximum $30,000. HPL has been looking to reduce its stakes in the voco hotel and Forum mall, excluding HPL House, people familiar with the matter said last year. The firm is now including the building in the assets put up for sale after talks with other interested parties fell through, the people said. HPL was given provisional government approval in 2023 to redevelop the three properties into a mixed project comprising a hotel, retail, office and residential components, as well as a rooftop garden and a performance theatre. As the sale of assets got under way, the redevelopment plans made some potential partners baulk due to uncertainties, the people said. These include concerns over the theatre’s profitability, and the lack of income for years arising from a big transformation, which is already likely to require significant capital outlay, they said. HPL’s Lim said at a shareholders’ meeting in April that the company was evaluating the redevelopment carefully as it would involve giving up recurring income from the properties. It was “focused on optimising development potential with the relevant authorities, including seeking revisions to certain approved parameters”. The company swung to a net loss of $39.1 million in the first half of 2026, compared with a profit of $11.4 million a year earlier. Its shares have fallen 6% over the past 12 months, compared with a 25% gain in the benchmark Straits Times Index. For Hongkong Land, a purchase of the assets will expand its presence in Singapore’s retail strip. A new fund backed by the firm said in July that it was buying Wheelock Place mall for $1.1 billion from longtime owner Wharf Real Estate Investment Co. Wharf’s controlling shareholder Hong Kong billionaire Peter Woo also owns about a fifth of HPL’s shares. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Wealthy investors can trust Singapore to manage their assets: Gan Kim Yong
events.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong speaking to Bloomberg TV on the sidelines of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi on Oct 14. DPM Gan Kim Yong said wealthy investors can trust Singapore with their assets, as the city-state works faster to stay a top global wealth hub. He said Singapore must build supply chain resilience by diversifying gas supplies, studying nuclear energy, and preparing for climate and geopolitical shocks. Gan said the ASEAN Power Grid will be a long, complex project, while Singapore’s 2027 ASEAN chairmanship will focus on trade and digital economy deals. NEW DELHI – The rich can trust Singapore with their assets, said Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, as the Republic seeks to strengthen its position as a global wealth management hub. He was speaking to Bloomberg TV on the sidelines of the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026 in New Delhi, India, on Oct 14. Gan is on a three-day visit to India from Oct 13 to Oct 15 to strengthen bilateral economic cooperation. “You can trust Singapore to manage your wealth. This is where the wealthy people want to put their assets,” said Gan, who is also Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) . Asked how Singapore compete s with the likes of Hong Kong and Dubai as a wealth hub, he said that Singapore has to work faster and harder. “Competition is a given. We continue to make sure that our regulations and rules are up to date and facilitate many of these operations for wealth management. We continue to improve ourselves and make sure that we are efficient,” he said. Earlier in the day, he also spoke on a panel with India’s Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Piyush Goyal, DP World group chief executive officer Yuvraj Narayan and Canada ’s Minister of International Trade Maninder Sidhu. Gan said it is important for Singapore to invest in supply chain resilience amid geopolitical uncertainties and climate change. Citing the Covid-19 pandemic and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz , Gan said that “the cost of disruption may be higher than the cost you are paying for resilience”. “In time to come, it may not be the Strait of Hormuz, it may not be geopolitics, it may not be (a) pandemic. It could be climate change. It could impact on supplies. We just have to prepare for the new future,” said Gan. To build supply chain resilience, the Republic is diversifying natural gas supplies and studying nuclear energy as an option, said Gan. “We are looking at different sources of natural gas, so that we don’t depend on a single source for our supply of natural gas,” he said. On the feasibility of nuclear energy , Gan said: “We are still studying today. We have not made a decision, but it’s important for us to keep pace with the development of technology, so we know what is available, and we continue to keep our options open. I think this is something that we consider very seriously.” Asked about the ASEAN Power Grid, he noted that while it is a major challenge for countries to come together to decide and to implement the initiative, there is a need. The ASEAN Power Grid is a regional energy integration initiative to connect electricity networks across ASEAN member states for cross-border power trading and clean energy security by 2045. “With the need for green energy, the interest in developing this project is there. It is going to be very complicated because it will involve cross-border electricity trading, and this is something that we need to develop,” said Gan. Acknowledging that it will be a multi-decade-long project, Gan said the countries “have to look at it from an incremental point of view”. “First, for example, Singapore will connect ourselves with Malaysia, with Indonesia. Next, Malaysia will connect to Thailand and the rest of ASEAN. It’s going to be a step-by-step, phase-by-phase approach and component by component. It’s also important to upgrade the internal domestic power grid in order to be able to carry that,” he noted. This comes ahead of Singapore assuming the ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, taking over the role from the Philippines on Jan 1, 2027, and serving through Dec 31, 2027. Gan said the priorities are implementing regional trade and digital economy agreements such as the Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which ASEAN is expected to formally sign in November under the Philippines’ chairmanship , and the Trade in Goods Agreement. Gan noted that he is optimistic that the upgraded Trade in Goods Agreement will facilitate further intra-regional trade. “This will also benefit our trading partners because we are able to trade among ourselves more efficiently. Other countries who are trading with us will find that their goods will be able to move more freely within ASEAN so it’s mutually beneficial for all.”

events.title: India's Bank of Baroda to 'defend interests' after BR Shetty's $15bn lawsuit
events.summary: India's Bank of Baroda on Wednesday ​said ​it would protect ​its interests, a day after UAE-based ⁠businessman and founder of NMC Health BR Shetty filed ⁠a $15 billion case against the lender and ​25 other defendants at Bombay High Court. Mr Shetty alleged ⁠the Bank of Baroda and several current and former employees helped facilitate a fraud that contributed to the collapse of the Middle East healthcare group, according to a ⁠court filing reviewed by Reuters. The firm, then the Gulf's largest private healthcare provider, ​was ⁠placed under administration in 2020 ‌after months of financial mismanagement and disclosed debts of $6.6 billion, way above previous estimates ​of $2.1 billion. Representatives for Mr Shetty did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a stock exchange notification on Wednesday, the country's second-largest state lender said: “The bank has not been served with such a suit and cannot comment on the contents of pleadings, which are untested in court. If and when the bank is served, the bank will defend the suit firmly and take all steps necessary to protect its interests.” The Bank of Baroda added that it was pursuing recovery and enforcement proceedings in India and the UAE against Mr Shetty for outstanding dues of 28 billion rupees ($294.5 million) and had obtained several decrees against him. The lender will ​not bear any immediate liability until any order is ‌passed or until it ⁠is required to make a provision on ​account of potential damages, the lender said. Bank of Baroda ​shares dropped ‌2.6 per cent on Tuesday after the legal action was reported. The lawsuit, which centres on the bank's lending to ⁠NMC Health and affiliated entities in the UAE, comes three months after the lender agreed to pay $600 million to settle claims brought by administrators of NMC. Mr Shetty alleged that bank officials enabled round-tripping transactions, ignored repeated anti-money laundering warnings and ​accepted documents bearing forged signatures. He is seeking $5 billion in direct damages, $5 billion in consequential damages and an additional $5 billion for reputational harm, the filing showed.

events.title: 'I applied for 200 jobs' - How 'spray and pray' AI job applications can backfire
events.summary: Could using AI in your job application be ruining your chances of getting hired? Published 14 October 2026, 00:04 BST Would you use AI to help you write a CV or cover letter? How about during an online assessment or video interview for a job? We are increasingly using the technology to help us with job applications, graduates , external and recruiters say, with many employers happy for us to do so within reason. But when does it cross a line from being acceptable to unethical, or even cheating? Tom, 22, from Maidstone graduated last year with a geography degree and says he applied for over 200 jobs before finally landing a role last month as a restaurant manager. He says the process was "exhausting" and "demoralising", with employers often not even getting back to him, and he wouldn't have got through it without some help from AI. "Employers want you to put your absolute best into the application, but if I'm applying for 10 to 20 jobs in a day, the reality is you can't do that." Tom says it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen applicants While Tom says he never used the technology in an assessment or interview, he did use it to help him with cover letters and CVs or to find the right "buzz words" that early stage screening in a recruitment process will pick up on. He also thinks it's "hypocritical" for companies to ask candidates not to use AI when some are using it themselves to screen candidates . "That's where it feels like a weird tightrope. You can't use AI too much because otherwise you're not human. But if you don't write like an AI, you may get skipped by the AI screening." This summer, the Institute of Student Employers (ISE) surveyed 155 of the UK's biggest graduate employers and found they were becoming "more accepting" of candidates using AI "at some stages of the recruitment process". According to the trade group, the most commonly accepted use was writing cover letters or CVs, followed by completing online application questions. However, it also found 92% of employers had encountered or suspected AI "misconduct" in the job selection process - up from 85% last year. Most commonly this included using AI as a real-time assistant during online video interviews or to complete online assessments. On top of this, the tech is helping candidates write multiple applications at the same time - something known in the industry as "spray and pray". Stephen Isherwood, joint chief executive of the ISE, says it is "driving up the competition and pressure on students" in an already competitive graduate recruitment market. EDF's Hollie Moody says the use of AI in job applications is a "moral dilemma" for both employers and employees Hollie Moody, head of early careers recruitment at energy giant EDF, says she doesn't blame graduates for using AI in applications given how "brutal" the jobs market is right now. But she does think it's becoming a problem. EDF opened its graduate recruitment scheme three weeks ago, but decided to close it early after receiving 12,000 applications - a 10% increase on last year. Moody says AI almost certainly contributed to this, adding that the tech is being used "a lot more freely" in the actual selection process. "What we don't have is a level playing field, because what you'll find is that some candidates will absolutely use AI throughout the whole process, and other candidates won't." Like many firms, EDF now issues guidance on the appropriate use of AI in job applications, and is trying to make its recruitment process as "AI-proof" as possible. It only reads CVs in the later stages of the hiring process and uses skills and behaviour-based online assessments and video interviews to better assess candidates. But Moody says some applicants still try to bend the rules, particularly in video interviews. "A lot of the answers [we hear] are the same. Or people might pause whilst they wait for AI to come back to them with an answer. It's almost like people are reading a script." AI job application rise 'risks hiring incapable staff' Published 25 March 2025 AI era 'not all doom and gloom' for graduates, say analysts Published 5 March Young jobseekers 'discouraged' by ghosting and AI Published 21 May One recently employed trainee accountant, who didn't want us to use his real name, told the BBC he'd applied for 50 graduate jobs and used AI in every application. But he says it was only for researching roles, tidying up his CV and generating mock practise questions for video interviews. While he says he would never use the tech to cheat on assessments he knows people who would. "I know people who have applied for 100 jobs and after a while they become desperate. If they see everyone else is using AI, they think how can I compete?" According to the ISE, the graduate market has stabilised after a sharp fall last year but remains tough. Graduate roles currently attract an average of 141 applications each, it says.

events.title: Singapore’s PDG seeks US$1.2 billion loan for Malaysia data centre
events.summary: A worker walking past a data centre in the state of Johor, which has become South-east Asia's fastest-growing data centre hub, on May 7. Princeton Digital Group is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion to fund a 198.8MW data centre campus in Johor, Malaysia and refinance debt. HSBC, Maybank Investment Bank, OCBC Bank Malaysia, Standard Chartered Bank Singapore and UOB are the lead arrangers for the three-year loan, Bloomberg reported. The move shows rising AI data centre borrowing, but investors are becoming cautious as high rates and market volatility hit demand and some IPO plans. SINGAPORE – Asian data centre operator Princeton Digital Group is seeking a syndicated loan of up to US$1.2 billion (S$1.54 billion) to fund its Malaysia build-out , according to a source familiar with the matter, as the debt binge to finance artificial intelligence infrastructure continues. HSBC Holdings Singapore branch, Maybank Investment Bank, OCBC Bank (Malaysia), Standard Chartered Bank (Singapore), and United Overseas Bank are the mandated lead arrangers and bookrunners for the three-year loan deal, said the source, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Proceeds from the loan to be taken by the company’s subsidiary, Princeton Digital Group Labuan Alpha, will be used to fund a 198.8MW data centre campus project in Johor, Malaysia and to refinance existing debt, the source said. Standard Chartered declined to comment. Representatives for Princeton Digital Group, HSBC, Maybank, OCBC Malaysia and UOB didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment. Data centre companies across the world have been taking on debt as they seek to raise capital to meet growing AI demand. Moody’s Ratings expects at least US$3 trillion to flow into data centre-related investments over the next five years, with much of the spending financed through debt. But there are signs global investors are starting to push back against what they see are frothy AI valuations as evidenced by the collapse of Nvidia-backed data centre operator Firmus Grid’s initial public offering earlier in October. Data centre firm AirTrunk, which counts Blackstone as a key investor, was reported to delay its planned IPO of a real estate investment trust in Singapore until 2027 as higher interest rates and market volatility temper investor demand. Headquartered in Singapore, Princeton Digital’s top shareholder is Warburg Pincus, and other investors include Stonepeak Partners, Abu Dhabi sovereign fund Mubadala Investment and Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan Board. The firm, founded in 2018, operates more than 1.8GW of data centre capacity across Asia including China, Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, according to its website. PDG has been on a borrowing spree as it seeks to expand across Asia. In May, the firm said it raised around US$856 million for its data centre build-out in Indonesia. Earlier in 2026, the company said it was targeting to raise US$5 billion in debt to support regional expansion plans. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Ossoff rejects 2028 buzz amid bruising night of Senate debates
events.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced. Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected. "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia. The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington. In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded , referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer. Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein. "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back , pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state. Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects. Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage. In his closing statement , Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger." In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge , as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points. Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel , saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine. Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war. Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

events.title: John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget
events.summary: Move aimed at firms such as Amazon and eBay could raise up to £1bn more for Treasury, says report A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget. The chancellor is said to be preparing to announce that online marketplaces will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by all retailers selling on their platforms. Marketplaces have been required to collect VAT for overseas businesses selling into the UK since 2021 but some foreign operators have posed as British retailers, using shell companies or other techniques to avoid this rule. Under the proposed change, websites would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, no matter where they are based. Healey is expected to announce this change will be made to fund cuts to business rates for high street shops, the Times reported. The government ran a consultation over the summer on changing the “deemed reseller” rules, saying “non-compliance persists among both overseas and UK-based businesses, distorting competition and disadvantaging compliant firms online and on the high street”. It consulted food delivery platforms as well as retail marketplaces, suggesting it was considering drawing them into the system. Amazon said it welcomed the prospect of a change to deemed reseller rules. “Closing this loophole will raise significant revenue for the exchequer and simplify compliance for both HMRC and legitimate sellers,” the UK’s biggest online marketplace said. The development comes as pressure continues to grow on Andy Burnham and Healey to relieve struggling small businesses on the high street before the budget on 28 October. Before he was elected in Makerfield, Burnham said he would increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high street retailers would not pay the tax. The government is facing calls from many factions to cut tax, with large retailers pushing for changes to national insurance to boost youth employment, for example. However, this week the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned Healey that his budget risks being a “ work of fiction ” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The IFS said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. In a boost for the Treasury, this week the International Monetary Fund upgraded its GDP growth forecast for the UK this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from its previous update in July . However, the IMF also cautioned that Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances. Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

events.title: Houthi attack hits Aramco's historic nerve centre in Saudi Arabia
events.summary: A missile attack on an administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state energy company Aramco hit the historic centre of the kingdom's oil industry , sparking a fire that authorities said caused no casualties. The strike by the Yemeni Houthi rebels hit a complex that serves as the nerve centre of the world's largest oil exporter, housing key research and development site, energy operations and thousands of employees and their families. People living near the building described moments of terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. "This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life," one woman told The National . Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area following the attack. While no further details have been released about the incident, the site is a key one for Aramco, serving as its central hub for oil, gas, and energy operations. More than an HQ Aramco, at the time known as the Arabian American Oil Company, moved its headquarters from New York City to Dhahran in 1952. Dhahran was where the kingdom’s first commercial oil was found in 1938, at Dammam No 7, the “Prosperity Well". The Saudi government gradually acquired the company, completing a full buyout in 1980, before it was renamed the Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Aramco) in 1988. Aramco’s headquarters is situated within a vast complex spread across 58 square kilometres, with a large residential area housing a reported 11,000 people, including employees and their families. The Dhahran district also has a research and development centre and the Expec Advanced Research Centre, which was inaugurated in 2008. Expec has been upgraded with a building to focus on upstream research and development. The Dhahran complex also houses a large-scale cooling plant, operated by Saudi Tabreed, with a 32,000 refrigeration-tonne capacity that includes thermal storage tanks for energy saving. The chilled water piping network stretches 16 kilometres to reach sites, meeting Saudi Aramco's requirements for cooling. The area also includes Ithra, the King Abdulaziz Centre for World Culture, which was built by Aramco as a cultural and creative destination for the public. The centre has attracted more than four million since its opening in 2018. Previous attacks The Dhahran area was attacked on February 25, 1991, during the Gulf War, when an Iraqi Scud missile struck a US Army barracks, killing 28 American soldiers and wounding 110. Aramco’s other sites in the Eastern province have also faced attacks in the past. Several drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing centres on September 14, 2019, knocking out about 50 per cent of the country’s crude oil production. The 17-minute strike by 18 drones and three low-flying missiles, claimed by the Houthis, caused a surge in oil prices and shut down more than 5 per cent of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia said about two weeks later that it had fully restored oil output. In March 2022, an Aramco plant in Jizan was also attacked by the Houthis with a drone laden with explosives, with a gas station in Khamis Mushait and a power station in Dhahran also hit. In early March this year, after the start of the Iran war, a fire broke out at Aramco’s Ras Tanura refinery , the kingdom’s largest, with 550,000 barrels per day of capacity, due to drone attacks. Operations were halted for 16 days. Ras Tanura, on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast, hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports. Other sites hit this year include Satorp in Jubail, a joint venture between Saudi Aramco and TotalEnergies processing 465,000 bpd and one of the world's largest export refining platforms, as well as Samref in Yanbu, a 400,000 bpd Aramco-ExxonMobil joint venture. Earlier this month, Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser said ​the company had ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required. Aramco can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million bpd available ⁠within days, ​he ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “Our system is intact,” he added. Aramco, which is listed on the Tadawul exchange, is majority owned by the Saudi government. It is due to release its third quarter financial results on November 3.

events.title: Pope's AI adviser warns Australia's copyright changes risk 'new form of colonialism'
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts As Australia considers copyright reforms, Pope Leo's AI adviser Father Paolo Benanti issues a warning Father Paolo Benanti has a background in engineering and is an advisor to Pope Leo XIV on artificial intelligence. ( Getty Images: Massimo Di Vita ) The AI adviser to Pope Leo has praised Australia for taking a considered approach to tech companies. Father Paolo Benanti warned Australia that changes to copyright laws to allow AI training would be risky. He believes tech companies openly court religious leaders to protect their business interests. Australia risks reviving a "new form of colonialism" if it allows AI companies to train on copyrighted work without permission and send profits offshore, warned an influential AI adviser to the Vatican. Asked about Australia's consideration of copyright changes to attract AI training, Father Paolo Benanti compared the risk with Europe's history of taking resources from other countries and profiting from them elsewhere. "You go, you take resources, and you monetise it outside the place where the resources [were]," he said. He said Australian writing could become another resource used by foreign companies, with the money and tax revenue ending up overseas. Father Benanti warns AI companies mining creative work risks repeating old patterns of colonial exploitation. ( Supplied: Microsoft ) “Is it ... a new form of colonialism from foreign power that could ... exploit from the resources and monetise it outside of the place where they are taken?" he asked. Those were questions he said he would ask before voting on such a change. Last month, the ABC reported that the Attorney-General's department was quietly consulting on changes that would mean AI companies could train on copyrighted content unless its owner had opted out. In June Attorney-General Michelle Rowland told 7.30: "This government has repeatedly said that there are no plans to weaken copyright protections when it comes to AI." Earlier this week, the federal parliament's AI committee took the unusual step of pre-empting its own process to write a letter that urged reforms to pave the way for AI training. Father Benanti praised Australia's efforts to regulate social media and AI when he met Prime Minister Anthony Albanese last week, and told 7.30 other countries should follow Australia's lead in reining in tech companies with policies like the teen social media ban. On his visit to Australia as a guest of the Italian Embassy, he described the country as being at the "foremost frontier" and defended it against aspersions about the effectiveness of laws like the social media minimum age. He said that the essential democratic principle was that "no one should be above the law". Father Benanti had a meeting with Anthony Albanese during his visit to Australia. ( Supplied: Instagram ) That included overseas social media companies, which he said could rely on protections in their home countries to avoid other governments' rules. He said Australia's first steps were important, and hoped other countries would follow. Working together would give governments more power to make technology companies comply with the rules in countries where they wanted to do business, he said. Father Benanti studied engineering before becoming a Franciscan friar and a professor specialising in the ethics of technology. He advised Pope Francis on artificial intelligence and now advises his successor, Pope Leo. Pope Leo's first encyclical, titled Magnifica Humanitas, focused on the rise of artificial intelligence. ( Reuters: Guglielmo Mangiapane ) In May, Pope Leo presented his first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas , a major papal letter sharing his teachings about humanity in the age of AI. The landmark document made global headlines for criticising autonomous weapons, as well as algorithms that could deny people access to healthcare, employment or security. Father Benanti said the encyclical resonated beyond the Catholic Church's followers because it addressed moral questions they were already asking about how technology could change their lives. The encyclical urged governments to slow the development of AI systems. ( Reuters: Yara Nardi ) He said its appeal came from keeping those questions open for public debate and allowing society to shape how AI is governed. Father Benanti's concerns about AI extend to the emotional attachments people can form with the technology. He is concerned that companies exploit loneliness and romantic attachment to their products to make money from people's emotions. "Those are not neutral things, but are things that are designed by someone," he said.

events.title: New bridge linking China and North Korea will open more than a decade late
events.summary: A new bridge linking China and North Korea is set to open more than a decade after the Chinese side of it was built, in the latest sign of closer ties between the two countries BEIJING -- A new bridge linking China and North Korea is set to open Thursday after more than a decade of delay in the latest sign of closer ties between the two countries. The official Chinese news agency Xinhua reported Wednesday that both sides will hold a ceremony for the launch of the New Yalu River Bridge. The four-lane, 3-kilometer (1.8-mile) bridge will connect the northeastern Chinese city of Dandong to the North Korean city of Sinuiju. The bridge initially was expected to enter use in 2014 after China apparently completed construction of access roads, customs facilities and other related infrastructure on its side. But the date passed with no sign of an opening and without North Korea doing corresponding works on its side. At that time, it prompted an unusually sharp report in the Global Times, a newspaper affiliated with the Chinese Communist Party, which quoted Dandong residents expressing frustration over delays in what they had hoped would be an economic boon for their border city. A lack of substantial work on the North Korean side prompted speculation that North Korea was wary of an increase in economic dependence or was unhappy with China voting for United Nations resolutions toughening international sanctions on the North over its nuclear program . Some observers said North Korea and China also differed over the location of the bridge. The new link is expected to lessen the burden on an existing yet aging bridge on the Dandong-Sinuiju route, which handles more than 70% of official trade between the two countries. The old bridge built in 1937 carries a railway line as well as cars and trucks, but vehicle traffic can move only one way at a time. The South Korean government said last year there were at least 17 active road and rail links across the porous North Korea-China border stretching more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles). The new bridge’s opening will likely boost bilateral trade and enhance logistical efficiency gradually. But in the short term, trade won't likely result in a sharp increase in Chinese exports to North Korea as Beijing would take Pyongyang's interests into consideration to some extent, according to a recent report by Gyubeom Kim, an expert at Seoul’s state-run Institute for National Security Strategy. North Korea’s export of processed goods, food products, cosmetics and alcoholic beverages to China could increase, Kim said. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hasan execution will be live-streamed, Pentagon official says The bridge’s opening comes about a month after North Korea and Russia opened a 1-kilometer (0.6-mile) road bridge over the Tumen River as part of their efforts to cement relations. Experts say Chinese officials likely felt uneasy about the opening of the North Korea-Russia bridge, which the Russian government said would allow daily passage of up to 300 vehicles through a newly built border crossing point. The North Korea-China bridge is much bigger and likely capable of carrying round-the-clock, two-way traffic including containers and heavy cargo trucks, according to Jeong Eun-i, an analyst from South Korea’s Institute for National Unification. China has long been North Korea's biggest trading partner and economic pipeline. But in past years, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has prioritized Moscow , sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine , apparently in exchange for military and economic assistance. Kim has recently drawn closer to China with the apparent intent to improve the economy and build a front against the United States. China, for its part, wants to restore its unique influence over North Korea. Last year, about 98% of North Korea’s external trade was with China. The bridge’s opening has been anticipated since Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit , Xi expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority. events.title: Hundreds of Royal Mail staff quitting each week under new efficiency plans
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 00:03 BST About 400 postmen and women are leaving Royal Mail per week, according to the Communication Workers Union (CWU), who claims this number has gone up since the company introduced a new delivery system earlier this year. The CWU says the firm had been losing about 330 postal staff a week from a workforce of 83,000 before it rolled out DM26, which reorganised routes to improve delivery performance. The union claims the new system is not working in hundreds of offices, and BBC Your Voice has heard from staff warning of a "nightmare" Christmas ahead as the number of parcels increases. Royal Mail says the reforms are part of its plan to deliver a more "efficient and financially sustainable" service. Over the last year we've been in touch with more than 30 postal staff in all four nations of the UK, as they have switched over to DM26. It allows for second class post to only be delivered every other weekday, and is supposed to guarantee first class mail and parcels are delivered every day, by putting workers into groups of three and changing the walking pattern of rounds. But posties speaking to us anonymously say parcels are still being prioritised, letters left behind, and time wasted in sorting and dividing mail into first and second class. "I didn't take any first class mail out on my last shift because I was on a road that's been behind for weeks," a worker in the West Midlands told me. "But I'm sure a manager would have ticked a box to say all first class mail went out." A Royal Mail spokesperson said the company always worked to ensure all mail - both letters and parcels - were delivered on time. Royal Mail plans to cut 2,500 jobs Published 7 days ago Only three-quarters of first class mail delivered on time Published 29 May Royal Mail letters sit undelivered 'for weeks' as parcels prioritised, staff say Published 16 February Some postal workers we've spoken to say the new model is also increasing their workload. We asked eight workers in different areas to track their average step counts. Since the switchover all their steps increased by a quarter or even a third, often up to around 25,000 steps a day. Several fear this Christmas will be a "nightmare". "We all think this Christmas will be the worst ever, for us and our customers," said one postman in the East Midlands. Bryn Dymott says he is speaking out now because he wants people to know what's really happening Bryn Dymott delivered post in the village of Wootton in Bedfordshire for nine years. For the most part he loved the job. But he left the company in July saying he couldn't face another "shambolic" Christmas. "People put things in the post for them to be delivered, not for them to be delayed because Royal Mail hasn't got the systems in place and enough people to get them delivered." Bryn says he wanted to speak out after leaving the company because he was sick of the fact that posties aren't able to say what's really happening. He says the company is "proving it's impossible to have four people's work done by three people. It shouldn't really come as a surprise." So far DM26 has been introduced in about 1,000 of Royal Mail's 1,200 delivery offices. Now the CWU has told its members to pause further roll-out of the new system until a plan can be agreed with Royal Mail to address problems. The union says that while it is operating successfully in around 500 offices, it has run into significant problems in hundreds of others. "Put simply, if a boat is already taking on water, adding more passengers is unlikely to solve the problem," says Martin Walsh of the CWU. The union believes most Royal Mail workers leaving the company are new starters on part-time contracts, but also says there has been an increase in staff on legacy contracts departing. Royal Mail, on the other hand, says the new system is on track to be up and running in all offices by Christmas. It says the roll-out is 90% complete and that it is now delivering to "95% of addresses every day across the UK, up from 88% before the roll-out. The roll-out continues across our network and we expect quality of service to improve as deployment progresses." The company says it is hiring, as usual, an additional 22,000 temporary workers over the Christmas period. The BBC saw returned post that couldn't be delivered so ended up back on the frames in a Royal Mail office Royal Mail has battled with increased competition and falling demand for letter deliveries in recent years, and last week announced plans to cut 2,500 head office and other supporting roles by the end of 2027. The company has also faced years of criticism from politicians and the public over slow letter deliveries - something which has continued since the new system has been rolled out. The regulator Ofcom has fined Royal Mail more than £37m in the last three years for missing delivery targets.

events.title: How To Define CPU And Software Stack Performance For Agentic AI
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Measuring the performance demands of agentic AI; assessing CPU bottlenecks, SW stack efficiency, and system-level tradeoffs. Agentic AI changes the CPU performance problem. A completed task can involve repeated model calls, retrieval, state management, tool execution, application interactions, policy checks and validation loops. Accelerators remain central to model execution, while CPUs coordinate and execute much of the surrounding system path from user intent to completed work. This paper proposes a use-case-driven framework for evaluating that CPU contribution. It separates CPU-visible work into two complementary areas: common agentic framework functions and use-case-specific tool workloads. Five representative workload archetypes are used to capture distinct deployment venues, tool classes and CPU stress profiles. The paper then describes two complementary measurement approaches: component benchmarking, which emphasizes reproducibility and attribution and end-to-end benchmarking, which emphasizes realistic task-level outcomes. The objective is not to prescribe a finished benchmark suite or a single figure of merit. It is to define the measurement boundaries, workload categories and methodological gaps that need industry agreement. In particular, replayable agent trajectories offer a path to separating CPU work from model and network effects while reducing the run-to-run variability introduced by non-deterministic agent behavior. Generative-AI workloads evolve on a quarterly cadence, with novel attention variants, quantization formats, and routing schemes appearing faster than fixed-function neural-processor silicon can be respun. This paper presents the General-Purpose Neural Processor (GPNPU): a single programmable processor architecture, delivered as configurable IP, that unifies scalar, vector, and matrix execution in one instruction-set architecture (ISA) and one programming model accessible from standard C++ and Python. events.title: Simplify Electronic-Photonic Design Workflows: eBook
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports The natural evolution of EDA, extending proven design methodologies to include photonic devices, circuits, and systems. Combining light-based components with traditional electronics is not straightforward. Conventional electronic design automation (EDA) workflows were never built to handle the complex physics and deep integration demanded by photonics. As optical and electronic technologies converge, engineers face tighter cross-domain coupling and unprecedented system-level complexity. Addressing these challenges requires a new design paradigm: electronic photonic design automation (EPDA). Driven by exploding bandwidth demands, power and latency constraints, and the rapid adoption of silicon photonics, EPDA is no longer optional — it is essential for delivering scalable, manufacturable electronic photonic systems. events.title: Accelerating Advanced IC Package Design: A Methodology for Early and Iterative Optimization of Chiplet Integration
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Optimizing chiplet integration, power integrity, and performance through early-stage IC package design and analysis. Today’s multi-chip and chiplet solutions are leading the way for the “More than Moore” vision, with companies leveraging packaging technologies to create value and differentiate themselves from their competitors. Through-silicon via (TSV), wafer-level packaging (WLP), and 3D stacking technologies offer a wide range of packaging options for all form factors. Figure 1 illustrates a common example of 3D die/wafer stacking vs the traditional 2D system-on-a-chip (SoC). Fig. 1: Common example for 3D die/wafer stacking. Source: Cadence As semiconductor packaging technologies such as chip-on-wafer-on-substrate with redistribution layer (CoWoS-R) and local silicon interconnect (CoWoS-L) increase in complexity due to the rapid growth in the number of signals and the integration of high-bandwidth memory (HBM), high-speed interface areas are a key focus for design and analysis. This complexity challenges traditional design and analysis workflows, as importing large designs into analysis tools and managing redesigns can exceed project time constraints, making it difficult to meet deadlines. This white paper presents a comprehensive methodology that enables early and iterative optimization of IC package designs. By integrating in-design analysis (IDA) directly into the design environment and leveraging scalable multiphysics simulation engines, IC package engineers can compress design cycles, reduce late-stage surprises, and achieve confident sign-off on complex advanced package designs.
