events.title: Why Heat Is Becoming A Bigger Chip Design Issue
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Complex designs now require voltage, timing, resistance, power, and temperature to be analyzed together, and in the context of each other. Vertical scaling will require new materials and cooling options. Agentic AI could help engineers cross traditional discipline silos, which will be necessary because thermal is a system-level problem. Experts at the Table : Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss the growing thermal challenges and trade-offs as dies are stacked, vertically integrated, and harder to cool, with Lang Lin, director of product management at Synopsys ; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Satish Radhakrishnan, head of semiconductor and electronics at Vinci ; Chris Mueth, director of new markets management at Keysight EDA ; and John Ferguson, senior director of product management at Siemens EDA . What follows are excerpts of that conversation, which was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. To view part one of this discussion, click here . Part two is here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Lin; Vinci’s Radhakrishnan; Keysight’s Mueth; Siemens’ Ferguson. SE: One of the big trade-offs in advanced designs is voltage versus current. How do you balance that? Lin : If you reduce the voltage, it will change your timing and reduce the performance. But it also reduces heat. If you keep running the chip fast, you will run into a lot of thermal problems. These are conflicting physics. You need to find the sweet spot for your chip. You need to try the real combination of, say, this voltage versus this timing budget. And you need to do a loop of timing, thermal, and supply voltage or power integrity co-optimization. You have to close this loop and run a couple different workloads to make sure there is not a failure or any other problems. We don’t have a tool yet to do this big loop, so the engineer may be asking how to solve their place-and-route problem while also running timing, thermal, and voltage. And then, they still have to make sure they can close the design. Radhakrishnan : Along with thermal, you also have the resistance change because of the temperature. You need to understand the dynamics of a temperature-based transient. As you pass the current, the temperature rises and the resistance changes. Are you going to keep the same performance? Are you going to change the total current. How much power do you budget? That’s where the coupled nature of the entire simulation is going, and that’s where a lot of focus in the industry will be. As power rises, temperature rises, so you’re going to allow more cooling, and you’re going to push up the power. All of this is going to be coupled, probably starting next year. SE: So given all these issues, is a full 3D-IC possible? Mueth : It’s just a matter of time. We’ll solve a lot of the problems. That will require a lot of materials science, which needs more investment. For the aging problem, we will use specialized materials science types of solvers, which need to be extended to achieve that. There are exotic things you can do, like stacked intercoolers with fluid circulation. Of course, that means it’s going to be incredibly expensive to make those, and you’re only going to use them for high-performance applications. You’re not going to use them for everything else. Radhakrishnan : People are already talking about 3D DRAM and 3D-IC. From a thermal view, there are different techniques like a cooled interposer, but the industry is going more toward a 3D-IC where everything is stacked together and you have optics coming in on the side. It will be more expensive, though, so maybe you need to start with a narrow application. Mueth : One thing that hasn’t been mentioned yet is heterogeneous technology, and how you can bring that in to use the right modal technologies for the right application and integrate that stuff together. That can help if you have a super high-performance application and you need a small size. You can use that for a specialty application to integrate the different technologies together. SE: This goes into orchestration, where it’s not just whatever you’re doing as a process, but also the materials that you use, as well. Berg : Absolutely. The materials are extraordinarily important, and the time constant associated with thermal is different from the speed of electrons through a transistor. That disconnect needs to be consistently taken into account. But for 3D-ICs, it’s not a matter of if we’re going to do them. It’s a matter of when. It will happen. SE: For full 3D-IC, or 2.5D or 3.5D? Berg : Well, you can call a stack of 16 HBMs in a single package a 3D-IC. So, depending on your definition, we already have it. But that z-level scaling is going to be very important, and it will take a group of very intelligent materials scientists, and people with thermal and mechanical skills to make that happen. Radhakrishnan : Hybrid bonding is enabling that. More innovation, like having nanometer-based TSVs, will allow that. Ferguson : The whole discussion is interesting. It reminds me of the early days of Moore’s Law, where every time we went to a new process, somebody would say, ‘That’s it. We can’t do it. We’re never going to get to the next node.’ But we get there. Maybe we don’t get there exactly when we want, but we do get there. And then we say, ‘Well, that was great, but now I need it to be faster. Now I need better signal intent.’ Now, as we bring in the MCPs (Model Context Protocols), it’s not just bringing in the intelligent people. Intelligent MCPs can do this so much faster than we can, and we need the people to find and build the right MCPs. One of the things we need to think about in this industry is that we’re looking at each thing almost in isolation. Here we’re talking about thermal. What are the thermal impacts? But in the meantime, somebody else is looking at changing the chemistry of some of the materials. And if you didn’t know that, they’re going to come together at the wrong time. We’ve got to think about bringing the whole ecosystem together so we’re all communicating and we know exactly when things are going to fit correctly. SE: We lost that with the end of the ITRS, and now we’re looking to AI to pick up the mantle. Mueth : Yes, and I’ve been surprised at how much AI has advanced in the last year. It’s astounding. We had a hackathon a couple months ago. We were doing an amazing number of things with the tools we never thought were possible. If the customer knows the problems they have to solve, it’s our job as vendors to supply the tools to help them out. events.title: China’s trade surplus hits $938 billion for Jan-Sep
events.summary: China’s customs agency says the country's exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier HONG KONG -- China’s exports surged 36.3% in September from a year earlier, its customs agency said Wednesday, bringing it on track to exceed last year's record trade surplus as pressure ramped up from its trading partners, including the European Union, to rebalance trade. The exports data, which was better than what economists had expected, accelerated from the 25% growth in August. High-tech goods such as semiconductors and autos have helped fuel its rising shipments overseas. September's export growth pace was the fastest since February, according to FactSet data. Imports climbed 31% in September year-on-year, also accelerating from August’s 28.2% rise. Still, China recorded a $133.5 billion trade surplus last month, widening from $119.1 billion in August. For the first nine months, China’s trade surplus reached $938 billion, with expectations growing that it could surpass last year’s full-year $1.2 trillion record . Strong exports have helped drive China’s overall economic growth this year, at a time when domestic consumption and investment remained sluggish, weighed on by a yearslong real estate sector downturn . However, China’s export resilience is now faced with mounting challenges, said Ecaterina Bigos, a senior market strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “While U.S.-China trade tensions have eased somewhat, the EU’s push to rebalance directly targets high-value exports,” she said. The U.S. has launched an ongoing probe against China and other trading partners this year on their excess industrial capacity, although Washington and Beijing last month reached an agreement to extend their trade truce and cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods . The 27-nation EU has particularly been struggling to rebalance a trade deficit exceeding $1.1 billion a day with China. EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič, following his visit to Beijing where he met his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao last week, said a deal has been reached with Beijing, including halving Chinese hybrid car imports into the EU over the next few years. Many of China’s trading partners are facing weak growth prospects and are fearful of their manufacturing industries being overrun by exports from China , said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Policymakers have also pointed to a weakened yuan, China’s currency, versus the U.S. dollar and other currencies contributing to Chinese exports being cheaper overseas when compared with goods from other countries, adding to trade imbalances. China has said it has “no need or intent” to gain competitive advantages through currency devaluation and that its trade growth has been driven by its industrial competitiveness in the global market. Between January and September, China’s semiconductor exports soared 108.1% year-on-year in terms of value, customs data showed. Its exports of automatic data processing equipment and parts jumped 54.6%, while auto exports rose 54.3%, driven by an increased global demand for Chinese electric vehicles and hybrids. China’s trade surplus and its high-tech export model depend on open markets, Bigos said, and while diversifying its exports into markets such as Southeast Asia and Latin America can help, it cannot fully substitute for Western demand. The country’s reliance on high-tech exports, meanwhile, could face challenges as some U.S. technology industry leaders called for a global slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence over safety reasons. “A slowdown in the global AI investment cycle could pose a greater threat to China’s export growth than trade restrictions imposed by other countries,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board. Chinese leaders have set an annual economic expansion target of 4.5%-5% for 2026. It is set to release its July-September quarterly economic growth figures next week. This week, the International Monetary Fund lowered its forecast for China’s 2026 economic growth to 4.5%, down 0.1 percentage point from its previous projection, as it warned that the country's robust exports were unable to fully offset domestic weaknesses. While Chinese officials have highlighted the need to bolster domestic demand, analysts believe that has yet to become a priority for this year even after authorities recently rolled out new measures to help lift its economy, including subsidies for homebuyers’ mortgage interest payments. events.title: China’s September exports soar, putting $1 trillion trade surplus in sight
events.summary: Exports soared 36.3% from a year earlier, outstripping August’s 25% rise and far exceeding expectations for 25.5% growth, customs data showed on Oct 14. China’s September exports rose 36.3% year on year, and imports grew 31.0%, widening the trade surplus to US$133.53 billion and putting a US$1 trillion surplus in sight. Semiconductors, green-tech goods and cars drove trade growth, while the US and EU surpluses stayed large. Analysts said demand should remain strong through year-end. The strong trade performance may help China meet its 4.5% to 5% GDP target, but it could also deepen trade tensions and raise the risk of new export curbs from major partners. BEIJING – China’s trade surplus widened more than expected in September as exports surged, keeping the country on track to surpass 2025’s record surplus and likely intensifying trade tensions with major partners. Global demand for semiconductors and green-tech products has helped keep China’s factories humming, easing pressure on policymakers to shore up economic growth against subdued domestic demand and investment. September’s growth was the fastest since February when exports expanded 39.6%. Imports also remained robust, up 31% compared with 28.2% growth in August and economists’ forecasts of a 24.5% gain. Wang Jun, a vice-customs minister, said at a press briefing there would be external uncertainties including geopolitical conflicts that might affect trade, but added there was foundation and support for continued growth in exports and imports in the fourth quarter. Analysts expect trade to remain buoyant, with tech products continuing to drive exports and imports. “Key trade ties look set to remain stable through the year end , which should keep this year’s key growth engine humming,” said Lynn Song, ING’s chief Greater China economist. China’s trade surplus topped US$1 trillion (S$1.28 trillion) in November 2025 and posted a record US$1.189 trillion for the whole year. The surplus reached US$938.11 billion in the first nine months of 2026, putting the manufacturing powerhouse on course to hit the US$1 trillion mark sooner unless exports slow sharply in the final quarter. For now, such a slowdown appears unlikely. September’s trade surplus widened to US$133.53 billion, helped by a 20-month-high US$34.01 billion surplus with the United States and a larger US$34.8 billion surplus with the European Union. A deal with the EU to limit Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc, announced earlier in October, is likely to weigh on China’s booming auto trade over time. But with the trade measures likely being laid out in December, exporters may drive up shipments to beat the deadline. “The widening trade surplus with Europe could spur broader EU restrictions beyond last week’s narrow deal, though we expect the resulting economic fallout for China to be small,” said Capital Economics’ China economist Nguyen Hoang Nam. President Xi Jinping’s September summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington secured an extension to their tariff truce and an agreement to cut tariffs on US$30 billion worth of goods from each side. High-tech goods and cars continued to underpin shipments, with semiconductor exports rising 108.1% year on year in value terms in the first nine months. Auto exports expanded more than 50% in both value and volume terms. With the global build-out of AI infrastructure showing little sign of slowing, analysts expect demand for Chinese-made technology products, including semiconductors, to remain robust. China’s factory-gate prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September, separate data showed, while consumer inflation edged up but lagged behind forecasts, underscoring an uneven recovery. The Canton Fair, China’s largest trade exhibition, kicks off on Oct 15 for Chinese manufacturers to showcase their products to foreign buyers. In commodities, September crude oil imports fell 21.5% year on year in volume terms, while soya bean imports were down 7.7% from the same month in 2025. The strength in exports indicates that policymakers could still rely on moderate policy support to meet China’s 4.5% to 5% annual gross domestic product growth target. Risks of curbs on Chinese exports loom as China continues to defend its industrial and monetary policies, which Washington and Brussels blame for Beijing’s massive trade surplus. China’s central bank last week pushed back against criticism of its exchange-rate policy with a lengthy statement, arguing that it never pursued competitive depreciation and rejecting claims that China keeps the yuan artificially weak to gain a trade advantage. Any major hit to exports, a key growth engine, could prompt policymakers to step up stimulus measures to address weak domestic demand and the years-long property market downturn. REUTERS

events.title: Public Media Co’s bridge fund for nonprofit radio stations turns from rescue to reinvention
events.summary: Public Media Co. celebrated its 25th anniversary with a $10 million donation from the Knight Foundation Public Media Co. celebrated its 25th anniversary Tuesday night with a $10 million donation from the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation to support its transformation into a major grantmaker — a role that would have been unthinkable two years ago. As recently as 2024, the nonprofit consultant that works to strengthen public radio stations reported $3.42 million in revenue, according to tax filings. Public Media CEO Tim Isgitt said he was proud of his “small, but mighty team” and the impact that they had on the sector. Then came the federal funding cuts . One day in June 2025, Isgitt told a roomful of funders that federal cuts to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting could create a “doom loop” with catastrophic effects on the entire public radio sector, requiring them all to act immediately. The next day, the House of Representatives voted to rescind all of CPB’s funding , about $1.1 billion that stations were already promised. Within weeks, the Senate followed suit. “It felt just like a wave that washed over us all of a sudden,” Isgitt told The Associated Press. Isgitt and Public Media were quickly pressed into service. His idea to help was suddenly in demand. “PMC had never been a grantmaking organization before, but everybody was saying, ‘You’ve got to do this,’” he said. “So we sort of turned ourselves inside out, hired some staff and became a grantmaking organization.” By August 2025, Public Media had organized a fundraising bonanza. It created the Public Media Bridge Fund to raise and quickly donate $100 million to stabilize public radio stations that depended on CPB funding for more than 30% of their annual budgets and were in danger of closing after the federal cuts. The fund launched with $27 million, including an initial $10 million donation from the Knight Foundation and support from Pivotal and the Ford, MacArthur, Robert Wood Johnson and Schmidt Family foundations. By December, it had distributed all $27 million to stabilize endangered stations. Stations with support from other sources, including the Bureau of Indian Affairs for tribal stations and the state of New Mexico for stations there, did not receive funding. “That was a good thing,” Isgitt said, “because we committed every dime that we had.” The Public Media Bridge Fund has raised about $87 million and stabilized 186 public radio stations that serve about 30 million people in the United States. The Knight Foundation’s additional $10 million donation, announced Tuesday, is part of PMC’s new $38 million fundraising effort to help stations become more financially sustainable without federal funding. Knight Foundation President and CEO Maribel Perez Wadsworth said she was impressed with how quickly and effectively Public Media deployed funds last year. “Now, it is really turning all of its attention to sustainability and the things that are critical to sustainability,” said Perez Wadsworth, adding that PMC’s focus on fostering collaboration between local news organizations can “drive the kind of business model change that will hopefully support sustainability in the long run.” The bridge fund will still support stations with unstable budgets; the fund is now also looking at projects with broader impact, Isgitt said. “Our attention now is more on the nationwide system and how it can sort of re-engineer itself to work more efficiently,” he said. The public radio network is a collaboration of three Maryland nonprofit stations owned by Salisbury University and the University of Maryland Eastern Shore. Cost-cutting and increased donations allowed Delmarva Public Radio to use part of its Public Media Bridge Fund grant to modernize equipment and purchase new marketing database software. It also established a content-sharing agreement with Baltimore Public Media. The changes tripled the number of donors and listeners in the station’s marketing database and increased membership revenue by 20% over last year's already unusually strong donations as supporters responded to the federal cuts, Diaz said. “I can now see a clear path for the foreseeable future,” she added. “We didn’t have that before.” Ashley Alvarado, president and CEO of Texas Public Radio, said Public Media and its bridge fund are helping her organization navigate a combination with the nonprofit newsroom San Antonio Report. The two nonprofits decided in July to join forces, believing they would be stronger financially together. “What we found is that the strengths and weaknesses of each organization would really benefit from that combination,” Alvarado said.

events.title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
events.summary: NVIDIA Announces New Investments in the UK Startup Ecosystem Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work — and the scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems. NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research. NVIDIA has been investing in the U.K. startup ecosystem, supporting companies including Basecamp Research , Ineffable Intelligence , Synthesia , Wayve and many more. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Boltz , Foresight , Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane . Boltz , a London-based AI startup founded by MIT researchers, builds biomolecular models and AI agents that help scientists predict molecular structures and interactions, and design potential new medicines. Foresight, a London-based startup, helps owners of major infrastructure projects, including hyperscale data centers, predict completion dates, mitigate risks and accelerate time to revenue. Hiverge , a Cambridge-based AI startup founded by researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Cambridge, builds an AI discovery engine that automatically writes and optimizes algorithms for tasks such as faster AI training and complex logistics planning. Prima Mente , a London-based AI biology startup, focuses on building biological foundation models to decode complex diseases and identify novel therapeutic targets, starting with Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and ALS. Riverlane, a Cambridge-based quantum computing startup, builds real-time error correction hardware and software that work across all major qubit types, helping quantum computers become reliable enough for practical use. In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize , joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges. Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households. Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems. In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients. Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence. Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed. Apian , Synnovis and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care. Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback. On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K. Digital Jersey , Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services. In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions. Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling. Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM , a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure. NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations. Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift. Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems. Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST. events.title: Saudi Ministry of Energy reports limited fire in building at Aramco compound targeted in attack
events.summary: The Saudi Ministry of Energy says a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province CAIRO -- A limited fire broke out Tuesday in an administrative building at Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in an attack in the country’s Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said. The ministry said no injuries were reported. The attack came as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition fighting them exchanged attacks Tuesday night. The fighting marked a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region, and the capital Riyadh. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes. The coalition of forces in Yemen led by Saudi Arabia carried out new airstrikes Tuesday on the Houthi rebel-held Yemeni capital, the Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah and residents said. The strikes came shortly after a coalition spokesman urged residents to evacuate the area for their safety. Witnesses reported hearing strong explosions in Sanaa hours after the coalition struck the Subaha fuel facility west of the city. In a rare statement earlier, the coalition had urged civilians in the Houthi-controlled capital to leave the Yemeni Oil Company site, on a hill overlooking the capital, and nearby storage areas ahead of a possible strike. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the facility and its underground fuel depots for their arsenal of missiles and drones. Houthi officials appeared to have anticipated the attack. The oil company said its storage facilities were empty and that a Saudi strike would not affect oil reserves or supplies for residents. Still, witnesses in the city said lines of cars formed at some gas stations amid fears of a shortage. Shortly after the warning, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that any Saudi attack on Sanaa would be met with a “firm and painful” response in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Hours later, Saudi Arabia issued alerts for incoming missiles heading for Riyadh and the Eastern Province but quickly said the danger had passed. The coalition said it had intercepted a series of Houthi-launched ballistic missiles, drones and cruise missiles in multiple areas in the country, including Riyadh and the southern province of Wadi al-Dawasir. Riyadh residents reported hearing loud explosions. Airlines moved a number of their planes out of Riyadh on Tuesday on the advice of insurers and government officials because of the threat of additional attacks. They needed to transfer the planes to other airports in the country so they can keep flying passengers to their destinations, said Osprey Flight Solutions Chief Intelligence Officer Matthew Borie, whose company advises airlines, insurers and countries on flight threats. “It’s not abnormal for this to occur especially in this day and age with the types of conflict zone situations that have occurred in the region,” Borie said. More than 3,120 flights scheduled to depart from airports across Saudi Arabia since Oct. 8 have been canceled or listed as not operating, representing about 41% of scheduled departures, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. That includes more than 300 flights that had been scheduled to depart Wednesday. Several airlines have suspended service to the kingdom because of the Houthi attacks on airports. It was unclear whether the Tuesday strike in Yemen was a signal of military escalation or a carefully measured response to recent deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport. The warning and the attack show “the Saudis’ aims of upping the ante and striking deep in the heart of Houthi-controlled territory while attempting to control the narrative by presenting themselves as more careful and humanitarian actors than the Houthis,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Washington-based New America institute. Saudi Arabia is still scrambling to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis , including an attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300.

events.title: NVIDIA Commits $250 Million to Advance UK Agentic Safety and Security Research Over the Next Five Years
events.summary: NVIDIA announces a compute donation valued at $250 million over five years to support U.K. agentic safety and security research. The program will support the wider U.K. research community, with a proportion of the commitment supporting BOLD, SOFAIR and Imperial College London across fundamental agentic foundation models and robotics safety. Compute access will be delivered through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners, supporting the nation’s research capability and compute ecosystem. NVIDIA today announced a five-year compute donation valued at $250 million to strengthen the United Kingdom’s agentic safety and security research capability. The commitment will provide $50 million in compute access annually to support agentic safety and security research across the U.K. The majority will support the wider U.K. AI safety and security research community, with a proportion supporting work with the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab (BOLD), the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab (SOFAIR) and Imperial College London. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “The U.K. brings world-class scientific rigor to this essential engineering challenge. With this $250 million commitment, NVIDIA will put accelerated computing in the hands of U.K. researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI. This is how the U.K. turns research leadership into real-world solutions — and scientific progress into a future that benefits everyone.” “This commitment is a vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research — and, in particular, frontier AI safety that is becoming ever more important as AI’s capabilities develop,” said U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan. “NVIDIA’s donation will help Britain’s AI innovators access the resources they need to bring their ideas to life — and, in the process, help build a distinctly British AI future that is safe, secure and that serves people’s best interests, objectives that will be central to the U.K.’s G20 presidency.” “To realise the opportunities of AI, people need to feel the technology is safe and secure. The government is committed to ensuring AI can be securely harnessed to fuel new discoveries and drive growth,“ said U.K. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. “NVIDIA’s investment will help British researchers continue to lead the world in that effort — accelerating the breakthroughs that build trust and help us deploy AI safely.” Strengthening UK Leadership in Agentic Safety and Security Compute provided through the initiative will be dedicated to agentic safety and security research. The program will connect complementary areas of U.K. research, including in AI safety and security. BOLD, led by the University of Oxford, is developing approaches that help AI systems learn, adapt and operate alongside people. SOFAIR, led by UCL, is exploring new open source AI architectures and more accessible ways to develop and deploy AI. Imperial’s work will include safety engineering and robotics. “We are experiencing a critical moment where AI safety as an afterthought is no longer appropriate for the open-ended, evolving world,” said Jakob Foerster, founding director of BOLD. “This compute will help us explore transparent and human-centric approaches to AI that allow us to collectively rise to the challenge by building in governance and human-AI co-improvement from the ground up.” “The next frontier of artificial intelligence is physical — robots, autonomous systems of agents that perceive, reason and act in the real world,” said Alessandra Russo, director of Imperial Frontier AI Research Lab and convening co-director of Human and AI, School of Convergence Science. “With NVIDIA and our industry partners, Imperial is working to ensure that safety and assurance is at the heart of this revolution, ensuring the U.K. leads not only in developing physical AI but in making it trustworthy for the communities and industries that will depend on it.” NVIDIA will fund compute access through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners , with infrastructure hosted in the U.K. This will support the U.K. compute ecosystem and provide a domestic platform for research. Provider selection, technical architecture and commercial terms are to be agreed. As part of the wider initiative, research programs will focus on secure agents, open-model security and real-world threat mitigations. The work will support secure sandboxes, reproducible research and safety assessment benchmarks, including research conducted using NVIDIA OpenShell™ open, secure runtime software and the NVIDIA Sentry reference design . Findings are intended to inform safeguards across the wider computing ecosystem. The commitment builds on NVIDIA’s collaboration with the U.K.’s research community, including on the University of Bristol’s Isambard-AI supercomputer, powered by NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchips. events.title: Businesses could be barred from non-essential water use amid supply threat
events.summary: Golf clubs, private schools and car washes may face tighter rules from water companies as England’s drought continues Three water companies are seeking to impose severe restrictions on businesses as the drought continues across most of England , putting rivers and wildlife under huge pressure. Golf clubs and private schools could be barred from using mains water to irrigate playing fields and courses, and commercial car washes stopped from operating, under “non-essential use bans” being sought by the companies. Eleven areas of England are still in drought, rivers are suffering from low flows, groundwater levels are declining and reservoir levels are at 54% – 21% below what is expected in the autumn. Yorkshire was the latest area to move into drought status on 9 October. Parts of Wales are experiencing the first signs of drought recovery after the whole country was declared in drought in July. Nineteen reservoirs or reservoir groups in England and Wales are less than 50% full, and eight are exceptionally low, up from five in August . The Met Office says above-average rainfall is needed over a sustained seven-month period to bring all areas out of drought. But last month England received about 65% of its typical September rainfall, with eastern and southern areas experiencing the greatest deficit. Businesses in drought-hit areas have been excluded from the hosepipe restrictions imposed on the public for the past three months. But South East, Southern and South West Water have applied to extend restrictions on water use to businesses via non-essential use bans in parts of their regions. If granted, water restrictions can be placed on golf clubs, private schools and commercial car washes to cut water use. Power hoses in car washes can use up to 25 litres of water per minute. Permission from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) is required, but the government has yet to respond to the water companies’ requests. Pressure on wildlife and the environment from the drought is continuing. River flows in seven areas in England are exceptionally low, according to the latest Defra figures, affecting habitats, fish and wildlife. They include the River Derwent in the north-east, the rivers Yare and Ely Ouse in east England, and the River Tone and the Hampshire Avon catchments in south-west England. When river flows fall to low flow levels they can take years to recover, with potentially severe effects on fish spawning and river health. Mark Owen, the head of fisheries at the Angling Trust, said: “When rivers and fish are suffering from the ongoing effects of a severe drought, the Angling Trust supports further restrictions on non-essential water use, alongside urgent action to reduce huge leakage from water companies and unsustainable abstraction from rivers. “We must continue to reduce unnecessary demand for water. It makes little sense to ban people from washing cars at home while commercial car washes can continue operating.” In Hampshire, where the chalk aquifer is exceptionally low, Southern Water is seeking a drought order that would allow it to draw water from an internationally prized chalk stream and rare salmon habitat, even at levels below what is deemed ecologically safe. Southern said it was applying for the permit for the River Test owing to “a clear threat to supplies” in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential The company is seeking a non-essential use ban on commercial premises and businesses to reduce demand as it seeks to draw more water from the Test at levels that were previously deemed unacceptable. As they seek permission to put restrictions on businesses’ water use, South East Water and South West Water have been allowed to alter the amount of water they draw from rivers to try to conserve water in their reservoirs. The Ardingly reservoir, near Haywards Heath in West Sussex, which serves 280,000 people, is exceptionally low, holding 1.05bn litres of water. Its total capacity is 5.2bn litres. In the south-west, Colliford reservoir on Bodmin Moor, which serves 255,000 households in Cornwall, is 37% full, holding 10.68bn litres against a total capacity of 28.5bn litres. Wimbleball in Somerset, which provides water for 390,000 people, is 18% full, with 3.8bn litres against a total capacity of 21.3bn litres. Sam Bottomley, South West Water’s director for drinking water services, said the region was entering a critical phase of an exceptionally prolonged drought. “Every day we continue to draw on our reservoirs to keep water flowing to homes, businesses and communities while river flows remain below the levels needed to support public water supply,” he said. “Many people understandably think a drought is over once it starts raining. In reality, recovery takes much longer.

events.title: Energy bills through the roof? Five signs your house is leaking heat
events.summary: From finding draughts to buying a thermal leak detector – there are simple, cost-effective ways to start sorting heat loss How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences 1. Cold draughts around windows, doors and loft hatches Pick a day when there is a good breeze, and heat the house to its usual temperature. Then wander around with a candle or smoke pen (about £20). Alternatively, buy a thermal leak detector. This flashes blue for cold, green for normal and red for warm. 2. Water trapped between window panes “Misting or water trapped between the panes of double glazing can point to a failed sealed unit,” says Antony Heath, the marketing and development director at Glevum Windows. “Once the seal has broken, the window may no longer insulate as effectively.” Condensation on the inside of windows, particularly first thing in the morning, can indicate cold surfaces where heat is escaping, says Oliver Novakovic, technical and innovation director at Barratt Redrow. It can have several causes, including poor ventilation. Older single-glazed windows allow more heat loss, which exacerbates the problem. 4. The heating is always on, but your house still feels cold If your home struggles to maintain a comfortable temperature, it may be losing heat through walls, floors or the roof. Uneven room temperatures can also be a sign that radiators are not working or heat is escaping faster in some areas. “The better a home is at retaining warmth through good insulation and airtightness, the less energy is needed to keep it comfortable,” Novakovic says. If snow melts quickly on your roof while nearby properties remain blanketed – or it is a hotspot for birds – this can be a sign that heat is escaping. An older or uninsulated home can lose 25% of its heat through the roof.

events.title: European Cities Deploy NVIDIA-Powered AI Agents to Run Smarter Urban Operations
events.summary: Keeping a city running means making decisions that affect residents every day — from when to repair a road to how to use energy more efficiently. Across the EMEA region, cities and local software, infrastructure and integration partners are using NVIDIA accelerated computing to build physical AI agents and digital twins that help teams make those decisions. These applications can anticipate maintenance needs, guide urban planning and make public services more responsive. Software partners including ABA Technology , Akila , Galene AI , Honeywell Technologies , K2K , Linker Vision , Milestone , Onetera , ThinkDeep and Younite AI are using NVIDIA physical and agentic AI to develop solutions for city operations and public services. NVIDIA Cosmos open models and the NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) help agents interpret video and identify conditions, such as traffic congestion, equipment condition, underused spaces and safety hazards, that need attention. NVIDIA Nemotron open models enable developers to build agents that reason over information, respond in natural language and deploy digital twins with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries. Projects span Belgium, Finland, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland, Sweden, the U.K. and elsewhere. In the U.K., the Liverpool City Region , K2K is exploring how to build AI factories using NVIDIA accelerated computing, Cosmos and the VSS blueprint that can support urban planning and public services — testing applications for mobility and safety. The Island of Jersey is working with K2K to strengthen decision-making, mobility and urban planning while advancing clean energy and public services. Innovation City Belfast is exploring a pilot with K2K focused on smart mobility, transport systems, citizen safety and event and response management. In France, the Department of Côte-d’Or , Akila and ThinkDeep built operations agents that combine sensor, infrastructure and historical data in a sovereign digital twin using NVIDIA Nemotron, Omniverse and accelerated computing, with Cosmos adoption planned for video data. Across more than 500 public buildings, the agents support energy, compliance, safety and climate resilience, and cut document search time from weeks to minutes and reduce total operating costs by 10%, targeting 30% at scale. In addition, Port Sud de France in Sète is working with ThinkDeep’s agentic platform that uses Cosmos and Nemotron to analyze cargo and safety data, coordinate operations and guide secure handling of hazardous materials. In Italy’s Milan region, Galene.AI , Dell Technologies and TD Synnex are deploying an NVIDIA-powered, locally operated AI factory, starting with Cinisello Balsamo and planning expansion to four additional municipalities. Services include real-time translation, citizen chatbots and assistance with procurement and funding. These applications aim to simplify administrative work and help people get access to municipal data in seconds versus hours, while keeping local governance of data. At Belgium’s Port of Antwerp-Bruges , Milestone and Dell Technologies are testing how agentic vision AI technologies, using NVIDIA Cosmos and the VSS blueprint, could support complex use cases such as oil-spill warnings by training models with synthetic data to prepare for incidents where real-world data is scarce. In the Nordics, Younite AI is developing a digital twin experience with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries for Gothenburg in Sweden as a part of the EU’s Citiverse initiative, focused on helping cities simulate changes and improve accessibility by providing event entrance previews, seating and crowd conditions before arrival. These cities point toward a broader ambition: adapting agentic applications to local needs and extending them across departments and neighboring municipalities and countries such as Poland’s city of Wroclaw. Elsewhere in the region, Honeywell Technologies is deploying Forge Cognition, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, Cosmos, Omniverse and the VSS blueprint, at the Dubai Fairmont Hotel to connect AI agents with building systems and improve reliability, energy efficiency and operations. Video courtesy of Honeywell Technologies. Building the AI Infrastructure for European Cities For European cities, scaling from pilots to everyday operations requires infrastructure that can process local data, customize models and run AI agents. System builders and infrastructure partners including Cisco , Dell Technologies , HPE , Lenovo and Supermicro are packaging NVIDIA accelerated computing, networking and storage into locally operated AI factories. These systems let cities customize and run intelligent applications locally while retaining control of their data, models and operations. Nebius and Net Zero Compute are part of the broader ecosystem building AI factories designed to accelerate deployment and reduce costs for agentic services. EY and Accenture provide the integration and operational expertise to connect applications with city systems. Their work helps cities build repeatable deployment blueprints that they can adapt across departments and expand as local needs grow. events.title: Demand for air-con servicing hots up amid worsening haze in S’pore
events.summary: The increase in demand comes as a combination of hazy conditions and hot weather prompts more families and businesses to check that their air-conditioners are working properly. PHOTOS: WIRA AIRCON SERVICES, AIRCON UNCLE, IAIRCON SINGAPORE Requests for air-conditioner servicing surged in September as the PSI first entered the unhealthy range in Singapore, with demand continuing to climb in October. Service firms said customer queries and bookings increased by 15 to 30 per cent, as homes and businesses checked units for poor cooling, dirtier filters and better sleep comfort. Job ads for air-con technicians more than doubled, but hiring remains difficult because suitable candidates are scarce; some firms are holding prices and staffing steady for now. SINGAPORE – More job postings for air-conditioner technicians surfaced in the l ast quarter, as demand for air-conditioner servicing rose sharply across residential and commercial venues. Requests for air-con servicing surged in September, when the PSI first entered the unhealthy range in Singapore , with demand continuing to climb in October. Sushil Acharya, co-founder of home services platform StringsSG, said September recorded the sharpest increase in requests for air-con servicing, coinciding with the onset of the haze. There were 792 requests in September, up from 297 in the same month in 2025. In October, the volume of requests increased further, in line with the worsening air quality across the island . He noted that requests received from Oct 1 to 10 were 23% higher than those received during the same period in September and October 2025. “In September, the number of requests generated per dollar of customer acquisition spending increased by 64% compared with in August,” he said. Air-con servicing companies told The Straits Times that customer demand and queries on air-con servicing have risen sharply, by up to 30%, in recent months. For Rafiuddin Ismail, sales operations manager at Wira Aircon Services, the prolonged haze and hotter weather mean handling a surge in customer queries about air-con performance. There has been about a 30% increase in new customers, he said, adding that he has observed more residential and commercial customers including hotels, shops and offices “experiencing insufficient cooling rather than reporting actual equipment faults”. Rafiuddin said: “We have also received more inquiries from customers who have not been using their air-conditioning units regularly and now want to have them checked before using them more frequently, especially at night. “Many are looking to ensure their units can provide a comfortable sleeping environment.” Similarly, Aircon Uncle operations manager Jeremy Chng has seen a clear uptick in bookings from households and businesses. “(They are) asking questions and looking for dependable support to keep their units running well,” he said. He added that customer demand and engagement have grown by about 20%, reflecting a heavier reliance on air-conditioning in Singapore’s climate as well as a growing awareness that regular servicing can prevent costly breakdowns later. A spokesperson for iAircon Singapore, who wanted to be known only as “Uncle Eric”, said demand for servicing has increased by 15% to 20% lately, with most customers having blower fans and filters that are “much dirtier than usual”. The company is able to monitor the cleanliness of the units closely as many of its customers have signed up for annual maintenance packages with quarterly servicing, he said. FastJobs founder and chief executive Julian Tan said job postings for air-con technicians have more than doubled in the last quarter, but the figure remained below that for the corresponding period in 2025. “Hiring for air-con technicians on FastJobs typically picks up in the hotter July-to-September period, and this year was no exception,” he added. There are typically more job postings for air-con technicians on recruitment platform FastJobs during the hotter July-to-September period. But employers have faced challenges finding suitable candidates. Tan said he has heard from recruitment partners that suitable technician candidates are difficult to find, with some agencies scaling back on these roles as a result. To this end, more air-con and maintenance companies are hiring directly rather than through recruitment agencies, he noted, adding that “roles posted directly by employers nearly doubled compared with the same period last year”. Despite the surge in demand, several air-con firms said they have not increased their prices and are not looking to hire more technicians for now. Wira Aircon Services’ Rafiuddin said: “Our current two teams of four air-con technicians each are sufficient to accommodate our customers’ requests, although we continue to monitor demand. “Hiring additional technicians comes with significant costs so we have to be careful with our recruitment decisions.

events.title: Rare earths company could be nationalised as China-linked investors fail to divest
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Northern Minerals is seen as vital to developing alternative sources of dysprosium and terbium, which are used in renewable energy and military technology. ( ABC Rural: Matt Brann ) China-linked investors are defying federal government orders to divest from a Perth-based rare earths company. Northern Minerals is seen as a key player in efforts by both the US and Australia to break China's stranglehold on the critical minerals supply chain. Resources Minister Madeleine King said "one option" is to nationalise the company, given the strategic national interest. The Resources Minister Madeleine King says nationalising a Perth-based heavy rare earths company is an "option" for the government as China-linked investors continue to defy orders to divest from the strategically sensitive miner. In May, federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers ordered six investors which hold around 17 per cent of Northern Minerals to divest by July 2 from the company, which is developing the Browns Range project in Western Australia's east Kimberley region. But Northern Minerals told the ASX later in July that the companies still held most of the shares they had been ordered to sell. Northern Minerals is seen as a key player in efforts by both the US and Australia to break China's stranglehold on the critical minerals supply chain and is already on track for about $500 million in funding from the Export Import Bank of the United States. Madeleine King told the National Press Club on Wednesday that the uncertainty was "holding up" the development of the project, which is vital to developing alternative sources of dysprosium and terbium, critical minerals which are used in both renewable energy infrastructure and advanced military technology. The minister also appeared to leave the door open to nationalisation when asked if the government would be willing to take that step — although she stressed that no decisions had yet been made. "I guess it is one option, but I wouldn't want to advance on any decision we're making there," she said. She also appeared to confirm that the companies had failed to pay the fines imposed by the federal government for non-compliance. Madeleine King says the critical minerals are important for Australia's national security. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Ms King said the government was "very active knowing what is going on" when it came to the project, and took aim at the China-linked investors refusing to sell, saying "failure to follow through or pay respects, quite frankly, to Australian government decisions, is a very serious matter we are looking at". "There have been a number of decisions made by FIRB [the Foreign Investment Review Board] but also divestment decisions as well, and that has not been done by those who hold those shares," she said. The comments from the minister come after a rolling series of government interventions designed at protecting the company from Chinese entities stalking it. In 2023, Mr Chalmers blocked a Chinese-linked investor Yuxiao Fund from boosting its stake in the company, and in 2025 he ordered another five companies linked to China to divest from it. One of those Chinese investors launched an unsuccessful bid earlier this year to topple the company's leadership. And at least some of the Chinese companies blocked from Northern Minerals seem to have made multiple efforts to circumvent federal government orders to divest from the company. Earlier this year the Foreign Investment Review Board wrote to Northern Minerals, saying three of the blocked investors last year had simply transferred their shares to Hong Kong Ying Tak Ltd, one of the six companies ordered to divest earlier this year. The Resources Minister said the saga highlighted the need for the federal government to press on with its review of foreign investment laws, which is due to wrap up next year. The ABC has approached Northern Minerals for comment.

Jimblebar iron ore mine, 41 kilometeres east of Newman in the Pilbara. Minister for the Pilbara Amber-Jade Sanderson said the decision was very disappointing. WA Electrical Trades Union (ETU) state secretary Adam Woodage called the cuts a "senseless attack". The cuts come amid an ongoing dispute between BHP and unions over pay and conditions at its Port Hedland operations that has included a series of recent strikes. events.title: Forcing gas producers to sell to Australia won't 'crash' prices, King says
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Gas reservation laws won't cause wholesale price 'crash', King says Madeleine King says the government has struck a careful balance in its bid to push down wholesale gas prices while keeping the sector profitable. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The resources minister has declined to detail how far she expects gas prices to fall under a proposed reservation law, saying the government's modelling is commercially sensitive. Madeleine King has introduced legislation to create a gas reservation scheme she says will create a "modest" domestic oversupply. The Coalition has indicated it will work with the government to pass the laws, but says questions remain about how future supply and investment will be assured. The resources minister says gas prices will not crash under national reservation laws, but refused to say how much they will fall as the industry warns the government is pushing too hard. Madeleine King said she wanted the proposed laws to make prices fairer while ensuring new gas projects would still be profitable enough to proceed. "Allow me to be clear: we need gas to support the rollout of renewables. We need gas to have a strong Australian manufacturing industry. We need gas to continue heating our homes," she said. The legislation introduced to parliament this morning would force producers to sell up to a fifth of their gas slated for export to Australia, pushing down wholesale prices by sparing the country from having to compete with the international market for its own resource. How much gas producers will be required to sell to Australia each year would be set by the energy regulator, with a target amount of 110 per cent of Australia's actual needs. The government says the "modest oversupply" will put downward pressure on prices for consumers. But after being burned by its failure to meet a previous promise to cut home power bills by $275 through renewables, which was thrown off course by Russia's invasion of Ukraine driving up gas and fuel prices globally, the government has been reluctant to put a price tag on how much prices would be expected to fall under the scheme. The resources minister told the National Press Club that the rules for gas producers had been carefully balanced, but that information was commercially sensitive. "We have done a lot of study and a lot of analysis and, I might add, that so has just about everybody else in relation to this," Ms King said. "A lot of the modelling that we have done, or the analysis that we have done, is commercial-in-confidence, so it is difficult." She said the government would release an impact assessment related to its gas reservation laws, but did not commit to that including estimated impacts on wholesale gas prices. "Our focus is on making sure there is this modest oversupply, and that demand calibration is really important, as well, in this," Ms King said. "We all know having too little gas to firm renewables or provide for the manufacturing industry is as dangerous as having a massive oversupply which crashes the market, but also it can undermine investment in renewables, so it is a really fine balance we have got to achieve here." The resources minister said the bill's focus was to make gas cheaper for heavy industry and energy generation, but added that an important element was ensuring cheaper gas prices "will be felt by the consumer". 'Sugar hit' will hurt in long-term, industry says The gas industry has warned that the government's plan could force the sale of gas at rates that are cheaper than it costs to produce. It says the scheme might provide a "sugar hit", but would make future gas projects unviable and dry up supply in the long-term. "The government cannot expect industry to invest billions of dollars in new gas supply while introducing policies that fundamentally undermine the commercial viability of those investments," Australian Energy Producers chief executive Samantha McCulloch said. "Any price impact is likely to be temporary because of the impact this is going to have on investment and future gas supply. "The [Australian Competition and Consumer Commission] has said that the marginal cost of new supply is somewhere between $9.50 and $13 [per gigajoule]. You need a price within that range to encourage investment in new supply." Australian Energy Regulator data shows wholesale gas prices have been between about $10 to $11.50 per gigajoule, depending on jurisdiction. events.title: Heating oil users facing fuel or food winter choice
events.summary: Liz Humphris said although she can afford it, she does not like to look at the price heating oil has reached Published 14 October 2026, 06:18 BST With the summer gone and the central heating going on, people who use heating oil in their homes are facing the prospect of filling their tanks, at much higher prices than they have been used to. Many will pay nearly double what they had to last year because of a rise in prices since the start of the Iran war. It has led people like Liz Humphris, from Bishop's Castle in Shropshire, to limit how much they buy at once to help ends meet. "Now, I just order 500 litres at a time because it costs too much," she said. Ministers said on Tuesday they would tighten up rules, promote competition and give customers clearer compensation routes if things go wrong . Minimum order levels, set for some customers, will be reviewed. As prices remain volatile, but significantly higher than in recent winters, campaigners have called for heating oil customers to benefit from a similar cap to that on mains gas and electricity tariffs in England, Scotland and Wales. There is no promise this will happen, but ministers said they would work to "develop a regulatory regime for the heating oil market, protecting consumers and promoting competition." Humphris said she had noticed the jump in prices: "It is costing over £500 for 500 litres, so it has gone up hugely." Humphris added that she felt for people she knew who had to use food banks, like the one she volunteers for. "I am reasonably OK because I've got a teacher's pension, so I am not destitute or anything," she said. "For people who are on a very fixed income, it literally is coming down to the point where it is fuel or food, which is awful because you've got to heat your home." According to Shropshire Council, about 15 per cent of households in its area rely on oil-fuelled central heating, which is between 16,000 and 21,000 properties. But within the county there are large variations, with the South Shropshire constituency having one of the highest percentages of homes without mains gas across the UK, at 53%. It has led to co-operatives forming to bulk buy heating oil at cheaper prices, including one set up by the charity Community Resource. , external Hanna Clarke, who is the fundraising lead at the charity, said people coming to them were struggling with rising prices. "It is different to your electricty and your gas. You can't necessarily put it on a direct debit and spread that cost out across the 12 months - you have to fill up your tank," she said. "To be able to do it, lots of the suppliers have minimum orders, so that is the one sort of key issue that we are having, that they just literally cannot afford that big increase in the cost per unit now." Campaign group Action with Communities in Rural England (ACRE) said the government's move to regulate the heating oil market did not go far enough. Chief executive Corrine Pluchino called for an immediate cut to VAT on heating oil and LPG. "While we welcome the government's announcement that they intend to accept the recommendations of the Competition and Markets Authority's study of the heating oil market, we do not believe the action will address the fundamental problem facing the 1.7 million UK households who are off the gas grid, mostly in rural areas," Pluchino added. "For those households, especially those nearing the end of their current supply, the real issue is the high and volatile price of heating oil, which is adding hundreds of pounds to their bills because the fuel has to be bought in bulk." events.title: Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George Monbiot
events.summary: Tom Watson has said ‘mob rule’ must not decide public contracts. Perhaps he should take a look at his new employer What a world we live in. Imagine: gangs dragging civil servants off commuter trains and beating them up because they handed government data jobs to the wrong contractor – and the government is changing its procurement decisions as a result. Well, OK, it might not have happened yet, but it’s only a matter of time. As the former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson asks : “Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want mob rule to lead procurement practices?” No, I absolutely don’t want the latter, and it’s always good to get ahead of trouble. But then I remember there are two common meanings of mob rule. One is intimidation by crowds of thugs. The other is a pejorative term for democracy. And while I’ve yet to see government procurement practices in the UK determined by pitchforks and flaming torches, democratic transparency could be a genuine threat to certain contractors. One might have hoped that Watson, who once took on the Murdoch empire , would have recognised the distinction. But then again, one might have hoped that Watson would not have taken a job as a senior vice-president at Palantir. Continue reading...

events.title: Rex grounds two routes 10 months after $60m rescue package
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fuel costs blamed as Rex suspends Orange and Port Macquarie services Regional Express has announced it will suspend two regional NSW services in late October. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor ) Rex Airlines will suspend its Orange and Port Macquarie services from October 25. The decision comes less than a year after the carrier was sold in a deal that featured a $60 million rescue package and a further $108 million to restructure Commonwealth debt. The airline says it will monitor fuel costs and reinstate the routes it becomes commercially viable. Less than a year after it was sold with the aid of a federal government rescue package, embattled airline Regional Express (Rex) has grounded flights to two NSW destinations. The carrier announced that flights to and from Sydney and Port Macquarie on the Mid North Coast and Orange in the Central West will be indefinitely halted from October 25. Independent MP Andrew Gee, whose federal electorate takes in Orange, described the decision as a "real shock". "It feels like a slap in the face or a kick in the guts for the whole region after everyone called for so much support and so much pressure was put on the government to deliver it," he said. Andrew Gee says Rex's decision comes as a blow after the effort put into ensuring its survival. ( ABC News: Nick Haggarty ) A Commonwealth bailout allowed the airline to keep flying its regional routes and, in late 2025, it was bought by US-based air services company Air T . The sale was endorsed by the federal government, which backed the bid with a $60 million support package and an additional $108 million to help restructure existing Commonwealth debt. In exchange for that support Air T made commitments to increase the number of aircraft in service, maintain an ongoing level of service to regional Australia, and increase frequencies of profitable flights across its network. The ABC has contacted Air T for comment. A spokesperson for Federal Transport Minister Catherine King issued a statement acknowledging the Rex decision would be "be disappointing for many". "In return for support from the Australian Government, Air T agreed to a set of regional commitments aimed at maintaining Rex's services to regional Australia," the spokesperson said. "Notwithstanding these changes, Rex continues to operate one of Australia's largest regional air networks. "The Government continues to work closely with Rex to understand market challenges and to monitor Rex's compliance with regional commitments." The statement noted that customers in both regional destinations would still be able to fly to and from Sydney on different carriers. A spokesperson for Catherine King says the government is continuing to "work closely" with Rex. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) A statement issued by Rex said the suspensions were indefinite, and affected customers would be offered "refunds or re-bookings". "The environment of entrenched high fuel prices driven by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, together with lack of demand, do not make these routes commercially viable at this time," the statement said. REX said it would monitor the situation and consider reinstating the routes "once fuel prices decrease to a level that makes it commercially viable for flights to resume". The carrier said it remained "committed to serving regional and remote Australia". In May, the airline cut two services in Tasmania and scaled back a service to Mildura in Victoria's north-west. Rex has blamed soaring fuel costs for the suspension of the flights. ( Supplied: Rex Airlines ) Port Macquarie Mayor Adam Roberts said the area's $700 million annual visitor economy would be hit by the Rex decision. "The reality is that it has a significant flow-on effect to our community," he said. "Living in a regional area, we absolutely need these vital services." Cr Adams said whether airport staff would lose jobs remained unclear, but discussions were underway to mitigate impacts. "The state and federal governments need to look at what's happening here and ask the question [whether] they could potentially help us stabilise our potential for travel," he said. "If it's a grant fund or if it's a carrot to entice more airlines to use this airport, we're already having some peripheral conversations." Orange Mayor Tony Mileto is pessimistic about the prospect of the service ever being reinstated. "I don't think they'll be backflipping on the decision," he said. Cr Mileto said there was clearly demand among the other airlines that serviced the airport, including Qantas and Link Airways.

events.title: Geeing up for 6G: What the next mobile standard promises and challenges it faces
events.summary: Over the past weeks, UAE telecom operators etisalat and du have announced further progress in their march towards 6G, the next generation of wireless communication. The industry is accelerating its preparations for the technology that being presented as vital to the world becoming more connected, underpinned by increasingly intelligent devices and services . Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries . Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi's etisalat – which recently rebranded back from e& – said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold. What is 6G and when would it be available? 6G promises faster speeds and efficiency than the current 5G mobile phone technology, which also has more advanced forms under names such as 5G+, 5G Advanced and 5.5G. Historically, new generations of wireless technology have emerged with every new decade, suggesting 6G could become available in the early 2030s. This is a widely shared industry expectation. The US introduced the third generation in 2002, the fourth in 2010 and 5G in 2018. The second and first generations were in the 1980s and early 1990s, respectively, with the “zero G” before that. While a 6G rollout is predicted in the early 2030s, not all of its features are expected to be available at launch, as the industry would continue testing its deployment. How fast is 6G? 5G's maximum transmission speed is 20 gigabits per second, which is already 20 times faster that 4G's 1Gbps rate under ideal circumstances. However, 6G's theoretical maximum compared to 5G, has varied from anywhere between 50 times faster, or 1 terabit per second, to 1,000 times, or 2.5 terabytes per second. One can only imagine how much that will increase transmission speeds. A multi-gigabyte file that used to take seconds or a few minutes to download could be done in a snap. Where is 6G use ideal? The consumer proposition of 6G will always be front and centre, especially as digital consumption and reliance on connected devices will only become more widespread. But on an industrial scale, 6G is expected to power advanced iterations of immersive and mass communication, ubiquitous connectivity, integrated sensing and communication, low-latency and hyper-reliable communication and artificial intelligence communication, according to the International Telecommunication Union, which leads the framework and standards-setting of wireless communications. Communications, business and economic gains aside, the power of 6G will also play a critical role in society by enabling affordable, resilient and energy‑efficient networks for health, education, agriculture and disaster response, the Geneva-based UN agency said. “Advanced networks also present a way to close the persistent digital divide that today leaves many people in low-income countries behind,” it added. Transport, home appliances and security, payment networks, financial transactions and a host of other products and services expected to be highly connected in the future will also rely on the speed 6G would offer. The challenges There are a number of issues that need to be addressed to ensure the reliability of 6G networks. Arguably the biggest challenge is to build 6G networks resilient to any AI-induced compromises. Networks of the future should be able to detect threats and adaptive enough to respond to them, according to the EC-Council University in New Mexico. Encryption, especially that which can protect against quantum threats, and integration to blockchain would also be important to avoid unauthorised data access and manipulation, the university added.
