events.title: Not building third runway would be 'huge missed opportunity', warns Heathrow boss
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 05:59 BST Not building a third runway at Heathrow Airport would be a "huge missed opportunity" for the UK, the boss of the country's busiest airport has warned. Thomas Woldbye told BBC Radio 4's Today programme it would be "good to know" the government's position on the project, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham refused to say whether he backed expansion. The airport's chief executive said if its owners could not invest in a third runway, the money "will be invested somewhere else in the world", suggesting a decision would be made in the new year. The Department for Transport said it was reviewing responses to a consultation and was "considering the appropriate next steps". A spokesperson added that the government supported airport expansion "across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting the tests on the environment". They said expanding Heathrow had the "potential to deliver around £40 billion in economic benefits across the country". Building a third runway at Heathrow has been debated for decades. The project has proved controversial, facing steep opposition from local residents, politicians and climate campaigners. Last year, then-chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government-backed expansion, saying that "a third runway is badly needed", and that the government could not "duck the decision any longer". Heathrow Airport is owned by a consortium of investors, the largest of which is French private equity firm Ardian. Others include the Qatar Investment Authority, Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and the China Investment Corporation. "If they cannot invest in Heathrow... then that money will be invested somewhere else in the world," Woldbye said. "It's not about allocating this money elsewhere. It's private money. It's not public money. So hence, it will not go into the UK. I think that would be really a sad, huge missed opportunity for this country." A third runway would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway. It is estimated it would cost £33bn to build. Heathrow serves more than 80 million travellers a year with its four passenger terminals and two runways. The number of flights, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average, if a third runway is built. This additional traffic would potentially lead to a huge surge in revenue for the airport's owners, and Heathrow has argued the expansion would provide a "huge economic boost" and create jobs. The new runway was scheduled to open by 2035, subject to plans being submitted and approved, but Heathrow has since suggested it would be delayed by four years to 2039 due to planning and regulatory issues. Whether the new-look government still backs a third runway is not yet clear. Burnham, who as Mayor of Greater Manchester opposed the scheme, said he believed the matter was "for London and Londoners". "I think we ought to hear the voice of people there first. It's not right for me to just jump straight in on the back of the consultation," he said, speaking to the BBC last month . Woldbye said he hoped the prime minister would "will come along" with the project, pointing out it was backed by the unions. Thomas Woldbye, seen here speaking to the BBC last year, has stressed the importance of Heathrow's third runway He added that a third runway was "not just for Londoners". "Benefits will be felt all over the country because our supply chain reaches all the way from the north all the way to the south of the UK." Downing Street declined to comment on Woldbye's remarks. Questioned about the noise impact on nearby communities of more planes taking off and landing, Woldbye claimed Heathrow had seen a "stark" reduction in noise over the past 40 years and said the "trend will continue". "My biggest concern is actually the years of uncertainty. And I think it's time that we give them certainty on what we want with this project so that we can move on and they can move on in their lives," he said. Andy Burnham refuses to back third runway at Heathrow Published 27 September Woldbye told the Today programme he had not yet met the current Chancellor John Healey, but if he did, he would outline that the airport "contributes dramatically to the economy" but that "we are now full". "That means we will stop contributing or stop growing that contribution. If we want to avoid that, we need to now take this decision, move forward and continue the work of the previous government to move at speed and deliver this," he said. The Department for Transport said it was still finalising its Airports National Policy Statement, which provides the basis for deciding whether to grant a new runway at Heathrow. It was last updated in 2018.

events.title: Government says perpetrators of financial abuse will be pursued in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government says perpetrators of financial abuse will be pursued in court under sweeping reforms The federal government will introduce new laws cracking down on perpetrators of financial abuse. ( ABC News: Patrick Thomas ) Perpetrators of financial abuse who use the tax and social security systems to create debts as a form of coercive control could soon be held liable. The federal government today announced consultation over whether courts should be given greater flexibility to transfer a tax or social security debt to the spouse responsible for financial abuse in family law proceedings. ABC News last month flagged that Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino was taking a range of steps to combat financial abuse. "Financial abuse is often one part of a broader pattern of coercion, control and abuse designed to remove a person's independence and limit their choices," Mr Mulino said. He said the effects could follow victim-survivors for years after a relationship ended, through debts, financial insecurity and lost opportunities. Family and domestic violence support services: If you need help immediately, call emergency services on Triple Zero. 1800 Respect National Helpline : 1800 737 732 Men's Referral Service : 1300 766 491 The Kids Helpline : 24-hour support on 1800 55 1800 The reforms form part of the federal government's response to the Parliamentary Joint Committee (PJC) inquiry into financial abuse. Reforms to stop death benefit payouts and super rollovers Other reforms announced include preventing perpetrators of family and domestic violence from receiving victims' superannuation death benefits, with draft legislation to be released later this year. The government also wants to stop coerced directorships, including providing protections for victim‑survivors pressured into company directorships and associated liabilities. Daniel Mulino says he wants to stop financial abuse through the tax and super systems. ( ABC News: Stuart Carnegie ) Mr Mulino said draft legislation would be released for consultation later this year and supported by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO). The government would also give the ATO powers to prevent rollovers into newly established self‑managed super funds, where there are concerns of fraud, financial abuse, misconduct, or potential consumer harm. ASFA chief policy and advocacy officer James Koval said currently a super fund may be legally obligated to pay a member's death benefit to a person who perpetrated family and domestic violence against that member. He welcomed moves to end it as well as stop rollovers of super in cases of abuse. "Once money leaves the safety of larger institutional super funds and moves into a self-managed fund, it can be very difficult to recover," he said. Perpetrators of domestic violence would be punished rather than rewarded for their actions when committing abuse against their former partners through the tax and super systems. Super Consumers Australia's director of advocacy Lily Jiang said the announcement was a positive step towards addressing the devastating impacts of financial abuse. "We need to address the risks built into the system, identify abuse before people's savings are transferred, and make sure the professionals people rely on aren't enabling that abuse," she said. Lily Jiang wants professionals who facilitate abuse to be held accountable. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) Mr Mulino said the government would invest more than $180 million to reform the child support system and close loopholes that facilitated financial abuse and coercive behaviour, including through legislation it introduced in September. Government proposes crackdown on economic abuse The federal government is consulting on major reforms to reduce financial abuse, including making it harder for directors to be appointed without clear consent. It would also expand Services Australia's powers to waive social security debts incurred as a result of family and domestic violence. Ann Kayis-Kumar, the founding director of UNSW's tax and business advisory clinic, noted one in six women and one in 13 men were impacted by "this insidious form of abuse" and hoped the law changes would soon be implemented. She has long been calling for the ATO to waive debts in cases of financial abuse. Ann Kayis-Kumar wants to see the ATO waive debts in cases of financial abuse. ( ABC News: Scot Preston ) Lody Stewart from Redfern Legal Centre's Financial Abuse Service called for increased funding for frontline services.

events.title: Spotlight on Hong Kong as APEC finance ministers gather to discuss region’s economic future
events.summary: The city is organising the 2026 meeting of senior financial officials, firmly demonstrating its positioning as an international financial hub [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hong Kong will be able to flex its growing strength and influence as a major international financial centre when the city stages the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) 2026 Finance Ministers’ Meeting (FMM) for the first time, from October 20 to 21. For the city’s Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po, it is an opportunity to “showcase Hong Kong’s comprehensive development in the economic, financial and social dimensions”, and more. “The FMM also helps deepen our collaboration with other APEC member economies,” said Chan, when the Hong Kong SAR Government announced the meeting would be held in Hong Kong SAR. That Hong Kong SAR was chosen as the venue for the gathering – part of the wider APEC China 2026 event being hosted around the nation by the Ministry of Finance – also reflects the city’s continued role as a “superconnector” across the finance industry and the region in general, according to Chan. Figures released by APEC underscore this, with total foreign direct investment inflows into APEC economies estimated at US$956.3 billion in 2024, of which more than US$126 billion flowed into Hong Kong. Gathering at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre over the two days will be finance ministers drawn from the 21 APEC member economies, as well as representatives of the globe’s leading financial institutions and assorted industry heavyweights and watchers. Among the items on the agenda will be a focus on how to tackle the challenges facing the region while preparing its financial markets for the future at a time of global uncertainty. Also on the table will be plans for cooperation and development across borders with a priority on growth, resilience, digital transformation and inclusive, sustainable prosperity. With APEC economies collectively accounting for 62 per cent of the world’s gross domestic product in 2021 (or US$67.7 trillion), these meetings will help shape the future of the region, and of the world. Andrew Weir has witnessed first-hand the impact the APEC ministerial meeting can have through his roles as vice-chairman of the Hong Kong Financial Services Development Council, chair of the Pacific Basin Economic Council, and former senior partner (Hong Kong) and vice-chairman of KPMG China. “There’s so much uncertainty and there’s so much friction in the world,” Weir says. “It’s a great opportunity to clarify any areas of potential misunderstanding or clarify areas of collaboration which need deeper engagement.” Weir, who began working in Hong Kong in 1991, believes the APEC meeting will give the city an opportunity to show off its strengths. “Hong Kong is one of the best places to work because of the concentration of human capital,” he says. “It’s always been an East-meets-West place, and the rule of law and the importance of good governance have always been in place in Hong Kong. “People forget that in Hong Kong, you can meet a lawyer, an accountant, a fund manager, a banker, a leading insurer – in one day. And people always give their time to meet. People are always looking to grow and develop. So that concentration of human capital and professional capability in financial services, I think, is second to none.” Meeting delegates will arrive in the city following the release in September of the Hong Kong SAR Government’s first five-year plan for economic and social development: one that places an emphasis on strengthening the city’s position as an international financial centre, as well as developing its position as a global offshore yuan business hub and the connectivity of its capital markets. The blueprint’s publication came on the same day that the Global Financial Centres Index reaffirmed the city’s status as Asia’s leading financial hub while ranking Hong Kong third globally, behind New York City and London. Marjorie Yang’s role as chairman of the Esquel Group, a leader in the textile and apparel industry, has given her unique insights into the way Hong Kong does business, while her roles on the Chief Executive’s Council of Advisers on Economic Advancement and Sustainability, as well as on APEC’s Business Advisory Council, mean she has been able to chart the role the city now plays across the region. “We are a superconnector, because we’ve been in this business for a long time – connecting with the mainland and other parts of the world. A lot of companies in Hong Kong have been doing this, so this knowledge is cumulative,” she says, adding that in a fragmented geopolitical environment that has disrupted the global supply chain, the meeting is important for the city to take a strategic position on future trade. Yang also believes that in organising this year’s meeting, Hong Kong can place itself in front of the world.

events.title: Chinese companies seek Gulf partnerships as physical AI takes shape
events.summary: Chinese robotics companies are looking to the Gulf as a possible manufacturing centre for the next generation of AI-powered machines, as the region's capital, energy resources and industrial ambitions create opportunities for partnerships. Beijing-based robotics company LinkerBot is among those exploring opportunities in the UAE, where it is in talks with major institutions on potential partnerships, Weber Su, the company's vice president and head of global markets, said during the AIM Summit in Dubai on Tuesday. One model being considered would involve Chinese companies supplying advanced robotics parts, while the UAE provides capital-intensive assembly and automated production. Such an arrangement could allow Gulf countries to take part directly in making advanced robots, rather than mainly buying the technology. “That could be the business model that we are exploring with Middle Eastern countries, particularly in UAE,” Mr Su said. LinkerBot specialises in dexterous robotic hands, enabling machines to grasp and manipulate objects. It has expanded into components including reducers and micromotors that control robotic movement. The potential collaboration reflects a broader trend in which Asian companies seek international manufacturing partners, while Gulf economies use their capital, energy and infrastructure to build higher-value industries. In September, Chinese electric and extended-range vehicle maker ROX Motor began producing vehicles in Abu Dhabi . The UAE, meanwhile, is also boosting manufacturing and under its Operation 300bn strategy aims to increase the industrial sector's contribution to gross domestic product to Dh300 billion by 2031. The country's industrial exports rose 25 per cent last year to a record Dh262 billion, with medium and high-technology exports increasing 42 per cent to Dh92 billion, according to the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology. The UAE is also investing in automation to improve manufacturing competitiveness. Mr Su said Chinese companies could increasingly focus on specialised robotics parts, while Gulf partners develop the capital-intensive assembly operations needed to bring those technologies to market. Turning that potential into commercially successful partnerships will require investment agreements, viable production models and sustained demand for AI-powered machines. The next wave of AI? The potential partnerships come as the technology industry moves towards what investors and developers describe as the next stage of artificial intelligence: physical AI. Chinese AI developers including DeepSeek , Zhipu AI and Moonshot AI are becoming increasingly competitive with their US rivals, offering advanced models at lower costs, according to Joseph Zeng, founder and chief investment officer of Hong Kong-based Arcadia Fund Management Group. While generative AI has focused on chatbots, content creation and software applications, the next phase is expected to bring intelligent systems into the physical world. Physical AI combines advanced AI models with robotics, allowing machines to interpret their surroundings, make decisions and perform tasks traditionally requiring human intervention. Introducing vision-based tactile sensing on the LinkerHand. 320 × 240 per fingertip. 0.05 mm spatial resolution. 0.1 N force sensitivity. More than 380,000 sensing points across the hand. Touch, made visible. #LinkerHand #LinkerBot https://t.co/0u9e0MMyd0 — Linkerbot (@LinkerbotHQ) September 27, 2026 Unlike conventional industrial robots, which are generally programmed for repetitive movements, the ambition is to develop machines capable of adapting to different situations. Applications could include robotic hands manipulating unfamiliar objects, autonomous machines working across production lines and robots assisting hospital patients. Mr Su said advances in computing power and AI models were making these capabilities increasingly possible. LinkerBot is developing robotic hands with built-in movement ability that could eventually be combined with sophisticated AI systems to perform a wider range of tasks. “We're going to have skill stores similar to the app stores,” Mr Su said. China's manufacturing scale could give its companies an advantage as the technology shifts towards commercial production. The country installed about 295,000 industrial robots in 2024, accounting for 54 per cent of global installations, according to the International Federation of Robotics . The figures refer to factory robots rather than humanoids, but demonstrate the scale of China's industrial automation industry and supporting supply chains. SK hynix held 50 per cent of the global high-bandwidth memory market by revenue in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung accounted for 33 per cent, according to Counterpoint Research data reported by the Yonhap news agency. Opportunities beyond robotics "Physical AI provides a lot of opportunities for investors,” said Mr Zeng, whose investments include ByteDance and Zhipu AI in China, as well as South Korea's SK hynix and Samsung. The next stage of AI would require advances in computing hardware and infrastructure, he added. He identified high-bandwidth memory, optical transceivers and robotics components among the technologies benefitting from rising investment. Health care could also become an important market. During a recent visit to Suzhou, near Shanghai, Mr Zeng said he encountered a company developing a voice-controlled robot designed to assist bedridden patients with repositioning and personal care. Mr Su said humanoid robots could eventually help to care for elderly people and children in smaller communities, where shrinking populations make it difficult to attract doctors and maintain healthcare services. While fully autonomous, general-purpose robots are still being developed, their potential to ease labour shortages, reduce care costs and extend essential services to underserved communities illustrates the social and economic impact physical AI could have beyond factories. For the Gulf, opportunities could include using autonomous systems in established industries. Mr Zeng highlighted electric and autonomous heavy-duty trucks for mining and industrial operations, alongside energy storage and cleaner power technologies. Energy is also becoming increasingly important to AI investment. Global data-centre electricity use is expected to more than double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency . The forecast highlights the importance of electricity generation, storage and cooling infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates. For Gulf countries with substantial energy resources and growing renewable power capacity, this creates another potential area of collaboration with Asian technology developers.

events.title: Judge orders White House to reinstate press access until litigation concludes
events.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday ruled the Trump administration must continue to grant CNN, MS NOW and Politico access to the White House grounds while the lawsuit filed by the three news organizations continues. Why it matters: It marks a major win for the news outlets as it maintains their White House access and signals the judge believes their legal claims could succeed on their merits. Judge Timothy Kelly, an appointee of President Trump, awarded a temporary restraining order to the plaintiffs on Sept. 24 that mandated the White House reinstate the outlets' credentials for 14 days. Last week, Kelly extended that through Oct. 13. The preliminary injunction preserves the outlets' access until the case is resolved, which could take weeks, months or years. Zoom in: "Defendants (except for President Trump) and their agents, representatives, and all persons or entities acting in concert with them, shall not execute, implement, or enforce the September 18, 2026, decision to revoke the White House 'hard pass' press credentials held by employees of CNN, MS NOW, and POLITICO," Kelly's court order said. What they're saying: In a statement, Theodore J. Boutrous, Jr., attorney for CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, said the ban "blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment." "The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound," he said. "The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this 'unconstitutional ban on the free press' for the foreseeable future." Yes, but: The judge's ruling doesn't guarantee that the plaintiffs have access to key areas, such as the Oval Office and Air Force One. The White House has continued to bar CNN and Politico journalists from press pool assignments onboard Air Force One, despite the temporary restraining order reinstating their credentials. A different White House lawsuit, brought by the Associated Press, could help clarify the extent of the president's power to bar reporters from those types of spaces. That case is ongoing . Catch up quick: The news outlets sued the White House, arguing it violated their First Amendment rights by blocking them in retaliation for their reporting and discriminating against their viewpoints. They also argued their Fifth Amendment rights were violated as they were banned without due process. The temporary restraining order and the preliminary injunction suggest the judge believes the plaintiffs have a strong case on the Fifth Amendment claims. Further legal proceedings, including a potential trial, would determine whether the White House violated the outlets' First Amendment rights. Reality check: Legal experts believe the news organizations have a strong case because of a precedent set by the 1977 Sherrill v. Knight case in which an appeals court ruled it was unconstitutional for the White House to arbitrarily revoke press credentials based on a journalist's reporting or viewpoint. They point to comments President Trump made to justify the ban, including, "They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration." What to watch: The broader White House press pool, which consists of outlets that cover the president and travel with him on rotation, has stood in solidarity with the barred outlets. The White House reached out to other outlets to fill CNN and Politico's spots in the press pool, but they have refused. Some outlets have indicated that they intend to continue withholding publication or distribution of images captured as part of the White House still photography pool, "until a court has the chance to hear arguments on the legal claims filed by those media organizations." Disclosure: The author of this article is a paid contributor for CNN. Editor's note: This story was updated to include a statement from an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

events.title: What will it take for AI-powered purchases to become the norm?
events.summary: ‘Full-stack agent-native solutions’ key to wider business adoption, Ant International’s chief innovation officer says Anyone who has spent time on the internet researching goods and doing lengthy price comparisons will be intrigued by developments in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) for agentic commerce. This new form of online shopping involves AI-powered agents – autonomous software systems that use reasoning, memory and external tools to complete multi-step tasks across different sites and platforms on their own. They can carry out each stage of the buying process, from the initial search to comparing different options from multiple sellers, perhaps even negotiating, and then complete a purchase based on broad customer prompts, or even without direct human intervention. However, the potential benefits of agentic commerce are not limited to online shopping. For businesses, AI agents can help humans execute tasks from end to end and support them on actions that have clear, measurable objectives and standard operating procedures. AI agents could organise an estimated US$3 trillion to US$5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030, according to a report published earlier this year by leading management consulting firm McKinsey & Company. The key to that will be ensuring payment functions are fully integrated with the rest of the ecosystem and are guaranteed to be secure, reliable and accessible around the clock anywhere in the world. “Businesses are already leveraging AI for faster, more efficient decision-making on a range of tasks,” says Jiangming Yang, chief innovation officer at Ant International, an affiliate of financial technology company Ant Group. He adds that in the past year, nearly 90 per cent of customers of Antom – a merchant payment and digitisation platform operated by Ant International – have already adopted agentic AI tools. “But to reach the next phase of agentic commerce – where AI can be used to generate new business opportunities – merchants need full-stack AI-native solutions [end-to-end systems where AI is built into every layer of the process] that allow agents to execute securely across functions like payments, accounting, foreign exchange, treasury and growth operations,” he says. Yang also believes that adoption is likely to take off more quickly in scenarios where results of agent deployment can be assessed easily, such as business-to-business purchasing and operations. With AI agents able to handle inquiries and transactions and resolve problems autonomously around the clock – based on clearly defined rules and boundaries – there is scope to cut operating costs, improve response times and increase all-round efficiency. However, to reach that point, a number of general challenges must still be addressed. One is the issue of trust and transparency, with users likely to be sceptical about autonomous agents making buying decisions and accessing their financial data when they first adopt the technology. “The agentic era creates new risks in finance,” says Yang, whose role at Ant International includes being responsible for anticipating customer needs and staying ahead of industry trends. “Accountability, safety and traceability are crucial considerations for merchants and users in adopting these technologies.” Ant International’s two-layered security architecture is key to meeting these needs, he says. It features a first layer that protects users from existing threats such as fraud and scams with a payment-specific AI model that can simultaneously interpret various types of data and user behaviours. The second layer, meanwhile, targets agent-specific risks through Ant International’s know-your-agent (KYA) framework, which verifies not only the agent’s digital identity, but also that it is acting within the authorised user-defined parameters such as the purpose or budget. Another issue is the so-called integration complexity, where fragmented payment systems can make the seamless deployment of AI agents technically challenging, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises with limited resources. Yang also stresses the importance of the use of an interoperable framework that can help businesses reduce duplicated work processes related to agentic commerce while maintaining trust and managing risks. One significant advance in AI agents enacting payments is Ant International’s Agentic Mobile Protocol (AMP). Launched in April, the company describes the framework as the world’s first mobile-first, “wallet-agnostic” open protocol designed for cross-border agentic commerce. Last month, Ant International announced that 10 digital wallets within its Alipay+ digital cross-border payment network will support AMP in their own agentic payment architectures.

events.title: Conflicting advice left prospector stranded on outback tenement
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Goldfields prospector allowed to retrieve equipment after being stranded on outback tenement Dale Richardson's tenement and belongings he had to leave behind in March. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) Conflicting advice over whether he could or could not legally access his outback tenement left Goldfields prospector Dale Richardson stranded for almost a month. Mr Richardson says he was forced to break the law to leave the site, more than 1,000km north-east of Perth, to return home. He says the confusing situation highlights the need for reform of WA's Aboriginal heritage and access laws. A prospector was left stranded on a remote tenement with dwindling supplies for almost a month due to conflicting advice from WA's former Aboriginal Affairs Minister and the state's planning and heritage bureaucracy. Prospector Dale Richardson had approval for the tenement near Cosmo Newbery, about 1,000 kilometres north-east of Perth, since 2021 under the WA Mining Act. But he has faced more than two years of confusion over whether he can drive out to the ground he has pegged without breaching WA's Aboriginal Heritage and Planning laws. Dale Richardson says the experience has been confusing. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) In a move WA's peak mining and exploration body says highlights the need for reform of the laws, the confusion culminated in Mr Richardson being stranded on the tenement, unsure if he could leave without breaching the law. He was on the tenement on February 27 this year when he received advice from the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage that he could no longer drive along the remote White Cliffs-Yarmarna Road, contradicting previous advice he had obtained. He stayed until his supplies ran low, leaving on March 21, but left his caravan and most of his prospecting equipment behind. In September, Mr Richardson was told by the department that he had breached Section 31 of act by using the road, but no formal action would be taken against him. The road at the heart of Mr Richardson's situation passes through the Cosmo Newbery West and South Aboriginal Reserves, generally requiring permission to access under the Aboriginal Affairs Planning Authority Act. But in December 2024, former Aboriginal Affairs Minister Tony Buti wrote to Mr Richardson confirming he did not need a permit to travel along the road. That advice was reversed in February, when the department advised the minister's earlier ruling had been incorrect, based on an additional investigation and information provided by Central Desert Native Title Services. The department initially advised the road Mr Richardson was using did not meet the gazetted route, and he would be obliged to use a track that had not been maintained for more than 60 years. Dale Richardson says this is the track Don Punch said he had to use to access his tenements. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) But in a subsequent update, it ruled a Federal Native Title decision meant the road was no longer gazetted, and he would need a separate mining permit to use it. A Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage spokesperson said advice on road access had been based on the information available when access to the tenements was initially sought. "I've done everything that I was legally supposed to do," Mr Richardson said. "I've tried to get a permit, I've tried to negotiate an agreement, they're just not willing to do so for some reason." The Yilka Talintji Aboriginal Corporation, which represents the area's native title holders, declined to speak to the ABC. White Cliffs-Yamarna road, at the start of Cosmo Newberry Reserve. ( Supplied: Dale Richardson ) While not at risk of prosecution, Mr Richardson said he had been left with little opportunity to retrieve his caravan and equipment. Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch intervened late last week, granting the prospector a three-month permit to return to the site, remove his property and secure his prospecting equipment. The limited permission does not allow Mr Richardson to resume prospecting. Don Punch granted Mr Richardson a three-month permit to access the site and secure his equipment. ( ABC News: Briana Shepherd ) Labelling the matter complex and unusual, Mr Punch said the Aboriginal Lands Trust had only wished to grant Mr Richardson seven days' access, but he had opted to overrule the body. "Since being made aware of the matter, my office has remained engaged with the relevant parties," he said. Mr Richardson said he wanted to work and rehabilitate his tenements, actions he continues to hold a license for.

events.title: Failed caravan company AOR allegedly traded insolvent since 2023
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Failed caravan company Australian Off Road allegedly traded insolvent since 2023 Australian Off Road suddenly shut its doors in September, leaving dozens of staff unemployed. ( ABC Sunshine Coast: Josh Dye ) Administrators for collapsed caravan company Australian Off Road have detailed fresh allegations against its directors. Nearly 50 customers who paid for caravans that were not built are among the creditors owed $14 million. Administrators say AOR may have been trading insolvently since 2023. A failed Queensland caravan manufacturer may have been trading while insolvent for three years, according to administrators, who say the company owes $14 million. Australian Off Road (AOR) shut its doors in September after 26 years operating on the Sunshine Coast, becoming the second local van manufacturer after Zone RV to collapse within a year. Nearly 50 customers face losing $2.25 million after making progress payments toward caravans that were not built. They include Sandra Muller from NSW Southern Highlands, who stands to lose $101,000. Sandra Muller has paid $101,000 towards her caravan, which was not built. ( ABC News: Lucas Hill ) In a report to creditors on Tuesday night, administrators DVT McLeods detailed fresh allegations against directors Russell Evans and Steve Budden and said AOR may have been insolvent for more than three years. Potential offences identified included insolvent trading, reckless or intentional dishonesty, failure to act in good faith, and improper use of position to gain advantage. "We have a preliminary view that the company traded whilst insolvent from at least 30 June 2023," the report stated. Administrators also said AOR's creditor bill had grown to $14 million, up from $9 million estimated last month . The administrators said further investigations were required and that the results would be reported to ASIC, the corporate regulator. The ABC has attempted to contact Mr Evans and Mr Budden. Mr Evans is one of two parties offering to purchase the company out of administration. He has pitched to investors seeking $2 million to resurrect AOR in a move that could leave existing customers empty-handed. It is legal for a director to buy and transfer a company's assets into a new business if the sale is approved by creditors. The ABC has seen an email from Mr Evans outlining his vision "to establish a new, financially disciplined premium off-road caravan manufacturing business". His proposal offered 20 cents in the dollar for the company's assets, while the existing company's debts would not carry across. The pitch pledged to "recognise customers who paid deposits" and "investigate practical solutions for affected customers" but did not clarify whether all progress payments would be honoured. Inside the Australian Off Road factory in China. ( Supplied ) Mr Evans said the new business would have "a clean financial structure" and "a clear pathway to sustainable profitability and growth". Mr Evans's proposal detailed projected annual revenue of $11.3 million with production of 84 caravans, or seven a month. The new venture would "create a new, low-cost and scalable caravan business", he wrote. Despite marketing itself as an Australian manufacturer and blaming imported Chinese vans for its demise, the ABC can reveal AOR was making chassis in China. A separate company with a factory north of Shanghai was established in 2025 to reduce AOR's production costs. The Chinese company is owed $518,000 but falls among the unsecured creditors. AOR made a loss in three of the past four financial years, and had a negative asset position of $3 million when it collapsed, the creditors report stated. Administrators engaged Argus Auctions to advertise the sale of the business or its assets. After receiving 200 enquiries, 20 parties signed non-disclosure agreements, with feedback that "stock was outdated and poorly managed" and there was a "lack of operational systems and structure". Russell Evans joined AOR about 2012 and became a director in 2021. ( Supplied ) Only two parties made offers to buy the company, including Mr Evans's proposal. The administrators said they were investigating allegations that caravans fully paid for by some customers had been delivered to other people. If you know more about this story, contact Josh Dye at dye.josh@abc.net.au The report noted the company's CCTV system ceased recording on September 9, the day the company stopped trading. "Due to the limited clarity and quality of the footage … we are unable to determine with certainty … whether any caravans were moved within or removed from the premises," the report stated.

events.title: Bank of America hit with $1.2bn fine for money laundering failings
events.summary: Published 14 October 2026, 03:05 BST Bank of America has been fined $1.2bn (£910m) for failing to detect potential money laundering and other illegal activity, the US Treasury Department said on Tuesday. The banking giant failed to report over $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, $1bn of which posed national security and illicit finance risks, the Treasury said. Those failures included not flagging transactions that possibly involved Chinese money laundering networks or trade-based laundering "with a substantial nexus to the southwest border", according to the Treasury. "Our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators," Bank of America told the BBC. The announcement came less 24 hours before Bank of America was due to announce its quarterly earnings on Wednesday morning. "Our third-quarter results will include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2 billion impacting net income by approximately 17 cents per share," the bank said in an emailed statement. "We have already dedicated substantial personnel and resources to our ongoing remediation efforts, and those costs are in the current expense base," it added. In announcing the fine, the third-largest the department has ever imposed, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said: "When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks." The Treasury said the bank overly relied on inquiries from outside parties like law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls. This meant that it "effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations," the department said. As part of the settlement, Bank of America admitted that it "willfully violated" the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to maintain a compliant anti-money laundering programme, conduct required due diligence on foreign correspondent accounts and file suspicious activity reports, the Treasury said. The $1.2bn fine included penalties imposed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) and the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The OCC's $750m fine marked the biggest penalty it has ever levied. OFAC said its settlement with the bank was tied to 475 apparent violations of sanctions programmes including those on Russia and Iran, narcotics, and global terrorism. The settlement amount of $11.6m reflected the determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were "non-egregious", OFAC said. events.title: Justice Department says North Koreans have infiltrated dozens of US companies
events.summary: Last two days at Disrupt are half off. Don’t miss any more moments. REGISTER NOW Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. The U.S. Department of Justice is warning that hackers working for the North Korean regime are increasingly relying on Americans to facilitate the hacking of U.S. companies. In an announcement on Tuesday, prosecutors said they have indicted and arrested at least two people, and conducted searches across dozens of suspected “laptop farms” in Texas. The computers were allegedly used by North Koreans to remotely hack into American companies and steal sensitive data. According to the DOJ, federal authorities seized over 180 computers that they believe American companies had shipped out to their newly hired employees, not realizing that they were sanctioned North Korean spies who had used stolen identities of U.S. citizens to gain employment. The DOJ said that it raided over 40 laptop farms across Texas, the largest disclosed number of homes and residences used for facilitating North Korean hacks, which were owned by at least two American facilitators. CrowdStrike, which helped the FBI investigate and disrupt the latest North Korean operations, said that laptop farms are “vital” to North Korea in helping its hackers overcome physical, financial, and legal challenges of not physically being in the United States. The prosecutors said at least 70 U.S.-based companies had been infiltrated by the hackers, who are believed to have generated around $3 million in stolen funds. The DOJ did not name the affected companies, but described them as healthcare, cyber support, retail, communications, and manufacturing sectors across Ohio and 16 other states, including the District of Columbia. “Increasingly, North Korean IT workers are turning to recruiting American facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. These workers are hiring facilitators to complete a wider variety of tasks, and in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to third-party foreign nationals,” the Justice Department said . Oftentimes, North Korean hackers use real-looking email addresses, spoofed LinkedIn profiles, and extensive online and social media accounts as cover for their activities. In a separate public service announcement , the FBI said that there are “thousands” of North Korean state-controlled IT workers working at Western companies, which “pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.” This is the latest wave of arrests, indictments, and enforcement action targeting North Korean activities in the United States in recent years. The breakaway regime has used this “remote IT workers” scheme to allow North Koreans to gain employment with U.S. and European companies, earn a wage, and then steal sensitive information and intellectual property while as employees. The victim companies are then extorted into paying the hackers further. The remote IT workers’ scheme is one of several strands of illicit revenue that the North Korean regime aims to generate, including hacking crypto exchanges and open source developer projects , with the aim of funding its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program. The regime is thought to have stolen at least $2 billion in crypto during 2025 alone. Experts on North Korea have put the number of hacked companies and the amount of stolen crypto as likely much higher than reported. Earlier this year, CrowdStrike said in a separate report that North Korean hackers were behind around half of all documented “hands-on-keyboard” intrusions over the past year, referring to hacks that are carried out by humans and not automated tools or AI. events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Federal Court declares Commonwealth's blocking of NSW goldmine 'invalid' Regis Resources argued the Commonwealth's decision rendered its goldmine unviable in its current form. ( ABC News: Lani Oataway ) A Federal Court judge has found an Aboriginal protection order that halted an approved goldmine in NSW was "invalid". Regis Resources launched the legal action in 2024, challenging the Commonwealth's decision relating to its McPhillamys Gold Project. Justice James Stellios ruled that the project must be referred back to the federal minister for re-determination. The Federal Court has overturned a Commonwealth decision that halted a billion-dollar goldmine in New South Wales. Regis Resources launched legal action against then federal minister for environment and water Tanya Plibersek in November 2024, challenging the validity of an Aboriginal protection order she granted over part of its McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney. The order applied to 400 hectares of the site, including an area where the company wanted to build a tailings dam, which is used to hold mining waste. It was made after the mining project received approval in 2023 . At the time, Ms Plibersek said the order would protect the headwaters and springs of the Belubula River and that the company could construct its tailings storage elsewhere. But Regis Resources disputed this, saying the decision affected a critical area of the project development site and meant the project was "no longer financially feasible". The Belubula River originates at the mine site. ( ABC News: Xanthe Gregory ) Justice James Stellios has presided over the Federal Court challenge and held two days of hearings in December 2025 . He delivered his judgment during a short sitting today, which found that Regis Resources was successful in the judicial review and the minister's "declaration is invalid". The Aboriginal protection order was granted after Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds lodged an application to protect the area under Section 10 of the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Protection Act in 2020. Tanya Plibersek granted the Aboriginal protection order over part of the McPhillamys mine site in 2024. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) The court heard the application was supported by the Wiradyuri Traditional Owners Central West Aboriginal Corporation (WTOCWAC) and referred to a Dreaming story called the Blue Banded Bee. Justice Stellios told the court that this information "constituted a new application" and should have been referred to the government reporter for consideration and to carry out a public consultation process. "The court's decision and my reasons say nothing about the merits of the claim ... whether it's a significant area or under threat of injury or desecration ... those are matters within the authority of the minister ... not the jurisdiction of this court." In a statement the WTOCWAC said it was "disappointed by the court's decision" and will take time to consider the implications of the judgment. "This case has always been about protecting places of profound cultural and spiritual significance to Wiradyuri people," the group said. "The court's decision does not diminish the cultural significance of these places, nor does it alter our obligation to speak for and care for Country." Regis Resources took the office of the federal environment minister, now held by Murray Watt, to the Federal Court. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Justice Stellios said the appropriate remedy was for the proposal to be sent back to the federal minister for environment and water, a position now held by Murray Watt, for redetermination. He ordered the parties to provide written submissions on costs to be submitted by October 27. In a statement, Senator Watt said he respected the ruling. "The Judge specifically made the point that his decision did not concern the merits of the Minister's decision … instead, the court's decision was based on an error in the process used to grant the declaration," he said. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told parliament during Question Time that the government was carefully considering the judgment. Senator Watt said it was "an example of how complex the current cultural heritage processes are for everyone involved". "We remain committed to working alongside [First Nations people, industry and state and territory governments] on a better system," he said. In a statement, Regis Resources said "after considerable delay and uncertainty, and more than two years of time lost" it was "eager to move forward" to advance one of the country's largest undeveloped gold projects.

events.title: MAS keeps Singdollar appreciation rate unchanged but warns of elevated inflation
events.summary: Unlike most central banks, which target interest rates, MAS uses S$NEER, a trade-weighted basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners. MAS kept Singapore dollar policy unchanged, but said the war-linked energy shock will keep inflation elevated until 2027. The bank said the S$NEER band will keep strengthening to curb imported inflation, after two policy tightenings in 2026. Core inflation rose to 2.1% in July to August, and MAS expects growth to stay steady as GDP grew 5.4% in the third quarter. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s central bank maintained its monetary policy stance, but warned that persistent energy price pressures from the Iran war will keep inflation elevated well into 2027. The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Oct 14 that it will keep unchanged the rate of appreciation of the Singapore dollar’s trade-weighted value, also called the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) policy band. Unlike most central banks, which target interest rates, MAS uses S$NEER, which is a trade-weighted basket of currencies of Singapore’s major trading partners. This is because, in a small and open economy such as Singapore’s – where gross exports and imports of goods and services are more than 300% of gross domestic product (GDP) and almost 40 cents of every dollar spent domestically is on imports – the exchange rate has a much stronger influence on inflation than interest rates. MAS said: “The current appreciating policy band will allow the S$NEER to continue to strengthen and lean against the anticipated near-term rise in imported inflation, ensuring the gradual easing of inflationary pressures in 2027.” Faced with sticky inflation amid an unresolved energy shock from the Iran war, MAS has tightened its policy stance twice in 2026 – in April and July – allowing for a stronger S$NEER that helps dampen the impact of rising import costs. Global crude oil benchmark Brent was trading around US$106 a barrel on Oct 14, up more than 70% since the start of the year, as supplies from the Middle East remained constrained amid the Iran war and the conflict between top oil exporter Saudi Arabia and Yemen. “Since September, energy commodity prices have risen anew and are projected to remain high in the near term,” said the central bank. Global and regional food prices are also expected to pick up as costlier inputs and adverse weather patterns impact food production. Firming imported cost pressures in Singapore will keep core and all-items inflation at the current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead, MAS said. Core inflation, which excludes the costs of accommodation and private transport from all-items inflation, rose to 2.1% on the year in July to August, from 1.5% in the second quarter. For 2026 as a whole, core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2%, while all-items inflation should come in around 2%. This is lower than MAS’ July forecast of 1.5% to 2.5% for both core and all-items inflation. MAS said inflation should ease more discernibly in the second half of 2027 as global energy prices gradually moderate. But with inflation running high all the way to mid-2027, both core and all-items inflation are projected to average 1.5% to 2.5% – higher than the historical average of 1.5 per cent. Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Danish investment bank Saxo, said MAS’ decision to leave policy settings unchanged was a surprise relative to market expectations. However, the pause should not be seen as a pivot. “After two rounds of tightening in 2026, policymakers appear comfortable giving earlier measures more time to work rather than responding aggressively to every inflation risk,” Chanana said. DBS Bank’s senior economist Chua Han Teng said the pause likely reflected a softer-than-expected 2026 inflation outlook, with MAS lowering the top end of its previous forecast. However, the relatively higher projection for 2027 alludes to the persistent risk of energy prices remaining volatile for longer. “MAS likely kept the door open for another calibrated tightening if needed,” he said. For now, economic growth is not a worry for the central bank, with strong demand for Singapore’s AI-related exports, such as semiconductors, and an increase in production capacity across the technology sector. In its quarterly Macroeconomic Review report, also released on Oct 14, MAS said technology-related sectors have accounted for around 75% of overall growth. While there was some moderation in electronics output growth in early third quarter, it said this likely reflected capacity constraints in the global supply chain as underlying AI-related demand remained firm. The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry’s (METI’s) advance estimates released on Oct 14 showed Singapore’s overall GDP grew by 5.4% year on year in the third quarter. In August, METI projected Singapore’s GDP to grow 4.5% to 5.5% in 2026.

events.title: 'A lot of emotion:' First round of redundancies to hit Whyalla steelworks
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts First round of redundancies to exit Whyalla steelworks by end of week More than 250 Whyalla steelworks employees have accepted redundancies since the permanent closure of the blast furnace. ( ABC News: Brant Cumming ) The first of more than 250 Whyalla steelworks employees to accept redundancies will leave on Friday. The plant's direct workforce will be reduced due to the permanent closure of the blast furnace last month. Workers have told the ABC they feel uncertain about their future in the steelmaking town. The first of more than 250 workers to accept redundancies at the Whyalla steelworks will finish up this week — but those who want to stay are still facing an anxious wait. The permanent closure of the blast furnace last month will reduce the plant's direct workforce from 1,700 to 1,200, while at least another 300 contractor roles will also be affected. Australian Workers' Union organiser Shane Karger said he expected about 270 direct employees to accept "genuine redundancies" by the end of this month. The first group of those will exit by this Friday. Mr Karger said following that, voluntary redundancies and early retirement scheme applications would be processed. Genuine redundancy occurs when a worker's role is no longer required, for example, those who were working at the blast furnace. He said voluntary redundancies would go to workers in departments that would reduce their numbers but not shut down entirely. Shane Karger said it's been a emotional time for workers in Whyalla. ( ABC News ) Mr Karger said the final number of redundancies should be known by November. "[That] will then sort out how many positions are up for redeployment," he said. Even for those who stay on, it is unclear what the future will look like. The steelworks has been in administration since early last year, with the announcement of a buyer expected by the end of 2026. Mr Karger said unions have been working with administrators KordaMentha to make the process as fast and smooth as possible. "There's been a lot of emotion," he said. "You've got other workers that are looking forward to a well-earned rest after a very long career at the steelworks." The steelworks was forced into administration in February last year. ( ABC News: Che Chorley ) Several contractors have confirmed to the ABC that they have already laid off staff, with more than one closing down entirely. Jack Taylor, 30, has done manual labour at the steelworks for 10 years but will clock off for the final time this week. His was one of the roles being cut and he has opted not to apply for redeployment, instead accepting a redundancy. "It was a big decision to make," he said. "I own my house here in Whyalla so going for redeployment [would have] meant I'd have a chance of keeping a job, having income coming in." Jack Taylor accepted a redundancy. ( ABC News ) Mr Taylor said years of uncertainty over the future of the steelworks had taken a toll. "We've been through administration two times. "I'm just a bit over all of it, to be honest." He plans to apply for fly-in-fly-out jobs in the mining sector, and hopes to stay in Whyalla. "I've got my family, the footy club, all my friends and that here," he said. events.title: SoftBank junk bond sale raises stakes for CEO Son’s all-in AI bet
events.summary: The scale of Masayoshi Son’s investments, which include backing of about US$64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. SoftBank’s record US$11 billion junk-bond sale shows pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to prove his huge AI bet will pay off, especially through OpenAI. The company is borrowing at up to 9.75% to keep assets it expects to rise in value, while investors worry about concentration risk and possible AI market overheating. Analysts say SoftBank’s AI bets are far bigger and riskier than before, with mixed past results, but supporters believe AI could still bring major financial gains. TOKYO – SoftBank’s promise to pay its highest-ever yields in a record US$11 billion (S$14.1 billion) junk-bond offering highlights the pressure on CEO Masayoshi Son to secure returns on his all-in bet on AI amid concerns about possible overheating in the market. The SoftBank debt issuance in September added to a sharp surge in corporate borrowing in 2026, including major bond sales from Amazon.com, Alphabet and Tencent. The scale of Son’s investments, which include backing totalling US$64.6 billion for ChatGPT maker OpenAI, has made the technology-and-investing conglomerate a bellwether for AI sentiment. Those fresh investments are now coming under sharper scrutiny by analysts and investors amid worries about the degree of concentration in SoftBank’s portfolio and whether a payoff from the expenditures by AI companies will come soon enough. SoftBank previously sold shares in Nvidia and T-Mobile US to fund its investments, but it is now borrowing at record yields of up to 9.75% to retain assets that it believes will appreciate, a senior SoftBank executive told Reuters. “We’ve borrowed money in large part because we don’t want to sell assets that we believe will keep rising in value,” said Alex Clavel, CEO of SoftBank Investment Advisers, which manages the Vision Funds. Sam Altman’s OpenAI is the core investment in the latest iteration of Son’s investment strategy, following lucrative bets on Chinese tech giant Alibaba and chip designer Arm. “Given OpenAI’s appreciation to date, 9.75% is still very reasonable,” Clavel said. Arm’s valuation has grown fivefold since it floated in 2023 and further listings from SoftBank’s private AI portfolio would clarify their value and more easily allow the assets to be monetised for additional investment activity. Altman has said OpenAI will not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns about artificial intelligence. It also faces competition from rival Anthropic and hyperscalers, as well as low-cost Chinese labs. SoftBank was previously “betting on a bunch of numbers at the roulette table. Now it’s red or black, either lose everything or gain everything”, said analyst David Gibson of MST Financial. Increased scrutiny of AI-related fundraising SoftBank will pay its highest-ever coupon of 9.75% on a bond issued in September that matures in 2034. That return compares with Alphabet offering 5.2% for a bond issued in August that matures in 2033. SoftBank’s shares surged to a record high of 8,632 yen in June, though they have fallen 38% since then, while its credit default swap spreads – the cost to insure its debt against a default or other credit event – jumped 24% over the same period. SoftBank’s higher yields reflect investor perceptions of their risk and concentration in large positions, analysts say. “The bets are much bigger than we’ve ever seen,” said Amir Anvarzadeh of Asymmetric Advisors, who recommends shorting the stock. James Athey, a fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough, said the fund was not allocating to high-yield bonds at this stage of the credit cycle, given current tight spread levels. “SoftBank is so aggressive, so concentrated and so all-in, I don’t think we’d be looking there first anyway,” he said. Clavel, however, says SoftBank’s OpenAI backing reflects their deep business ties. “We see OpenAI as a partner, building a relationship that can deliver strategic value as well as financial returns,” he said. OpenAI is also an investor in and customer of data centre company SB Energy, which SoftBank is looking to list and may seek a valuation of US$50 billion, Reuters has reported. “SoftBank is taking advantage of hyper-excitement around AI-driven businesses, applying very high valuations for relatively low revenues, and they are looking to capitalise,” said MST’s Gibson of the potential valuation. Son’s bets have a mixed track record – his investment in Chinese tech giant Alibaba was a major success, but Son also directed US$16 billion to Adam Neumann’s WeWork, which ultimately went bankrupt. Other setbacks included a crash in the value of its investments as central banks moved to hike rates in 2022. “OpenAI’s value appreciation to date far exceeds the losses in our 2021 vintage investments,” Clavel said.

events.title: Singapore’s GDP grew by 5.4% in third quarter of 2026
events.summary: On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the Singapore economy expanded by 1.1%, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter. Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter of 2026, slower than 6.2% in the previous quarter, said METI on Oct 14. Manufacturing rose 7.5%, while construction grew 8.8% as public and private projects increased. Services also grew, led by wholesale trade, transport, IT, finance and hotels. METI said fuller third-quarter GDP data, including inflation, jobs and productivity, will be released in the Economic Survey of Singapore in November 2026. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s economy grew by 5.4% in the third quarter, moderating from 6.2% in the previous quarter. This was higher than the 5.1% consensus estimate in a Bloomberg poll. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the economy expanded by 1.1%, easing from the 1.5% growth in the second quarter, said the Ministry of Energy , Trade and Industry (METI) on Oct 14. The manufacturing sector grew by 7.5% year on year in the third quarter, slower than the 12.9% growth in the previous quarter. The construction sector expanded by 8.8% year on year in the third quarter, faster than the 6.1% growth in the preceding quarter, as both public- and private-sector construction output increased. Among the services sectors, the wholesale and retail trade, and transportation and storage sectors collectively grew by 8% year on year in the third quarter, extending the 6.9% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the retail trade sector. Growth in the wholesale trade sector was led by the machinery, equipment and supplies segment, which saw strong growth in tandem with the robust increase in electronics exports over the same period. Meanwhile, growth in the transportation and storage sector was supported largely by the water and air transport segments. On a quarter-on-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the wholesale and retail trade, and transportation and storage sectors as a whole grew by 2.2%, improving from zero growth in the second quarter. The group of sectors comprising the information and communications, finance and insurance and professional services sectors expanded by 4.3% year on year in the third quarter, easing from the 5.1% growth in the previous quarter. All sectors within the group grew during the quarter. Growth in the information and communications sector was driven by the IT and information services segment, while that in the professional services sector was largely supported by the architectural and engineering, as well as the technical testing and analysis services segments. Growth in the finance and insurance sector was led by the fund management and banking services segments. On a quarter-to-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, this group of sectors expanded by 0.4%, moderating from the 2.8% growth in the second quarter. Growth in the remaining group of services sectors, comprising accommodation and food services, real estate, administrative and support services, and other services industries, came in at 2.1% year on year in the third quarter, extending the 2.4% growth in the preceding quarter. All sectors within the group expanded during the quarter, except for the food and beverage services sector. In particular, the accommodation sector grew on the back of an increase in gross lettings in the higher value-added hotel segments. On a quarter-to-quarter seasonally adjusted basis, the sectors in this group collectively expanded by 0.6%, easing from the 0.8% growth in the second quarter. Selena Ling, chief economist and head of OCBC group research, said Singapore’s economic growth continued to be driven by AI- and electronics-related activity, trade and transportation services, as well as construction and infrastructure. She noted that construction growth accelerated sharply in the third quarter, supported by both public- and private-sector activity, while trade and transportation services strengthened on the back of robust regional trade and continued demand for AI-related electronics. Finance, information and communications, and professional services also continued to expand at a solid pace, but consumer-facing and other domestic services lagged. “This divergence creates a dual-speed expansion where businesses linked to construction, trade and advanced electronics may continue to benefit from strong demand, while consumer-oriented sectors face a more challenging environment, especially on the domestic cost front and tightening financial conditions,” she said. Zavier Wong, market analyst at trading platform eToro, said the strong economic growth has yet to translate into tangible benefits for many households. “Most households aren’t seeing that growth in their wallets,” he said.

events.title: Global standard-setting bodies publish final report on guidance for FMIs on general business risks and general business losses
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) CPMI and IOSCO issue their final report on FMIs’ management of general business risks and losses. The report provides supplemental guidance to the CPMI-IOSCO Principles for financial market infrastructures . The Bank for International Settlements’ Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) and the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) today published a final report on financial market infrastructures’ (FMIs) management of general business risks and general business losses. The report sets out guidance for FMIs and relevant authorities, including in the context of FMIs’ recovery and orderly wind-down, on: i. identifying, monitoring and managing general business risks; ii. determining the minimum amount of liquid net assets funded by equity to be held against potential general business losses; and iii. governance and transparency in managing general business risks. The final report builds upon the consultative report on general business losses published in November 2025. It takes into account the findings of the Level 3 assessment report on the implementation of PFMI Principle 15 (General business risk), which identified issues relating to FMIs' management of general business risks and the liquid net assets funded by the equity they hold to cover potential losses. Consultation responses can be found here . CPMI and IOSCO appreciate the thorough responses and engagement received from respondents.

The "why" being the joy of being together, as well as the chance to wear yellow mesh, she joked. Girls was considered groundbreaking. The show will be executive produced by Judd Apatow. Production will begin in 2027, a decade after the season six finale. Girls won two Emmys, including Outstanding Casting for a Comedy Series, and was nominated 19 times. Girls ran from 2012 to 2017 and was set in New York City. events.title: Oil rises as Middle East attacks increase uncertainty over flows
events.summary: An escalation of Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz threatens the recent rebound in Gulf supply. Oil prices rose because more Middle East attacks made oil flows from the Persian Gulf less certain. The US said it helped move more than 19 million barrels through the Strait of Hormuz, while Iranian and Houthi attacks kept pressure on shipping and Saudi Arabia. Brent has surged more than 70% in 2026, and tanker firms are using ship-to-ship transfers to keep exports moving and reduce risk. Oil rose as a flare-up in attacks in the Middle East increased uncertainty over a recovery in energy flows from the Persian Gulf. West Texas Intermediate advanced toward US$95 a barrel, after edging higher in the previous session, while Brent declined to close below US$106. The US said it assisted in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude through the Strait of Hormuz, even as an escalation of Iranian attacks on tankers in the waterway threatens the recent rebound in Gulf supply to near prewar levels. Elsewhere in the region, Saudi Arabia intercepted more missiles and drones launched by Yemen’s Houthis, as fighting with the Iran-backed militant group showed few signs of subsiding. The headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco in the east of the kingdom was hit in the latest attacks. Brent has surged more than 70% in 2026 as the US-Iran war roils energy markets. Risks have intensified as Iran-backed Houthis attacked Riyadh’s main airport earlier in October and Saudi-backed forces launched a campaign to reclaim rebel-held territory in Yemen. Tanker strikes in Hormuz have also prompted more supertankers to turn away from the Persian Gulf. “While the day-to-day headlines constantly move, the overarching picture in the Persian Gulf has been little changed throughout the past three months,” said Pavel Molchanov, an analyst at Raymond James. Tanker companies are becoming more adept at moving crude between vessels at sea to keep exports flowing, while reducing exposure to Iranian attacks, he said. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Mike Johnson's Latino voter problem keeps getting worse
events.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) needs Latino voters to stick with Republicans as they did in 2024. But new polling shows they're drifting back toward Democrats at levels not seen in years. Why it matters: Latino voters souring on President Trump has been part of the mood music of the president's second term. Democrats hope this helps them replicate the landslide from Trump's first midterm in 2018. The big picture: Democrats have their widest lead of the year against Republicans, 57% to 31%, on the generic congressional ballot, according to new polling from Equis Research. In battleground districts, Democrats lead 62%–38% among likely Latino voters in two-way races, ahead of the party's 2022 level of 57%. That's well above the 49% of Latinos who voted Democratic in 2024, but below the 67% who backed Democrats in 2018, according to Equis , a leading authority on Latino voting behavior. Zoom in: Republicans were convinced that Trump's undeniable gains in 2024 represented the beginnings of a real realignment, but poll after poll this year has indicated that Latino voters haven't found a permanent home in the GOP. In Florida, GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has addressed Trump directly in a campaign ad about his immigration crackdown. The Equis survey, conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2, provides fresh evidence of Trump's declining support among Latino voters. Trump's approval rating stands at just 30%, compared with 65% disapproval. That's a 35-point deficit — and a new low in Equis surveys. Between the lines: Economic concerns — and rising gas prices — are driving much of the dissatisfaction, particularly the cost of living. 76% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump's handling of the cost of living, which 52% identify as their top issue. 54% trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 33% who trust Republicans. That gives Democrats a 21-point advantage on the economy, up from just 7 points in February. The bottom line: Latino voters helped put Trump back in the White House. The Equis survey is the latest indication they could help Democrats take back Congress. Note: The Equis survey was conducted Sept. 23–Oct. 2 via phone and text-to-web with 1,800 registered voters who identify as Hispanic or Latino nationally. The sample was weighted to match the composition of registered voters modeled as Latino by state, gender, age, education, vote history, voter registration date, VCH score and 2024 vote recall.
