events.title: Social Security benefits will rise 3.6% in 2027, but that may not be enough to offset healthcare costs
events.summary: Increasing Social Security benefits annually helps millions of older Americans afford necessities. Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Monthly checks for the nearly 76 million Americans who receive Social Security benefits will rise by 3.6% in 2027. The increase, announced on Oct. 14, 2026, is the largest since the one that took effect in 2023. This cost-of-living adjustment , or COLA, is how the government tries to make sure that the value of Social Security benefits keeps up with inflation. Without it, the same payment would cover less of what recipients are spending on medical care, housing, groceries, clothing and other necessities. I am a finance professor , and one of the topics I research is how inflation affects retirees’ investment choices . And I believe the upcoming bump doesn’t capture the inflation challenges that many people who receive Social Security benefits face. The percentage increase in Social Security benefits depends in part on the annual inflation rate as of September 2026. It stood at 3.7% that month , as the Bureau of Labor Statistics, a government agency, also announced on Oct. 14. But the size of the increase is only part of the issue. The index used to set the COLA reflects what working people buy, not retirees, and that is a mismatch at the heart of a long-running debate over how the adjustment should be measured. Calculating the COLA The government has annually increased Social Security benefits to keep up with inflation since 1975. Congress previously had to pass a law each time it increased benefits. As a result, years could pass without an adjustment, despite climbing prices. The metric that the government uses is its consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers , known as the CPI-W. The Bureau of Labor Statistics tracks changes in the prices of goods and services that working households typically buy to calculate this index. The Social Security Administration then compares the average CPI-W reading for July, August and September with the average for those same months in the prior year to set the COLA adjustment, which kicks in the following January. If the economy contracts and prices fall, however, benefits stay the same . That happened in 2009, 2010 and 2015. Spending much of the bump on premiums One big problem with this calculation is that it understates healthcare inflation. Out-of-pocket health costs, including Medicare premiums, deductibles and copayments for medical care and prescription drugs, typically consume nearly 30% of Social Security benefits, according to research from the nonpartisan Center for Retirement Research at Boston College . For example, the government deducts Medicare Part B premiums directly from many retirees’ Social Security checks. The standard monthly Part B premium rose by US$17.90 in 2026, from $185 to $202.90. That increase alone consumed roughly one-third of the average $56 monthly gain in benefits from the 2026 COLA. More broadly, this big jump in healthcare costs for people covered by Medicare, as most Americans getting Social Security benefits are , helps explain why there is a long-running debate over how the program measures inflation. Finding other options Critics of the system the government uses to adjust benefits for inflation, including the Senior Citizens League and the National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare , say the CPI-W reflects the spending habits of working people, who shell out less on medical care than retirees. Retirees also tend to spend less on clothing, education and transportation than people with jobs. There are other ways the government measures inflation, including the consumer price index for Americans 62 and older , known as the CPI-E, that could be more accurate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics began to calculate this experimental index in the 1980s, but the Social Security Administration has not used it to set benefits yet despite some efforts in Congress to make the switch. The National Committee to Preserve Social Security and Medicare has researched how much more older people spend on medical care. People 65 and older spend more than twice as much as younger Americans on out-of-pocket health and medical costs, the group estimates. Those 75 and older spend nearly three times as much, the committee estimated after reviewing data from 1982 through 2014. It argues that a CPI-E weighted more toward medical care, housing and recreation would yield slightly larger cost-of-living adjustments than the CPI-W. But an index tied to how older people generally spend their money does not always lead to a bigger cost-of-living adjustment. The CPI-E has increased less than CPI-W in some years . What’s more, the CPI-E was not designed to set benefits and would need a larger survey sample before it could be used for that purpose. This article was originally published on Oct. 13, 2026. It has been updated with the latest cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security benefits. Pankaj Agrrawal does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: Inside Trump, Netanyahu's dilemma: Strike Iran before elections or wait
events.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Trump last week discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two U.S. officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. Netanyahu said during the call that he was concerned about Israeli intelligence indicating Iran was taking troubling steps to reconstitute its nuclear program, according to the Israeli official. The Israeli leader's call with Trump about the possible attack took place before Trump said he would not strike Iran ahead of the midterms. Why it matters: Resuming major combat operations in Iran would inject a volatile new issue into the Oct. 27 Israeli elections and the U.S. midterms a week later. But the Israeli and U.S. militaries are still on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind, sources said. " Bibi seems to want to go in again. He has talked to the president about it a couple times, and the president has said, 'Well, you know, Bibi, go ahead and get ready.' But there's really no commitment. 'Go ahead and get ready' is maybe now, maybe later, maybe never," a U.S. official said. A White House official said it's "false" that Trump and Netanyahu discussed resuming the war. "The President has said that we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," the person said. Netanyahu's office said that "the prime minister maintains regular contact with President Trump and senior U.S. administration officials and does not comment on the content of their conversations." Driving the news: Netanyahu has had several calls with Trump over the last two weeks about returning to major combat operations in Iran. According to the sources, Netanyahu and Trump spoke about a potential joint U.S.-Israeli operation that would hit military and nuclear targets. Netanyahu expressed concern about steps Israel believes Iran is taking to reconstitute all of the various parts of its nuclear program. Israel is especially concerned about Iran potentially operating Pickaxe Mountain as a uranium enrichment site. Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David on Oct. 2 to discuss next steps in the war and the possibility of resuming strikes. Behind the scenes: An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant. A U.S. official said Trump has been going back and forth on the issue. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the leadership of U.S. Central Command are the strongest backers of resuming strikes in Iran, a source familiar with the discussions said. But most of Trump's advisers favor keeping up economic sanctions and other forms of pressure for now. "They claim this economic choking is working better and better. Let's keep it up," the second U.S. official said. Between the lines: Renewed strikes would carry major political implications for both leaders. Resuming the war could dramatically affect the Israeli elections, since Iran would likely fire hundreds of ballistic missiles at the country in retaliation. Israel Defense Forces Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir spoke last week with Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine and discussed the possibility of resuming full-scale fighting against Iran within the next three weeks, according to a source briefed on the call. Zamir said that restarting the war in that timeframe could cause the Israeli elections to be postponed, given that Iran would probably retaliate, the sources said. Caine's spokesman, Joe Holstead, declined to comment. It's a big dilemma for Zamir because a strike ahead of the elections could be seen as a political ploy by Netanyahu that would erode public trust in the military, which is largely viewed as apolitical. The intrigue: The White House is aware of Netanyahu's domestic political considerations. "Bibi's got an election before the midterms. He believes his strength is being a wartime prime minister," one of the U.S. officials said. In meetings with his security and intelligence chiefs in recent days, Netanyahu claimed it was Trump, not him, who initiated the discussion about possibly hitting Iran before the elections, an Israeli official said. According to this account, Trump asked Netanyahu if Israel would join. Resuming the war before the U.S. election could backfire on Trump by reminding voters of the unpopular conflict and potentially sending gas prices higher. The big picture: Qatari mediators are still waiting for Iran to respond to the latest U.S. counterproposal to end the war, which includes demands for nuclear concessions. "The negotiations are not really dead, but they're not really alive. We're just here, piling on the pressure and there's a belief that smarter heads will prevail over there," a U.S. official said. "The Iranians thought this president would back down because of the pressure and the midterms. He has shown them the error of their ways," the official added. Trump repeated a familiar refrain Tuesday, telling reporters that "Iran is a failed country" and "we will make a decision on Iran very soon."

After waiting a year for a battery system that never showed up, Bob Emery's frustration boiled over. He says the installer, Lux Solar, "can't be trusted". Mr Emery paid a $1,000 deposit last October for a 48kwh system which he hoped would slash his power bills at his Perth home. After lengthy delays, he unsuccessfully requested a refund. The retired electrician also pursued his case with a consumer protection body and industry groups without resolution. He joins a growing number of customers raising concerns about the conduct of some companies selling and installing batteries under the federal government's Cheaper Home Batteries Program. The program has sparked unprecedented demand, with more than 530,000 batteries installed since July 2025. Over four years, the scheme has covered estimated costs of more than $7.2 billion. There has also been a spike in complaints to federal and state watchdogs with the NSW energy and water ombudsman saying complaints in that jurisdiction had doubled since last year. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) has several investigations underway and South Australia has announced a crackdown on "dodgy solar companies". Queensland's Office of Fair Trading confirmed Lux Solar is under investigation. It is the second solar company in as many months being probed for allegedly charging customers for deposits to install battery systems under the federal scheme that were never delivered. Bob Emery is still waiting for his solar battery. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) In June, Lux Solar was kicked out of the voluntary industry-run consumer protection scheme, the New Energy Tech Consumer Code (NETCC) for "major failures," including continuing to take payments without showing it could deliver the systems. The company has continued to advertise itself as an "approved seller" on its website, despite the Clean Energy Council requesting that wording be removed. Consumer advocate and CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre, Erin Turner, has called for the ad to be investigated. "That's really potentially misleading and I hope a regulator looks at it because that's a part of the consumer law where we can see really significant court actions with fines of up to $100 million," Ms Turner said. 'I don't have any trust in anyone installing it' In November 2025, Mr Emery was told the installation of his battery system was two to four weeks away. Two months later there was still no progress, so he emailed the salesman and asked for a refund. Bob Emery has waited over a year for his solar battery from Lux Solar. ( ABC News: Dominic Briggs ) Again, he was told the "install team" would make contact within a week or two. Mr Emery grew alarmed when the salesman stopped answering his calls and voice messages with Lux Solar weren't returned. Lux Solar is based in Western Australia but also operates in Queensland and New South Wales. Mr Emery made a complaint to Consumer Protection WA but the watchdog said it was up to him to take the matter to court. "The government bodies need to lift their game," he said. "It's put me off the whole (federal battery) program, I don't have any trust in anyone installing it," he said. Lux Solar told customer Justin Albin that installer issues were the reason for delays getting his solar battery. ( ABC News: Brigham Edgar ) His frustration is shared by Brisbane man Justin Albin and his Queensland work colleague who both waited about a year after paying deposits to Lux Solar last October. In January, a salesman told Mr Albin there had been "some installer issues" but he would get his system as promised. He received an email which said Lux Solar had more installation teams "ramping back up" and confirmation would come soon. He sent a legal letter demanding Lux Solar install the system or he would start court proceedings. Justin Albin has waited about a year after paying a deposit last October. events.title: Hegseth wants a livestream execution. Here's how firing squads work
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plans to livestream the December execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan by using a firing squad, one of the rarest forms of capital punishment in the United States. Why it matters: The planned livestream would mark the first public U.S. execution in roughly 90 years, but it has already drawn scrutiny , with President Trump expressing doubt it'll happen. Catch up quick: Hegseth said Oct. 8 that Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 shooting , will be executed in December, and the execution will be livestreamed. Trump has expressed apparent uneasiness despite giving his initial endorsement , Axios' Marc Caputo reported. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) expressed some concerns, too, while Vice President Vance said he wouldn't watch if it were aired. Zoom out: Execution by firing squad is rare, with only six since capital punishment resumed in 1977, per the Death Penalty Information Center. . The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945, when it executed Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion in France, per NPR . The military's last execution was in 1961, when it hanged John A. Bennett . How a firing squad works State of play: The Pentagon hasn't disclosed its firing squad procedures for Hasan's execution and didn't respond to Axios' request for comment Tuesday. Past executions offer a glimpse of what the method typically involves. How it works: The procedure typically begins with a prisoner strapped to a chair placed before a wall and surrounded by sandbags to absorb blood. A medical professional will typically mark a target over the prisoner's heart, while a black hood covers the prisoner's head. The shooters fire simultaneously, aiming at the heart, from a set distance away from the prisoner. If shooters miss the heart, the prisoner can still die from blood loss. Zoom in: States have different approaches to the firing squad method. For example, Utah uses five shooters, one of whom has a blank round, while South Carolina has three shooters, all with live ammunition. Hasan uses a wheelchair, potentially complicating how the execution would be carried out at Fort Hood. Yes, but: Firing squads don't always work as intended. Last year, prisoner Mikal Mahdi was executed in South Carolina by firing squad. An autopsy later found that only two bullets struck him and missed his heart. Where firing squad is legal The method is legal in Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah, according to the DPIC . It is the main execution method in Idaho as of this past summer. The only authorized method for capital punishment in Texas is lethal injection. Yes, but: State laws don't govern military executions. Data: Death Penalty Information Center ; Note: New Hampshire abolished the death penalty but retains one prisoner on death row; Map: Erin Davis/Axios What we know about the execution livestream Few specifics are known about the livestream execution, where it would streamed, or how people would watch it. It will happen on Thursday, Dec. 3, at 1pm CT, in Fort Hood. It's unclear if the execution would stream on social media or a website. TikTok and Kick said the event would violate their policies. What we're watching: The Army. Army Regulation 190-55 assigns the Army responsibility to choose the method, date and location of the execution.

events.title: What it takes to trust AI with real-world fixes
events.summary: Copilot to autopilot: Why no single safeguard is enough We designed a layered model that lets an AI agent resolve production network incidents on its own within defined identity, authorization, tooling, and human-approval boundaries. It’s 2:00 am. A pager goes off. A link somewhere in a datacenter has started flapping, a handful of alarms have correlated into one incident, and the on-call engineer is now doing what on-call engineers have always done: opening five tabs, one per system, and reconstructing what happened from fragments. We built an AI agent to do that reconstruction. It works. It pulls the device state, reads the telemetry, correlates the recent changes, classifies the failure, and writes a clean summary into the incident before the human has finished logging in. It also knows the fix. And that is where the demo stops being a demo. Because the agent “knows the fix,” the question is whether the system should allow it to shut a BGP session on a device that’s carrying live customer traffic. A “read” is something you can double-check. A “write” is an action that already happened. The moment an agent can change production, every property you were relaxed about at the read stage becomes a potential source of customer impact and risk. This post is about what we learned building an agent that’s trusted to take that action, as well as the uncomfortable conclusion we kept arriving at: There is no single thing you can build that makes an agent safe to run in production. Not a smarter model, not a stricter prompt, not a clever guardrail. Safe autonomy requires a stack. Ask 10 builders for a definition, and you’ll get 10 answers—and most of them are really examples (“You know, like a coding agent”) rather than definitions. That’s fine; we’re still in the relatively early days of agentic AI. But the fuzziness hides what matters here. An agent is not the model. The model is the brilliant, non-deterministic part in the middle. The agent is the deterministic software wrapped around it—the part that decides what the model is asked, what it may do with the answer, which tools it can reach, and what happens when it is wrong. The model supplies intelligence. The agent supplies judgment about how far to trust that intelligence and what to let it touch. Seen that way, the interesting engineering in an agentic system is usually the wrapper. And the whole safety question reframes with that distinction: Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it. Concretely, the harness we wrap around the model during execution is a mostly-deterministic workflow with a few narrow, schema-checked model steps inside it. It is what turns “the model worked something out once” into “these steps run the same way every time.” You don’t need its full mechanics yet—that’s another layer. For now, just hold the picture: a deterministic workflow with the model kept on a short leash inside it. Harness, agent, orchestrator, playbook, call it what you like. The load-bearing idea is the same: deterministic software putting a non-deterministic model to work, on purpose, within limits. The “holy grail” of agentic development is an agent that can investigate a problem, work out a fix, and carry it out without a human directing every step. But getting there in production means building safety into each step. More autonomy should not mean fewer controls. Imagine giving that agent a service account with broad access, a shell that can run anything, and a stern system prompt listing everything it must never do. It might have everything it needs to fix the problem. But what actually prevents it from taking an action it shouldn’t take? A broadly privileged service account can give the agent more access than the person who invoked it. An unrestricted shell can put anything that account and machine can reach within the impact radius. A system prompt helps guide behavior, but it can’t enforce permissions. The model can misinterpret an instruction or be influenced by malicious text in a log or tool response. Production safety can’t depend on instructions to the model alone. The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence. Modern models are frighteningly good at figuring out the fix. The real question is: “What is this thing allowed to do, under whose identity, through what interface, and with whose sign off?” It’s boring, it’s deterministic, and it’s the whole game. The mental model: Four boundaries, layered Once we started stacking boundaries, the architecture fell into four layers. Each answers a different question. None of them are sufficient alone, and that’s the point. Read bottom to top, it’s defense in depth across identity, tool, mutation, and time. Read as a sentence: The agent acts only as the human who summoned it (identity), reaches production only through a controlled interface (tool), can read freely but must pause before it changes anything (mutation), and gets less reliant on live reasoning the more it runs (time). Two of these are security controls in the literal sense: identity and tool access are where an attacker or a hallucination does its damage, so that’s where the hardest walls go. Layer 1: The agent never has more access than you The agent doesn’t get its own powerful account. It acts on behalf of the human who invoked it, bounded by that person’s real permissions. Where a service identity is unavoidable, it gets the narrower of the two. Identity is compound: the human plus the agent, and the stricter one wins. Access policies are owned by the teams that own each tool, defined per tool, and changed through a normal pull request (PR) with the tool team as a required reviewer. Merging a PR grants access; reverting it revokes access. Layer 2: One tool interface, not a bare shell The agent never gets a bare shell. Every capability it has sits behind a single typed tool interface, each tool is individually authorized, and each call is structured and logged. Note the careful wording: The enemy is not the command line; it is the unbounded one. A raw shell cannot be governed, because you cannot put a permission boundary, a schema, or a clean audit trail around bash. But a command line invoked as one narrow, declared tool, behind the interface, is fine. This is why the framing of “MCP vs. CLI” is a false dichotomy. You want both, chosen by trust level. Put everything behind the tool interface, then pick the implementation per call: a plain function or a sandboxed CLI for low-risk local work inside the trust boundary, and MCP for anything that crosses it, because MCP gives you least privilege, credential isolation, structured audit, human approval hooks, and rate limiting for free. You can secure a CLI, too, but only by paying for per-user sandboxes with tightly limited access, and even then, you can’t match per-tool granularity. Layer 3: Read freely, pause before you write Diagnostics run on their own.

events.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
events.summary: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House directed Axios to the president's remarks to reporters Tuesday. He said described the agreement as a "diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices. And when you knock out diesel refineries, that's not a great thing, but they're not releasing that to us. They're releasing it to the entire world." Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting that they halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. events.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
events.summary: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. events.title: US home sales rose in September, but slowed from a year earlier
events.summary: Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes rose in September from the previous month, but slowed compared to a year ago, the latest sign the housing market remains stalled as rising mortgage rates and home prices discourage prospective homebuyers. Existing home sales rose 1.5% last month from August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million units, the National Association of Realtors said Tuesday. One of the factors in the monthly increase is that sales in August were revised lower. Sales fell 2.2% compared with September last year. The latest sales tally is slightly above the 3.98 million pace economists were expecting, according to FactSet. Home sales have been mostly hovering close to a 4-million annual pace going back to 2023, far short of the historic norm that is closer to 5.2-million. September is the second month in a row that the annual sales pace has remained below 4 million. Home prices continued to rise nationally last month. The U.S. median sales price increased 1.3% in September from a year earlier to $417,500, an all-time high for the month of September based on data going back to 1999, NAR said. Home prices have risen on an annual basis for 39 months in a row. “This is a very tough market out there, especially with mortgage rates rising,” said Lawrence Yun, NAR’s chief economist. The U.S. housing market has been in a slump since 2022, when mortgage rates began to climb from pandemic-era lows. Sales of previously occupied U.S. homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. This year, sales have been in a rut in large part due to rising borrowing costs, as mortgage rates have marched higher in the months since the war between the U.S. and Iran started in late February. Expectations of higher inflation amid surging oil prices have pushed up the long-term bond yields that lenders use as a guide to pricing home loans, driving mortgage rates higher. The average rate on the benchmark 30-year mortgage hit 7.4% last week , its highest level in nearly three years. It briefly dipped below 6% before the war started. Many of the homes purchased last month likely went under contract in August and July, when the average rate on a 30-year mortgage ranged from 6.43% to 6.69%, according to Freddie Mac. Mortgage rates are not likely to drop meaningfully any time soon, given the ongoing uncertainty over oil prices, geopolitical tensions, the exploding U.S. government debt and other factors that have been driving rates on home loans higher, Yun said. Greta Gerwig's 'Narnia: The Magician's Nephew' film adaptation gets trailer Ukraine received no intelligence from partners on incoming missile strike on Kyiv Apple's new HomeView smart display to cost $299 Homebuyers should consider mortgage rates at 7%, or slightly above 7%, “the new normal,” he said. The sharp rise in mortgage rates, which can add hundreds of dollars a month in costs for borrowers, has led many would-be home shoppers to put their home shopping plans on hold. However, those who can afford to buy at current rates, or pay all cash, have a much wider selection of homes to choose from than they've had in years as properties sit on the market longer. Although home inventory levels remain below historical norms, there were 1.6 million unsold homes at the end of last month — the highest level of unsold inventory on the market since November 2019, NAR said. All told, unsold home inventory rose 1.9% last month from August and climbed 4.6% from September last year, NAR said. September’s month-end inventory translates to a 4.8-months’ supply at the current sales pace. Traditionally, a 4- to 6-month supply is considered a balanced market between buyers and sellers. The more balanced market gives home shoppers potentially more leverage in negotiating better terms with sellers, especially if a property has not fetched offers in weeks or months. Consider, in September, the national median home listing price fell 1.2% from a year earlier to $419,250 as about 21% of listings had their initial price lowered, according to Realtor.com. “The market is clearly tilting in favor of buyers able to negotiate for better prices,” Yun said. events.title: CVS agrees to pay $315 million to settle case over opioid prescriptions
events.summary: CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids WASHINGTON -- CVS Pharmacy Inc. and various subsidiaries have agreed to pay $315 million to resolve a Justice Department case alleging it unlawfully dispensed medically unnecessary prescriptions of highly addictive opioids, officials said Tuesday. The settlement resolves a lawsuit brought in 2024 that accused the healthcare giant of prescribing massive amounts of opioids and other controlled substances “to fuel its own profits at the expense of public health and safety.” It’s the latest effort by the federal government to hold accountable companies that officials have alleged helped fuel the U.S. addiction and overdose crisis. “Today’s settlement is a significant milestone in the Justice Department’s efforts to combat the opioid epidemic by cracking down on pharmacies who unlawfully fulfill prescriptions for controlled substances," Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said in an emailed statement. CVS said in a statement that its pharmacists were trained “in the safe and appropriate use of all medications” and that it had implemented “best-in-class” programs to help them “make the best decisions on behalf of patients.” The company said it strongly disagreed with the claims made in the lawsuit and that the settlement admits no wrongdoing. The company said in 2024 that pharmacists were being held to “vague, undefined, and ever-changing standards of practice” when it comes to filling prescription opioids. The lawsuit filed under President Joe Biden's administration accused CVS of violating the Controlled Substances Act by filling illegitimate prescriptions for high doses of potent opioids that “fed dependence and addiction.” The Justice Department alleged it dispensed large quantities of opioids based on prescriptions from known “pill mills," or providers that hand out prescriptions for drugs without a legitimate medical purpose. The prescriptions were often billed to and reimbursed by Medicaid and other federal healthcare programs, the lawsuit says. Under the settlement, CVS must also "implement additional safeguards to ensure that prescriptions for opioids and other controlled substances are dispensed only when medically appropriate,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate, who leads the Justice Department’s Civil Division, said in a statement. Over the last decade, drugmakers, wholesalers, pharmacies and other companies have agreed to settlements with governments in the U.S. totaling over $50 billion. Most of the money is intended to go to address the crisis, which has been linked to more than 100,000 deaths in the U.S. some years, though the numbers have fallen sharply recently. Most of the settlements -- and dollars -- have been with state and local governments, but the U.S. has reached several deals, including in the last two years with the pharmacies Walgreens and Walmart. events.title: Cyberattack targeting refrigeration systems hits 700 supermarkets
events.summary: Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France PARIS -- Cyberattacks have disrupted European supermarket chains, causing refrigeration systems to overheat at hundreds of stores in France and forcing a major grocer to shut down websites serving customers in Europe and the United States. French Finance Minister Roland Lescure told Parliament on Tuesday that about 700 of the country’s 10,000 supermarkets were affected. He said there was no risk to France’s food supplies but acknowledged that the attack “touches the heart of our food security.” ″It was a wake-up call for everyone,” he said. The Paris prosecutor’s office said Tuesday that its cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack, including the extent of damage caused by spoiled food and possible fires. Dominique Schelcher, CEO of French grocery chain Cooperative U, said 80 of the company’s 2,000 stores were affected. Most managed to prevent disruptions to refrigeration, but some had to discard food, he said in a post on X. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products is an attack on the French food supply chain. It is unprecedented, extremely serious, and unacceptable,” Schelcher said. Danish technology company Danfoss, which supplied the refrigeration management software, said Monday that most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates. “Danfoss has long advised customers to keep supported systems updated with the latest firmware, as well as to operate behind a firewall,” the company said. events.title: UK's Burnham weighs approval for oil and gas drilling in the North Sea
events.summary: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham faces a crucial decision on whether to allow oil and gas drilling in the North Sea LONDON -- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing a key test of his environmental policies as he decides on whether oil and gas companies should be allowed to drill in the North Sea. Burnham's government has been under heavy pressure from climate campaigners and businesses over whether to approve two oil and gas fields in waters north of Scotland, including one said to be the U.K.'s largest untapped oil resource. Environmental groups have urged Burnham to refuse permission for the projects, known as Rosebank and Jackdaw, saying they would accelerate climate change at a time when the U.K., like the rest of Europe, faces record extreme heat linked to human actions including burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. But opposition politicians, the oil and gas industry and U.S. President Donald Trump have piled pressure on Burnham to give the green light, arguing it would protect jobs, cut household bills and boost Britain’s energy security. British officials have been expected to make a decision since August, when public consultations on the two projects closed. Rosebank is an oil field that also will produce gas. Located 80 miles (130 kilometers) north of Scotland's Shetland Islands, it is estimated to be the largest undeveloped oil and gas field in the U.K., reportedly with capacity to produce 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil within about 25 years. Jackdaw is a gas field 150 miles east of Aberdeen on Scotland's northeast coast. Production there was expected to last under a decade. The Shell Group, one of the project's co-developers, predicts the field can produce around 6.5% of the U.K.’s gas production at its peak. The opposition Conservative Party, which has pushed for the developments to go ahead, said the Jackdaw field could start heating 1.4 million homes in the U.K. this winter if approved. The former Conservative government previously approved production at both sites, which were scheduled to start operations later this year. But a court in Edinburgh ruled last year that the approvals were unlawful, after considering a legal challenge from Greenpeace and another nonprofit. “The public interest in authorities acting lawfully and the private interest of members of the public in climate change outweigh the private interest of the developers,” judge Andrew Stewart ruled at the time. Critics have argued that the oil and gas reserves in Britain's North Sea holdings are small and would make little difference to energy bills because prices are decided by international markets. They contend that new developments would increase carbon emissions while failing to contribute to Britain's energy security. Analysts at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a London-based nonprofit, estimated that more than 90% of the oil and gas likely to be produced from the North Sea has already been extracted. “We’ve just had record-breaking heat waves this summer, wildfires, half of the country’s still in drought. We’re facing potential crop failures and food shortages this winter from a super El Niño ,” said Victoria Smith, a Fossil Free London activist protesting on Tuesday. Almost 600 climate and health experts wrote a joint letter to the government last month arguing that approving the projects would breach the U.K.'s national and international climate commitments. Separately, critics also have raised concerns about Rosebank's links to Israeli company Delek Group, which activists say profited from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Green Party leader Zach Polanski is among critics who have asked how the U.K. can ensure revenue from any oil and gas production did not finance the settlements. Supporters of further drilling say it will not make a significant difference to emissions and is vital for protecting jobs. Some also argue that domestic production will result in less carbon emissions than importing oil and gas. The governing Labour Party is split on the issue. Some warned that going ahead will renege on the party's pledge in its 2024 manifesto not to issue new licenses for oil and gas exploration in the North Sea. Others disagree. “If we do not proceed with Jackdaw and Rosebank, investment will leave the UK, jobs will disappear and expertise will be lost,” lawmaker Graeme Downie said. The issue became more politicized after Trump waded in. The U.S. president, who criticized former Prime Minister Keir Starmer's energy policies, claimed in August that people in Aberdeen were “dancing in the streets” following reports that Burnham would approve new drilling.

events.title: White House pushes out Kimberly Guilfoyle after misconduct reports
events.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, announced her resignation Tuesday, shortly after the White House asked her to step down and following reports alleging misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The exit of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday during her first press briefing that Guilfoyle was asked to resign. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Driving the news: "My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote in a post on X on Tuesday. "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again." "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America." Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president. Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines. Zoom in: In her statement, Guilfoyle once again said that the allegations against her are "false." "I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service." Zoom out: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador." A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true. Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025. What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun. Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath. events.title: Europe's alternative to Trump's China trade war
events.summary: Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0 , betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach. Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb. Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe. The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December. The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters . Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.) Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs. The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point." "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said. What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade official, tells Axios. Washington is pushing trading partners to join forces against China's industrial overcapacity. "It's really hard for any one country to make progress on that if you don't have allies on your side," Mullaney says. By the numbers: Chinese automakers ramped up hybrid shipments to Europe after the EU imposed steep tariffs on fully electric vehicles in 2024. New data released yesterday shows that China's global passenger vehicle exports surged 64% in September, to 919,000, even as domestic sales fell 27%. What to watch: Europe's deal could shift pressure to other industries — or perhaps even other nations — without addressing the underlying imbalances driving China's export boom. Economist Michael Pettis argued over the weekend that the agreement would do little for European manufacturing overall. "EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers," he wrote on X . The bottom line: Europe's deal may provide breathing room for its automakers. But China's industrial might — and the pressure it is inflicting on manufacturers around the world — is not going away.

events.title: Bumble bought for $1.3bn in 'bet on the future of humanity'
events.summary: Dating app Bumble has been bought for $1.3bn (£980m) in what the new owners called "a bet on the future of humanity". Investment firm Ithaca Holdings is taking over the loss-making firm and it directors, Ravi Gupta and John Hegeman, will become co-chief executives of the company which once differentiated itself by having a "women-first" chat rule. Bumble ditched the rule in August this year. Whitney Wolfe Herd, Bumble's founder and current chief executive, said she would remain "actively involved" with the business she set up 12 years ago. While it is unclear what Wolfe Herd's role at the dating app will be, she said she will work closely with the new owners. Gupta and Hegeman said they wanted to use technology to "renew and accelerate businesses...in a world transformed by AI". They said: "Technology should work in service of our deepest source of fulfillment, human connection and this investment is a bet on the future of humanity." This contrasts with a recent debate over the safety of AI, with some experts claiming the speed of its development threatens the future of humanity . Bumble's share price has soared as news of the deal began to emerge. The jump lifted its company valuation to over $580m but that is still far below a peak of more than $14bn it reached after it floated the business on the Nasdaq stock index in 2021 . Since becoming a public company, it has made an annual pre-tax profit only once, in 2023. In the following two years, it reported steep losses, though during that period Bumble had been working to incorporate new technology, including AI, into its app. Its chief executive in 2024, Lidiane Jones, told the BBC she believed AI had "exciting potential" in dating apps related to safety, and Bumble had been looking at research that found Gen Z and milliennials were interested in AI assistance with creating profiles. This year, the dating app unveiled several new AI features, including profile guidance to help people create dating profiles. Bumble was launched in 2014 by Wolfe Herd who built the brand around a distinctive feature that only allowed women to initiate conversations with matches. It recently abandoned that rule , prompting debate among users over whether the app had lost what set it apart from rivals. "Today, our community is asking for more flexibility, less pressure, and more opportunities to create real, meaningful connections and that is what this new experience provides," Wolfe Herd said in August. Dating apps like Bumble have come under pressure in recent years as some younger users have grown disillusioned with browsing for dates. Bumble said in 2025 that it would cut almost a third of its workforce as the industry grappled with what Wolfe Herd described as an "inflection point" in online dating. Investments in other dating companies have also soured as apps have struggled to convince users to pay for their services. Match Group - which owns apps including Tinder, OkCupid and Hinge - has also seen its shares fall sharply from their peak in 2021. According to a report by media watchdog Ofcom in 2025, adults in the UK were spending less time on dating apps compared to three years earlier. Some single people are instead turning to board game get-togethers , book clubs and other group activities in the hope of finding a partner. events.title: Kroger to lay off 3K corporate employees over 3 years as it leans into AI
events.summary: Grocery store chain Kroger says it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations. “Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.” Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.” Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer. Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO . Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities. Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells. Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed. A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value. Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee. Kroger shares fell 1.6% in morning trading Tuesday, to $61.66. Time: 10am – 11.30am | Location: Bank of England, 20 Moorgate, London, EC2R 6DA The Chair thanked members for attending and confirmed that the Minutes of the Money Markets Committee (MMC) June 2026 meeting had been published on the Bank’s website. footnote [1] The Chair updated on recent usage of the Bank’s market-wide repo facilities. Members were reminded that use of the Bank’s facilities, including against a broad range of eligible collateral, was consistent with the intended transition to a repo-led operating framework. The Chair provided a brief update on the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC’s) September decision on Quantitative Tightening footnote [2] , including the exchange of letters between the Governor and the Chancellor regarding QT and the APF. footnote [3] The Chair also noted the related announcements made by the Bank and HM Treasury that came out at the same time. footnote [4] Item 2 – Discussion on market conditions Members noted that money markets continued to function smoothly and that funding conditions remained stable, even during recent increased bond market volatility. Liquidity was reported to be ample, with limited signs of stress. Members also reported stable cross-currency funding conditions despite recent geopolitical developments and broader market volatility, with quarter-end and year-end conditions expected to remain orderly. While some highlighted the potential for volatility in outright asset markets to transmit into funding conditions through reduced risk appetite or position unwinds, the overall assessment was that money market functioning remained robust. Some nevertheless noted emerging funding pressures further out the euro curve as Eurosystem liquidity continued to decline. Members also discussed developments in European Commercial Paper (ECP) markets, noting increased issuance activity and growing use of these funding channels. Members also discussed the Financial Policy Committee’s proposed changes to the leverage ratio framework footnote [5] . Members generally welcomed the direction of the proposals but considered that leverage requirements are just one of a number of constraints on their activity including stress-testing assumptions, investor expectations and risk-weighted capital requirements. As a result, members considered that it was difficult to predict the extent to which the proposals would lead to a material increase in leverage or balance-sheet deployment in UK money markets in the near-term. Some noted that greater releasability of constraints in stress could support increased use of gilts and reverse repo within buffers. Members noted increasing competition for retail and corporate deposits. While this had not materially affected funding plans, some observed that sustained competition for deposits could increase wholesale funding requirements and funding costs over time. Members agreed this would remain an area to monitor. From a market infrastructure perspective, strong trading activity across gilt and international markets was reported, with no material change in cleared repo conditions. Members also welcomed the predictability provided by the MPC and Bank's recent balance sheet announcements and noted that the Bank's liquidity facilities continued to support confidence in firms' ability to manage reserves and liquidity needs.

events.title: Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K: What to know about smart hub and updated console
events.summary: Apple has introduced HomeView, a device that the company says incorporates artificial intelligence-driven Siri and an easy-to-use interface to help people at home. A video posted to Apple 's website and social media accounts shows a busy family in the kitchen using the device to answer questions, communicate with others and set reminders. “Siri, ping me my keys,” a woman asks HomeView as she tries to leave her home. The HomePod speaker causes her keys to give off a beeping noise, presumably with the help of Apple 's AirTag. In the video and on the HomeView webpage, Apple says the product is only “available in English to start”. The company says HomeView will be available on November 13 with prices starting at $299. Two options will be available: a device that rests on surfaces and a version that mounts on a wall. Before Apple's HomeView announcement, Anshika Jain, principal analyst for the technology market analysis firm Counterpoint , said that such a device would help the US technology giant strengthen its consumer product offerings. “The upcoming display-based device could become a central interface for controlling smart home products, accessing content and services, and interacting with Apple’s AI capabilities, potentially giving Apple a stronger foothold in the smart home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. Apple also seems prepared to allow devices made by other companies to work with HomeView. “Designed in collaboration with Apple and select brands, Apple Home Collection accessories – including smart cameras, thermostats and a door lock – are simple to set up, easy to use, and private with data that’s encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home,” the company posted to its site. It added that the collection of devices would arrive at a later date. Mohit Agrawal, research director with Counterpoint, said that this aspect was intriguing. “Rather than buying its way in, as Amazon did with Ring and Google with Nest, Apple is partnering with LG and Schneider Electric,” he explained. “This lets it fill out the home quickly, from the front door to the thermostat, while keeping control of the experience through Siri and the Home app.” Apple seems to be positioning the forthcoming HomeView product as a device that is used passively in day-to-day life. “HomeView does the heavy lifting when you’re busy around the house,” a description reads. “And with a vibrant display and powerful acoustics, your music, videos and calls look and sound amazing … meet the new heart of your home.” According to technology news outlet, The Verge , HomeView will be initially available in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and India. HomePod mini 2 Also on Tuesday, Apple announced its HomePod mini speaker devices would be getting an upgrade. “Siri on HomePod mini 2 puts a powerful, AI assistant right at the centre of your home,” the company said. “Once set up with your iPhone or iPad , Siri draws on broad world knowledge and your personal context to help you find what you need and get more done every day.” The HomePod 2 will be available on October 30, with prices starting at $149. Apple touts improved sound, touch controls, a mesh design and a woven power cord among the HomePod's improvements. “With Apple Intelligence and a more capable Siri, the company is positioning HomePod as an entry point into an AI-powered home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said. “Still, shipment growth is likely to remain modest in low single digits YoY [year over year] as the market continues to face saturation and longer replacement cycles.” Apple TV Apple's TV console has gone several years without an update, but that changed on Tuesday with the unveiling of Apple TV 4K. The company says the updated console has an A19 processor that assists in delivering 4K video quality, and it will also have a Siri remote. Apple TV 4K will be available on November 13, with prices starting at $299. “Apple TV 4K delivers the ultimate cinematic experience, from shows and movies to games and workouts,” the company said. “With the new, more powerful Siri AI and built-in microphones, enjoying what you love is as easy as using your voice.”

events.title: Saudi attacks shake the confidence of foreign investors
events.summary: Oil prices ticked down on Tuesday as Saudi oil executives sought to reassure the market following a major attack on the capital’s airport. International energy bosses were largely absent from this week’s World Petroleum Council Energy Congress, held in Riyadh for the first time, after the Houthi attack. The CEOs of BP, Shell, and TotalEnergies, along with a host of international ministers, including US Energy Secretary Chris Wright, dropped out due to the strikes. That left a thinner-than-expected crowd, mostly made up of local executives, to hear the kingdom seek deeper international cooperation to secure energy supplies and trade routes. Saudi Arabia can build more pipelines and boost storage capacity, but “no one nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone,” Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said. His comments reflect the growing role of foreign investors in the region’s energy industry, already expanding even before the Iran war. Long relegated to minor roles, the Gulf energy companies increasingly see international energy firms and global investors as an integral part of their plans to lock in customers for their hydrocarbon exports, invest in their infrastructure, and bind other states into their security in a way that the old expectations of oil for security arrangements have failed to guarantee. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Trump’s Russian energy strategy could backfire
events.summary: Tim’s view The contradictory tangle of energy policy actions taken by US President Donald Trump toward Russia over the weekend risks repeating mistakes that he and his allies often slammed his predecessor for. On Friday, Trump announced the US would waive sanctions on Russian diesel exports until the spring and permit it to release 300,000 metric tons of diesel into the global market, before announcing an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv. The diesel deal was quickly condemned by a bipartisan group of senators , who argued that the volume was too small to make a difference — equal to less than a day of US consumption — and extended a “financial lifeline” to Russian President Vladimir Putin. This, they said, contradicted both a 2022 US ban on Russian energy imports and the spirit of the new sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to penalize countries like China and India for the very same kinds of purchases the president is now pursuing. The diesel relaxation, former State Department energy diplomat Geoff Pyatt told me, is “enough of a sweetheart deal to encourage [Russian Direct Investment Fund CEO Kirill] Dmitriev and Putin to keep fighting in hopes Trump will deliver Kyiv.” As for the “ceasefire,” Russia seems to have violated it almost instantly . A Ukrainian official told me on Monday that Kyiv was temporarily holding off on further long-range drone strikes against Russian refineries while it assessed Moscow’s behavior and was waiting for a chance, potentially later this week, to clarify details of Trump’s proposal with US officials. Axios reported the deal could apply only to refineries , which would make little sense for Ukraine to participate in given that it has only one barely-functional refinery. Kyiv is more worried about the power sector, which a recently leaked Russian military planning document makes clear is still directly in Moscow’s sights . Dangling a limited ceasefire deal that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy can’t accept sends the same message to the Kremlin as the diesel deal: Ukrainians are the problem in this war, and US resolve in support of Ukraine is barely paper-thin. The past few years have shown repeatedly that accommodating Putin pushes him away from the negotiating table, not toward it . Trump and his energy officials have criticized Biden often and loudly for authorizing, in 2022, a record release of oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which they framed as an irresponsible stab at tamping down US fuel prices ahead of an election at the expense of long-term American security interests. They also criticized Biden’s decision in 2021 to relax sanctions on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline in the interest of repairing relations with Moscow, which helped embolden Putin to undertake the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. With just three weeks until the midterms, Trump is clearly riled about diesel prices and the slow recovery of exports of refined products from the Persian Gulf. But it’s counterproductive to capitulate to Putin: In addition to the uncountable human toll, a longer war in Ukraine means more energy market distortion ahead. Notable A new poll found that even if Trump managed a political feat like ending the Iran war or bringing down gasoline prices by $1 ahead of November’s midterms , a majority of voters would not be more likely to vote Republican.

events.title: Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment and manage the home
events.summary: Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods TV & Home Entertainment Accessories Support Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home A person cooking in their kitchen looks at HomeView. A person sits at their kitchen table and reads a book next to HomeView. A user’s HomeView sits on their living room countertop. HomeView is shown in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray. A person touches the screen of HomeView and moves the hinge. The back of HomeView is shown, complete with ports and a color-matched charging cable. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence Siri AI pulls up information from a user’s Calendar app on HomeView. Siri AI is shown on a user’s HomeView and iPhone 18 Pro. Rich Entertainment Anywhere in the Home Connecting Users to What Matters Most HomeView shows a group of people on a FaceTime call. HomeView shows a recipe for butternut squash soup. HomeView shows a timer a user set for 15 minutes. Customers in Australia , Canada , India , New Zealand , the UK , and the U.S. can pre-order Apple HomeView in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray for $299 (U.S.), and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) in space gray and silver for $299 (U.S.), starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Customers in Singapore can pre-order starting Thursday, October 15, at 9 a.m. SGT. Both models will be available in these countries beginning Friday, November 13. Customers in South Africa will be able to pre-order Apple HomeView and Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) through Apple Authorized Resellers, with availability beginning Friday, November 13. Apple HomeView is not available for sale in the European Union, as Siri AI is currently unavailable in iOS in the EU. Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward. HomeView (Wall Mounted) will be available with a choice of three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home. Power Mount USB‑C Wall Connector, available starting at $59.95 (U.S.), and Power Mount AC Wired, available starting at $79.95 (U.S.), can be ordered starting today from apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app. Power Mount PoE Wired will be available starting in early 2027 for $129.95 (U.S.). Siri AI on HomeView is available in English in the U.S., Australia , Canada , India , New Zealand , Singapore , South Africa , and the UK. Canadian French-language support will be offered later via a free software update. Text of this article October 13, 2026 PRESS RELEASE Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home Apple HomeView is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI and built with privacy and security at its core CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today introduced Apple HomeView , designed to be central to the home and personal to everyone in it. With a stunning 7-inch Liquid Retina display, HomeView brings entertainment, connection, and smart home management together in one place, from playing music and making FaceTime calls to home monitoring and hands-free automations with voice control — all designed with privacy and security at the core. 1 HomeView recognizes users by their faces, adapting so they can access their personal content in Messages, FaceTime, Calendar, Reminders, and Find My. HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that’s profoundly more capable and conversational, with broad world knowledge that powers richer music discovery and onscreen awareness. When paired with an Apple Intelligence-enabled device, it can also draw on a user’s personal context, such as their Calendar, Messages, and relevant information across their apps, to provide more helpful, personalized responses. 2 Designed to fit in any space, HomeView can be placed on a tabletop as the center of the home or wall-mounted to fit in spaces like the entryway or hallway. Pre-orders start today, with availability beginning November 13. “Apple HomeView is designed to be shared by everyone in the home yet feel completely personal to each user,” said Greg Joswiak, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Marketing. “It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home. And it’s powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI at its core, drawing on personal context from your iPhone to help you find what you need and get more done, all while keeping everyone’s information private and secure.” Elegantly Designed for Any Space HomeView features a beautiful aluminum design with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display connected to a domed speaker base by a stainless steel hinge that provides a smooth tilt for comfortable viewing on tabletops of any height. The perfect addition to a kitchen counter, nightstand, or side table, HomeView comes in four beautiful colors — silver, starlight, rose pink, and space gray — each finished with a matching cable. The elegant design and Liquid Retina display seamlessly blend into any space while remaining clearly visible from across the room. It features adaptive display technologies, including True Tone, that react to changing light throughout the day. Automatic brightness adjusts from 500 nits — bright enough to stay vivid and easy to see even in a sunlit room — down to just 0.3 nits, making it ideal for the nightstand. The HomeView interface intelligently adjusts based on the user’s distance, showing simpler information that’s viewable from across the room and richer detail as they step closer. A separate wall-mounted HomeView model — available in space gray and silver — offers the same 7-inch Liquid Retina display, powerful set of features, and rich audio. It can be attached to a wall using three purpose-built mounts from Schneider Home, with options for self-installation or professional installation. A Personalized Experience for Each User in the Home HomeView recognizes up to six people and delivers a personalized experience for each one. Each user gets their own personalized Home Screen with apps and widgets. Personal content stays private from others, while shared photo albums and music can be easily enjoyed by everyone in a household, including guests. Featuring Siri AI, Powered by Apple Intelligence HomeView features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence and advanced Apple silicon. Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding and onscreen awareness. With broad world knowledge, anyone in the home can ask Siri about virtually any topic and get an answer.
