events.title: OPay readies $4B New York IPO
events.summary: The News OPay, the Lagos-based fintech firm backed by Softbank and Chinese billionaire Zhou Yahui, more than doubled its revenue in the first half of 2026 as lending overtook payments as its top source of income, according to a filing ahead of a planned New York listing likely set for next month. The company has applied to trade under the ticker OPAY, with a potential Nigerian secondary listing to follow. The filing lays out a business growing rapidly after jumping 137% to $467 million in revenue in the first half of 2026 while net income rocketed by over 300% to $91 million. OPay launched in Nigeria as a payments company in 2018 backed by Chinese investors and later funded by venture investors led by Softbank. OPay hadn’t disclosed an IPO price range or a listing date as Semafor was going to press but based on the normal sequence of filings and roadshows, investors will be expecting pricing to be revealed in mid-November. Previous reports have put the initial valuation estimates around $4 billion. The fintech firm also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. Know More A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise and presence to expand across Africa. Step Back OPay took off in 2019 in Nigeria with ambitions to be a super app that offered various features, including motorcycle taxi bookings, food deliveries, and quick loans. But it narrowed its focus to financial services in recent years and raised $570 million in venture funds between 2018 and 2021. A handful of African tech companies have successfully listed in the US, notably e-commerce platform Jumia and telecom towers provider IHS but have had mixed performances. An OPay listing in the US would be the first by a fintech company with a mostly Nigerian customer base.

events.title: Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon. [Read more]
events.summary: Today we are announcing our biggest bet yet on our own silicon. Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services. And we’re introducing Maia 300, which delivers 40% more tokens per watt compared to leading GPU-based systems. We are already deploying Maia 200 across the US, Europe, and Australia, delivering up to 1.7x more tokens per watt across experiences in Teams and Copilot. Our goal is to build on the full-stack efficiency gains we’ve already seen, while continuing to bring the latest innovations from across the ecosystem into our fleet. Read more: https://lnkd.in/g68XQtxE This is encouraging. If AI is going to become part of practically every product and workflow, the cost of running it has to come down significantly. More efficient hardware could open the door to use cases that simply aren't economical today. Spot on, Satya Nadella! Transitioning toward custom silicon and multi-gigawatt infrastructure deployments represents a fundamental milestone in redefining enterprise AI economics and operational scalability. Maximizing tokens per watt through proprietary hardware architecture is critical for mitigating latency and curbing the exponential energy demands of large-scale agentic AI. Integrating full-stack silicon efficiency directly into cloud services sets a new benchmark for sustainable enterprise IT. As hyperscalers aggressively pivot toward custom silicon to optimize inference economics, what core engineering or supply-chain challenge do you view as the primary bottleneck for scaling multi-gigawatt deployments over the next cycle? "Tokens per watt". What an absurd metric. As if there's a uniform, consistent definition of a token or a generic correlation to compute. Not. And such a metric would inherently reward verbosity. Utterly stupid. I'm assuming this is good news. Anyone else consider themselves "tech savvy" and dont understand much of what they just read? It seems great though! Good job Microsoft: more power is always good:) 40% more tokens per watt, but at what context length? The workloads you named, sustained multi-step agents, carry long contexts, and every agent's working memory grows with each step. At that point the binding constraint is memory, not compute, and the specs that lead this launch are memory specs. Tokens per watt measured on short contexts says little about tokens per watt once agent memory dominates. The bigger announcement may be co-design. With Maia as the primary engine, Copilot's models get shaped around Maia and each next Maia around Copilot's workloads. That's where the gain compounds, and it's very hard to copy from outside. It also splits the market: integrated model-plus-chip stacks on one side, open models on general-purpose GPUs on the other. As agents multiply token demand, that gap becomes the price difference between closed and open AI. Who gives open models what Maia gives Copilot? I’d love to be in the room for Microsoft’s next GPU pricing negotiation when NVIDIA knows Maia is already running Copilot workloads 😅 Having a credible alternative at that scale might be worth almost as much as the efficiency gains themselves. Incredible milestone, mr.Satya! As custom silicon scales to multi-gigawatt deployments with Maia 300, optimizing tokens-per-watt highlights a critical industry truth: physical thermal management at the hardware level is becoming just as vital as architectural efficiency. We’ve been tackling this exact frontier through advanced passive thermal architectures designed for high-density AI hardware. If you or your silicon team are ever open to a brief exchange on bypassing the thermal wall at scale, I'd love to share a few notes. Exciting times ahead for full-stack optimization!" The focus on tokens per watt is particularly interesting. As AI workloads continue to grow I think energy efficiency and infrastructure costs will become just as important as raw computing power. Im curious how Microsofts custom silicon strategy will reshape the economics of AI at scale while maintaining flexibility across different workloads. Werden die Effizienzgewinne von Maia zeitnah auch in günstigere PTU-Reservierungen für Enterprise-Kunden weitergegeben, oder bleibt die Hardware primär für Microsofts eigene SaaS-Dienste reserviert? Gerade bei fest gebuchten Kapazitäten entscheidet am Ende der Preis pro garantiertes Token über den tatsächlichen Nutzen im produktiven Betrieb. Tokens per watt is the number I watch from Manila, where available power decides where AI capacity can go. A 40% gain stretches the same megawatts further. In markets like ours, that makes it easier to run inference in-country, close to the users and their data, and every in-country deployment pulls demand into local data center space and domestic fiber. events.title: Ecobank agrees to join Chinese payment platform
events.summary: Ecobank agreed a partnership with China’s payment system to enable transaction settlements in the yuan currency. The Togo-based bank, which operates in 34 African countries — more than any other continental lender — will sign an agreement this month to join the China Interbank Payments System (CIPS). South Africa’s Standard Bank and the African Export Import Bank have taken the same step in the last year. The move follows increasing demand from businesses on the continent to transact and settle deals using China’s currency. An 18% rise in China-Africa trade last year — marked by a surge in the continent’s imports of Chinese solar power equipment — underscored the growing commercial relationship between both parties, highlighting the appeal of financial systems that make transactions easier to complete. China this year removed tariffs for imports from all African countries except Eswatini. Its move to increase bank integrations with its payments system furthers a push led by the BRICS bloc against the US dollar’s dominance in international trade. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel memorial prize in economics
events.summary: STOCKHOLM -- American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford won the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics Monday for their work on models that have helped governments and central banks manage economic shocks, such as energy crises and inflation. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners in Stockholm, noting that their work created the theoretical foundation to better understand how consumers decide whether to save or spend, insights that make it easier for policymakers worldwide to stabilize economies after fluctuations. “The laureates’ research has made it possible to manage major macroeconomic crises far more effectively than before,” the Nobel committee wrote. “It has been hugely beneficial during the pandemic and the energy crises of recent years." Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone from New York: “It’s a tremendous honor. It’s a surprise." For decades, governments responded to economic shocks by following the Depression-era prescriptions of the British economist John Maynard Keynes: Intervene in the economy by lowering taxes and hiking government spending, thereby encouraging consumers and businesses to spend and invest and help restart growth. “This is the Keynesian recipe and it worked well — until it didn’t,’’ said Timo Boppart of the Nobel economics committee. Policymakers had thought economic management involved simple trade-offs — unemployment, for instance, would stay low at a time of high inflation and rise when inflation fell. But the “ stagflation ’’ of the 1970s — when the world economy experienced simultaneous high inflation and high unemployment — proved the formula was simplistic. Some economists argued that government attempts to intervene in the economy were doomed to fail. But Hall and Woodford, in separate contributions, set about improving the Keynesian model to take into account how consumers and businesses actually make decisions about whether to invest and spend. “Economic outcomes are the result of millions of decisions made at the microlevel by households and businesses,’’ the Nobel committee wrote. “Using models based upon this approach, rather than simply studying the economy from a macro perspective, like a bird’s eye view," Hall and Woodford’s research "generated a paradigm shift in the theory of stabilization policy.’’ Hall studied the way that consumer decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be. “If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes. In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80% of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth,’’ the committee wrote. “The prize is for research that pushes our understanding of macroeconomics from the bottom up, from families and firms making decisions over time, while looking ahead,” Ivan Werning, an economist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said in an email. Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Selma Blair released on bond after alleged Delta flight altercation Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’ Therefore, central banks such as the U.S. Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do.’’ Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing. During the phone call broadcast at a news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending.” The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896. Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine , physics , chemistry , literature and peace.

events.title: First Utility-Scale Enhanced Geothermal Plant Goes Live
events.summary: This article was originally published by Canary Media . The geothermal startup Fervo Energy is now selling power to the grid from its Cape Station project in Utah—marking the first time a utility-scale, next-generation geothermal facility has achieved such a feat worldwide. The Houston-based firm turned on an initial 33-megawatt unit late last week and has been testing and ramping up output since. On Thursday, Fervo will officially begin commercial operations, supplying carbon-free electricity to Shell Energy, a retail power provider in California. Cape Station, a $2 billion project that will eventually be 500 MW, is unique among the world’s commercial geothermal plants. While other facilities draw on naturally occurring hot water and steam, Fervo has engineered its own geothermal resource deep underground. The startup uses drilling techniques from the oil and gas industry to create reservoirs in hot, dry rocks that generate steam to produce electricity. “Traditional geothermal would have never been done in southern Utah,” sa ys Dawn Owens , Fervo’s senior vice president and head of development and commercial markets. With the first unit online, Fervo sa ys it is working to commission two more 33-MW power blocks by 1 Jan uary , 2027. The project’s remaining 400 MW—which is supported by a new agreement with Google —is under construction and slated to come online in 2028. Fervo’s Next-Generation Geothermal Journey Fervo already operates a 3.5-MW commercial pilot plant in Nevada, which went online in late 2023. Owens sa ys the pilot, called Project Red, was important for demonstrating the technology itself. But firing up Cape Station proves that Fervo’s approach can achieve utility scale and export power to wider markets. “This is massive for both Fervo and the geothermal industry at large,” she sa ys . Fervo , which went public in May, is leading the fast-growing movement to develop clean, always-on geothermal power to meet soaring demand from data centers and balance growing supplies of intermittent solar and wind energy. Next-generation geothermal firms have raised billions of dollars in private capital in recent years to develop and deploy technologies that can harness energy in harsh, deep environments. Drilling continues at Fervo Energy’s Cape Station geothermal plant in Beaver County, Utah, where the company plans to ramp up production to 500 MW. Fervo Energy Today, geothermal represents just 0.4 percent of total U.S. electricity generation every year. Expanding geothermal’s share of the mix will require not just building more projects like Cape Station but also tackling high upfront drilling costs and other economic and regulatory barriers —all while working to limit potential impacts on communities and the environment, experts say. “ Fervo’s first power achievement shows investors the size and scale of the opportunity to fuel many more such milestones across developers and sites in the future,” sa ys Mitchell Smith , who serves as grid lead for the Mountain West Geothermal Consortium. The bipartisan initiative is calling for increased public and private financing “ to help bring more projects online responsibly and at the speed of demand,” he added. Enhanced Geothermal Energy Gets Cheaper Fervo has declined to disclose the terms of its power purchase agreements for in-progress and future development, which together represent about 1,000 MW, or enough to power roughly 1 million U.S. homes every year. Phase 1 of Cape Station is set to deliver power at $7,000 per kilowatt, while Phase 2 should come at $5,500 per k ilowatt , the company previously told Canary Media. (By comparison, the average cost to build a natural gas–fired power plant was $2,157 per k ilowatt in 2025.) Along with slashing drilling costs, enhanced geothermal projects could improve their economics by delivering power when it’s most valuable to utilities, according to researchers . While geothermal plants traditionally provide around-the-clock, baseload power, next-generation facilities might operate flexibly during certain periods—like in the evening, when solar output declines—to reduce overall grid costs. Geothermal plants could also operate “ behind the meter” to directly power data centers so that the costs of adding new electricity capacity aren’t passed on to utility customers, Owens sa ys . “We’ve been saying all along that our technology makes geothermal more scalable and affordable in more places,” she sa ys . On Cape Station’s powering-up, she add s , “ That’s just something no next-generation geothermal company has ever been able to do before.”

events.title: Turmoil within Dolly Parton’s estate underscores the precariousness of family businesses after founders die
events.summary: Dolly Parton waves to her fans at Dollywood in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in March 2024. Amy Harris/Invision via AP Dolly Parton’s nephew Bryan Seaver announced the legendary singer’s death on Aug. 25, 2026, in a prerecorded video. Seaver, the son of one of Parton’s 11 siblings , had been her head of security for many years. But Seaver is currently embroiled in a messy dispute with She’s Alive LLC, the company Parton established to manage her business assets after her death . This unusually acrimonious fight highlights some of the business succession problems that can arise when the founder of a company dies but wants its other leaders to keep it going. Parton, a legendary American singer, actress, entrepreneur and philanthropist, left behind an estimated US$450 million estate . She’s Alive LLC terminated Seaver’s involvement with the business, and a court has issued a restraining order against him. Seaver is accused of engaging in “ an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats” against Parton’s estate . He denies the allegations. As professors who research and teach topics related to inheritance law, we are fascinated by the Parton case. It illustrates some of the pitfalls of planning for the transition of a privately held business after the founder’s death – a concern for celebrity and noncelebrity estates alike. Following Dolly Parton’s death, there has been turmoil in her management involving her nephew Bryan Seaver. Managing celebrity estates after death Celebrity estates, like Parton’s, are distinct because they often contain valuable intellectual property. This includes copyrights, which protect creative works , such as songs and recordings, including Parton’s catalog of hits. Another valuable asset in these estates are publicity rights , which protect the use of the celebrity’s name or likeness, such as the use of Parton’s face on a T-shirt sold for profit. These rights can be enormously valuable long after the celebrity has died. Without careful planning beforehand and appropriate management after death, the estate may never get the full value of these property interests. Prince, for example, died in 2016 without a will or any formal estate plan. The twice-divorced Minneapolis pop star had no surviving children. His estate passed to his siblings, who were his sole heirs . It took more than six years to administer his complicated $156 million estate , which concluded with the heirs establishing corporate entities to manage his intellectual property rights. One of those entities, Prince Legacy LLC, recently became embroiled in litigation when some of Prince’s heirs sought to fire the managers who had been hired to manage their share of the intellectual property rights. Marilyn Monroe, who died in 1962, also without any children, left behind a professionally drafted will under which her longtime acting coach, Lee Strasberg (and his then-wife) inherited most of her publicity rights. But Strasberg remarried, and his widow – a woman whom Monroe never met – hired various professional managers, including a company known as CMG Worldwide , which specializes in the management, marketing and promotion of publicity rights associated with dead celebrities. Because of the successful management of her estate’s publicity rights, Monroe became known as one of the highest-paid dead celebrities – with large sums enriching a woman she’d never met. Marilyn Monroe’s will is seen on display at Julien’s Auctions in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2012. Joe Klamar/AFP via Getty Images Should a founder’s relatives remain in charge? Many much-less famous family businesses face similar questions about how to keep their profits and revenue flowing and who should manage the company after the founder of a family business dies. A continuation of business operations may have many benefits for a deceased founder’s family. The founder may have relayed their succession plans to them. Relatives often have institutional knowledge and loyalties that can enhance the value of the business and make it last longer. Studies have not conclusively shown, however, whether continuing a business within the family is clearly better or worse for its bottom line than having outsiders manage it. As one study found, family managers often have a “ sense of kinship obligation ” and enjoy “personal and social fulfillment” from working together in the business. That, in turn, creates incentives to manage the firm carefully with an eye toward long-term survival. By contrast, another study of small and medium-size businesses after the sudden death of a CEO-owner found that, in the short run, nonfamily successors are better equipped to run the company . Relatives, by contrast, may be hampered by grief and the emotional impact of the death. But the study also found that in the long run, family members may be more successful in managing the business because they “are likely to view the firm’s survival as a way to stay connected with the deceased family member and keep their memory alive. In turn, this is expected to inspire great stewardship towards the firm.” Other studies, however, have found that maintaining family control over the management of a company after its founder’s death can hurt its performance. Restricting the pool of potential managers to relatives excludes better-qualified candidates who can bring expertise and experience that members of the family lack. Research has shown that hiring pros tends to be best for the business . Death can be bad for business When the owner of a privately held business dies, their assets, including real property, intellectual property and investments, will pass to others according to the estate plan, if the owner created one. But in many cases, the true value of a business is more than just the sum of all its assets. Some of the value may reside in the owner’s talent, knowledge and business acumen. In some cases, the owner maintained personal relationships with employees or customers that may have played a key operational role. In others, the owner may have relied upon unique personal qualities to achieve success in business. Parton herself, for example, was likely the most significant driver of value for her business because of her creativity and star power. According to a 2022 study by economists who studied what happened to startups following the death of nearly 1,500 business founders, growth and profitability fell after the founder’s death. Smaller companies are at risk of having to close altogether. The study found that the negative effects on business continuity “appear to be driven by entrepreneur specialness rather than leadership transition,” which suggests that the founder’s unique contributions to the business can be difficult to replicate after death even with excellent transition planning. What this means for Parton’s estate Parton’s full estate plan is not yet publicly known, but she did not have any children, and her husband died before her. According to cour

events.title: Business faces a more interventionist Washington post-midterms
events.summary: Both parties will be pressured to intervene more in markets after the midterms as economic frustration animates the new Congress, according to an FGS Global sketch of 2027 Washington scenarios, shared first with Axios. Why it matters: In a Trump-dominated Washington, Congress ceded much of its power and relevance. That'll change three weeks from Tuesday if Democrats win the House, as expected, and perhaps the Senate in the midterms. The new analysis by FGS , a worldwide strategic leadership advisory with huge clients, is a sequel to a popular FGS report that Jim VandeHei and I used as the basis for a series of popular "Behind the Curtain" columns before the 2024 elections. FGS bills "Alternative Futures: Beyond November" as a framework for processing the epic battles ahead: how power will get used, how both parties will evolve, and how business leaders can navigate the uncertainty. "The 2026 midterms will begin — not end — a 27-month period of unusually high strategic uncertainty," the report says. Zoom in: Michael Feldman — FGS partner and co-chairman, North America — tells me that for Republicans, "intervention may mean tariffs, industrial policy, domestic manufacturing incentives, and other measures aimed at strengthening U.S. production capacity, economic security, and competitiveness." "For Democrats, intervention may mean affordability policies, labor protections, antitrust enforcement, plus regulation designed to reduce costs, curb concentrated corporate power and address inequality." "Everyone is focused on who controls Congress," Feldman added. "We think the more important question for business is what happens next. The midterms are the beginning, not the end, of a period of significant political and policy uncertainty." Left: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) campaigns in Linden, N.J., last year. Right: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) campaigns in Davenport, Iowa, last week. Photos: Getty Images Zoom out: Three structural shifts will drive the post-midterm operating environment for businesses of all sizes, FGS warns. " Voter dissatisfaction may be the most important force pushing both parties away from established policy orthodoxies. A frustrated electorate could push both parties toward more populist, interventionist and less predictable approaches to business." "Technological disruption could reshape the political agenda as profoundly as traditional partisan conflict. AI and related technologies are becoming a political variable — not merely a sector-specific policy issue." "Generational turnover will weaken established political assumptions even where ideology remains unchanged. The next generation of leaders may inherit existing parties without inheriting their relationships, orthodoxies or governing style." The bottom line: "Divided government does not necessarily mean lower political/legislative risk," FGS writes. "It may mean that policy/political conflict moves in less predictable ways." events.title: The Download: moon city problems and drone traffic controllers
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will. Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon . —Robin George Andrews This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday 21 October!   10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals Brimstone is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer. During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated. Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks. Discover how it’s making strides on two industrial problems . —James Temple Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from geothermal power plants to smart turbines and semi-solid-state cells. Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.” Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or remote pilot in command, at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, they oversee fleets of drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses Here’s what it takes to become a drone air traffic controller . —Eamon Whalen The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 An Anthropic AI model submitted a fake tip about an unsolved murder The tip was in a new group of rogue actions Anthropic disclosed. events.title: Trump privately expresses doubts about livestreaming execution
events.summary: President Trump has privately shared misgivings about livestreaming the firing-squad execution of a former Army major who murdered 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas, according to four people who have spoken with the president. Why it matters: Trump has been deluged with "negative input" about the idea from a bipartisan chorus of lawmakers as well as advisers inside and outside of his White House, a senior administration official said. A livestream of former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan's execution on Dec. 3 "might not happen," Trump told one confidant, who doesn't work in the administration and shared the comment with Axios. "He didn't sound particularly enthusiastic" about webcasting the execution, the source said. "That's why he's calling around, doing the Trump thing, asking people what they think." Zoom in: Hasan faces a firing squad at Fort Hood, where he went on his murderous shooting rampage 17 years ago. He would be the first person in the U.S. whose execution would be livestreamed. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the norm-shattering idea Thursday on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it — that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said. Zoom out: The idea was roundly condemned domestically and internationally . In the ensuing days, Trump started to publicly shift his positions: At first, Trump was full-throated in his support. "Absolutely, I approve," Trump told reporters early Friday evening. Later that night, Trump was more nuanced : "They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision." On Saturday, Trump took control by telling reporters he would have the final say: "There are two thoughts: Don't show it and show it. 'Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won't be doing what he did. So I'll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we'll make a decision," the president told reporters at the White House. Behind the scenes: Vice President Vance has signaled where he thinks the president is going with the decision, according to a source. "I don't know if that's actually going to happen," Vance, speaking off the cuff, told reporters Friday. He has privately repeated that to others. "I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said. Between the lines: Trump, Vance and everyone else in the administration is clear about supporting Hasan's execution. But the president is grappling with competing pressures. "The president wants the bastard to pay, and a public execution might be that extra humiliation [Hasan] deserves," another confidant who spoke with the president said. "At the same time, he doesn't want to make the guy a martyr." Said another: "This is an old dude in a wheelchair we're shooting. We want to livestream that?" (Hasan, 56, was permanently injured when he was shot during his capture.) Friction point: The divide in opinion over livestreaming the execution is another point of disagreement between Vance and Hegseth. They've been on opposite sides when it comes to the use of military force in Yemen and Iran , to the leadership of the Army . Advisers say the men have a good relationship. Context: Whether at the state or federal level, executions often are witnessed only by family members or select media. They haven't been livestreamed. Executions used to be viewed in public squares, but that practice was discontinued in the 1930s, according to NPR . Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's 2001 execution was viewable to loved ones and bombing survivors via a private closed-circuit telecast. Flashback: Yelling "Allahu Akbar!" Hasan fatally shot 13 people — including a pregnant woman — and wounded 32 others on Nov. 5, 2009, when they lined up for medical checks at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center. The rampage was the worst terrorist attack on U.S. soil since 9/11. A special Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee report criticized the military for "political correctness" that blinded authorities to the major's increasingly clear Islamist radicalization. The bottom line: Hasan will be executed unless something unexpected happens. The only real doubt is whether private citizens with no attachment to the case will be able to witness it. "If I had to bet, I would bet the president doesn't authorize this," said one administration official. "But I'm not gonna get ahead of the boss and try to predict what he'll do." "Hasan will be executed for his crimes," the official said, "and that's what matters."

events.title: Israel mints tech unicorns. Can it keep them from leaving for New York?
events.summary: The Scene Israel has produced more tech unicorns per citizen than any country in the world, twice as many as the US. Ittai Ben-Zeev’s job is getting them to stay there. The CEO of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is tasked with convincing the next Wiz, Monday.com, and Fiverr, which all went public in New York or sold to US rivals, to list at home instead. He’s also courting global investors whose money will help boost trading and valuations. His biggest tailwind, he said, is the takeover of US markets by a handful of AI giants. Israeli startups worth a few billion dollars can’t get the attention of investors rhapsodizing about trillion-dollar IPOs from SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI. “New York is no longer an option,” said Ben-Zeev, the exchange’s CEO since 2016. After the Oct. 7 attacks, 7% of its workforce was called up for military service and the bear case for its stock market was obvious. Since Oct. 8, 2023, the TA-125 has beaten the S&P 500 by 50 percentage points and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite by 23. The country is on track this year for a record 30 IPOs . Foreign holdings of Israeli shares more than doubled from September 2023 to the beginning of this year. Ben-Zeev dismissed wartime nationalism as a reason for Israeli founders to list at home, or for Israeli investors to buy their shares. “Israelis will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange,” he said. But he said the Jewish diaspora has increased its investments. Bill Ackman and his Israeli-born wife, Neri Oxman, bought 4.9% of the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange in 2024 after a 45-minute meeting with management, Ackman said in an interview. “Owning a stock exchange is the purest way to bet on a country,” he said, taking a minute to run the numbers: His $23 million investment is worth $230 million today. He said AI’s productivity-enhancing potential will overcome Israel’s economic weakness, its small population. “There will be a trillion-dollar company coming out of Israel, and that value will be shared among a tiny country.” The war also gave TASE cover to move its Sunday-to-Thursday trading to Monday through Friday. It wasn’t an easy pitch in a country that takes Shabbat seriously, but a way “to signal the world that we are part of it” and gain entry into global indexes that have long snubbed it, Ben-Zeev said. Anti-Israel sentiment and antisemitism are fueling campaigns at many US institutions to divest from Israel. Politicians will politick, he said, but “investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return.” Q&A Liz Hoffman: Israel has produced more tech unicorns per capita than any other country in the world, but they all want to go public in New York. How do you hold onto them? Ittai Ben-Zeev: It used to be that a tech company with $100 million [in annual revenue] could IPO in New York. That’s no longer the case. The $100 million became $500 million. And because of the gigantic IPOs that are coming, for most Israeli tech companies, New York is no longer an option. Six or seven years ago, if an Israeli company couldn’t do an IPO on Nasdaq or NYSE, they were looking at Singapore, Toronto, Australia. We managed to change the perception. And I believe that in 2027, maybe before the end of 2026, we’ll start seeing global investment banks leading global IPO offerings on TASE, and only for TASE. I’m mindful, speaking to you the week of the anniversary of Oct. 7 — is patriotism part of the pitch? No. Post-Oct. 7, I see a genuine change in the way that Jewish people in the diaspora, especially in the States, want to invest in Israel, not only to make a return but also to get a broader connection to Israel. But that’s not the case with the Israeli entrepreneurs. Israelis, I have to tell you, will be patriotic about certain issues, but that’s not the way they view the exchange. Then what’s the pitch? You are Israeli. You don’t understand the American mentality. The American market can be brutal. You miss your estimates by one cent, your share price goes down, and then what? Start in the Israeli market and, once you’re ready, you can always do a dual listing. Think about TASE as a stop on the way to New York. You’ve also courted global companies to dual-list in Tel Aviv. Palo Alto Networks did that after buying [Israeli startup] CyberArk, but why would most companies bother? We have data that shows you get more liquidity and more demand for your shares. You can argue that it’s not significant enough, but it’s a free option. And not too many people are aware of it, but if you look at the amount of money Israelis have in cash deposits in Israeli banks and you compare it to GDP, we are No. 1 of any western society. That’s money that is just ready to be invested. You’re in New York this week, selling the Israeli economy to investors. But the Middle East is a volatile place to invest right now, and there are big anti-Israel divestment campaigns at some US institutions. In the old days, people would ask me: What will happen to Israel if something happens in Iran? I remember being in New York a couple of years ago, telling one of those American investors that if something happened in Iran, you should be more worried about your American portfolio than your Israeli portfolio. Israel is more well-positioned than it used to be, and I’m not sure that everybody fully understands it. In terms of BDS [the push for boycotts, divestment, and economic sanctions against Israel], there are politicians all over the world. Investors, at the end of the day, want to make a return. And the Israeli market is a good marketplace to make a return. Also, I think Israel can do a better job of PR. This is part of what we tell companies: You need to know how to sell the pitch. It’s not only about facts; it’s also about storytelling. As a country, this is something we need to do better. You shifted trading from Sunday to Thursday to Monday to Friday. Was that a hard sell? We were in the middle of a war. Everybody understood that it’s important for us to signal the world that we are part of it. We needed to get aligned to global standards, and this is what we did this year. What’s it like having Bill Ackman on your cap table? For sure it has helped change the perception. Israeli tech guys, they look to New York. When they will read what you’re writing, they will give it much more credit than what the Israeli newspaper writes. So a very successful businessman like Bill talking about the Israeli economy, putting faith in the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, helps my pitch.

events.title: Saudi Arabia’s resolve, and fears of a ‘forever war’
events.summary: The Scene Riyadh Season — the Saudi capital’s biggest suite of events that had been key to its tourism push — opens next week with concerts, UFC, the Epcot-esque Boulevard World, and the world’s top ranked tennis players set to compete at the Six Kings Slam. Since 2019, it has been the capital’s answer to anyone asking whether Riyadh is the place to be. After the Houthi strikes over the weekend, residents are asking themselves the same question. Traffic on King Fahd Road is lighter and some companies — mostly those based in the King Abdullah Financial District — told staff to work from home on Sunday. Schools in the city have moved to remote learning for the week, with no clear date yet on when students will return to class. When I ask Saudis — friends, relatives, and sources — how they are doing, most say: , thanks to God, the catchall for everything from the greatest blessings to the mantra mourners repeat when family members die. It’s the same expression they used in March when Iranian missiles first reached the capital, but the tone now is different after more than a dozen people were killed and hundreds wounded in attacks on King Khalid International Airport. Fear is breaking through. Social media and WhatsApp group chats have been filled with eulogies for Captain Hamoud Alkalthami, the Saudia Airlines pilot killed on Thursday, and for Saturday’s dead — eight of them foreign residents from countries including Bangladesh, Egypt, and Sudan. People are posting about and queuing to donate to blood banks. The crown prince himself did so last week, part of an annual campaign, and that image was used to spur urgently needed donations. The captain’s death in particular has become a symbol for many Saudis: The war now has a martyr, with a name and face that looks like theirs. Manal’s view Saudis broadly trust their government. When they wrap themselves in the flag, or share statements of solidarity after attacks (at least for those who use their real names), it’s genuine and reflects how people speak in private. But there has been a shift. Some are talking about leaving, which a few months ago would have been seen as a betrayal. Most are still confident and say the kingdom has come through worse. What’s pretty universal is the desire for the disruption to be over and to get back to living. While the conflict with Iran was clear — we have been told to be wary of the Islamic Republic from the time we understood what an enemy was — the confrontation with the Houthis is more complex. Riyadh has tried a mix of strikes and diplomacy for more than a decade, and the UN-brokered truce in 2022 held long enough for people to stop thinking about the issue. It’s clear now that it’s a forever war, and few people I speak to can describe what winning would look like. Without public polls, it’s impossible to gauge exactly what the Saudis think. Speaking to more than 25 people this weekend showed a split. One camp wants the Houthis finished for good, whatever that may meanOthers worry about the toll on Yemenis, our poorer neighbors, who make up the kingdom’s largest foreign community and share ties of kinship and history with Saudis. Over the past six months, those who lived through the 1991 Gulf War used it to explain why they weren’t worried. Those six weeks of Iraqi strikes had one Saudi business leader “ more frightened of the uncertainty of the Scud than anything else. ” Uncertainty is again, 35 years later, the greatest fear. Notable The strikes sharply raise the risk of Saudi Arabia being drawn into a wider war, after a decade in which Riyadh worked to contain the Yemen conflict rather than escalate it , Bloomberg reported. Eulogies for the 12 killed in Saturday’s strike filled Saudi social media, among them a Flynas flight attendant killed on duty and a university student in her final year , Arab News reported.

events.title: Two U.S. professors win Nobel prize in economics
events.summary: Stanford University's Robert E. Hall and Columbia University's Michael Woodford won the Nobel Prize in economics for research on how policymakers can stabilize economies , the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday. Why it matters: Their work helped shape how central banks set interest rates and communicate policy. The win comes as those institutions fight energy-driven inflation and risks to economic growth. Zoom out: For decades, policymakers relied on economic models that linked higher inflation with lower unemployment. But that framework broke down during the 1970s stagflation when both prices and joblessness surged at the same time. "The solution by Robert Hall and Michael Woodford was to build a new framework ground up," Timo Boppart, a member of the Nobel economics prize committee, said on Monday. What they're saying: Woodford, who called into Monday's press conference hosted by the committee, said he was "elated" by the win. " It's a tremendous honor. It's a surprise — but I'm feeling very good about it," Woodford said. The intrigue : Asked by a reporter about the threat to the global economy, Woodford said the Middle East conflict has disrupted energy markets and driven price changes with consequences far beyond the region. He pointed to the 2008 financial crisis as a key test of his research, when central banks cut interest rates to near zero but struggled to revive economic activity. His framework helped explain how other tools, including forward guidance and asset purchases, could support the economy. Zoom in: In research culminating in a landmark 2003 book, Woodford developed a framework linking businesses' pricing decisions to inflation and monetary policy. Hall — a Stanford professor who chaired the committee that dates U.S. recessions for 46 years — showed in a 1978 paper how consumers' spending decisions reflect expectations about future income. Of note: The prize comes with an award of 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), up from 11 million kronor last year, to be divided between the two winners. Flashback: Recent economics Nobels have recognized research on technological progress, economic prosperity and labor markets. Last year's prize went to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for their work explaining how innovation drives economic growth. In 2024, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won for their research on how institutions shape economic prosperity. Harvard economist Claudia Goldin won in 2023 for research that advanced the world's understanding of women's labor market outcomes.

events.title: US, European yields unlikely to fall soon, economists say
events.summary: Borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated across the US and Europe for the foreseeable future, economists said. Experts surveyed by The Wall Street Journal projected that US 10-year Treasury yields would decline only slightly from current levels to end the year at 5.1%, and would dip to around 4.8% 12 months later: “ It has been a sea change in the fundamentals underlying the fixed-income market and the economy,” one told the Journal. A key factor, as the economist David Skilling wrote in a recent note, has been that “ state capitalism … is a much more capex-intensive regime ” just as “the global economy is moving from a savings-abundant environment towards one in which available capital is becoming scarcer.” — Prashant Rao

events.summary: Economists and executives warned of thinning global oil buffers, with conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine piling pressure on the energy supply chain. events.title: Tanzania seeks investment to tackle youth job pressure
events.summary: The News Tanzania is counting on increased investment to accelerate industrialization and create jobs for its young population, the prime minister said. The government has targeted $15 billion in annual foreign direct investment, roughly triple last year’s figure, as part of its long-term economic plans . Mwigulu Nchemba, speaking on the sidelines of an investment forum in London, said the government had put money into rail and port infrastructure, as well as expanding power generation to create an industrial base. This was on top of cutting the cost of doing business, and strengthening supply chains. Nchemba said increased industrialization would boost local processing of natural resources leading to more employment opportunities. Tanzania, like many African countries, has a rapidly expanding population. The UN estimates 42% of people are aged 14 or under . The prime minister said the path to creating work for all the country’s school leavers rests on developing the private sector through investment. “There is no way you can absorb all those graduates,” the prime minister told reporters. “The only way you can solve the issue of job creation is by empowering the private sector to create those vacancies for our youth.” Know More Tanzania has large offshore gas resources and deposits of minerals needed for the energy transition and digital infrastructure — such as copper, lithium, and cobalt — as well as precious metals and stones, including gold and diamonds. In August, the country commissioned a 2,115 MW hydropower plant that more than doubled its electricity generation capacity and ​created a surplus that officials said could support power exports and industrial growth. Tanzania, like governments across the continent, is looking for ways to add value locally instead of raw minerals exports. In neighboring Kenya, President William Ruto has focused on job creation through industrialization as a key plank in his campaign to secure a second term in next year’s election. Notable Liquefied natural gas development offers Tanzania its most obvious means of monetizing its giant gas reserves after the wars in Ukraine and Iran upended global energy markets, wrote Neil Ford in African Business.

events.title: Dangote's Kenya refinery triggers political battle
events.summary: The News The $16 billion project to build Aliko Dangote’s refinery on the Kenyan coast is at the center of a high-stakes political battle ahead of elections in 10 months. President William Ruto is hinging his second-term bid on a series of major infrastructure developments. He has argued that the refinery could raise Kenya’s annual gross domestic product by 12%. Additional expected benefits include 500MW added to the national grid and thousands of new jobs. But mounting litigation, some initiated by his political rivals, is threatening to delay its construction, scheduled to be completed by 2030. Groups behind the legal action allege that the project is only the latest in a series of “secretive deals” signed by Ruto and his administration. The government’s refusal to make public key agreements related to the refinery has been criticized by opposition leaders, including one of Ruto’s main challengers, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has launched a bid in parliament for the documents, including the refinery contract, to be released. Unanswered questions remain over the impact on the environment, the community living near the refinery, and taxpayers. The president and his allies have warned that legal hurdles and uncertainty affecting key projects could dampen investor confidence. Ruto’s government is no stranger to court challenges to its financial deals. Its plan to privatize the country’s fuel pipeline company was eventually approved after various cases were dismissed. Last month, the $1.6 billion sale of a government stake in telecoms company Safaricom to UK’s Vodafone was declared illegal by the courts — the administration has launched an appeal. Both deals are meant to fund Ruto’s infrastructure push, according to government documents. Know More Ekuru Aukot, leader of the opposition Thirdway Alliance,told Semafor he would “definitely file a suit” if the government failed to meet an Oct. 23 deadline in his access to information request seeking more details about the refinery including the names of those who stand to benefit. “We are not opposed to investment. What we are saying is follow the law, follow the constitution,” he said. “The era of secretive deals negotiated in the dark will end when we kick this current regime out and return our country back to the rule of law,” Sifuna said on social media , adding that Ruto was frustrating his parliamentary push for more details. He insisted that the disclosure was “a constitutional imperative.” The threat of protracted litigation also looms over a suit launched by more than 100 Lamu residents arguing that the site of the refinery is part of their ancestral lands, with a court halting construction until the matter is heard. In addition, campaign groups have raised the alarm over the government’s failure to publish the environmental impact report, with Greenpeace threatening legal action . Last year, its five-year effort to block the construction of a $2 billion coal plant in Lamu ended in success for the activists. Despite the legal cases, Dangote and Ruto, who broke ground on the refinery project on Sept. 30, have expressed confidence that the project will overcome the legal hurdles. Step Back Seen as the candidate for the young and downtrodden in the last election, Ruto’s popularity has waned especially among the youth after the deadly 2024 Gen Z-led protests in which dozens of demonstrators were killed by police. Instead, Ruto is now leaning heavily on his infrastructure plans and the promised opportunities to shore up support for his re-election campaign. He has promised to move Kenya “from third world to first world” within 10 years, and unveiled a $38 billion infrastructure fund meant to finance various projects. The View From Nigeria Dangote is taking the objections in his stride. Speaking to investors in Nairobi ahead of the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said legal challenges were “normal for us in Africa. In fact, this is small.” He drew parallels with concerns over his cement plant in Senegal , which faced delays over land-related legal disputes. “They stopped our factory for one year. We went up to the Supreme Court to get a judgment,” he said. Notable Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority approved the Dangote IPO , enabling local investors to participate on the Nairobi Securities Exchange.

events.title: Obama cuts ad in Mississippi Senate race
events.summary: Former President Barack Obama has cut an ad for Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom, the latest sign of Democrats putting real effort behind boosting their candidate in the deep red state as they eye a potential upset next month. The Colom campaign will run the 30-second spot on digital and radio statewide in Mississippi as part of a seven-figure media buy in Mississippi, according to details shared first with Semafor. In the ad, Obama tells voters: “Mississippi, it’s time for a change.” “You need to send Scott Colom to the US Senate,” Obama continues in the ad . “Scott made his community safer, prosecuting violent crimes as a district attorney and fighting corruption.” Colom is running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a conservative GOP senator who blocked Colom’s nomination to a federal judgeship under then-President Joe Biden. Colom currently serves as a district attorney in Mississippi. The race to defeat Hyde-Smith is not a must-win for Democrats to retake the Senate and Colom remains an underdog in deep red Mississippi. But national Democrats have been eying the race for months due to the state’s large Black population, and Obama’s ad is a clear effort to juice turnout. Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., will appear with Colom on Wednesday in Jackson and Democratic Sens. Cory Booker of New Jersey, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware have also previously campaigned with the Democratic candidate.Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has also listed Mississippi as a target for Democrats. Democrats tried to beat Hyde-Smith in the past and failed. She defeated former Democratic Rep. Mike Espy by 7 points in 2018 and a wider margin in a 2020 rematch. But most Senate Democrats think Colom, a young father, is a stronger candidate in a tough environment for Republicans.

events.title: Learning to Play Like a Pro: Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking for Humanoid Robots
events.summary: This White Paper provides roboticists and control engineers with a comprehensive overview of how motion planning and motion tracking can be decoupled to preserve professional athletic style in humanoid robots, and why adaptive, speed-aware control is essential for closing the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. What you will learn about: Why combining a professional athlete’s motion style with reliable task performance remains an open challenge in humanoid ball-sports robotics, and how separating a high-level planner from a low-level tracker addresses this trade-off. How motion data extracted from broadcast video and motion-capture recordings can be reconstructed, retargeted, and physically corrected into reference motions a humanoid robot can safely track. Why the sim-to-real transition introduces compounding tracking errors, and how training a tracker on randomized execution speeds, paired with a learned motion-speed adapter in the planner, improves robustness on physical hardware. How this adaptive framework was validated across two humanoid platforms, including full-size, in-the-wild serving performed without any motion-capture system. Download this free whitepaper now!

events.title: What it would take to build a city on the moon
events.summary: Welcome to the second space race. You can be forgiven for experiencing déjà vu. Last time, it was the Soviet Union and the United States vying to be the first to plant some flags. Now it’s a sprint to the lunar surface between America and China—alongside a host of varyingly friendly and rival nations—plus a cornucopia of private spaceflight companies. And this time it looks like they’re getting ready to set up camp. There will be, the contenders say, bases on the moon, permanently inhabited castles under the stars. The notion of a moon base, fanciful as it might sound, isn’t new. But this year, under the leadership of Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA has been flooding the zone with bold announcements . If all goes according to plan—a plan that will likely cost tens of billions of dollars to start—there will be drones , robotic landers, communication satellites , and a nuclear power plant ; there will be plant terrariums and moonquake sensors; there will be mechanized scouts exploring craters for water. Initial astronaut missions to the lunar surface, which the US is currently planning to start in 2028, will be focused on exploration and technological experimentation. But the idea is that we will—some time in the 2030s—get to a point where there will be habitation quarters for long-term stays, surrounded by a network of scientific research stations, resource mining and processing plants, and landing pads for spaceships. “It’s going to be an expanse,” says Carlos García-Galán, NASA’s moon base program manager—one that will add up to “hundreds of square miles.” The effort is undoubtedly being fueled by nationalistic competition. China has near-identical plans to build its own base on the moon. And being first matters, because the “victor” gets to define the terms. What is the moon, exactly? Is it a militarized outpost? Is it a manufacturing hub? Is it a wilderness to be studied and preserved? But there are also other reasons to go. Earth’s companion contains primeval rocks that hold clues to the formation of the entire solar system. The lunar surface, with virtually no atmosphere in the way, is an ideal place to put telescopes that could examine the most ancient epochs of the cosmos. The far side of the moon would be “a fantastic place to explore the further universe,” says Josef Aschbacher, the European Space Agency’s director general. And it’s way more energy efficient to launch rockets from the low-gravity lunar surface than it is from Earth, meaning sending astronauts—or robotic spacecraft—farther into the solar system will become much less difficult. “The moon is critical. It will be a stepping stone for going further—that means to Mars and beyond,” says Aschbacher. SELMAN DESIGN But if these bold visions are to become reality, there’s a daunting amount of work to be done. A sprawling moon base must be safe for its astronaut inhabitants—protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining, so that it can weather changing political fortunes and not cost ruinous amounts of money to maintain. For that, we’ll need to find a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating—and ideally generating revenue. And we’ll need autonomous robots that can build, maintain, and expand the base even when their human masters aren’t present. “It’s almost like starting civilization from scratch,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales. Assuming we can overcome these starting challenges, decades from now—let’s say, by the year 2100—our initial moon bases could grow from barely visible structures into luminous cities, perhaps not too dissimilar from those dreamed up by authors and screenwriters the world over. “It’s like science fiction today that we really want to turn into a reality,” says García-Galán. Will anyone succeed? The moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. In general, daytime temperatures can reach more than 250 °F; at night, they can plummet to less than –200 °F. Exposed to the vacuum of space, the surface is constantly showered in carcinogenic radiation and frequently hit by meteoroids. And its volcanic dust is sticky and corrosive, a destroyer of equipment and choker of lungs.  Sadly, the lunar south pole—the area NASA is targeting—is even harsher. NASA wants to build a base there because its permanently shadowed craters are thought to harbor caches of water ice, which would be more precious than gold. Purify it, and you can water crops and hydrate astronauts; split it into oxygen and hydrogen, and you have breathable air and rocket propellant. But the temperature in those craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. On the surface outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. But there is only so much money we can spend on safety. “What it comes down to is acceptable risk of death,” Philip Metzger , a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute, said while pondering some of the dangers. “What can we reasonably survive without breaking the bank?” Temperature is one of the easiest problems to handle. Materials science has come a long way, and there are myriad metals, ceramics, plastics, compounds, and alloys that can resist wild temperature swings. Radiators keep things cool; heaters keep batteries from dying prematurely. Astronauts survive just fine too, with their fancy spacesuits—but that technology has proved itself only during brief excursions. It’s not yet clear how long this equipment could operate under such tempestuous conditions. The temperature in the moon’s south pole craters can be lower than –410 °F, making them some of the coldest places in the known universe. Outside those pits, astronauts would be bathed in the scorching sun for 14 days before experiencing an equally long frigid night. Space radiation, which can wreak havoc on electronics and trigger a cancerous division of cells, is far more pernicious. And as Stuart George, a physicist at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, explains, it comes in two unpleasant forms.  The first is galactic cosmic rays , which rain down on the moon almost constantly. “They’re made by supernovas and neutron star mergers—all these kinds of things,” says George. And because the atomic nuclei, protons, and electrons that make them up are moving at significant fractions of the speed of light, these cosmic rays have oodles of kinetic energy, meaning they can punch through thin shielding (say, a metal wall) with ease. “They also have this habit where the heavier ions are fragmenting in that shielding and making secondary particles,” says George. That means if your shield is too thin, the astronauts behind it will be blasted with a surprisingly large dose of radiation.

events.title: The ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests
events.summary: In a research station in central Panama, you can walk through a century of forest time, watching scrubby plots of adolescent trees give way to cathedral-­like canopies of mature growth. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, oversees this sequence of plots across the Barro Colorado Nature Monument, some of which date as far back as the 19th century. Not one of the trees she surveys was planted by human hands. She maps, measures, and tracks each trunk that emerges, revealing how waves of tree life rise from bare earth.  Tropical forests like these are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land . As part of an international network of researchers, Dent is deciphering the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has built a body of evidence that such large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. Few places are better to demonstrate this than Barro Colorado, a reserve covering the forested peninsulas and islands that formed when construction of the Panama Canal flooded the area in 1914. Under the management of the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute, generations of ecologists have amassed more than a century of records.  That means Dent can trace why some plots rebound after clear-cutting for farming and forestry while others falter. Fruit-eating animals—including spider monkeys, bats, and parrots—are responsible for planting more than 70% of trees in tropical forests, and Dent’s dataset can tell which built each patch of trees by depositing seeds in their nutrient-rich droppings. Many of these creatures worked together to plant a diverse 70-year-old patch whose canopy is approaching the stunning structure and richness of an ancient jungle. In contrast, a patch of similar age populated by narrow trunks of a single long-lived species, Gustavia superba , hints that tropical rodents called agoutis are more or less the sole animal architects behind this more homogeneous forest.  The data she collects helps write a playbook for when to let ecosystems regenerate and when to give them a helping hand. One 2024 estimate in Nature found that some 215 million hectares of forest worldwide (an area larger than Mexico) could regenerate naturally. “Tropical forests are underpinned by this massive network of interactions,” Dent says—interactions between life-forms like the fungi that help trees take up nutrients, as well as pollinators and seed-distributors. Supporting those relationships is key to growing forests that lock up carbon and help sustain local communities and wildlife.  Filling in the gaps Just over a decade ago, as the landmark Paris Agreement was being codified in 2015, forest recovery seized global attention as a solution to the climate crisis. Global leaders rallied behind plans to regrow a trillion trees , after the ecologist Thomas Crowther highlighted their potential to capture a decade’s worth of global carbon emissions. But the biggest question has lingered: How, exactly, do you regrow two trees for every star in the Milky Way? While startups have proposed seed-spraying drones and nutrient-coated seed bombs , Dent has spent two decades studying what happens when we let forests rebuild themselves. As a PhD student around the turn of the millennium, she researched old-growth forests in northern Borneo but felt hopeless watching entire landscapes felled for palm oil plantations. Rather than despair, she turned to restoration. Then, as a postdoc in 2005, she joined Panama’s Prorena, a joint initiative between the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute and the Yale School of Forestry and Environmental Studies, which aimed at determining how best to establish diverse native forests on clear-cut land. Back then, secondary forests—ones that grow naturally after the original forest was lost—had been “a bit of a niche research area,” Dent says. But as farming and human infrastructure have driven deforestation, resurgent forests now account for some 70% of all tropical canopies. Prorena initially followed the usual playbook of transplanting nursery trees to rangelands, but Dent began to question whether planting was necessary. In 2009, she published an encouraging paper showing that animal populations rebound quickly as forests naturally regrow. In 2010, she began working in Barro Colorado on the plots established by the pioneering American ecologist Julie Denslow. In 1994, Denslow identified plots that had been regenerating naturally for 20 to 100 years, and Dent would add younger ones to continue the sequence.  The site provides not just general data on forest regrowth but in-depth demographic information over time, says Robin Chazdon, a professor emeritus of ecology and evolutionary biology at the University of Connecticut who collaborated with Denslow when she established the plots. “It tells you more about the actual processes that are happening in the site,” she says.  For example, previous research had shown that fast-growing “pioneer trees,” the first to thrive in the damaged land, are eventually overtaken by larger carbon-storing trees. Dent’s research helped fill in gaps about the mechanics of how this happens—or doesn’t happen—in individual cases. In the Gustavia -dominated patch, for instance, stubborn grasses planted by cattle ranchers smothered most other trees before they could take root. These trees can hang around, crowding out the light, for 150 years, blocking the second wave of large-trunked trees.  To plant or not to plant Dent found herself well placed for the massive influx of interest in reforestation that began in 2015. She’d already become a principal investigator for 2ndFor, an international research network aiming to learn how best to manage secondary forests. Using data gathered from the Barro Colorado plots, the team authored a 2016 paper in Nature showing that a hectare of naturally regenerated secondary forest can capture 11 times as much carbon each year as an old-growth one, with young trees absorbing it quickly as they compete to grow toward the sun. Then, in a 2022 study published by the Royal Society, Dent and colleagues showed that locations such as Barro Colorado are among the best-case scenarios for what can be achieved without planting a single seed. Clearings are often surrounded by lush environments filled with birds, bats, and other animals, all of which help tree cover regain old-growth levels of richness and abundance within a few decades. events.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
events.summary: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda." The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." The White House referred Axios to Trump's Truth Social post last week last week, in which he described the ads as a "positive promotion" for the U.S. Representatives for the DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Tuesday to discuss next steps in the case. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs and the White House's response to a request for comment.
